group_a.h1: Video Interview Software That Actually Stops Deepfake and Proxy Candidates

persona.name: Executive & Compliance Buyer
persona.lens: CHRO/CXO or legally minded enterprise HR who signs off on the video interviewing purchase and answers for the selection process later; needs each vendor's integrity controls (proctoring, lockdown, ID/face match, deepfake and proxy detection) evidenced from the vendor's own security and product documentation, plus the consent, bias-audit (NYC Local Law 144, EU AI Act) and recording-retention terms that make the choice defensible.
persona.why: Vendor comparison at decision stage built on security documentation, legal duties, and data retention, which routes to the buyer who carries the risk, not the recruiter running the funnel.

group_a.ai_overview: defines them as "cloud-based software tools that let companies conduct live or pre-recorded candidate interviews remotely," then runs a best-for vendor list — HireVue (large enterprises, skill validation, workflow automation, structured AI assessments), VidCruiter (structured customizable workflows, ATS integrations), Spark Hire (SMBs and staffing agencies, one-way), Jobma (multi-format scalable video screening, AI assistant), Hireflix (simple, affordable, lightweight async, no candidate logins) — followed by four capability buckets in this order: Asynchronous (One-Way) & Live Video, AI & Analytics (transcription, response summaries, communication scoring), ATS Integration (Workday, Greenhouse), Candidate Experience (mobile-friendly, no app download or forced account creation). Fraud, identity verification, proctoring, deepfake and proxy detection appear nowhere in its skeleton.
table_stakes: At-a-glance comparison table of all vendors before the write-ups
Per-vendor sections, one heading per tool, then a second deeper review pass on the same tools
Selection criteria or methodology ("how we chose", "what makes the best")
What video interviewing software is / introduction to the category

sections_menu.h2: Why remote video interviews became the fraud target

h3.h3: Remote, contractor, and third-party hiring lost the in-person checkpoints

evidence.gloss: Remote, frontline, and third-party hiring lack the physical and procedural checkpoints
evidence.verbatim: Remote, frontline, and third-party hiring environments amplify these risks because they often lack the physical and procedural checkpoints that once helped verify identity and intent[3].

evidence.gloss: No in-person onboarding means reliance on digital interactions just as AI deception gets cheaper
evidence.verbatim: Without in-person onboarding, employers rely heavily on digital interactions, making it easier for malicious actors to exploit weaknesses at exactly the moment when AI-generated deception is becoming cheaper, more convincing, and easier to scale[3].

evidence.gloss: Who is most exposed: staffing firms placing contractors and enterprise teams hiring for sensitive access
evidence.verbatim: Staffing firms placing contractors across many clients carry outsized reputational risk if a fraudulent worker is placed at a customer site, and enterprise talent teams face similar exposure when a role involves access to code, financial systems, or customer data[6].

evidence.gloss: The shift to contractors, gig, and third-party workers opened the vulnerabilities attackers now exploit
evidence.verbatim: As the workforce evolves to include more contractors, gig workers, and third-party specialists, the way organizations hire and who they hire has fundamentally changed, opening the vulnerabilities state-sponsored actors and sophisticated scammers now exploit with AI-generated deepfakes, stolen identities, and impersonation tactics[3].

evidence.gloss: Why remote onboarding is targeted: volume, distributed teams, replicable workflows, cheap AI
evidence.verbatim: Remote onboarding is increasingly targeted because of its volume and reduced physical oversight: high hiring volume enables automated fraud attempts, distributed teams reduce in-person checks, standard workflows are easier to replicate, and AI tools lower the cost and effort of creating synthetic identities[12].

evidence.gloss: Remote, frontline, third-party hiring lacks physical and procedural checkpoints
evidence.verbatim: Remote, frontline, and third-party hiring environments amplify these risks because they lack the physical and procedural checkpoints that once helped verify identity and intent.

evidence.gloss: Reliance on digital interaction coincides with cheaper, more convincing AI deception
evidence.verbatim: Without in-person onboarding, employers rely heavily on digital interactions, making it easier for malicious actors to exploit weaknesses at exactly the moment when AI-generated deception is becoming cheaper, more convincing, and easier to scale[46].

h3.h3: The $20 deepfake: identity fraud got cheap, not new

evidence.gloss: The trigger is falling cost of identity fraud, not its novelty
evidence.verbatim: The trigger is not that identity fraud in hiring is new, but that the cost of running it collapsed.

evidence.gloss: Fraud that once needed nation-state resources now costs $20 and 20 minutes
evidence.verbatim: What once took nation-state resources now takes a $20 tool and 20 minutes[1].

evidence.gloss: AI democratized hiring fraud rather than inventing it
evidence.verbatim: AI did not create hiring fraud; it made it available to everyone[1].

h3.h3: A screening stack built for rare fraud, with evidence split across teams

evidence.gloss: Fragmented onboarding across HR, IT, and partners breaks the chain from applicant to Day 1
evidence.verbatim: Fragmented onboarding across HR, IT, and third-party channels adds another layer: when verification is split across disconnected systems, departments, and partners, it becomes harder to confirm that the person who entered the hiring process is the same individual who arrives at onboarding and Day 1, which increases exposure to fraudulent hiring while also creating more candidate friction, higher drop-off, and greater inefficiency[3].

evidence.gloss: The screening stack rests on assumptions that no longer hold
evidence.verbatim: The screening stack most companies use was built for assumptions that no longer hold.

evidence.gloss: Veriff CEO John Zoldak: the assumption that the applicant is the person showing up is broken at scale
evidence.verbatim: Dr. John Zoldak, CEO of Veriff, put the same point in Q1 2026: "Traditional background checks were designed for a world where the person applying was the person showing up. That assumption is now broken at scale.

evidence.gloss: Attack surface expanding faster than any single checkpoint tracks
evidence.verbatim: Synthetic identities, AI-generated documents and deepfake video are expanding the attack surface faster than any single checkpoint can track[1]

evidence.gloss: Current hiring workflows were designed for rare, not scaled, fraud
evidence.verbatim: the hiring workflows most organizations still run were designed for a world where identity fraud was rare rather than a scaled, tool-assisted threat[2]

evidence.gloss: Evidence is scattered across systems, teams, and stages
evidence.verbatim: Remote hiring makes verification harder because evidence is scattered across different systems, teams, and stages of the process[7].

evidence.gloss: Recruiter sees the ATS resume, hiring manager sees only the video interview
evidence.verbatim: A recruiter reviews a polished resume in an applicant tracking system; the hiring manager may only see the candidate during a video interview[7].

h3.h3: The Proxy Interview Market and Why It Pays

evidence.gloss: No reliable industry-wide statistic exists for proxy interviews
evidence.verbatim: On proxy interviews specifically, precise statistics are difficult to obtain because of the clandestine nature of interview fraud and no reliable industry-wide figure exists

evidence.gloss: Proxy interview attempts grew with remote hiring; prevention is now standard practice
evidence.verbatim: what is clear is that the problem has grown noticeably since fully remote hiring removed the physical verification barriers in-person interviews naturally provided, and hiring teams for high-demand technical roles report attempts often enough that proactive prevention is now standard practice rather than optional[6].

evidence.gloss: Kuczynski on payroll incentive: location fraud can mean a 600% salary increase
evidence.verbatim: That risk is concrete on the payroll side too: as Kuczynski puts it, if someone is an engineer in Ukraine but claims to be an engineer in San Francisco, "suddenly that's a 600% salary increase — for free"[40].

evidence.gloss: Pattern: passes screen, starts in three weeks, PIP six months later for inability to code
evidence.verbatim: In one described pattern, a candidate passes the technical screen, negotiates well, and starts in three weeks; six months later a manager opens a performance improvement plan because the person cannot write basic code.

evidence.gloss: The worker and the interviewee were different people
evidence.verbatim: The person who showed up to work and the person who interviewed were not the same person[45].

evidence.gloss: Proxy interview fraud grew over 300% between 2023 and 2025
evidence.verbatim: Proxy interview fraud incidents grew over 300% between 2023 and 2025 (HireVue 2025 report)[45].

evidence.gloss: About 1 in 20 candidates estimated to have used a proxy surrogate
evidence.verbatim: Approximately 1 in 20 candidates (5%) are estimated to have used a proxy surrogate at some point in the hiring process[45].

evidence.gloss: Proxy interviews framed as a rational market response, not a moral failing
evidence.verbatim: Proxy interviews are described not as a moral failing of individual candidates but as a rational market response to a specific economic condition: remote hiring dramatically lowered the cost of deception while employer verification methods stayed frozen in a pre-2020 model[45].

evidence.gloss: Candidate pays $500-$2,000 to gain a $90,000-$140,000 role
evidence.verbatim: A candidate faces a $500–$2,000 fee to an organized proxy network (Reuters, October 2025) and stands to gain a $90,000–$140,000 remote tech or finance role[45].

evidence.gloss: Employer's only tools are a video call and a resume
evidence.verbatim: On the other side, the employer relies on a video call and a resume, tools that were never designed to establish identity continuity[45].

evidence.gloss: Six-figure payoff plus near-zero detection means supply meets demand
evidence.verbatim: As long as a single successful proxy interview yields a six-figure salary and the detection rate hovers near zero, supply will meet demand[45].

evidence.gloss: Organized networks advertise surrogate interview services openly (Veriff CEO)
evidence.verbatim: Organized networks now advertise surrogate interview services openly, per Leon Rodrigues, CEO of Veriff (2025)[45].

evidence.gloss: Josh Bersin: proxy interviews are the new resume padding and screening is blind to it
evidence.verbatim: Josh Bersin (2025) frames the employer's blind spot the same way: most companies still treat interview fraud as an edge case, and in a remote-first world proxy interviews are the new resume padding while the screening process is probably blind to it[45].

evidence.gloss: The goal is raising the cost of fraud so networks route around you
evidence.verbatim: The goal is not to detect every fraudster; it is to raise the cost of fraud high enough that the proxy networks route around you.

evidence.gloss: Target hardening: multi-point verification pushes networks to easier employers
evidence.verbatim: This is target hardening from behavioral economics: if your interview process requires identity verification at multiple points, proxy networks will prioritize employers who don't[45].

evidence.gloss: Google brought back in-person technical rounds to counter AI interview fraud
evidence.verbatim: Second, the direction of travel is not purely toward more software: Google reintroduced in-person technical interview rounds specifically to counter AI interview fraud, a move confirmed in multiple industry reports through 2025, and environments where keystrokes and process can be observed are described as particularly effective[10].

evidence.gloss: No reliable industry-wide figure exists for proxy interview prevalence
evidence.verbatim: First, precise statistics on proxy interview prevalence are difficult to obtain due to the clandestine nature of interview fraud, and no reliable industry-wide figure exists

evidence.gloss: The problem grew after remote hiring removed physical verification barriers, making prevention standard practice
evidence.verbatim: what is clear is that the problem has grown noticeably since the shift to fully remote hiring removed many of the physical verification barriers that in-person interviews naturally provided, and hiring teams for high-demand technical roles report seeing attempts often enough that proactive prevention is now considered standard practice rather than optional[6]

evidence.gloss: Sources conclude proxy interviews need proactive prevention, with four measures that cut vulnerability
evidence.verbatim: Second, the sources' own conclusion is that proxy interviews are a serious threat to technical hiring integrity requiring proactive prevention rather than reactive detection, and that camera-on requirements, identity verification, interactive interview formats, and consistency checks across multiple rounds together reduce vulnerability substantially, with the investment paying off not just in avoided bad hires but in a fairer, more trustworthy hiring experience for honest candidates competing on merit[6].

h3.h3: What a Fraudulent Hire Costs After Onboarding

evidence.gloss: Kohn: candidate fraud creates cybersecurity risks worse than a bad hire
evidence.verbatim: Candidate fraud creates cybersecurity risks that can be far more serious than making a bad hire.

evidence.gloss: SHRM 2025: average cost per hire is $5,400, compounded by re-hires after fraud
evidence.verbatim: SHRM's 2025 data puts average cost per hire at $5,400, with re-hires needed after fraudulent candidates compounding that[2].

evidence.gloss: IBM 2026: global average data breach cost reached $4.99 million
evidence.verbatim: IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found the global average breach cost reached $4.99 million[3].

evidence.gloss: A fraudulent hire's access enables breaches, sabotage, and day-one entry to POS terminals or patient records
evidence.verbatim: Beyond the direct figures, a fraudulent hire's access can be used to commit data breaches, sabotage operations, or funnel sensitive information to malicious actors, and in frontline and third-party environments it can mean immediate access to shared systems, POS terminals, patient records, or other business-critical tools from the very first shift[3].

evidence.gloss: Financial fallout beyond salary: investigations, remediation, penalties, and wages that may fund hostile states
evidence.verbatim: Financially, organizations can lose far more than salary dollars: fraudulent hires can trigger costly investigations, remediation, breach response, delayed productivity, and regulatory penalties, and in some cases the wages paid may fund sanctioned or hostile state programs[3].

evidence.gloss: Legal and commercial exposure: sanctions and export control violations, client trust, liability
evidence.verbatim: A fraudulent hire can expose sensitive systems, violate sanctions and export control rules, damage client trust for staffing firms, and create legal liability for the hiring company[6].

evidence.gloss: Reputational fallout: governance and workforce-integrity concerns with employees, customers, and regulators
evidence.verbatim: Reputationally, discovering that an organization unknowingly hired an impostor raises governance, security, and workforce-integrity concerns with employees, customers, partners, and regulators[3].

evidence.gloss: Catching a mismatched identity pre-offer is dramatically cheaper than the aftermath
evidence.verbatim: Catching a mismatched identity before an offer is extended is dramatically cheaper than untangling the aftermath, which can include security incidents, wasted onboarding costs, and legal review[6].

evidence.gloss: Impact appears long after onboarding: access, data exposure, compliance risk, lost trust
evidence.verbatim: In many cases the impact appears long after onboarding — unauthorized system access, exposure of sensitive business or customer data, compliance risks in regulated environments, and breakdown of internal trust in identity verification — which is what makes early detection critical[12].

evidence.gloss: Data breaches: documented insider actions after infiltration
evidence.verbatim: **Data breaches.** Documented insider actions include releasing proprietary code in some instances, copying code repositories to personal accounts or cloud storage, and harvesting credentials or session cookies for future compromise opportunities.

evidence.gloss: Breaches trigger notification duties in several jurisdictions
evidence.verbatim: Taken together these can lead to significant data breaches requiring notification to individuals and authorities **in several jurisdictions**[30].

evidence.gloss: Sanctions and US export control exposure from hiring sanctioned-jurisdiction workers
evidence.verbatim: **Sanctions and export control violations.** Employing workers from sanctioned jurisdictions like North Korea can open a company to sanctions violations, and depending on the nature of the work and information accessed, companies may also face exposure under **U.S. export control laws**[30].

evidence.gloss: Financial cost of remediation after an infiltration

evidence.verbatim: **Reputational harm.** Beyond immediate operational disruption, companies may suffer **erosion of client trust and loss of business relationships**, particularly where regulated work is involved[30].

evidence.gloss: Consequences of a fraudulent hire: systems, sanctions, client trust, liability
evidence.verbatim: A fraudulent hire can expose sensitive systems, violate sanctions and export control rules, damage client trust for staffing firms, and create legal liability for the hiring company[2].

evidence.gloss: Vendor dollar ranges for identity fraud, insider and nation-state incidents
evidence.verbatim: One vendor puts explicit dollar ranges on the exposure: average cost of identity fraud at $500K–$1M+ per incident, $1M–$5M+ for a malicious insider, and $5M–$50M+ for a nation-state actor hired as an IT engineer[1].

evidence.gloss: Vendor claim of 42 recruiter hours saved per job posting
evidence.verbatim: The same vendor quantifies the recruiter-time drain at 42 hours saved per job posting when fraudulent candidates are removed from the funnel, multiplied by the number of open roles[1].

evidence.gloss: The documented costs of not verifying: wasted interviews, delays, security and reputational risk
evidence.verbatim: The documented costs of not verifying are wasted time interviewing and onboarding people who misrepresent themselves, operational delays that slow offers and disrupt workforce planning, and compliance, security, and reputational risks when fraudulent hires gain access to systems or sensitive data[47].

evidence.gloss: The framing is when a team implements proxy detection, not whether, before a $50,000 bad hire
evidence.verbatim: the question is framed not as whether proxy detection will become standard but whether a team implements it before a $50,000 bad hire forces the conversation[45]

evidence.gloss: Fabric researchers price a fraudulent hire in re-recruitment, wasted onboarding and access risk
evidence.verbatim: Hiring fraud researchers at Fabric put the direct cost of a fraudulent hire in terms of re-recruitment, wasted onboarding, and the security risk of giving a bad actor access[10].

evidence.gloss: Onboarded fraudulent hires become long-lived insider threats with financial, operational and regulatory costs
evidence.verbatim: Once onboarded, fraudulent hires may have privileged access to critical systems, facilities, and sensitive workflows before detection, creating long-lived insider threats that are difficult to unwind, with costs ranging from financial losses and operational disruption to reputational damage and regulatory scrutiny[46].

evidence.gloss: 23% of businesses lost over $50,000 and 10% over $100,000 from a fraudulent placement
evidence.verbatim: Accidentally placing a fraudulent candidate proves costly, with 23% of businesses reporting a loss of over $50,000 and 10% losing more than $100,000[51].

evidence.gloss: 23% of businesses lost over $50,000 and 10% over $100,000 from a fraudulent placement
evidence.verbatim: Twenty-three percent of businesses reported a loss of over $50,000 from accidentally placing a fraudulent candidate, and 10% lost more than $100,000 [51].

evidence.gloss: Gartner's Jamie Kohn on candidate fraud creating cybersecurity risks beyond a bad hire
evidence.verbatim: Gartner's senior research director in the HR practice, Jamie Kohn, framed the consequence rather than the frequency: candidate fraud creates cybersecurity risks far more serious than making a bad hire[8].

evidence.gloss: Cost comparison: a bad hire costs a quarter of salary; a planted identity costs something unpriceable
evidence.verbatim: A bad hire costs a quarter of salary and some goodwill; a planted identity inside your systems costs something you cannot easily price[8].

evidence.gloss: High-access roles turn fraud into an identity and access-control problem
evidence.verbatim: In roles tied to engineering, finance, cybersecurity, IT administration, or customer-data operations, the same issue becomes an identity and access-control problem, because the wrong person may receive credentials, devices, or sensitive system access[7].

evidence.gloss: Fake candidate uses the interview to get documents, equipment, and system access
evidence.verbatim: A fake candidate can use a synthetic interview to obtain internal documents, receive equipment, manipulate onboarding, or gain access to systems before the organization verifies employment details[27].

evidence.gloss: Frames the cost of a compromised assessment: an unverified candidate whose performance gap only appears on the job, compounding weekly
evidence.verbatim:
A fraudulently passed assessment does not just produce a bad hire. It inserts an unverified candidate into a role where the performance gap surfaces on the job rather than in the screening process, and the cost compounds with every week the hire remains in seat.
Talent management strategies built on assessment data are only as reliable as the integrity of those assessments. Enterprise talent management programs that use assessments as a primary filter are directly exposed to fraud at the top of the pipeline.

evidence.gloss: Direct hiring cost of assessment fraud: SHRM's 50-200% of salary replacement cost, the 60-90 day detection lag, and the 90-day quality-of-hire mark
evidence.verbatim:
SHRM estimates the cost of replacing a bad hire at 50 to 200% of that role’s annual salary, covering recruitment fees, onboarding investment, productivity loss, and manager time on performance management. In technical and senior-level positions, the figure approaches the upper end of that range.
A software engineer or finance analyst who passed a technical assessment fraudulently typically goes 60 to 90 days before the performance gap becomes actionable. At that point, the full hiring cycle restarts, and the cost of that cycle doubles against the original budget.
Most HR teams track quality-of-hire at the 90-day mark. Assessment platforms that generate auditable session logs give HR teams the evidence to identify fraud before that mark, rather than attributing poor performance to onboarding variables.

evidence.gloss: The cost of a fraudulent hire: direct dollar figures plus legal liability, security exposure, and team damage
evidence.verbatim:
A single fraudulent hire caught after onboarding costs an average of $17,000 in direct costs (SHRM), rising to three to four times annual salary for senior roles once you add lost productivity, management time, and rehiring costs. Gallup research places the cost of replacing any employee at 50-200% of their annual salary. Gem and Crosschq estimate the U.S.-wide aggregate at over $600 billion annually.
The financial figure is the visible part. Three costs typically exceed it.
Legal liability. In regulated industries – healthcare, finance, childcare, education – hiring an unqualified candidate who causes harm exposes the employer to negligent hiring claims. Michigan’s Authentic Credentials in Education Act has been used to recover damages directly from employees who used false academic credentials to obtain employment. The employer’s exposure scales with how little verification they ran.
Security exposure. The North Korean synthetic identity operations documented by the FBI are not an edge case – they are a documented, repeating pattern. Amazon’s December 2025 disclosure confirmed that a systems administrator had worked inside the company for months before the fabricated identity was discovered. One fraudulent hire with appropriate permissions is an insider threat by definition.
Team damage. Fraudulent employees underperform and teams absorb the shortfall. When the fraud surfaces – and it usually does – it erodes trust in your hiring process and demoralises the people who worked alongside the hire.
Key Takeaway: Running a live skills test and making two independent phone calls costs under an hour and effectively zero budget. One fraudulent hire who reaches day 90 costs more than the entire annual verification overhead for most mid-size teams.

sections_menu.h2: The two candidate frauds this software has to stop: proxy stand-ins and deepfakes

h3.h3: What counts as proxy fraud and what counts as a deepfake

evidence.gloss: Gartner's Jamie Kohn frames candidate fraud as an identity problem, not a quality-of-hire problem
evidence.verbatim: Jamie Kohn, senior research director in Gartner's human resources practice, framed the problem as an identity problem rather than a quality-of-hire problem: "It's getting harder for employers to evaluate candidates' true abilities, and in some cases, their identities.

evidence.gloss: Definition of cosmetic enhancement: inflating skills with AI-generated technical narratives
evidence.verbatim: Cosmetic enhancement means inflating skills the candidate does not have, with AI generating plausible technical narratives to back it up

evidence.gloss: Definition of identity fraud: a different person takes the interview, sometimes with deepfakes or real-time AI prompting
evidence.verbatim: identity fraud is the extreme, where a different person entirely takes the interview, sometimes using deepfake technology or real-time AI prompting to simulate expertise they do not possess[2].

evidence.gloss: The distribution pattern: cosmetic fraud is everywhere, identity fraud concentrates where verification is weakest
evidence.verbatim: The pattern the sources draw from this: cosmetic enhancement is everywhere, while identity fraud concentrates where verification is weakest[2].

evidence.gloss: Definition of proxy interviewing
evidence.verbatim: Proxy interviewing means a stand-in sits the technical interview or assessment[4].

evidence.gloss: Definition of AI-driven misrepresentation, including AI avatars
evidence.verbatim: AI-driven misrepresentation covers using AI tools to generate answers during technical tests or written assessments, real-time answer generation, and candidates using AI avatars to appear for interviews on their behalf[4].

evidence.gloss: Definition of interview fraud, including outside help from a friend or an AI chatbot
evidence.verbatim: Interview fraud covers any candidate deception during the interview, including a candidate using outside help such as a more qualified friend or an AI chatbot to answer questions, and there are well-reported instances of candidates using stand-ins on camera who pretend to be the person the employer is trying to hire [3].

evidence.gloss: Fraud spectrum: reading ChatGPT answers at the simple end, faked image/voice/background at the complex end
evidence.verbatim: Fraud during an interview can be as simple as someone reading answers generated by ChatGPT while questions are asked, or as complex as a candidate faking image, voice, and background in a video to deceive hiring managers, particularly for remote jobs [3].

evidence.gloss: Candidate fraud differs from resume embellishment: it questions who is evaluated and who gets access
evidence.verbatim: Candidate fraud is distinct from ordinary resume embellishment because it raises the question of who is actually being evaluated and who receives access after hiring[7].

evidence.gloss: The recurring fraud patterns list: fake resumes, synthetic identities, fake references, proxy interviews, deepfakes
evidence.verbatim: The recurring patterns are fabricated resumes with invented employers, projects or credentials; synthetic or stolen identities; fake references; proxy interviews where someone else answers for the applicant; and deepfake-assisted video interviews involving face swaps and voice manipulation[7].

evidence.gloss: Human proxy defined as a stand-in taking the interview
evidence.verbatim: One is a human proxy: a stand-in who takes the interview for someone else.

evidence.gloss: Synthetic identity defined as face swap, injected feed, or voice clone
evidence.verbatim: The other is synthetic identity: a face swap, injected video feed, or voice clone placed in the interview seat.

evidence.gloss: Both attacks exploit the video call being the primary identity evidence
evidence.verbatim: Both attack the same weakness, which is that the video call itself has become the primary evidence of who a candidate is[27].

evidence.gloss: The employer's question shifts from answer quality to answer ownership
evidence.verbatim: That is the exposure in one sentence, and it is why the employer's problem is not "was this answer good" but "whose answer was it.

evidence.gloss: The named fraud behaviors in this exposure set
evidence.verbatim: The specific fraud behaviors named in this exposure set: face swaps, voice clones, or AI filter impersonation; AI-generated work samples with unclear authorship; real-time coaching during interviews; and location misrepresentation that surfaces later during payroll, tax, or access review[7].

evidence.gloss: Live deepfakes differ by what changes and where it enters the path
evidence.verbatim: Live video-call deepfakes are differentiated by what the attacker changes and where the change enters the communication path.

evidence.gloss: Face swap defined: visible face replaced, body and movements preserved
evidence.verbatim: Face swaps replace the visible face with another person's while preserving the attacker's body, background, or facial movements[27].

evidence.gloss: Proxy sitting is misrepresentation of identity, which verification exists to catch
evidence.verbatim: Having someone else sit the interview is misrepresentation of identity, and identity verification exists precisely to catch it.

evidence.gloss: Introduces the four fraud categories and notes each needs a different detection method
evidence.verbatim: The 4 types of resume fraud active in 2026 are traditional inflation, AI-generated fabrication, deepfake interview fraud, and state-sponsored synthetic identity fraud. Each type requires a different verification method – a process built only to catch traditional fraud will miss the other three entirely.

h3.h3: How the attacks are actually run in an interview

evidence.gloss: "Bait and switch" hiring is a named and growing tactic
evidence.verbatim: "Bait and switch" hiring, where one person interviews and another shows up to do the job, is a named and growing tactic[3].

evidence.gloss: Scammers recruit U.S.-based accomplices to appear on camera and even fill an office seat
evidence.verbatim: In some cases scammers recruit U.S.-based accomplices who agree to appear on camera for video interviews, and even show up in the office to fill a seat on the fraudster's behalf[3].

evidence.gloss: Tactic: compromised identities used to pose as legitimate candidates
evidence.verbatim: **Compromised identities** — using stolen identities to pose as legitimate candidates.

evidence.gloss: Tactic: online job marketplaces and talent intermediaries used to secure interviews under stolen identities
evidence.verbatim: **Online services** — using job marketplaces, freelance platforms, and intermediary talent firms to secure interviews under compromised identities.

evidence.gloss: Tactic: real-time deepfakes to manipulate video or audio during an interview
evidence.verbatim: **Deepfake technology** — using real-time deepfakes to manipulate video or audio and impersonate a legitimate person during an interview.

evidence.gloss: Tactic: VPNs and masking tools to hide true location after employment starts
evidence.verbatim: **Remote work** — using VPNs and other tools to mask true location and identity after employment is secured.

evidence.gloss: Glider AI: AI video and voice tools made proxy interviewing far more convincing
evidence.verbatim: Glider AI's research into deepfake technology and candidate fraud found that AI-generated video and voice tools have made proxy interviewing far more convincing than it used to be[6].

evidence.gloss: A human interviewer may not spot a synthetic face, which is why liveness and deepfake detection is added
evidence.verbatim: The material is direct that a skilled operator can use a synthetic or altered face during a live video interview and a human interviewer may not notice, which is why identity solutions increasingly include dedicated liveness and deepfake detection rather than relying on a recruiter's judgment alone[6].

evidence.gloss: Synthetic faces in live video can go unnoticed by human interviewers
evidence.verbatim: AI-generated video and voice tools have advanced enough that a skilled operator can use a synthetic or altered face during a live video interview and a human interviewer may not notice[2]

evidence.gloss: Reported cases of candidates using on-camera stand-ins
evidence.verbatim: there are well-reported instances of candidates using stand-ins on camera who pretend to be the person the employer is trying to hire [3].

evidence.gloss: Assessment-stage fraud shows as a gap between submitted work and live explanation
evidence.verbatim: At the assessment stage, fraud typically appears as a gap between submitted work and live explanation: a take-home assignment looks well-prepared but the candidate cannot explain how they approached it, or the work is stronger than their resume, screening call, or interview answers suggest[7].

evidence.gloss: Interview-stage issues: proxy interviews, AI-assisted answers, voice spoofing, deepfakes
evidence.verbatim: At the interview stage, the issues that surface are proxy interviews, AI-assisted responses, voice spoofing and possible deepfake use[7].

evidence.gloss: Proxy interviews run on credential sharing or remote access software
evidence.verbatim: Proxy interviews work through credential sharing: candidates share their login credentials with the proxy, giving access to the virtual interview platform such as Zoom or GoToMeeting, or through remote access software like TeamViewer and AnyDesk that lets the proxy control the candidate's device[34].

evidence.gloss: Two shapes of proxy fraud in spoken virtual interviews
evidence.verbatim: During traditional spoken virtual interviews the proxy is either on camera completing the interview as the candidate, or the candidate stays on-screen while the proxy feeds them responses[34].

evidence.gloss: In non-spoken technical assessments the candidate stays on camera while the proxy controls the device
evidence.verbatim: On technical interviews and pre-hire skills assessments that do not require spoken responses, the candidate usually stays on camera while the proxy controls their device and does everything, solving the problems[34].

evidence.gloss: Who the proxy is: a paid expert, friend or colleague, or an underground professional interview proxy
evidence.verbatim: The proxy may be a paid subject matter expert, a friend or colleague[34], or a paid expert from an underground service or a professional "interview proxy" hired through illicit networks that have emerged to exploit remote hiring[6].

evidence.gloss: Legacy cheating methods (tab-switching, screen sharing, notes, phone lookups) persist but are now combined with AI rather than replaced by it
evidence.verbatim:
Before addressing newer threats, the traditional ones never went away. Tab-switching, screen sharing to a helper, notes documents open in adjacent windows, and phone-based lookups still account for a significant share of detected violations in high-volume hiring pipelines.
The key difference in 2026 is that these lower-sophistication methods are now combined with AI tools rather than replaced by them. A candidate who opens a second screen is increasingly likely to run an AI query, which changes the quality and speed of the output compared to a basic search.

evidence.gloss: How LLMs and purpose-built exam tools changed cheating economics: polished answers in seconds, passive secondary-device generation that defeats browser lockdown and copy-paste detection
evidence.verbatim:
Large language models changed the economics of cheating in online assessments. A candidate with access to any major LLM can paste a technical question and receive a polished answer within seconds, then rephrase and type it naturally to avoid copy-paste detection.
More recently, tools built specifically for exam contexts have entered circulation. These tools monitor on-screen content through a secondary device and generate answers passively, without any copy-paste activity from the candidate.
Standard browser lockdown does not catch this behaviour because the secondary device operates entirely outside the controlled environment.
Cognitive ability assessments face additional complexity here since AI tools can generate plausible responses to logic and reasoning questions within typical time limits.

evidence.gloss: Cheating method: candidates use AI chatbots like ChatGPT and deepfakes, exploiting weak photo-only proctoring instead of full video/audio monitoring.
evidence.verbatim:
Candidates are found to use AI chatbots and even deepfake technology to manipulate assessments. Candidates may use tools like ChatGPT to search for answers during assessments, bypassing their own knowledge and skills.
Many companies use basic proctoring systems, such as taking random candidate photos during the examination, rather than full-length video and audio proctoring.
This allows candidates to cheat, as live proctoring solutions are often available only for high-end examinations.

evidence.gloss: Cheating method: screen sharing, remote collaboration tools, and a second device (phone/tablet) used to get outside help during unproctored assessments.
evidence.verbatim:
Candidates often resort to using screen sharing and remote collaboration tools to get help from others during online assessments. Since AI in pre-hire assessments happens without an external proctor, candidates take this as an opportunity to cheat without raising suspicion.
Some may even use a second device, such as a phone or tablet, to search for answers online during the assessment.

evidence.gloss: Deepfake interview fraud: face-swap and voice-cloning during video interviews, enabled by platforms with no live identity verification
evidence.verbatim:
Gartner’s 2026 research found 6% of job seekers admitted to deepfake fraud during a video interview – using AI to alter their face or voice on a live call, or having a more qualified person sit in their place entirely. On the employer side, 15% of hiring professionals said they had already witnessed face-swapping or voice cloning during an active interview.
Remote hiring created the attack surface. Most video interview platforms have no live identity verification. A candidate with a deepfake overlay passes a face-to-face screen while never being physically present.

evidence.gloss: Synthetic identity fraud, including state-sponsored operatives, plus a comparison table of the four fraud types by detection difficulty and target sector
evidence.verbatim:
At the extreme end: fully fabricated identities. The FBI has documented North Korean state-sponsored operatives creating complete synthetic personas – work history, LinkedIn profiles, GitHub repositories, references – to secure remote IT roles at U.S. companies. Amazon confirmed in December 2025 that a systems administrator’s identity had been entirely fabricated using this method.

h3.h3: How common it is and why it got cheap

evidence.gloss: Sterling: identity misrepresentation runs 2.3x higher in remote-first roles than on-site
evidence.verbatim: Sterling's 2025 screening report found identity misrepresentation runs 2.3x higher in remote-first roles than in on-site positions[2].

evidence.gloss: The economics: tailoring an application went from hours of work to seconds of compute
evidence.verbatim: The economics behind that curve are simple: a decade ago, tailoring an application to a specific job description took hours of human work; today it takes seconds of compute, and the marginal cost of producing a flawless, customized resume has collapsed[2].

evidence.gloss: Sets up the section on today's cheating landscape, arguing fraud is now systematic and repeatable rather than opportunistic
evidence.verbatim: Assessment cheating in 2026 is systematic, not opportunistic. The tools candidates can access allow for repeatable fraud that standard proctoring alone cannot detect, and understanding each threat type is a prerequisite for building controls that actually work.

evidence.gloss: Two forms of identity fraud, account takeover and deepfake impersonation, with the Palo Alto 1,300% deepfake growth figure and Gartner's 1-in-4 fabricated profiles by 2028
evidence.verbatim:
Identity fraud in remote assessments takes two forms. The first is account takeover: a candidate completes registration legitimately, then hands the live session to a more capable substitute.
The second form is deepfake impersonation: the substitute uses a synthetic video feed that matches the registered applicant’s appearance closely enough to pass a webcam check at session start. Candidates who bypass video-based identity checks using deepfake technology can sustain the deception for the duration of a standard proctored session.
Palo Alto Networks found that deepfake fraud across digital channels grew 1,300% from 2023 to 2024. Gartner projects that by 2028, 1 in 4 candidate profiles across enterprise hiring pipelines will contain fabricated information, and assessment platforms that rely on a single webcam snapshot at session start are insufficient against either method.

evidence.gloss: Sets up the cheating problem with the claim that ~50% of candidates cheat on AI-driven assessments, introducing the list of methods that follows.
evidence.verbatim: Research found that about 50% of candidates cheat at AI-driven assessments, nearly half of the candidate pool. Though companies take multiple guidelines and precautions, candidates still find a way. Some of these include:

evidence.gloss: Cheating method: identity fraud and fake qualifications, with 15-20% of candidates misrepresenting themselves, 92% rise in fraud since the pandemic, bad-hire cost of 30% of salary and $4,700 per hiring cycle.
evidence.verbatim:
Some candidates fake identities or qualifications during the hiring process. LinkedIn studies show that about 15-20% of candidates lie about presenting themselves. Additionally, there has been a 92% increase in candidate fraud since the pandemic.
Hiring fraud can be costly for companies, especially as one bad hire costs almost 30% of the role’s salary. Not only that, but the total cost of recruiting and onboarding for one hiring cycle is $4700.

h3.h3: What stops each fraud type

evidence.gloss: Same-person continuity across application, assessment, interview, offer, credentials
evidence.verbatim: The core concern is same-person continuity: whether the person who submitted the application is the same person who completed the assessment, joined the interview, accepted the offer, and will receive credentials[7].

evidence.gloss: Opening answer: stack four defenses (identity verification, environment lockdown, unscriptable follow-ups, pre-interview skills assessment), backed by Gartner and survey data on interview fraud, candidate AI use, and lying rates.
evidence.verbatim:
Try for free
Book a demo
Cheating in online interviews is now an AI problem, not a notes-under-the-desk problem. To prevent it, stack four defenses: verify who is on camera, lock down the test environment, ask follow-up questions that scripted or AI-fed answers cannot survive, and score a skills assessment before the live call so the interview confirms a real person instead of carrying the whole decision. That combination catches proxy candidates, deepfakes, and real-time AI copilots without turning every interview into an interrogation.
The scale is not small. In a 2025 Gartner survey of 3,000 candidates, 6% admitted to interview fraud, either posing as someone else or having a stand-in pose for them. In that same survey, only 26% of candidates trusted AI to evaluate them fairly, yet 40% already use AI somewhere in the application. Gartner also expects 25% of candidate profiles to be fake by 2028. Add the 60% of workers who admit to lying in a job interview (64.2% have stretched the truth about skills, experience, or references at least once, and 72.4% would use AI to help), and the case for a structured, verified process is hard to argue with.
Summarise this post with:

evidence.gloss: TL;DR bullets summarizing the six core recommendations, from identity-first verification to publishing an acceptable-AI-use policy.
evidence.verbatim:
- Modern interview cheating is mostly identity fraud and real-time AI help: proxy candidates, deepfakes, and answer overlays, not hidden notes.
- Verify identity first. Government ID plus face and voice matching across stages catches most impersonation before it costs you an offer.
- Design beats detection. Application-specific questions and pointed follow-ups expose AI answers faster than any single tool.
- Score a skills assessment before the interview. The live call then verifies a person you already have evidence on.
- Proctoring and lockdown controls create the clean environment, but a human reads the evidence and makes the call.
- Set an acceptable-AI-use policy up front. Clear rules and stated consequences cut casual cheating on their own.

evidence.gloss: Defines the modern cheating landscape and gives a five-row table of methods (proxy interview, deepfake, real-time AI copilot, secondary device, fabricated credentials) with how each works and its specific counter.
evidence.verbatim:
It has shifted from low-tech to high-tech. The old playbook was memorized answers, hidden notes, and the occasional stand-in. The 2026 playbook is a proxy candidate on a spoofed video feed, a deepfake avatar, or a transparent AI overlay that reads answers onto the screen during the call. These tools produce fluent first answers, which is exactly why a fluent first answer is no longer proof of anything.
The five methods below cover almost every case worth planning for. The counter for each is a specific control, not a vibe check.
Cheating methodHow it worksHow to counter it
Proxy interviewA paid stand-in takes the call, or feeds answers off-screen.Photo ID check, face match, and voice matching across every stage.
Deepfake or video spoofA synthetic face or filter masks who is really answering.Liveness checks and lip-sync analysis; watch for audio that lags the mouth.
Real-time AI copilotA hidden overlay shows AI answers the candidate reads aloud.Sharp follow-ups, application-specific questions, and delay or eye-movement cues.
Secondary device or off-screen helpA phone or second monitor supplies prompts and notes.Environment scan, full-screen enforcement, and a second-camera view.
Fabricated credentialsSkills, references, or history are invented on the resume.Skills assessments plus reference and background verification.

evidence.gloss: Key takeaways expanding each recommendation with the reasoning and the cost of skipping it, from treating cheating as identity fraud to keeping humans as the decision-maker.
evidence.verbatim:
- Treat interview cheating as identity fraud first. Proxy candidates and deepfakes are the expensive failures, so verifying who is on camera matters more than catching a glance at hidden notes. Skip this and a stand-in can reach an offer.
- Verification beats suspicion. ID, face match, and voice matching across stages give you a defensible reason to advance or pause a candidate, instead of a gut feeling you cannot act on.
- Design out the easy wins. Application-specific questions and two-deep follow-ups expose AI-fed answers without special tools, because the model was never told the candidate’s own story. This is the cheapest control you have.
- Move evaluation earlier. A scored skills assessment before the call means the interview verifies a person you already have evidence on, which shrinks the payoff of faking the live conversation.
- Keep humans in the decision. Proctoring produces evidence and flags, not verdicts. A person reviews the signal and decides, which protects honest candidates and holds up under scrutiny.
- Publish the rules. A stated acceptable-AI-use policy with real consequences cuts casual cheating before the interview even starts.

evidence.gloss: FAQ answering how to prevent and detect cheating, what a proxy interview is, how to spot candidate AI use, and whether Testlify detects cheating.
evidence.verbatim:
How can you prevent cheating in online interviews?
Combine four layers: verify identity with ID and biometric checks, lock down the environment with proctoring, ask follow-up questions that expose memorized or AI-fed answers, and score a skills assessment before the live call so the interview confirms a real person rather than carrying the whole decision.
How do you detect cheating in a video interview?
Watch for tells that scripted or AI-assisted answers produce: eyes reading off-screen, a beat of delay before fluent replies, answers that fall apart under a specific follow-up, and audio that drifts slightly out of sync with lip movement. Pair those human cues with automated proctoring signals for a defensible read.
What is a proxy interview?
A proxy interview is when someone other than the actual candidate takes the interview, either by impersonating them on camera or feeding answers off-screen. Identity verification, voice matching across stages, and an environment scan are the main defenses against it.
How do you know if a candidate is using AI in an interview?
Real-time AI tools produce polished opening answers but stumble on pointed follow-ups, ask you to repeat questions to buy processing time, and create small delays or eye movement toward a second screen. Application-specific questions about the candidate’s own stated work are hard for an AI overlay to answer convincingly.
Does Testlify detect cheating in interviews?
Yes. Testlify applies identity verification, AI-assistance detection, and configurable proctoring controls such as full-screen enforcement, tab-switch detection, and webcam monitoring, then hands recruiters reviewable evidence so a human makes the final call rather than an automated flag.

evidence.gloss: Detecting live AI assistance through second and third follow-up questions, plus behavioral tells like reading eye movement, restate requests, and reply delay; includes a two-probe pro tip.
evidence.verbatim:
AI copilots are strong on the opening answer and weak on the second and third. Ask a candidate to walk through a decision they just described, then push on a specific tradeoff. A real practitioner adds detail; an AI-fed answer either loops back to the general case or stalls while the tool catches up. Look for reading eye movement, a repeated request to restate the question, and a small delay before fluent replies.
Pro Tip: Keep two follow-ups in your back pocket for every core question. Ask “what would you do differently” and “why that and not the obvious alternative.” Those two probes catch far more AI-assisted answers than any single detection tool, because they need lived reasoning the model was never given.

evidence.gloss: Real-time detection of outside help: unexpected voices, screen changes, off-screen attention, AI-assistance detection, talking prohibition, and dual-camera room coverage
evidence.verbatim:
Proctoring also has to notice behavior that signals outside help: an unexpected voice, a sudden screen change, eyes drifting off-screen, or AI-assisted answering. The point is speed. A strong platform flags these moments live so your team can act or review them later, instead of finding out after the offer goes out.
AI assistance detection helps teams catch suspicious behavior during the assessment.
In Testlify, this includes AI-assistance detection, talking prohibition, a live environment check, and dual-camera support that builds a fuller, 360-degree view of the room without leaning only on a human proctor.

evidence.gloss: AI assistance detection plus extras (dual-camera, question-level logs, question shuffling, study prevention, beta live proctoring) and EEOC compliance note
evidence.verbatim:
Beyond the controls above, Testlify adds AI assistance detection to flag likely unauthorized chatbot use, dual-camera proctoring (laptop plus phone) for a wider view of the room, question-level activity logs, random question shuffling so no two candidates see the same order, logout on environment exit, and study prevention. Live video proctoring is available in beta for teams that want a human watching in real time.
All of these comply with EEOC guidance on fair, non-discriminatory testing, and they sit alongside Testlify’s wider anti-cheating controls.

h3.h3: What a one-way (async) video interview is and where it sits in the funnel

evidence.verbatim: In an asynchronous one-way video interview, the candidate records answers on their own time and the employer reviews the file later[1][2].

evidence.verbatim: Once recording starts, response length is typically capped, usually between 1 and 3 minutes per answer, and these timings can differ per question [22][28].

evidence.verbatim: Employers typically allow 1 to 3 retakes per question, set by the employer, and some platforms allow limited or unlimited attempts to record a response per question [22][28].

evidence.verbatim: A February 2026 case of a candidate caught using real-time AI prompting during a live technical interview at a FAANG company was notable only because the detection succeeded[2].

evidence.gloss: Volume sits at the recorded stage where a stand-in is cheapest
evidence.verbatim: Note what that split implies for integrity: the recorded stage is where volume sits and where a stand-in is cheapest to deploy, while the closer look happens only later.

h3.h3: Why the recorded stage is the cheapest place to send a stand-in

evidence.gloss: The absence of a live interviewer is the structural weakness
evidence.verbatim: That same absence of a live interviewer is the structural weakness.

evidence.gloss: Remote hiring removed the in-person touchpoint and the gap is being exploited
evidence.verbatim: Fully remote hiring removed the in-person touchpoint that older processes retained, and that gap has been noticed and exploited [6].

evidence.gloss: Async shifts effort onto candidates at the least committed point
evidence.verbatim: The candidate cost of async is described as real and under-discussed by vendors: asking someone to record themselves before any human has spoken to them shifts effort onto the candidate at the earliest and least committed point[24].

evidence.gloss: Async volume with no human present is the fraud exposure
evidence.verbatim: The same structural fact drives the fraud exposure — the async stage is where the largest volume passes through with no human on the other end.

evidence.gloss: Scale advantage and identity exposure are the same fact
evidence.verbatim: The scale advantage and the identity exposure are the same fact.

evidence.gloss: The same convenience removes the environmental control a live proctored session keeps
evidence.verbatim: the same property that makes the format convenient for a genuine candidate is what removes the environmental control a live proctored session retains.

evidence.gloss: Candidate AI assistance during unmonitored recorded interviews makes the signal problem more pressing
evidence.verbatim: This is more pressing as candidates use AI assistance during unmonitored recorded interviews[35].

evidence.gloss: Signal quality is bounded by the format: a retakeable recorded answer is a rehearsed artefact with no follow-up
evidence.verbatim: And signal quality is bounded by the format, because a recorded answer to a fixed prompt, with retakes allowed and no follow-up possible, is a rehearsed artefact — it cannot distinguish a candidate who understands a subject from one who prepared a polished paragraph about it, since nothing in the format can ask "why did you make that choice?"[35].

evidence.gloss: On the asynchronous side the exposure is structural
evidence.verbatim: On the asynchronous side, the exposure is structural.

evidence.gloss: Virtual exams have real upsides but make cheating easier without anti-cheat tools or proctoring
evidence.verbatim: Virtual exams, despite upsides such as testing from anywhere, allowing more candidates to test, and being less costly, may make it easier to cheat using outside tools and other people, especially when employers do not have anti-cheat tools or proctoring set up[48].

evidence.gloss: Applicants send substitutes or enlist coordinated help, sharing screens, answers or logins
evidence.verbatim: Some job applicants arrange for another person to take their pre-employment exam in their place, or quietly enlist help from a friend or a coordinated group, often remotely, where test-takers can share screens, send answers in real time, or hand over login credentials entirely[48].

h3.h3: No unscripted follow-up: what the missing interviewer removes

evidence.gloss: What async removes: no unscripted follow-up, no real-time observation, no one to hear a second voice
evidence.verbatim: In an async recording there is no one on the call to ask an unscripted follow-up, no real-time observation, and no interviewer to notice a second voice off camera.

evidence.gloss: No live challenge means attacker can retake, edit, coach off-camera or synthesize offline
evidence.verbatim: Nothing has to survive a live challenge, so the attacker can retake, edit, coach off-camera, or synthesize offline at any quality they can afford.

evidence.gloss: Recorded format gives the attacker unlimited render time and no interlocutor
evidence.verbatim: The recorded format hands the attacker unlimited render time and no interlocutor.

evidence.gloss: The challenge mechanism structurally disappears in asynchronous mode
evidence.verbatim: The asynchronous mode is where the challenge mechanism structurally disappears.

evidence.gloss: A recorded one-way interview has no recipient present to issue an unplanned request
evidence.verbatim: A prerecorded stream fails when the recipient asks an unexpected question or requests an unplanned action[27], which is precisely the move a recorded one-way interview cannot make: there is no recipient present to issue an unplanned request at the moment of answering.

evidence.gloss: Probing is by definition unavailable in the asynchronous format
evidence.verbatim: Probing is, by definition, unavailable in the asynchronous format, and the collected material draws that line in several places.

evidence.gloss: The unscripted pivot and pair-programming formats both require a live interviewer reacting in real time
evidence.verbatim: The entire mechanism of the unscripted pivot depends on a live interviewer reacting to the candidate's last answer[42][7], and the pair-programming and debugging formats depend on the candidate responding in real time to interviewer suggestions and direction[6].

h3.h3: What a live video interview is, and how the two formats differ

evidence.gloss: Definition of a live video interview
evidence.verbatim: A live video interview is a real-time conversation between a recruiter or hiring manager and a candidate, conducted through a video interviewing platform rather than in person[32].

evidence.gloss: Live vs one-way video interview comparison table
evidence.verbatim: Compared with one-way video interviews, live interviews offer real-time conversation instead of no real-time interaction, require scheduling coordination instead of candidate-side flexibility, allow immediate feedback instead of review at the recruiter's convenience, and are described as offering a more personal touch[32].

evidence.gloss: The two interview formats are not variants of one control
evidence.verbatim: The two formats are not two settings of the same control.

evidence.gloss: Core definition: recorded = submitted file, live = conversation under a per-frame time budget
evidence.verbatim: A one-way recorded interview is a file submitted with no human present; a live interview is a conversation happening inside a per-frame time budget.

evidence.gloss: Format difference determines cheap fraud, available signals, and what a flag can do
evidence.verbatim: That difference decides which fraud is cheap, which detection signal exists at all, and what a flag can do about it.

evidence.gloss: Async is instrumented, live is observed
evidence.verbatim: The async format is instrumented; the live one is observed.

h3.h3: Live presence as the detection mechanism, and its limits

evidence.gloss: Live human presence changes the fraud surface rather than removing it
evidence.verbatim: That live human presence changes the fraud surface rather than removing it.

evidence.gloss: Tab switching is behavioural not technical in the live format
evidence.verbatim: Tab switching is not a technical flag in this format, because the interviewer is already on the call; the risk is behavioural rather than technical, meaning that if the candidate's eyes drift to another monitor or their attention visibly shifts, the interviewer picks it up[33].

evidence.gloss: The behavioural-risk point applies to any live video call, not just HireVue
evidence.verbatim: This is stated to be true of any live video call, HireVue or not[33].

evidence.gloss: The detection mechanism in live interviewing is the human on the other end
evidence.verbatim: In other words, the detection mechanism in live interviewing is largely the human on the other end, unless the platform adds something on top.

evidence.gloss: In live HireVue interviews tab switching is not a technical flag because the interviewer is present
evidence.verbatim: In a live two-way HireVue interview with a human interviewer present, "tab switching itself isn't a technical flag in this format — because the interviewer is already on the call"[4].

evidence.gloss: Live risk is behavioral not technical; true of any video call
evidence.verbatim: The interviewer sees the camera feed and notices an extended look away from the screen, but "the risk here is behavioral, not technical," and it is true of any live video call, HireVue or not[4].

evidence.gloss: Live HireVue interviews monitor like a normal video call with a watching interviewer
evidence.verbatim: In a live HireVue interview with a human interviewer present, monitoring works like a standard video call: the interviewer sees the camera feed, and if the candidate looks away from the screen for an extended period, they notice[4].

evidence.gloss: In live format tab switching is a behavioural risk, not a technical flag
evidence.verbatim: Tab switching itself is not a technical flag in this format, because the interviewer is already on the call; the risk is behavioural rather than technical, in that visibly shifting attention or drifting eyes to another monitor is what registers, and this is true of any live video call, HireVue or not[4].

evidence.gloss: HireVue's live two-way format monitors like a normal call; tab switching is not a technical flag
evidence.verbatim: The same limit holds in HireVue's live two-way format. Monitoring works like a standard video call, and tab switching is not a technical flag in that format because the interviewer is already on the call.

evidence.gloss: In live formats the risk is behavioural: the interviewer notices drifting eyes or shifting attention
evidence.verbatim: The risk is behavioural, not technical: if the candidate's eyes drift to another monitor or their attention visibly shifts, the interviewer notices. That is true of any live video call, HireVue or not[4].

evidence.gloss: Live interviews still need authenticity review beyond behavioural observation for high-risk roles
evidence.verbatim: Live interviews still need more than behavioural observation when synthetic video or voice manipulation is a concern, and for high-risk interviews live meeting protection can add audio and video authenticity review before a candidate advances[7].

h3.h3: What each format actually logs

evidence.gloss: HireVue async logs focus-blur but cannot see other tabs, history or outside apps
evidence.verbatim: In HireVue's asynchronous format the platform logs a focus-blur event when the candidate leaves its tab, though it cannot see the content of other tabs, access browser history, or view any application outside its own interface[4].

evidence.gloss: HireVue prep time is unmonitored: no camera, audio or focus events until the candidate starts
evidence.verbatim: Prep time before each question is explicitly unmonitored: the interface shows a "Not Recording" indicator, and no camera data, no audio, and no browser focus events are captured until the candidate clicks to start the answer[4].

evidence.gloss: Recording starts only when the candidate clicks
evidence.verbatim: Recording begins only at that click[4].

evidence.gloss: HireVue prep time is fully unmonitored, with a Not Recording indicator and no data captured
evidence.verbatim: Prep time is completely unmonitored: HireVue's interface shows a clear "Not Recording" indicator during the preparation window before each question, and no camera data, no audio, and no browser focus events are captured during prep[4].

evidence.gloss: Recording starts only when the candidate clicks to begin the answer
evidence.verbatim: Recording begins only after the candidate explicitly clicks to start their answer[4].

evidence.gloss: Async one-way interviews capture focus, backgrounding and blur events; HireVue's app logs backgrounding
evidence.verbatim: The async one-way format captures browser focus events, backgrounding, and blur events technically, and HireVue's mobile app logs an "application did enter background" event, with some versions pausing recording when backgrounded and others continuing audio capture only[4].

evidence.gloss: Amazon: HackerRank assessments log tab switching, copy-paste, code similarity; Chime video rounds have no automatic monitoring
evidence.verbatim: The same split shows up in Amazon's stack: for HackerRank online assessments, tab switching, copy-paste, and code similarity are all logged; for Chime video rounds it is human observation only, with no automatic monitoring[5].

evidence.gloss: What a generic recorder (Zoom, Teams, Otter, Loom) fails to do
evidence.verbatim: A generic recorder (Zoom, Teams, Otter, Loom) captures the conversation with no structure on top, produces a generic transcript with no competency or rubric anchoring, leaves recordings in someone's personal drive or a shared folder, offers no cross-interview view, and leaves the scorecard and notes to be done manually after the call[19].

evidence.gloss: An interview-aware capture stack is built around what the recording becomes
evidence.verbatim: An interview-aware capture stack is built around what the recording becomes: structured notes written for you, a transcript anchored to your scorecard rubric and competencies, and role-based access, retention windows and a candidate-rights workflow built in[19].

evidence.gloss: Feature comparison checklist of Testlify against other tools: one-way and two-way video, question randomisation, live scheduling, custom question banks, time limits, recording and monitoring, cheating detection, multi-language, mobile, ranking and reports, ATS integration, branding and scoring

h3.h3: After-the-fact detection in async, and its false-positive cost

evidence.gloss: Async detection can be slow and expensive because the deadline has passed
evidence.verbatim: Detection can be slow and expensive because the deadline has already passed.

evidence.gloss: Offline forensic analysis: what it inspects, and that it cannot help a live decision
evidence.verbatim: What is left is offline forensic analysis, which examines a recorded file after the event, inspecting original frames, metadata, audio spectrograms, encoding history, source files, and chain of custody in greater detail. That supports incident response and legal review, but it does not protect a person who must decide during a live call whether to approve the request in front of them[27].

evidence.gloss: Text AI-authorship detectors carry severe false-positive economics as the async substitute
evidence.verbatim: Where the async substitute is a text-based AI-authorship detector, the false-positive economics are severe

evidence.gloss: Stanford Patterns study: seven GPT detectors, 91 TOEFL essays, 61.22% average false positive rate on non-native writers, 97.8% flagged by at least one
evidence.verbatim: Stanford research published in the Cell Press journal Patterns, by Weixin Liang and colleagues, ran seven widely used GPT detectors against 91 human-written TOEFL essays and 88 essays by US eighth graders, and found near-perfect accuracy on the American students but an average 61.22% false positive rate on the non-native English writers, with 97.8% of the TOEFL essays flagged as AI-generated by at least one detector[8].

evidence.gloss: Perplexity explains the bias: enriching vocabulary cut the false positive rate from 61.3% to 11.6%
evidence.verbatim: Unanimously misclassified essays had significantly lower perplexity, meaning detectors penalise writers with a narrower range of linguistic expression; when researchers used an LLM to enrich the same essays' vocabulary, the false positive rate fell from 61.3% to 11.6%, confirming the tools were measuring vocabulary range rather than authorship[8].

evidence.gloss: Without a human probe, the compensating controls are automated and after-the-fact
evidence.verbatim: Where a human probe is absent, the compensating controls are automated and after-the-fact.

h3.h3: Choosing the mix: which format at which hiring stage

evidence.gloss: Format choice matters more than vendor choice
evidence.verbatim: The choice between one-way and live is documented as mattering more than the vendor choice, because using the wrong format at the wrong stage costs candidates rather than money[24]:

evidence.gloss: Format table: what each format removes
evidence.verbatim: | What it removes | All scheduling, and the phone screen entirely | Travel and room booking, but not scheduling |

evidence.gloss: Format table: best stage for each format
evidence.verbatim: | Best stage | First screen, when volume is the problem | Later rounds, when judgement is the problem |

evidence.gloss: Format table: candidate reaction to each format
evidence.verbatim: | Candidate reaction | Mixed; some find it impersonal and drop out | Broadly accepted as a normal interview |

evidence.gloss: Format table: team benefit of each format
evidence.verbatim: | Team benefit | Several people assess identical answers | Follow-up questions and genuine conversation |

evidence.gloss: Format table: risk of each format
evidence.verbatim: | Risk | Losing strong candidates who dislike the format | No efficiency gain over a phone screen at volume |

evidence.gloss: One-way interviews remove timezone coordination but feel impersonal with no real-time follow-up
evidence.verbatim: One-way video interviews eliminate timezone coordination for global hiring and scale screening, but some candidates find one-way recording impersonal and follow-up questions are not possible in real time[1].

evidence.gloss: Live video suits sales, client-facing and senior leadership roles but carries scheduling overhead
evidence.verbatim: Live video interviews happen in real time like an in-person interview over video, and sales roles, client-facing positions and senior leadership hires benefit most, since interpersonal skills and quick thinking need to show up in conversation; the tradeoff is scheduling overhead across candidates, interviewers and panel members, which async formats avoid[1].

evidence.gloss: Recommended mix: async for first-round screening, live for final rounds
evidence.verbatim: Most teams benefit from both: async for first-round screening to filter a large pool to a shortlist, then live video for final-round conversations where interpersonal signals matter[1].

evidence.gloss: Spark Hire and VidCruiter support both formats natively
evidence.verbatim: Spark Hire and VidCruiter support both formats natively[1].

evidence.gloss: Format coverage across vendors: Spark Hire and VidCruiter do both modes, Willo is async-first
evidence.verbatim: Format coverage matters for which failure mode a buyer is buying against: Spark Hire and VidCruiter support both one-way and live formats natively, while Willo is async-first[1].

evidence.gloss: One-way async removes timezone and scheduling overhead but feels impersonal and blocks follow-ups
evidence.verbatim: One-way (async) video interviews eliminate timezone coordination for global hiring and remove the overhead of scheduling individual calls; the tradeoff is that some candidates find one-way recording impersonal, and follow-up questions are not possible in real time[1].

evidence.gloss: Live video suits sales, client-facing and senior leadership roles where interpersonal skill must show
evidence.verbatim: Live video interviews happen in real time, like an in-person interview over video, and benefit sales roles, client-facing positions, and senior leadership hires most — any context where interpersonal skills and quick thinking need to show up in conversation.

evidence.gloss: Recommended split: async for first-round screening, live for final rounds
evidence.verbatim: Most teams benefit from both formats: async for first-round screening to filter a large pool down to a shortlist, paired with remote interview questions designed for the format, then live video for final-round conversations where interpersonal signals matter[1].

evidence.gloss: The async/live split decides which integrity features are needed where, since real-time follow-up exists only live
evidence.verbatim: That is precisely the split that decides which integrity features a buyer needs where, because the real-time follow-up that exposes a stand-in is available only in the live mode[1][7].

evidence.gloss: Compares the three proctoring approaches (record and review, AI-assisted live, fully automated) in a table of how each runs, best fit, and trade-off, recommending record-and-review for top-of-funnel, AI-assisted live for expensive roles, and fully automated only for practice tests.
evidence.verbatim:
Three approaches cover almost every hiring use case. They trade off cost, candidate friction, and how fast you get a verdict. Match the approach to the stakes of the role, not the other way around.
ApproachHow it runsBest forTrade-off
Record and reviewAI records the session and scores it; a human reviews flags afterwardHigh-volume screening where a same-day result is fineNo real-time intervention; issues are caught after the fact
AI-assisted liveAI watches every session in real time and pushes alerts to a proctorFinal-stage or credential-bearing assessmentsNeeds staffed reviewers; costs more per candidate
Fully automatedAI flags and scores with no human in the loop by defaultPractice tests and very low-stakes screensFalse positives go unchecked; unsuitable for hiring decisions
For most hiring teams, record and review handles the top of the funnel and AI-assisted live covers the roles where a bad hire is expensive. Fully automated proctoring belongs on practice runs, never on an assessment that gates a decision, because nobody is there to overturn a wrong flag. If you run certifications, the rules tighten again; see how this plays out in certification testing.

h3.h3: The endpoint of the format logic: in-person assessment

evidence.gloss: Gartner recommends in-person assessment and found 62% of candidates more likely to apply when in-person is required
evidence.verbatim: For final stages there is a case for in-person assessment on two grounds: Gartner recommends in-person assessment as part of a multi-layered fraud strategy, and separately found 62% of candidates said they were more likely to apply to a position that required in-person interviews[8].

evidence.gloss: Assessment-testing parallel: the in-person re-sit catches score inflation better than browser and webcam monitoring
evidence.verbatim: The parallel from assessment testing is that browser and webcam monitoring matter less than the in-person re-sit that catches score inflation[5].

evidence.gloss: Endpoint of the format logic: in-person removes the video channel from the attacker's control
evidence.verbatim: This is the endpoint of the format logic: the recorded interview offers no live challenge, the live remote interview offers a challenge but a contested video channel, and the in-person stage removes the channel from the attacker's control entirely.

sections_menu.h2: What identity verification actually covers, and the checks people mistake for it

h3.h3: Background and reference checks verify history, not the person on camera

evidence.gloss: The misconception that a background check already covers this risk
evidence.verbatim: A common misconception is that a background check already covers this risk; it does not[6].

evidence.gloss: What a background check does and does not confirm about the person in the interview
evidence.verbatim: A background check confirms facts about a person's history, such as employment dates, education, or criminal record, but it does not confirm that the person sitting in the interview is the same person those records belong to[6].

evidence.gloss: Background checks run late, sometimes post-offer, and rarely repeat through onboarding
evidence.verbatim: Background checks are also typically run late in the process, sometimes after an offer has already been made, and they rarely repeat throughout onboarding[6].

evidence.gloss: The different question identity verification asks: is this candidate who they say they are, right now
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification asks a different, more fundamental question: is this candidate really who their resume and application say they are, right now, at this stage of the process?[6]
