evidence.gloss: The core misconception: a background check does not cover this risk
evidence.verbatim: The most common misconception the sources address directly is that a background check already covers this risk. It does not[2].

evidence.gloss: Background checks confirm history, not that the interviewee is that person
evidence.verbatim: A background check confirms facts about a person's history, such as employment dates, education, or criminal record, but it does not confirm that the person sitting in the interview is the same person those records belong to[2].

evidence.gloss: A check on a stolen identity comes back clean
evidence.verbatim: A background check run against a stolen or borrowed identity will often come back clean, because it is genuinely checking a real person's history, just not the history of the person actually applying[6].

evidence.gloss: Background checks run late and rarely repeat during onboarding
evidence.verbatim: Background checks are also typically run late in the process, sometimes after an offer has already been made, and they rarely repeat throughout onboarding[2].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification asks a different, present-tense question
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification asks a different, more fundamental question: is this candidate really who their resume and application say they are, right now, at this stage of the process[2].

evidence.gloss: Background checks verify a history, not the identity of the person applying; identity fraud is now named in HireRight benchmark data
evidence.verbatim: Background checks do not close this gap — they verify a person's history, just not the history of the person actually applying, which is why identity fraud has become a distinct, named concern in HireRight's benchmark data rather than something background checks alone are expected to catch[6].

evidence.gloss: Reference checks verify history and stated background, not who is in front of the camera
evidence.verbatim: These verify a candidate's history and stated background, not who is sitting in front of the camera.

evidence.gloss: Background checks test safety to hire, not identity, and confirm fraud if identity is fake
evidence.verbatim: Background checks do not substitute for this: they are designed to assess whether a candidate is safe to hire, not whether the person being evaluated is actually who they claim to be, they happen late in the process, and they depend entirely on candidate-provided data, so if the identity is fraudulent to begin with, a clean check only confirms the fraud holds up[51].

evidence.gloss: Two boundaries limit what a passing record certifies
evidence.verbatim: Two boundaries limit what a passing record actually certifies.

evidence.gloss: Identity verification does not replace work authorization, Form I-9, or E-Verify
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification at intake does not determine a candidate's legal authorization to work or replace an employer's Form I-9 or E-Verify obligations; it provides identity verification and document-authenticity screening to help recruiters identify potential fraud earlier [56].

evidence.gloss: A clean background check confirms safety, not identity, and can confirm the fraud
evidence.verbatim: And a clean background check does not close the identity question at all: it tells you whether a candidate is safe to hire, not whether the person being evaluated is the same person who applied, because those checks happen late and depend entirely on candidate-provided data, so a fraudulent identity produces a clean check that only confirms the fraud holds up [51].

evidence.gloss: An identity check is not a background check
evidence.verbatim: A separate compliance point sits underneath all of this: an identity check is not a background check.

evidence.gloss: Definition split: background check verifies history; ID verification confirms the person is who they claim
evidence.verbatim: A background check verifies a candidate's history, employment, education, and criminal record for the person named on the application, while ID verification confirms that the person actually applying and interviewing is that same named person, a different and earlier question [16].

evidence.gloss: Requirements vary by industry and jurisdiction; voluntary adoption is rising with remote hiring fraud
evidence.verbatim: Requirements vary by industry, role, and jurisdiction; some regulated industries and government contracts mandate specific identity checks, but even where not legally required, more employers are adopting it voluntarily given the rise in remote hiring fraud [16].

h3.h3: The three documented forms of identity check, and where proctoring begins

evidence.gloss: The core claim: 'identity verification' on an invite tells you nothing about scope
evidence.verbatim: The source's own conclusion is the argument the article's integrity column is built on: "'identity verification' on an invitation email tells you almost nothing about scope. A webcam snapshot and a document-plus-liveness check are both called the same thing"[26].

evidence.gloss: Vendor documentation is the most reliable source because depth varies
evidence.verbatim: Vendor documentation is named as "the most reliable source here, because the depth of the check varies more than candidates expect"[26].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification vs proctoring: two different questions
evidence.verbatim: The same source also separates the two capabilities the article scores independently: identity verification asks "are you the person whose name is on the application," proctoring asks "what were you doing during the assessment"[26].

evidence.gloss: The three documented forms of identity check
evidence.verbatim: Identity checks bind a real human to an application record and take one of three documented forms — a webcam photo stored in the candidate report for later human review; a document-and-selfie match where software compares the two; or live re-verification, where a recruiter or interviewer confirms on camera that the person in a later round is the person from the earlier one[26].

evidence.gloss: Identity checks don't examine code, browser or machine; proctoring is a separate toggleable system
evidence.verbatim: "None of these examine your code, your browser, or your machine. That is what HackerRank's proctoring signals and session recording do, and it is a separate system with separate settings. A test can have identity verification on and proctoring off, or the reverse"[26].

evidence.gloss: Configurability warns against scoring a vendor on feature presence alone
evidence.verbatim: That configurability is a direct warning against scoring a vendor by feature presence alone: a documented capability may be switched off in the buyer's configured instance.

evidence.gloss: Identity verification is the most direct countermeasure to fake profiles and interview fraud
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification is described as the most direct countermeasure to both the fake-profile and interview-fraud patterns, because it addresses the question underneath every other check: is this actually the person we think it is [6].

evidence.gloss: Core ID verification techniques: government document verification and biometric facial matching
evidence.verbatim: Most modern ID verification systems combine a few core techniques, including government ID document verification, which checks the authenticity of a passport, driver's licence, or national ID against known security features and formatting rather than accepting a photo of it at face value, and biometric facial matching, which compares a live selfie or video capture against the photo on the document [6].

evidence.gloss: Higher-assurance stack adds deepfake-resistant liveness detection to confirm a real present person
evidence.verbatim: Higher-assurance approaches add deepfake-resistant liveness detection alongside government ID verification and biometric matching, with the objective of confirming each candidate is a real, present individual rather than a synthetic, spoofed, or impersonated identity, using biometric, document, and data-based validation [30].

h3.h3: Why manual document review and a human watching the video fail against AI-driven fraud

evidence.gloss: Traditional checks, document scans, and manual review fail against AI-driven attacks
evidence.verbatim: Traditional background checks, document scans, and manual review processes fail against AI-driven attacks[3].

evidence.gloss: Deepfakes now pass basic onboarding because systems were not designed for this realism
evidence.verbatim: Deepfake tools can now replicate human appearance and speech closely enough to pass basic onboarding interactions — most systems are not failing, they are just not designed for this level of synthetic realism[12].

evidence.gloss: Short video calls, document uploads and lightweight steps miss subtle AI-media inconsistencies
evidence.verbatim: Onboarding flows that rely on short video calls, document uploads, or lightweight verification steps may not capture the subtle inconsistencies AI-generated media introduces[12].

evidence.gloss: Cloned voices, synthetic video and combined media create artificial identity presentations
evidence.verbatim: Cloned voices can replicate tone and cadence in voice checks, synthetic video can simulate facial expressions during interviews, and combined media can create consistent but artificial identity presentations[12].

evidence.gloss: Chip verification carries its own limits and demands careful attention
evidence.verbatim: Chip verification has its own separate limits, listed above, and the general warning applies to it too: careful attention must always be paid during verification processes[13].

evidence.gloss: Human review of the recording is not a substitute for identity verification
evidence.verbatim: Human review of the recording is not a substitute.

evidence.gloss: Only 24% of subjects detected well-made deepfakes; Alan Turing Institute on the impossibility of discerning synthetic media
evidence.verbatim: Studies have shown humans are overwhelmingly inept at distinguishing real faces from deepfakes, with one study finding only 24% of subjects could detect well-made deepfakes, and the Alan Turing Institute states it is now "increasingly challenging, potentially even impossible, to reliably discern between authentic and synthetic media" [13].

evidence.gloss: Human inspection and video calls are not viable; biometric liveness detection is essential
evidence.verbatim: Human inspection and video call interviews are not a viable solution, and science-based biometric liveness detection is described as essential [13].

evidence.gloss: Async integrity rests entirely on a recruiter watching a recording, so the human failure rate lands there
evidence.verbatim: Since the async format's entire integrity model is a recruiter watching a recording, sometimes only after an AI has ranked it, this failure rate lands directly on the one-way surface.

evidence.gloss: Two candidate-side realities complicate reading a recording for fraud signals
evidence.verbatim: Two documented realities complicate reading a recorded submission for fraud signals.

evidence.gloss: 62% of candidates report technical problems during online interviews, most avoidable with a 15-minute test run
evidence.verbatim: First, technical failure is common: according to industry data on online interview statistics, 62% of candidates report technical problems during online interviews, most of them avoidable with a 15-minute test run [22].

evidence.gloss: Ordinary technical glitches produce the same artefacts as a manipulated feed
evidence.verbatim: A buffering freeze mid-sentence, an unrecognised microphone, or a session that stalls produces the same surface artefacts a manipulated feed might.

evidence.gloss: Standard candidate advice rewards rehearsal and staging: practice videos, lighting, virtual backgrounds
evidence.verbatim: Second, the recorded format actively rewards rehearsal and staging: candidates are advised to record practice videos before the real thing, calibrate energy deliberately because visible engagement reads flat on video, light from the front rather than behind, use a clean or neutral virtual background, record in landscape on mobile, and test the platform before the deadline [22].

evidence.gloss: Because staging is the recommended norm, polish is no longer a usable fraud tell
evidence.verbatim: The result is that a heavily prepared, virtual-background, front-lit, retaken submission is the recommended norm, which removes staging and polish as usable fraud tells and leaves the async reviewer with fewer honest signals, not more.

h3.h3: AI interview scoring is a performance signal, not an identity control

evidence.gloss: Spark Hire's AI stack is triage and scoring: transcription, AI Summary, AI Video Review
evidence.verbatim: Spark Hire's documented AI stack is scoring and triage rather than integrity: transcription with captions during playback across 50+ languages, an AI Summary that generates a short summary of key points below each recorded response and inside email notifications so reviewers can triage, and AI Video Review, which evaluates English responses and scores them across four competencies and two personal qualities to produce an overall score shown in the Assessments list and on the candidate profile[21].

evidence.gloss: Spark Hire's named competencies
evidence.verbatim: The named competencies include Communication, Execution and Comprehension[21].

evidence.gloss: Scoring AI is not an identity control, which is the distinction the rating makes visible
evidence.verbatim: None of that is an identity control, which is precisely the distinction the rating exists to make visible.

evidence.gloss: HireVue's AI is a competency engine, and it has withdrawn facial expression and vocal tone signals
evidence.verbatim: The AI analyses recorded responses across thousands of data points, and as of 2026 relies primarily on language-based signals, having discontinued facial expression analysis in January 2021 following criticism from researchers and advocacy groups, and later removed vocal tone scoring as well[23].

evidence.gloss: What remains in HireVue's scoring: word choice, vocabulary, sentence structure, response characteristics
evidence.verbatim: What remains is word choice and vocabulary, and sentence structure and response characteristics[23].

evidence.gloss: Harver: strong ATS integration, but needs a dedicated integrity layer added
evidence.verbatim: Harver integrates with major ATS platforms, but teams that need strong proctoring signals alongside assessment should plan to supplement it with a dedicated integrity layer[8].

evidence.gloss: Submitted video is pre-screened by Spark Hire AI Video Review before a recruiter watches
evidence.verbatim: At many companies the submitted video first passes through Spark Hire's AI Video Review system before a recruiter watches it; the system was validated on 68,236 candidate submissions and achieves over 90% accuracy against human ratings, scoring responses and surfacing highlights for the hiring team [22].

evidence.gloss: Validation stats: 68,236 submissions, over 90% accuracy against human ratings
evidence.verbatim: the system was validated on 68,236 candidate submissions and achieves over 90% accuracy against human ratings, scoring responses and surfacing highlights for the hiring team [22].

evidence.gloss: Spark Hire AI scores six dimensions, including Communication and Execution
evidence.verbatim: Per Spark Hire's official AI Video Review documentation, the AI scores candidates on six dimensions, including Communication (clarity and organised sentences, penalising rambling, trailing off, or heavily fragmented answers) and Execution (whether the question asked was actually answered, catching vague or off-topic responses that sound polished) [22].

evidence.gloss: General AI scoring criteria for recorded answers and the ranking it produces
evidence.verbatim: More broadly, AI scoring of recorded answers assesses clarity, use of concrete examples versus vague language, competency-relevant keywords aligned to the job description, and overall answer organisation, then produces a score or ranking that helps employers decide which recordings are worth a human reviewer's time [23].

evidence.gloss: The scoring dimensions are performance signals, never identity signals
evidence.verbatim: First, these six dimensions and the wider scoring criteria are all performance signals, not identity signals: none of them asks whether the person on camera is the applicant.

evidence.gloss: A well-scoring fraudulent submission can be advanced with human review effectively skipped
evidence.verbatim: Second, the ranking decides which recordings a human ever watches, so a fraudulent submission that scores well can be advanced with the human review step effectively skipped.

evidence.gloss: Scoring is opaque to candidates: no feedback, undisclosed criteria, a top job-seeker complaint
evidence.verbatim: The scoring is also opaque to the candidate: candidates receive no feedback on their AI score and the scoring criteria are not disclosed to applicants, which is one of the most consistent complaints from job seekers [23].

evidence.gloss: Spark Hire confirms no AI score report goes to candidates; data is internal to recruiters
evidence.verbatim: Spark Hire confirms this from the platform side, stating candidates will not receive an AI score report because that data is for internal recruiter use, and offering no candidate-facing feedback on why an applicant was not advanced [22].

evidence.gloss: Who can access the recordings: hiring team, the AI system, and Spark Hire staff for support only
evidence.verbatim: Access to the recordings sits with the hiring team at the company applied to, plus Spark Hire's AI scoring system where the employer has that feature enabled, with Spark Hire staff able to access recordings only for support and account management purposes, per their official candidate FAQ [22].

evidence.gloss: When rating a vendor, name the exact capability rather than the category
evidence.verbatim: When building a per-vendor rating, name the exact capability rather than the category.

evidence.gloss: Jobma's documented proctoring checks and its native technical-candidate assessment plus searchable transcription
evidence.verbatim: Jobma's proctoring is documented as detecting multiple faces and voices, copy-and-paste, and window-switching, and it is the one vendor reviewers at SSR found that adds native technical-candidate assessment (coding tests) on top of recorded and live video, written, multiple-choice and audio questions in a single platform, plus transcription that is searchable, editable and shareable[18].

evidence.gloss: Adjacent modules should be scored for what they verify, not assumed to cover identity
evidence.verbatim: Adjacent modules should be scored for what they verify, not assumed to cover identity.

h3.h3: Collecting and keeping the minimum identity data

evidence.gloss: The scope rule: define what is needed, who accesses it, retention, and whether only a derived output is required
evidence.verbatim: The general rule for sensitive data in HR tooling applies directly to a live identity check: define exactly what is needed, who may access it, how long it is retained, and whether the business needs the underlying data at all or only a derived output [71].

evidence.gloss: Applied to interviews: retaining a face template indefinitely versus retaining only a match result
evidence.verbatim: Applied to biometrics in an interview, that is the difference between retaining a face template indefinitely and retaining only a match result.

evidence.gloss: Collect and retain only the minimum identity data needed
evidence.verbatim: only the minimum identity data needed should be collected and retained[33]

sections_menu.h2: ID verification and face match: proving the person on camera is the candidate

h3.h3: What an identity check actually answers

evidence.gloss: The second layer links the live face to a document
evidence.verbatim: The second layer links the live face to a document.

evidence.gloss: Remote identity verification must answer two separate questions
evidence.verbatim: Remote identity verification must answer two separate questions[37]:

evidence.gloss: Question one: who is this person, checked against authoritative records, documents, and biometrics
evidence.verbatim: - **Who is this person?** The system compares a submitted identity claim against authoritative records, identity documents, and biometric characteristics[37].

evidence.gloss: Question two: is this capture genuine, checking for injected or generated media
evidence.verbatim: - **Is this capture genuine?** The system checks whether the camera, microphone, document image, and transmission reflect a live, untampered interaction rather than injected or generated media[37].

evidence.gloss: Answering only one question leaves exposure: deepfakes pass identity-only, stolen identities pass liveness-only
evidence.verbatim: A failed answer to either creates exposure: a system that confirms only the identity claim can accept a deepfake, and a system that confirms only liveness can approve a real person using a stolen or synthetic identity[37].

evidence.gloss: NIST SP 800-63-4 separates resolution, validation, verification, and presentation attack detection
evidence.verbatim: The 2025 NIST Digital Identity Guidelines, published as NIST Special Publication 800-63-4, separate identity resolution, validation, verification, and presentation attack detection — a model that prevents "passed the selfie check" from becoming shorthand for "this person is legitimate"[37].

evidence.gloss: Deepfake verification is an identity-linkage discipline, not a single detection feature
evidence.verbatim: The framing to carry into a vendor conversation is that deepfake identity verification is an identity-linkage discipline rather than a single detection feature, because a convincing face proves nothing on its own, and remote checks combine several signals because no individual signal answers every fraud question[37].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification matches live photo or video to a government ID
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification matches a live photo or video against a government-issued ID, which is a different question from what a background check answers, and the two work best together[2].

evidence.gloss: The full named component stack for identity verification
evidence.verbatim: The named components are real-time identity document verification (Glider claims coverage across 150+ countries), biometric face matching between a candidate's ID and a live selfie or video, liveness detection and deepfake screening to catch AI-generated or manipulated video, checkpoints at application, interview, and offer or onboarding stages, integration with existing ATS and interview tools including the vendor's own AI proctoring environment so identity and exam integrity are checked together, and audit-ready records documenting when and how each candidate's identity was confirmed[2].

evidence.gloss: Definition of liveness detection
evidence.verbatim: Liveness detection specifically confirms the face being presented is a live person in real time rather than a photo, a recording, or an AI-generated deepfake[6]

evidence.gloss: FBI has pointed to identity verification as a meaningful response
evidence.verbatim: is designed to catch the visual and behavioral signals that distinguish a live person from a deepfake or recorded video, which is why the FBI has pointed to identity verification as a meaningful response[6].

evidence.gloss: HireRight benchmark names identity fraud separately because background checks verify a real person, not the applicant
evidence.verbatim: Identity fraud is now a distinct, named concern in HireRight's benchmark data rather than something background checks alone are expected to catch, because a background check can confirm a real person's history while not confirming the history of the person actually applying[16].

evidence.gloss: For impersonation the control is verification
evidence.verbatim: For impersonation, verification is the control.

evidence.gloss: HireRight benchmark treats identity fraud as distinct because background checks verify a history, not the applicant
evidence.verbatim: Identity fraud has become a distinct, named concern in HireRight's benchmark data rather than something background checks alone are expected to catch, precisely because a background check can verify a person's history, just not the history of the person actually applying[16].

h3.h3: The document check and the face match, step by step

evidence.gloss: Face match works from a government ID plus selfie and returns a score, not a yes/no
evidence.verbatim: In practice this means the candidate submits a government-issued ID and a selfie, and the system returns a facial match score rather than a yes/no verdict.

evidence.gloss: Onfido (Entrust, April 2024) combines ID analysis, biometrics and liveness, strong on global document coverage
evidence.verbatim: Onfido, acquired by Entrust in April 2024, combines government ID analysis, facial biometrics, and liveness checks to confirm candidates match their submitted documentation, and is chosen for global document coverage and depth of analysis rather than hiring-specific workflow tooling[11].

evidence.gloss: Document authenticity is a separate check from face match, with two levels
evidence.verbatim: Matching a face to an ID only helps if the ID itself is genuine, which is a separate check. Two levels exist.

evidence.gloss: Lighter level: analysing ID images for manipulation artifacts and structural inconsistencies
evidence.verbatim: At the lighter end, identity document images can be analysed for manipulation artifacts and structural inconsistencies that may indicate tampering or synthetic generation[12].

evidence.gloss: ID verification requires the candidate to hold a physical government document
evidence.verbatim: Where ID verification is enabled, the candidate must produce a physical government document.

evidence.gloss: TestGorilla's accepted documents: passport, national ID card, driver's licence
evidence.verbatim: TestGorilla accepts a physical passport, national ID card, or driver's licence [16].

evidence.gloss: Market-wide accepted documents are passports, driver licences, national identity cards
evidence.verbatim: Across the wider market, most platforms accept common government issued documents such as passports, driver licences, and national identity cards, with better solutions supporting documents from well over a hundred countries and reading the machine readable zone found on many IDs to cross check the printed data, which matters most for organisations hiring across borders or through distributed contractor pools [17].

evidence.gloss: Better solutions cover 100+ countries and read the machine readable zone for cross-border hiring
evidence.verbatim: with better solutions supporting documents from well over a hundred countries and reading the machine readable zone found on many IDs to cross check the printed data, which matters most for organisations hiring across borders or through distributed contractor pools [17].

evidence.gloss: Candidate side of the check: document scan plus live selfie or video with liveness detection
evidence.verbatim: The candidate side of that check is a document scan plus a live selfie or short video with liveness detection, which checks for natural movement, depth, and behaviour that a static photo, printed mask, or injected video feed cannot reproduce [17].

evidence.gloss: Glider claims document verification coverage across 150+ countries
evidence.verbatim: real-time identity document verification (Glider claims coverage across 150+ countries)

evidence.gloss: Biometric face matching between ID and live selfie or video
evidence.verbatim: biometric face matching between a candidate's ID and a live selfie or video

evidence.gloss: How AI identity tools work: match, tamper-check, manipulation markers, human review
evidence.verbatim: AI-based identity tools compare a live selfie or video against submitted identification, check the document for signs of tampering, and analyze the live footage for markers of digital manipulation such as unnatural blinking, lighting mismatches, or face-swap artifacts, returning results in seconds and flagging anomalies for human review[2].

evidence.gloss: AI fraud-detection beyond the face: behavior models, document reading, IP patterns
evidence.verbatim: Beyond the face itself, AI adds fraud-detection models that flag unusual applicant behavior or mismatched documents, automated document reading, and pattern recognition that spots suspicious behaviors such as multiple logins from different IP addresses[7].

evidence.gloss: Facia: a convincing face match does not prove liveness, so the two are rated separately
evidence.verbatim: Facia's material notes that a convincing face match does not by itself establish that the face presented was live[15], which is why face match and liveness are rated as separate columns rather than merged into a single "identity verification" tick.

h3.h3: How the vendors implement it

evidence.gloss: Interviewer.AI's match-score bands: LOW at 50 or below, MEDIUM 50-80, HIGH above 80
evidence.verbatim: Interviewer.AI's implementation is explicit about the banding it applies: a score of 50 or below is categorised **LOW**, above 50 up to and including 80 is **MEDIUM**, and above 80 is **HIGH**[9].

evidence.gloss: Interviewer.AI switches ID verification on per interview via a flag in the application form
evidence.verbatim: The feature is switched on per interview through an "Is Identity verification required" flag, after which candidates are prompted to provide the ID through the application form and the system processes the details and returns the band[9].

evidence.gloss: Interviewer.AI ID verification is a priced add-on quoted within 24 hours
evidence.verbatim: Buyers should note this is a purchased add-on rather than a default: Interviewer.AI asks organisations to specify the number of candidate assessments they want ID verification enabled for and quotes a price back within 24 hours[9].

evidence.gloss: Persona verification takes seconds and flags higher-risk sessions for review
evidence.verbatim: Verification takes seconds and higher-risk sessions are flagged for additional review[10].

evidence.gloss: Dimension 1 scoreable artifact: ID submitted, compared to live face, result exposed to reviewer
evidence.verbatim: The scoreable artifact is a documented flow: candidate submits a government-issued ID, the system compares it to the live face, and the result is exposed to the reviewer as a score or band.

evidence.gloss: Interviewer.AI's ID verification flow, flag-gated, with LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH face match score bands
evidence.verbatim: Interviewer.AI documents this concretely: an ID verification feature is enabled per organisation via a flag, candidates are prompted during the interview to provide a government-issued ID through the application form, and the system returns a facial match score bucketed as LOW at 50 or below, MEDIUM above 50 and up to 80, and HIGH above 80[14].

evidence.gloss: Interviewer.AI ID verification is not self-serve: email the vendor, priced per assessment, 24-hour reply
evidence.verbatim: The feature is not self-serve; buyers email the vendor with the number of candidate assessments they want ID verification enabled for, and the team responds within 24 hours with pricing[14].

evidence.gloss: Gating and per-assessment sale is itself a rating input
evidence.verbatim: That gating detail is itself a rating input: a capability sold per-assessment on request scores differently from one included in the platform.

evidence.gloss: Where a face-match score exists, the framework interrogates the threshold
evidence.verbatim: Where a face-match score exists, the framework asks what the threshold means.

evidence.gloss: Identity verification features: photo ID checks, face detection, no-face and multiple-face alerts, and how Testlify implements them
evidence.verbatim:
The first job is making sure the right person is taking the test, and that they stay in the seat. Look for photo ID verification, face detection, and alerts when a face is missing or more than one appears. These checks cut impersonation risk before the assessment even starts.
Candidate photo capture adds an identity check before the assessment begins.
Photo ID verification helps confirm that the right person is taking the test.
In Testlify, identity is supported through face detection, photo-based verification, and proctoring flags that give reviewers more context on unusual behavior.

evidence.gloss: Identity assurance features: face detection and periodic webcam snapshots to prevent impersonation and stand-ins
evidence.verbatim:
Face detection. Confirms a real human face is present throughout the test, not an empty chair or a swapped person.
Snapshot proctoring. Captures periodic webcam stills so reviewers can confirm the same candidate stayed for the whole test.

evidence.gloss: Identity verification mechanics: ID document checks with liveness detection, continuous facial comparison, webcam environment monitoring, and gaze tracking
evidence.verbatim:
Identity verification at session start combines document checking against a government-issued ID with liveness detection to prevent static image or video replay attacks. Continuous facial comparison throughout the session catches identity swaps that occur after login.
Webcam monitoring records the candidate’s environment and flags activity associated with forward and rear-facing secondary devices. More advanced implementations use gaze tracking to identify sustained attention shifts away from the primary screen, a pattern associated with reading from a secondary source.
Skills-based assessments that layer identity verification on top of role-specific questions produce a stronger combined signal. A candidate who passes both identity verification and a well-designed skills test has cleared two independent controls, not one.

evidence.gloss: Explains periodic webcam snapshots as identity verification and a visual audit trail that deters impersonation and outside help.
evidence.verbatim:
In the world of online assessments, maintaining the integrity and authenticity of the test-taker’s identity is paramount. This is where the webcam snapshot feature in our talent assessment tool comes into play. By capturing periodic snapshots throughout the test, we create a robust deterrent against various forms of cheating, most notably impersonation.
Impersonation is a serious concern in online assessments, as candidates might try to have someone else take the test on their behalf. With webcam snapshots, we can be certain that the person taking the test is the same individual who registered for it. These snapshots serve as a visual audit trail, confirming the test-taker’s identity and ensuring that the assessment process remains fair and secure.
Moreover, webcam snapshots also act as a deterrent against any unauthorized assistance during the test. Knowing that they are being monitored, candidates are far less likely to seek external help, browse the internet for answers, or use any other means to gain an unfair advantage. This feature not only safeguards the integrity of the assessment but also upholds the credibility of the entire recruitment process.

evidence.gloss: Explains location access and IP tracking to confirm candidates test from approved, secure places and to add a second layer of identity verification.
evidence.verbatim:
One of the significant challenges in online assessments is ensuring that candidates take the test from approved and secure locations. Location access and IP address tracking in our talent assessment tool provide a robust solution to this challenge.
By leveraging these features, recruiters can rest assured that candidates are not attempting tests in unauthorized locations, such as public spaces or internet cafes, where the risk of cheating is higher. This not only maintains the integrity of the assessment but also protects the confidentiality of the test content.
Location access and IP address tracking are also effective in reducing the risk of candidate impersonation. Knowing the precise location and IP address of the test-taker adds an additional layer of identity verification, ensuring that the person taking the test is indeed the registered candidate.
These security features not only bolster the fairness and integrity of online assessments but also provide recruiters with a sense of confidence that their talent selection process is free from cheating and other unethical practices. It’s a win-win situation, benefiting both candidates and recruiters by ensuring that the best talent is identified and hired through a transparent and secure process.

h3.h3: Where in the hiring funnel the check runs

evidence.gloss: A well built verification step takes under a couple of minutes: ID scan, selfie or short video, instant result
evidence.verbatim: Vendor-side, a well built verification step typically completes in under a couple of minutes on a mobile phone or desktop browser: the candidate uploads or scans an ID, takes a quick selfie or short video, and the system returns a result almost immediately [17].

evidence.gloss: Verification speed is framed as funnel protection against drop-off
evidence.verbatim: Speed is framed explicitly as a funnel-protection measure, so that the check does not become a drop off point in an otherwise smooth application funnel [17].

evidence.gloss: Verification may be requested of the candidate more than once
evidence.verbatim: Verification can also be asked of the candidate more than once.

evidence.gloss: Day-one or onboarding re-verification confirms the hire is the person assessed
evidence.verbatim: Many platforms support a day one or onboarding re verification step, confirming that the person who shows up to start the job is the same person who was assessed and interviewed, which closes a gap a single upfront check cannot, especially for remote roles where nobody meets the new hire in person [17].

evidence.gloss: Because formats fail differently the verification stack runs at more than one point
evidence.verbatim: Because the live and recorded modes fail differently, the verification stack is expected to run at more than one point.

evidence.gloss: Verify at multiple stages, not once at account creation, so a later switch gets caught
evidence.verbatim: The recommended pattern is verification at more than one stage rather than a single check at account creation, so a switch later in the process still gets caught

evidence.gloss: Request government-issued ID at pre-screen onboarding, framed as standard process
evidence.verbatim: Practical front-end steps include requesting a government-issued ID as part of pre-screen onboarding, framed as standard process rather than suspicion, with legitimate verification platforms handling it professionally and unobtrusively[10].

evidence.gloss: Run the identity check once, at the first live stage, as a real check not a behavioural guess
evidence.verbatim: The identity check should happen exactly once, at the first live stage, and should be a real identity check rather than a behavioural guess[8].

evidence.gloss: Verification requirement: check at more than one stage, not just account creation
evidence.verbatim: verification at more than one stage rather than a single check at account creation, so a switch later in the process still gets caught

evidence.gloss: Identity verification step: government ID on camera, face match, and voice matching across screening, assessment, and final interview to defeat proxy candidates.
evidence.verbatim:
Verify identity before you evaluate anything else. Ask for a government-issued ID on camera, match the face on the ID to the person answering, and match the voice across screening, assessment, and final interview so a swap between stages stands out. This one step defeats most proxy attempts, because the fraud depends on you never checking.
A proxy interview is the clearest case: someone other than the real candidate takes the call. Voice matching is the quiet workhorse here, since a paid stand-in can look plausible on a still ID photo but rarely matches a voiceprint captured earlier in the process.

h3.h3: What to require from a verification stack

evidence.gloss: Use liveness and deepfake detection instead of static photo comparison
evidence.verbatim: liveness and deepfake detection rather than static photo comparison, given how cheap convincing synthetic video has become

evidence.gloss: Integrate identity, behavior and skill signals in one view (Glider's Candidate 360)
evidence.verbatim: integration with proctoring and assessment data so identity, behavior and skill signals are reviewed together instead of in separate systems, the approach behind Glider's Candidate 360 view

evidence.gloss: Low-friction experience plus audit trails attaching specific evidence to a flagged mismatch
evidence.verbatim: a fast, low-friction candidate experience; and clear audit trails so a flagged mismatch arrives with the specific evidence attached, which matters for internal review and compliance documentation alike[16].

evidence.gloss: Pair identity verification with AI proctoring and a genuine skill assessment
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification should be paired with AI proctoring during the assessment itself and with a genuine skill assessment rather than a self-report[16].

evidence.gloss: Full list of what an identity check requires in practice
evidence.verbatim: What that check requires in practice: verification at more than one stage rather than a single check at account creation, so a switch later in the process still gets caught; liveness and deepfake detection rather than just a static photo comparison, given how much cheaper convincing synthetic video has become; integration with proctoring and assessment data so identity, behavior, and skill signals can be reviewed together rather than in separate systems; a fast, low-friction candidate experience, since a verification step that feels invasive or slow can hurt completion rates for legitimate candidates just as much as it blocks fraudulent ones; and clear audit trails, so a flagged mismatch comes with the specific evidence attached, which matters for internal review and compliance documentation[16].

evidence.gloss: Verification requirement: liveness and deepfake detection, not static photo comparison
evidence.verbatim: liveness and deepfake detection rather than just a static photo comparison, given how much cheaper convincing synthetic video has become

evidence.gloss: Verification requirement: integrate with proctoring and assessment data
evidence.verbatim: integration with proctoring and assessment data so identity, behavior, and skill signals can be reviewed together rather than in separate systems

evidence.gloss: Verification requirement: low-friction experience so completion rates do not drop
evidence.verbatim: a fast, low-friction candidate experience, since a verification step that feels invasive or slow can hurt completion rates for legitimate candidates just as much as it blocks fraudulent ones

evidence.gloss: Verification requirement: audit trails with evidence attached to a flag
evidence.verbatim: and clear audit trails, so a flagged mismatch comes with the specific evidence attached, which matters for internal review and compliance documentation[16].

sections_menu.h2: Face match and ID check accuracy: what the error rates actually are

h3.h3: What a face match check actually does

evidence.gloss: Face match to ID photo produces the most durable and regulated artifact
evidence.verbatim: Face match against an ID photo is the check that generates the most durable and most regulated artifact.

evidence.gloss: Definition of the face-match comparison: similarity score, match threshold, one-to-many vs one-to-one
evidence.verbatim: The comparison itself is a similarity score against an operator-assigned match threshold, a number representing a minimum acceptable similarity score, run either as one-to-many identification against a database or one-to-one verification between two images [37].

evidence.gloss: How a conventional face recognition system computes and evaluates a match score
evidence.verbatim: A conventional face recognition system computes a matching score between two images and thresholds it into a binary match/no-match decision, and performance is assessed by comparing score distributions for same-identity and different-identity pairs[55].

evidence.gloss: NIST is the independent US biometric evaluator and FRVT is the benchmark
evidence.verbatim: NIST is the US agency that independently evaluates biometric technologies, and its FRVT is the benchmark[55].

h3.h3: False positive versus false negative, and which one costs the candidate

evidence.gloss: Definition of false positive versus false negative in face matching
evidence.verbatim: A false positive means the software wrongly treated photos of two different individuals as the same person; a false negative means it failed to match two photos that do show the same person[60].

evidence.gloss: Grother quote on the asymmetric consequences of false negatives versus false positives
evidence.verbatim: Patrick Grother of NIST framed the asymmetry in consequences directly: "In a one-to-one search, a false negative might be merely an inconvenience — you can't get into your phone, but the issue can usually be remediated by a second attempt... But a false positive in a one-to-many search puts an incorrect match on a list of candidates that warrant further scrutiny"[60].

evidence.gloss: What the error asymmetry means in hiring: retake a selfie versus being flagged an impostor
evidence.verbatim: Applied to a hiring context, that is the difference between asking a candidate to retake a selfie and flagging them as an impostor.

evidence.gloss: False positives are the security-relevant error because they can admit impostors
evidence.verbatim: False positives are the security-relevant error here, because they may admit impostors[60].

evidence.gloss: A false non-match is a rejected genuine candidate, unevenly distributed
evidence.verbatim: For an employer, the operational translation is that a false non-match is not a neutral event. It is a rejected genuine candidate, and the error rate is unevenly distributed across demographic groups.

h3.h3: The gap between algorithms is wider than the gap between demographic groups

evidence.gloss: NIST demographic evaluation is the largest evidence body on accuracy variation across people, with release and update dates
evidence.verbatim: The single largest body of evidence on how face-matching accuracy varies across people is NIST's demographic evaluation of face recognition algorithms, released 19 December 2019 and last updated 3 February 2025[60].

evidence.gloss: Central NIST result: algorithm-to-algorithm spread is larger than demographic-group spread
evidence.verbatim: Its central result is that the spread between the best and worst algorithms dwarfs the spread between demographic groups.

evidence.gloss: 17 top verification algorithms had similar false-negative rates for black females and white males
evidence.verbatim: Among the highest-performing verification algorithms, 17 had similar accuracy for black females and white males: false-negative rates of 0.49 percent or less for black females (an error rate of less than 1 in 200) and 0.85 percent or less for white males (less than 1.7 in 200)[37].

evidence.gloss: Worst algorithms in the same test hit false-negative rates as high as 99 percent for all races
evidence.verbatim: Against that, the lowest-performing algorithms in the same test had false-negative rates, for blacks and whites alike, as high as 99 percent[37].

evidence.gloss: NIST's open submission policy means untested lab code sits alongside production systems in the range
evidence.verbatim: Part of that range is an artifact of who submits: NIST accepts an algorithm from anyone, from large companies with production systems to small research groups whose code has never left the lab, and tests them whether or not they are in any commercial product[37].

evidence.gloss: False-positive rates varied by up to a factor of 100 depending on the algorithm
evidence.verbatim: Depending on the individual algorithm, false-positive rates varied by a factor of up to 100 times[60].

evidence.gloss: False-negative rates range from under 1 percent in the best algorithms to 99 percent in the worst
evidence.verbatim: Against false-negative rates under 1 percent for black females and white males among the highest-performing algorithms, the lowest-performing algorithms had false-negative rates for blacks and whites as high as 99 percent[37].

evidence.gloss: Some algorithms hit uniform similarity scores with 99%+ accuracy across all races and sexes
evidence.verbatim: Several algorithms produced uniform similarity scores across demographic groups while maintaining true positive and true negative accuracy above 99 percent for all races and sexes[37].

evidence.gloss: Some algorithms differ across groups while holding true-positive and true-negative accuracy above 99 percent for all races and sexes
evidence.verbatim: Some algorithms perform differently on one group than another while still maintaining true-positive and true-negative accuracy rates above 99 percent for all races and sexes[37].

evidence.gloss: Several algorithms produced uniform similarity scores across race and gender, implying small differentials at a threshold
evidence.verbatim: Several algorithms produced uniform similarity scores across demographic groups, meaning similar match and non-match scores regardless of race and gender, which implies small demographic differentials once an operator applies a threshold[37].

evidence.gloss: Some highly accurate algorithms had undetectable false-positive demographic differentials in one-to-many search
evidence.verbatim: NIST found some highly accurate algorithms had false-positive demographic differentials so small as to be "undetectable" for one-to-many searches[37].

evidence.gloss: The most equitable algorithms are also among the most accurate
evidence.verbatim: Not all algorithms produce high one-to-many false-positive rates across demographics, and those that are the most equitable also rank among the most accurate[60].

evidence.gloss: The four image types NIST measured error rates across
evidence.verbatim: NIST assessed these false positive and false negative rates across four image types: mugshots, application photographs from immigration benefit applicants, visa photographs, and other images [37].

h3.h3: Which candidates the errors actually fall on

evidence.gloss: Stored biometric templates carry measured demographic error
evidence.verbatim: The stored template also carries measured demographic error.

evidence.gloss: NIST FRVT demographic error findings by age, sex, and race
evidence.verbatim: NIST's FRVT reported increased false positive identifications in women, children, and the elderly, alongside higher false negatives in under-represented racial groups, particularly Black, East Asian, and Native American individuals [55].

evidence.gloss: Krishnapriya et al.: false match vs false non-match rates differ by racial cohort
evidence.verbatim: Krishnapriya et al. found African-American cohorts exhibit higher false match rates while Caucasian cohorts face higher false non-match rates, showing the interplay between race and matching thresholds [55].

evidence.gloss: Klare et al.: balancing training data alone did not eliminate accuracy disparities
evidence.verbatim: Klare et al., in the pre-deep-learning era, found that underrepresented groups such as females and Black individuals benefited from increased representation in training data, but that balancing the dataset alone did not fully eliminate disparities in recognition accuracy at test time [55].

evidence.gloss: Majority of tested algorithms performed better on men and lighter skin tones
evidence.verbatim: The uncomfortable half of the finding is that the majority of algorithms NIST tested generally performed better on men and on individuals with lighter skin tones[37].

evidence.gloss: US-developed algorithms showed high one-to-one false positives for Asians, African Americans and native groups, worst for American Indian
evidence.verbatim: Among U.S.-developed algorithms there were similar high rates of false positives in one-to-one matching for Asians, African Americans, and native groups (Native American, American Indian, Alaskan Indian, and Pacific Islanders), with the American Indian demographic showing the highest false-positive rates[60].

evidence.gloss: One-to-many matching showed higher false positives for African American females; test used a 1.6 million mugshot FBI database
evidence.verbatim: For one-to-many matching, the team saw higher false-positive rates for African American females; NIST flags this as particularly consequential because the outcome can include false accusations, and notes the one-to-many test used a single FBI database of 1.6 million domestic mugshots rather than the full photo set[60].

evidence.gloss: Algorithms developed in Asian countries showed no dramatic Asian/Caucasian false-positive gap
evidence.verbatim: A notable exception cuts against a simple story about the technology itself: some algorithms developed in Asian countries showed no such dramatic difference in one-to-one false positives between Asian and Caucasian faces[60].

evidence.gloss: Grother quote naming training-data diversity as the hypothesis behind more equitable outcomes
evidence.verbatim: Grother stopped short of a causal claim but named the obvious hypothesis and research direction, the relationship between an algorithm's performance and its training data: "These results are an encouraging sign that more diverse training data may produce more equitable outcomes, should it be possible for developers to use such data"[60].

evidence.gloss: Differentials that run the other way: black men beat white men on false negatives; some top algorithms favour white women over white men
evidence.verbatim: For most algorithms, black men had lower false-negative rates than white men, and several top algorithms had better false-negative rates for white women than white men[37].

evidence.gloss: Most verification algorithms had higher false-negative rates for women than men
evidence.verbatim: It is also true that most verification algorithms had higher false-negative rates for women than for men[37].

evidence.gloss: Most verification algorithms fail women more often than men on false negatives
evidence.verbatim: Most verification algorithms had higher false-negative rates for women than men[37].

evidence.gloss: FR performance is unequal across race, gender, age and across the whole score space
evidence.verbatim: Face recognition systems frequently exhibit unequal recognition performance across race, gender, and age groups, and the disparities are not confined to one error type: accuracy differences exist across demographic splits and can manifest at various scoring thresholds, meaning they are present throughout the score space rather than tied solely to false match or false non-match errors[55].

evidence.gloss: NIST FRVT found higher false positives for women, children, elderly and higher false negatives for under-represented racial groups
evidence.verbatim: NIST's Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) reported increased false positive identifications in women, children, and the elderly, alongside higher false negatives in under-represented racial groups, particularly Black, East Asian, and Native American individuals[55].

evidence.gloss: Krishnapriya et al: higher false match for African-American, higher false non-match for Caucasian cohorts
evidence.verbatim: Research by Krishnapriya et al. found African-American cohorts exhibit higher false match rates while Caucasian cohorts face higher false non-match rates, showing the interplay between race and matching thresholds[55].

evidence.gloss: VisionLabs: a 4x nationality gap that is still only a 0.63 percent worst-case error rate
evidence.verbatim: Because error rates are so low, small absolute differences look large in relative terms: VisionLabs' Visionlabs-007 had a false-negative rate four times higher for its worst nationality (Somalian) than its best (Salvadoran), yet that worst-case rate was 0.63 percent[37]

evidence.gloss: Camvi: 13x false-positive gap that equals roughly one false match per 10,000 comparisons
evidence.verbatim: a Camvi verification algorithm had a false-positive rate 13 times higher for American Indian females than white men at one threshold, where the algorithm produced barely more than one false match per 10,000 imposter comparisons within that group[37].

evidence.gloss: Hiring is named alongside border crossing, law enforcement and security as a domain where fairness and accuracy are paramount
evidence.verbatim: The stakes are named explicitly for hiring alongside border crossing, law enforcement, and security, where both fairness and accuracy are paramount[55].

h3.h3: The stored face template is a regulated artifact, and employer duties are unsettled

evidence.gloss: US biometric privacy litigation has not settled employer obligations for stored data
evidence.verbatim: US biometric privacy litigation has not resolved what that stored data obliges an employer to do.

evidence.gloss: Unresolved questions on non-identifying data leave conflicting lower-court guidance
evidence.verbatim: Courts have yet to consider fundamental questions relating to the viability of claims where the data at issue is not capable of identifying the individual such that a business cannot feasibly provide the requisite notice or obtain consent, leaving companies relying on conflicting rulings of lower courts that give uncertain guidance on what separates lawful and unlawful uses of biometric technology [54].

evidence.gloss: Daichendt v. CVS: BIPA claim turns on capacity to identify the plaintiff from the data
evidence.verbatim: Some courts have held that the plain language of the statute and the practical realities of biometric-identification technology require the collected data to be at least capable of identifying a person; in *Daichendt v. CVS* the court explained that the most foundational aspect of a BIPA claim is whether the defendant had the capacity to identify the plaintiffs with the data collected, and the claim failed because plaintiffs initially pled no facts suggesting the defendant could identify them or any individual from the data collected [54].

evidence.gloss: The Daichendt litigation continues after amended pleadings on stored contact data
evidence.verbatim: That litigation is ongoing after plaintiffs amended to allege the defendant collected and stored their real-world identifying personal contact data [54].

h3.h3: What to ask a vendor about demographic testing

evidence.gloss: Ask whether the system was trained and tested for unbiased results across demographics
evidence.verbatim: Ask whether the system is tuned for your candidate population: an effective solution will have undergone rigorous testing and extensive training to deliver unbiased results across race, gender, age, and other demographic variables, and a system built without that testing, layered or not, will implement unwanted discrimination and false positives[28].

sections_menu.h2: Liveness, presentation attack detection, and injection detection: what each check actually catches

h3.h3: What liveness detection measures, and active versus passive checks

evidence.gloss: Liveness detection defined as confirming a biometric trait comes from a living human
evidence.verbatim: The foundational layer is liveness detection, the technology used to confirm that a biometric trait comes from a living human being rather than an artefact held up to the camera[7].

evidence.gloss: PAD is the formal name and ISO/IEC 30107 is the governing standard
evidence.verbatim: The formal name for the check is presentation attack detection (PAD), and it is governed by ISO/IEC 30107, the standard that covers techniques for the automated detection of presentation attacks and defines the terms used for PAD testing and reporting[8].

evidence.gloss: Liveness comes in two forms and the distinction affects candidate experience
evidence.verbatim: Liveness comes in two forms, and the distinction matters for candidate experience as much as for security.

evidence.gloss: Active liveness requires user actions like blinking or head turns
evidence.verbatim: **Active liveness** requires the user to perform specific actions, such as blinking or turning their head.

evidence.gloss: Passive liveness needs no user action and runs invisibly
evidence.verbatim: **Passive liveness** requires no action at all and works invisibly in the background[7].

evidence.gloss: Vendors offering both frame it as a security-friction balance
evidence.verbatim: Vendors offering both position it as a balance between security and friction[7].

evidence.gloss: Liveness detection runs at capture and assumes the camera feed is genuine
evidence.verbatim: Liveness detection runs at the point of capture and assumes the camera feed is genuine[21].

evidence.gloss: What liveness detection measures: physiological or behavioral signals like blinking, facial movement, depth
evidence.verbatim: Liveness detection techniques assess physiological or behavioral signals such as blinking, facial movement, or depth information to determine whether the input originates from a live human subject[25].

h3.h3: Presentation attacks versus injection attacks: two attack classes, two defenses

evidence.gloss: Definition of an injection attack: synthetic stream inserted into the software capture layer before liveness or face-match runs
evidence.verbatim: An injection attack defeats biometric verification by inserting a synthetic or pre-recorded video stream directly into the software capture layer, before any liveness or face-match check runs[21][22].

evidence.gloss: No physical scene, lens, or genuine capture event exists in an injection attack
evidence.verbatim: There is no physical scene, no lens, and no genuine capture event; the system receives frames that look like they came from a camera but were placed there by the attacker[21].

evidence.gloss: Definition of a presentation attack: a fake artefact held in front of a real camera
evidence.verbatim: A presentation attack, by contrast, holds a fake artefact in front of a real camera: a printed photo, a screen replay, a pre-recorded video played back to the lens, or a 3D mask[22][23].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines four canonical presentation attack types
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines those four canonical presentation types[22].

evidence.gloss: Operational difference: presentation attacks need physical sensor access, injection does not
evidence.verbatim: The operational difference is that a presentation attack requires physical access to a sensor and an injection attack does not[24].

evidence.gloss: Presentation attacks occur at first interaction, making them easiest to perform and most common
evidence.verbatim: Presentation attacks, by contrast, happen at the very first moment of interaction with the system, when data is being collected, which makes them the easiest-to-perform and therefore the most common attack type[23].

evidence.gloss: The two attack classes need different defenses; detecting one does not imply detecting the other
evidence.verbatim: The two classes require different defenses, and detecting one does not mean a system can detect the other[21].

evidence.gloss: Injection sits upstream of liveness, so liveness, face-match, and decision engine all evaluate the injected stream as genuine
evidence.verbatim: Injection places the deepfake upstream of that check, so the liveness model, the face-match, and the decision engine all evaluate the injected stream as though it were genuine[21].

evidence.gloss: Camera-based tells (glare, screen bezel, missing depth) do not exist because no physical scene was recorded
evidence.verbatim: Camera-based tells simply do not exist: there is no glare, no screen bezel, no missing depth, because no physical scene was ever recorded[21].

evidence.gloss: Attacker rationale: bypassing the capture stage is easier than beating liveness head-on
evidence.verbatim: This is precisely why attackers moved to injection: modern liveness systems can readily spot a screen or mask presented to a lens, so the rational move is to bypass the capture stage where that detection lives rather than try to beat it head-on[21].

evidence.gloss: Face-swapping advances make traditional PAD methods increasingly vulnerable to virtual-camera video injection
evidence.verbatim: Recent advances in face-swapping technologies have significantly improved the realism of deepfakes, making traditional PAD methods increasingly vulnerable and less effective against sophisticated video injection attacks using virtual camera software[25].

evidence.gloss: In an injection attack the real face in front of the camera is irrelevant because the signal is replaced en route
evidence.verbatim: In an injection attack it does not matter if the face in front of the camera is real, because somewhere between input and output the signal has been replaced with pre-rendered deepfake frames or an external live feed[26].

evidence.gloss: Presentation attack vs injection attack defined, needing different detection mechanisms
evidence.verbatim: Certification also does not cross the presentation/injection boundary: a presentation attack holds a spoof (photo, screen, mask) in front of the physical camera, while an injection attack bypasses the camera and feeds a synthetic video stream directly into the capture software, and the two require different detection mechanisms[22].

evidence.gloss: Injection attacks match angle, illumination and framing so the feed seems native
evidence.verbatim: Injection-style attacks match angle, illumination and framing so the system perceives the feed as native, real-time input[13].

h3.h3: Challenge-response prompts and what a passed challenge proves

evidence.gloss: Definition of challenge-response as a check judging live human presence in the moment
evidence.verbatim: Challenge-response is the family of checks that asks the person on camera to do something in the moment, and then judges whether the response could only have come from a live human physically present in front of the camera.

evidence.gloss: Active liveness defined against passive liveness (selfie only, no prompts)
evidence.verbatim: Active liveness detection is the version that asks users to complete those challenge-response actions, in contrast to passive liveness, which asks the user only to take a selfie and follow no prompts or gestures at all[28].

evidence.gloss: The four kinds of action a liveness check can request
evidence.verbatim: A liveness check can request a head turn, a spoken phrase, an eye movement, or the placement of an object in frame[27].

evidence.gloss: Real-time randomized challenges make stream injection harder and more detectable via session timing
evidence.verbatim: Against stream injection, real-time challenge-response makes the attack significantly harder because the synthetic feed must respond to a randomized, unpredictable challenge at the moment it is issued, which is materially more difficult than replaying a pre-recorded deepfake, and the additional session-timing signals make injection attempts more detectable[22].

evidence.gloss: Challenges do work against replay: prerecorded streams fail on unexpected questions or unplanned actions
evidence.verbatim: Where a challenge does still bite is against replay: a prerecorded stream often fails when the recipient asks an unexpected question or requests an unplanned action[27].

evidence.gloss: Challenge failure framed as a wrong-problem failure: responsiveness solved, not video authenticity
evidence.verbatim: An adjacent framing from the field is that challenge failure is often a wrong-problem failure rather than a technology failure: the check was solving for responsiveness, not for video authenticity[28].

h3.h3: Where liveness falls short: Level 3 spoofs, hyper-real masks, and real-time face swaps

evidence.gloss: Level 3 spoofs defeat active liveness with mechanical eyelids or responsive deepfake animation
evidence.verbatim: Against active liveness, where the system requires an action such as blinking or a head turn, Level 3 testers craft spoof prompts that mimic the required response — a mask with mechanically controlled eyelids that blink on command, or a deepfake animation that smiles and replicates head movement — so even dynamic liveness checks lose their protective value because the spoof appears animated and responds convincingly to instructions[13].

evidence.gloss: The Level 3 question shifted from stopping a spoof to surviving an expert-grade targeted spoof
evidence.verbatim: The Level 3 question is no longer "can you stop a spoof" but "can you survive a precision-engineered, expert-grade spoof designed specifically to defeat your system"[13].

evidence.gloss: Liveness works on many presentation attacks but falls short on sophisticated video injection that mimics live behavior
evidence.verbatim: These methods are effective against many presentation attacks but may fall short against sophisticated video injection scenarios where the spoofed content convincingly mimics live behavior[25].

evidence.gloss: Liveness testing proves physical presence but not absence of real-time face swap or synthetic voice
evidence.verbatim: The core limitation is that liveness testing asks whether a live human is physically present rather than a photograph, screen replay, mask, or prerecorded clip, and it does not necessarily detect a real-time face swap or a synthetic voice responding to the prompt[27].

evidence.gloss: iBeta Level 3 spoof prompts: mechanically blinking masks and deepfake animations that smile or move the head
evidence.verbatim: At iBeta Level 3, testers craft "spoof prompts" that mimic the required response when a system asks the user to blink or turn their head: a mask with mechanically controlled eyelids that "blink" on command, or a deepfake animation capable of smiling or replicating head movements.

evidence.gloss: Result of spoof prompts: dynamic liveness checks lose protective value
evidence.verbatim: The stated result is that even dynamic liveness checks lose their protective value, because the spoof appears animated and responds convincingly to system instructions[13].

evidence.gloss: Hyper-realistic mask construction detail and its ability to fool visible-light-only algorithms
evidence.verbatim: Hand-finished hyper-realistic masks recreate the thickness and semi-transparent look of natural skin, with built-up skin tones, pores, capillaries, freckles and micro-textures so the mask never appears flat, individual eyebrow and eyelash hairs inserted for realism, and some models carrying thin wire armatures or pull strings that allow controlled movement of the lips or cheeks to mimic expressions; the result can fool the human eye and some algorithms relying solely on visible-light cameras[13].

evidence.gloss: Full-body reenactment makes a head-turn request less reliable
evidence.verbatim: Full-body reenactment drives a digital representation of a person's face, posture, gestures, or upper body, imitating a speaker's movements while generating new words and expressions, which makes a simple request to turn the head less reliable[27].

h3.h3: The standard and the metrics behind a vendor's detection claim

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-3 metrics: APCER, BPCER for subsystems and IAPMR end-to-end
evidence.verbatim: Testing still follows ISO/IEC 30107-3: subsystems are scored via APCER (attack success rate) and BPCER (user rejection rate), and end-to-end systems are assessed with IAPMR, which reflects whether the full identity pipeline is compromised by a spoof[13].

evidence.gloss: No single test data source is dispositive for face recognition and old testing data dates quickly
evidence.verbatim: Assessing how well face recognition performs requires careful, nuanced analysis across several sources, no single source of test data is dispositive across all use cases, and old testing data loses relevance quickly as the technology improves[18].

sections_menu.h2: Presentation and injection attacks on video interviews, and the detection layers that catch them

h3.h3: Presentation attacks and PAD: the four attack types and where detection sits

evidence.gloss: ENISA's four facial presentation attack types: photo, video replay, 3D mask, deepfake
evidence.verbatim: The attack taxonomy the rating checks a vendor against comes from ENISA's remote verification research, which identifies four types of facial presentation attack: photo, video replay, 3D mask, and deepfake[15].

evidence.gloss: A remote verification system should prevent all four attack types
evidence.verbatim: A remote verification system should be able to prevent all four[15].

evidence.gloss: PAD operates at the capture stage, before face matching or an access decision
evidence.verbatim: PAD operates at the capture stage, before the system moves to face matching or an access decision, so that fake faces are stopped before they reach facial recognition[15]

evidence.gloss: FIDO's biometric requirements: PAD is automatic detection, and it must happen before recognition
evidence.verbatim: FIDO's biometric requirements likewise state that PAD is the automatic detection of a presentation attack, and that detection must happen at the capture stage before a recognition decision[15]

evidence.gloss: 1:1 facial matching without PAD is vulnerable at the input layer
evidence.verbatim: A facial recognition system doing 1:1 matching without PAD is vulnerable at that input layer[15].

evidence.gloss: Presentation attacks need no knowledge of the system's base components, unlike software attacks
evidence.verbatim: Presentation attacks differ from software attacks against the system architecture in that they do not require information about the system's base components[15].

evidence.gloss: Detection techniques a vendor should name: skin texture analysis, 3D scanning, micro-movements
evidence.verbatim: The underlying detection techniques the rating expects a vendor to name include texture analysis of the skin surface at small scale (sebaceous glands, pores, hair follicles, which printed photos and masks cannot reproduce), 3D scanning via structured light, time-of-flight or stereo cameras, and detection of micro-movements that indicate a live face such as pulse-driven skin tone changes, eye blinking and breathing[15].

evidence.gloss: Synthetic video detection centres on compression artifacts, time inconsistency, and texture/depth-passing faces
evidence.verbatim: For synthetic video specifically, detection work centres on three problems: rare compression artifacts, time-inconsistent synthetic video, and faces generated to pass texture and depth tests that catch overlays and prints[15].

h3.h3: Injection attacks and the virtual camera

evidence.gloss: Injection is the live-interview attack class: a plug-in streams a real-time deepfake, as in the $25M Arup case
evidence.verbatim: Injection is the attack class most relevant to a live hiring interview: with a simple plug-in, attackers can create a real-time deepfake and stream it into video conferencing calls, the methodology used in the $25M Arup Zoom-based deepfake incident[13].

evidence.gloss: Generative AI makes deepfakes cheap to reproduce, so one attack scales across employers
evidence.verbatim: Deepfakes are also cheap to repeat, since generative AI makes them quickly reproducible, so one working attack scales across many employers[13].

evidence.gloss: Injection methods span trivial to highly technical; most fraud clusters at the easy end
evidence.verbatim: Injection methods range from trivial to highly technical, and most real-world fraud clusters at the easy end, while the sophisticated methods are what make injection so hard to shut out completely[21].

evidence.gloss: Definition of a virtual camera: software posing as a webcam that feeds attacker-chosen video
evidence.verbatim: A virtual camera is software that presents itself to the operating system as an ordinary webcam while feeding in whatever video the attacker chooses[21].

evidence.gloss: Legitimate virtual camera uses (background replacement on calls) make the technology accessible
evidence.verbatim: Legitimate versions of this technology exist for background replacement on video calls, which is part of what makes it so accessible[21].

evidence.gloss: How the virtual camera attack is executed: point the app at the virtual camera and pipe in a deepfake
evidence.verbatim: The attacker points the verification app at the virtual camera instead of the real one and pipes in a deepfake[21].

evidence.gloss: Virtual cameras are the most common injection method because they need little sophistication
evidence.verbatim: This is the most common injection method by a wide margin, precisely because it requires so little sophistication[21].

evidence.gloss: The OS cannot tell a legitimate OBS virtual camera from a fraud-purpose one
evidence.verbatim: The operating system cannot distinguish a legitimate OBS virtual camera from a fraud-purpose one[22].

evidence.gloss: Two virtual-camera variants: static image/synthetic video injection, and real-time face swap processed inside the virtual camera software
evidence.verbatim: Two variants exist within this category: injection of a static image or synthetic video, and real-time face swap, where data is captured by a real camera and then undergoes additional processing within virtual camera software before it reaches the application[25].

evidence.gloss: Virtual cameras defined, and why they are the most common injection method by a wide margin
evidence.verbatim: Virtual cameras, software that presents itself to the operating system as an ordinary webcam while feeding whatever video the attacker chooses, are the most common injection method by a wide margin, precisely because they require so little sophistication[21].

evidence.gloss: Legitimate virtual-camera uses like video-call background replacement make the technology accessible
evidence.verbatim: Legitimate versions of the technology exist for background replacement on video calls, which is part of what makes it so accessible[21].

evidence.gloss: Most real-world fraud is at the easy end, but sophisticated methods make injection hard to fully shut out
evidence.verbatim: Most real-world fraud clusters at the easy end, but the sophisticated methods are what make injection hard to shut out completely[21].

evidence.gloss: Real-world attackers blend deepfakes with injection techniques including iOS and noise injection
evidence.verbatim: Attackers in the wild combine deepfakes with injection techniques, blending methods, partial injections, mirror-based attacks, injections on iOS devices, and sophisticated noise injections in videos[78].

h3.h3: The other injection vectors: emulators, rooted devices, SDK hooking, API interception, USB substitution
