evidence.gloss: Attack vector: running the verification flow inside an emulator stack or on a rooted device
evidence.verbatim: Instead of a virtual camera on a normal machine, an attacker can run the verification flow inside an emulator stack or on a rooted device[21][26].

evidence.gloss: Attack vector: SDK function hooking and manipulated SDK calls replayed with substituted video
evidence.verbatim: Attackers intercept and replay SDK calls with substituted video[21][26].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 testing explicitly covers function hooking as a method
evidence.verbatim: CEN/TS 18099 testing explicitly covers function hooking as a method[21].

evidence.gloss: Attack vector: transport-layer and API-level interception hijacking media feeds in software
evidence.verbatim: Manipulated network traffic and API-level video injection techniques hijack media feeds on the software level[21][26].

evidence.gloss: Direct injection downstream of the face recognition pipeline without any virtual camera
evidence.verbatim: There is also direct injection downstream of the face recognition pipeline without using a virtual camera at all[25].

evidence.gloss: Attack vector: USB camera substitution tested by independent labs under CEN/TS 18099
evidence.verbatim: Independent labs test against USB cameras as a distinct injection method under CEN/TS 18099[21].

h3.h3: How fast injection attacks are growing, and why

evidence.gloss: Benchmark 2024-2026: injection attacks surged ninefold year over year, the fastest-rising vector tracked
evidence.verbatim: One benchmark spanning early 2024 to early 2026 found injection attacks surging ninefold year over year, the fastest-rising vector it tracked[21].

evidence.gloss: iProov: native virtual camera attacks up 2,665% year over year
evidence.verbatim: iProov recorded native virtual camera attacks up 2,665% year over year[21].

evidence.gloss: Entrust: injection attacks up 40%, deepfakes one in five biometric fraud attempts
evidence.verbatim: Entrust reports injection attacks up 40%, with deepfakes now one in five biometric fraud attempts[21].

evidence.gloss: NISA: injection incidents surged in 2022 at roughly five times presentation attack frequency; deepfake presentation and injection ranked hardest to mitigate
evidence.verbatim: NISA reports that injection-attack incidents surged in 2022, occurring roughly five times more frequently than presentation attacks and in more sophisticated form, and ranks deepfake presentation and injection attacks among the two attack types hardest to mitigate[26].

evidence.gloss: Growth driver: accessible deepfake generation on consumer hardware from a document scan and a few social photos
evidence.verbatim: **Accessible deepfake generation.** Photo-to-video deepfake synthesis now runs on consumer hardware in seconds using publicly available models trained on a handful of reference images; an attacker needs only a document scan and a few social media photos to generate a usable face video[22].

evidence.gloss: Growth driver: virtual camera drivers installed for legitimate uses are trivially repurposed for fraud
evidence.verbatim: **Virtual camera proliferation.** Virtual camera drivers installed for legitimate purposes such as video conferencing, streaming, and content production are trivially repurposed for injection fraud[22].

evidence.gloss: Growth driver: fraud rings run industrialized pipelines combining both attack types with synthetic identity packages
evidence.verbatim: **Industrialized attack pipelines.** Fraud rings have automated both attack types, combining them with synthetic identity packages, fabricated documents paired with generated faces, to pass layered verification flows at scale[22].

evidence.gloss: Benchmark from early 2024 to early 2026 found injection attacks surging ninefold year over year
evidence.verbatim: One benchmark spanning early 2024 to early 2026 found injection attacks surging ninefold year over year, the fastest-rising vector it tracked[21].

evidence.gloss: Injection attacks surged ninefold year over year in a 2024-2026 benchmark, fastest-rising vector
evidence.verbatim: A vendor that cannot speak to any of these three is not measuring the fastest-growing threat: one benchmark spanning early 2024 to early 2026 found injection attacks surging ninefold year over year, the fastest-rising vector it tracked[21].

evidence.gloss: Injection frequency now comparable to presentation attacks, growth likely due to automation
evidence.verbatim: Injection frequency has already become at least comparable to that of presentation attacks, and its high potential for automation and scalability makes continued growth likely[78].

h3.h3: Where the verification pipeline is actually vulnerable: the trusted-camera assumption

evidence.gloss: The capture / transit / comparison three-layer model and what each layer does
evidence.verbatim: The three-layer model is capture, transit, and comparison: capture analyzes content when it is created using controls such as passive liveness and deepfake detection; transit verifies that content was not injected, altered, or replaced before it reaches the verification system; comparison evaluates templates, profiles, behavioral patterns, and known fraud signals[28].

evidence.gloss: A remote verification system has four stages: capture, processing, matching, decision
evidence.verbatim: A remote verification system moves a biometric through four stages: data capture, signal processing, matching against a reference, and a final decision[21].

evidence.gloss: Liveness detection runs at data capture assuming the camera feed is trustworthy
evidence.verbatim: Liveness detection almost always runs at the data capture stage, on the assumption that the camera feed is trustworthy[21].

evidence.gloss: The trusted-camera assumption is the whole vulnerability
evidence.verbatim: That assumption is the whole vulnerability.

evidence.gloss: A fake inserted after the camera but before the software lands upstream of all three checks
evidence.verbatim: An attacker who inserts a deepfake after the physical camera but before the software reads the frame lands the fake upstream of liveness, match, and decision, and all three then trust it[21].

evidence.gloss: The vendor question is about the path, not the image
evidence.verbatim: So the question to a vendor is not "do you check the image?" but "do you check the path?"

evidence.gloss: Pixel-only scoring cannot see a virtual camera or hooked SDK; the camera path carries the strongest signals
evidence.verbatim: A system that scores the pixels but never asks where the frames came from cannot see a virtual camera or a hooked SDK, and the camera path carries the strongest injection signals[21].

evidence.gloss: Session metadata, not the picture, is where the detection signal lives
evidence.verbatim: Metadata about the session, not just the picture inside it, is where the signal lives.

h3.h3: Virtual camera detection: what it does and how it works

evidence.gloss: What VCD does: identifies whether the stream comes from a physical camera or a software-based virtual device
evidence.verbatim: VCD targets the input source itself by identifying whether the video stream originates from a physical camera or a software-based virtual device[25].

evidence.gloss: VCD is the layer specifically relevant to countering virtual-camera video injection
evidence.verbatim: It is the layer specifically relevant to countering video injection attacks that exploit virtual camera tools to feed synthetic or pre-recorded content into the system[25].

evidence.gloss: Liveness detection and VCD are two complementary layers in the face anti-spoofing pipeline
evidence.verbatim: Liveness detection and VCD serve as two complementary layers within the face anti-spoofing pipeline[25].

evidence.gloss: Distinguishing physical from virtual cameras during a session is inherently challenging
evidence.verbatim: Distinguishing a physical from a virtual camera during a user session is inherently challenging[25].

evidence.gloss: Virtual cameras mimic physical devices; differences are subtle and must be inferred from authentication metadata
evidence.verbatim: Virtual cameras are designed to mimic the behavior of physical devices, and any differences are often subtle, context-dependent, and difficult to detect; the distinctions must typically be inferred from metadata collected during authentication[25].

evidence.gloss: Behavior under varying configurations differs markedly and shows consistent patterns despite platform, browser, and OS influence
evidence.verbatim: Although virtual cameras are designed to emulate physical ones, their behavior under varying configurations can differ markedly, and certain consistent patterns emerge despite the influence of software platform, browser, and operating system[25].

evidence.gloss: Heuristic: physical camera reconfiguration incurs hardware delay, virtual camera changes happen faster in software
evidence.verbatim: Reconfiguring a physical camera typically incurs a delay due to its interaction with hardware, whereas a virtual camera processes such changes entirely in software, often more rapidly[25].

evidence.gloss: VCD needs machine learning because no single feature reliably distinguishes virtual from real across cameras, platforms, and browsers
evidence.verbatim: VCD is a challenging task that requires machine learning methods, because the wide variety of real cameras, platforms, browsers, devices, and virtual camera software makes it impractical to manually isolate a single factor that reliably distinguishes a virtual from a real camera; only a complex combination of features achieves reasonably high accuracy[25].

evidence.gloss: Sessions are categorized into three types: bonafide, static-image/synthetic-video virtual camera attack, and real-time face swap
evidence.verbatim: Sessions are categorized into three types: legitimate (bonafide), virtual camera attacks using static images or synthetic videos, and virtual camera attacks involving real-time face swapping[25].

evidence.gloss: Other detectable traces of virtual camera injection: driver signatures, video metadata, sensor noise, timing anomalies
evidence.verbatim: Virtual camera injection leaves abnormal driver signatures, inconsistent video metadata, missing sensor-noise patterns, and session timing anomalies that live camera captures do not produce[22].

evidence.gloss: VCD is underexplored in academic literature with limited coverage of practical detection methods
evidence.verbatim: VCD remains an underexplored area in the literature, with limited coverage of practical detection methods tailored to this challenge[25].

evidence.gloss: VCD is already implemented and widely used in industry despite sparse academic literature
evidence.verbatim: Although VCD methods are already implemented and widely used in industry to counter video injection attacks, the academic literature on them remains sparse[25].

evidence.gloss: Published work mentions VCD in Unissey's remote biometric system without elaborating on the method
evidence.verbatim: Some published work briefly mentions VCD as part of the protection layers in Unissey, a French company's remote biometric system, without elaborating on the method[25].

evidence.gloss: Virtual-camera detection research distinguishes three session types: bonafide, static/synthetic injection, and real-time face swap
evidence.verbatim: Research on virtual-camera detection distinguishes three session types for training and annotation: legitimate (bonafide), virtual camera attacks using static images or synthetic videos, and virtual camera attacks involving real-time face swapping, where data is captured by a real camera and then processed within virtual camera software[25].

evidence.gloss: How the virtual-camera detection method works: query camera capabilities, adjust frame parameters, measure response time
evidence.verbatim: That approach queries the camera's capabilities and limitations, adjusts parameters such as frame rate, frame height, and frame width, and measures response time to those requests, using heuristic-based tests in a web application; video and session metadata serve annotation while the performance metrics train the model[25].

evidence.gloss: A virtual camera detection model was trained on real-world session metadata and validated empirically
evidence.verbatim: Detection research supports this: one study built a machine learning model for virtual camera detection trained on **metadata collected from real-world authentication sessions** in browser-based applications, validated empirically against video injection attacks carried out through virtual camera software[25].

h3.h3: The layered defence stack a vendor should be able to describe

evidence.gloss: iProov's suite documents presentation protection, injection protection, and active threat management above 98%
evidence.verbatim: iProov's Biometric Solutions Suite documents protection against presentation attacks (distinguishing a real person from photos, videos or masks) and, separately, protection against digital injection including deepfakes that bypass device sensors, plus active threat management that detects and responds to emerging threats in real time with continuous updates delivered without disruption to the customer or end user, at stated success rates above 98%[13].

evidence.gloss: Carta et al. (2023) three protection layers: PAD, VCD, and IT security safeguards
evidence.verbatim: Carta et al. (2023) identified three layers of protection against these threats: presentation attack detection (PAD), virtual camera detection (VCD), and IT security safeguards[25].

evidence.gloss: Injection attack detection interrogates media sources to spot emulator stacks presenting a synthetic device and camera
evidence.verbatim: Injection attack detection interrogates media sources to determine if an emulator stack is being used to present a synthetic device with a synthetic camera[26].

evidence.gloss: Defense principle: score the capture path, not just the image
evidence.verbatim: Defense means scoring the capture path, not just the image[21].

evidence.gloss: The defensive stack components: genuine-camera confirmation, virtual camera/emulator/rooted-device detection, SDK and session integrity, payload detection
evidence.verbatim: That means confirming frames come from a genuine camera, detecting virtual cameras, emulators, and rooted devices, verifying SDK and session integrity, and detecting the deepfake payload itself[21].

evidence.gloss: Payload detection closes the gap from both directions, the layered defense-in-depth approach CEN/TS 18099 and NIST push toward
evidence.verbatim: Payload detection closes the gap from both directions, which is the layered, defense-in-depth approach that CEN/TS 18099 and NIST's guidelines now push toward[21].

evidence.gloss: Injection attack detection defined by function: protecting capture and authentication pipeline integrity via media source interrogation and SDK call monitoring
evidence.verbatim: Injection attack detection is focused on protecting the integrity of biometric capture and authentication pipelines from injected or tampered inputs: it interrogates media sources to detect emulator stacks presenting a synthetic device with a synthetic camera, and monitors SDK calls that may be intercepted and replayed with substituted video[26].

evidence.gloss: One vendor collects 200+ fraud signals per session: device integrity, browser/OS environment, session consistency
evidence.verbatim: Alongside the PAD model, one vendor collects over 200 fraud signals per session including device integrity signals, browser and OS environment analysis, and session consistency checks[22].

evidence.gloss: Relevant controls are device attestation, camera-source checks, and transport analysis because attackers alter media before the app receives it
evidence.verbatim: Device attestation, camera-source checks, and transport analysis are the relevant controls, because the attacker does not need to compromise the video-conferencing platform at all; they can alter the media before the application receives it[27].

evidence.gloss: No single challenge is a control on its own
evidence.verbatim: No single challenge is a control on its own.

evidence.gloss: Deepfake detection alone cannot prevent identity fraud; layered controls needed
evidence.verbatim: Deepfake detection cannot alone prevent identity fraud, because identity fraud also includes presentation attacks, template injection, altered transmission channels, stolen identity data, and tactic switching, so organizations need layered controls[28].

evidence.gloss: PAD strategies include combining multiple biometric modalities
evidence.verbatim: PAD strategies also include combining multiple biometric modalities for more robust defense against spoofing[29].

evidence.gloss: Continuous identity verification beats a one-time check, but high-value transactions need more
evidence.verbatim: Continuous identity verification, which repeatedly reassesses whether the person, device, behavior, and session remain consistent after login or initial verification, is stronger than a one-time check, but high-value transactions still require deepfake detection and independent approval controls[27].

evidence.gloss: Injection has two halves (method and payload) so defence needs capture-path integrity plus synthetic-media detection
evidence.verbatim: Because injection has two halves, the delivery method and the payload, no single signal suffices, and effective defence addresses both: capture-path integrity stops the method, synthetic-media detection stops the instrument[21].

evidence.gloss: Defences are stacked: protect the payload in transit and layer synthetic-media detection
evidence.verbatim: Defences are stacked, protecting the payload in transit and layering synthetic-media detection to catch the deepfake itself[21].

sections_menu.h2: How Deepfake Detection Works in an Interview, and Where It Breaks

h3.h3: Liveness, presentation-attack detection and deepfake detection are three different checks

evidence.gloss: Liveness asks if a human is live, deepfake detection asks if media was generated
evidence.verbatim: Where liveness asks "is this a live human," deepfake detection asks "was this media generated or manipulated."

evidence.gloss: Deepfake detection evaluates audio and video for synthetic generation and strengthens rather than replaces checks
evidence.verbatim: It evaluates whether audio and video inputs show signs of synthetic generation, and it is designed to strengthen existing checks rather than replace them[12].

evidence.gloss: Liveness signals in onboarding reduce risk from replays and pre-generated interactions
evidence.verbatim: **Liveness signals** in onboarding workflows can be evaluated for active human presence, reducing risk from replayed recordings or pre-generated synthetic interactions[12].

evidence.gloss: PAD is most critical for unsupervised remote identity validation, and the four imaging technologies it may use
evidence.verbatim: Presentation attack detection is described as most critical where no person can oversee the validation of identity, typically remote identity validation from home on a consumer smartphone[66]; the technologies it may use are standard RGB imaging, multi-spectral imaging (exploiting the different reflective properties of human skin at different wavelengths, compared against values for materials such as skin, latex, or paper), 3D imaging (measuring depth to separate a live face's contours from a 2D spoof), and thermal imaging (using the different infrared signatures of humans and synthetic materials)[66] — each of which generates the kind of biometric data the rules above govern.

evidence.gloss: A deepfake detector's coverage is a defined technical scope, not a universal claim
evidence.verbatim: A detector's coverage is a defined technical scope rather than a universal claim: a model trained primarily on face swaps can miss a cleanly generated voice clone, and a service that analyzes a still image cannot assess whether a speaker's words match movement in a video[63].

evidence.gloss: The four categories of deepfake detection targets: video, audio, audio-video relationships, metadata and file signals
evidence.verbatim: Detection targets span video (face swaps, reenactment, lip-sync manipulation, generated presenters, altered gestures, composited scenes), audio (voice cloning, speech synthesis, spliced statements, converted voices, unnatural acoustic patterns), audio-video relationships (mismatched phonemes and lip movement, inconsistent timing, unnatural blinking, voice characteristics misaligned with the visible speaker), and metadata and file signals (editing history, encoding patterns, inconsistent timestamps, evidence of repeated re-recording or processing)[63].

h3.h3: The signals a scan actually reads: audio, video, cross-signal, behaviour and device

evidence.gloss: Audio analysis detects speech irregularities or synthetic artifacts
evidence.verbatim: **Audio analysis** detects speech irregularities or synthetic artifacts[12].

evidence.gloss: Video analysis identifies facial or frame inconsistencies
evidence.verbatim: **Video analysis** identifies facial or frame inconsistencies[12].

evidence.gloss: Cross-signal checks validate voice-visual alignment
evidence.verbatim: **Cross-signal checks** validate alignment between voice and visuals[12].

evidence.gloss: Behavioral and interaction signals: response timing, flow, engagement as supporting indicators
evidence.verbatim: **Behavioral and interaction signals** evaluate response timing, interaction flow, and engagement behavior; unnatural consistency or irregular response patterns act as supporting indicators of synthetic activity[12].

evidence.gloss: Voice biometric test suites are called essential as synthetic audio gets harder to detect
evidence.verbatim: Voice deserves a named line of its own. Biometric test suites for voice analyze audio patterns to prevent deepfakes and recordings, and these are described as essential as synthetic audio becomes more common and harder to detect[7].

evidence.gloss: What video and audio detection tools watch for
evidence.verbatim: Video and audio tools watch for gaze drift, unnatural pause structure before answers, keystroke patterns, and lip-sync artefacts.

evidence.gloss: Credible scans examine several signals rather than one universal deepfake artifact
evidence.verbatim: That is why credible scans examine several signals rather than searching for one universal deepfake artifact[63].

evidence.gloss: Good detectors sample deliberately across opening, middle, close, transitions and movement; segment analysis stops a short fake hiding
evidence.verbatim: Sampling in a good detector is deliberate rather than random, inspecting the opening, middle, and closing portions of a video along with transitions and moments of facial movement, because a manipulation that looks natural during a still pose can destabilize during a head turn, blink, expression change, or lighting shift; segment-level analysis also prevents a short manipulated section hiding behind a benign overall score[63].

evidence.gloss: Technical fingerprints: virtual cameras, device anomalies, behavior patterns
evidence.verbatim: On the technical side, detectable fingerprints include use of virtual cameras, injected video feeds, or face-swapping tools during live interviews; device and browser anomalies such as emulators, remote desktop tools, or environments designed to conceal identity; and suspicious behavior patterns including automation, scripted interactions, or unusual multitasking that suggests real-time assistance or impersonation.

evidence.gloss: Convincing profiles are easy to fake; technical fingerprints are not
evidence.verbatim: Surface-level profiles can look convincing, but these underlying technical fingerprints are described as extremely difficult to fake consistently[69].

h3.h3: Real-time face swaps leave artifacts the per-frame compute budget cannot hide

evidence.gloss: Live face swap must run the full six-stage pipeline inside the per-frame budget for 24-30 fps
evidence.verbatim: It "isn't a file you analyse later, it runs in the call right now," and the entire pipeline (face detection, landmark extraction, synthesis, and the rest of the six stages) must finish inside the per-frame budget needed to hold 24 to 30 fps[3].

evidence.gloss: Real-time constraint forces smaller quantized models, which leaves jitter, blink and gaze artifacts
evidence.verbatim: That constraint forces the attacker into smaller, distilled, quantized models running at lower resolution, and those compromises are precisely what leave the temporal jitter, blink and gaze artifacts that detectors target[3].

evidence.gloss: Synthesis consumes most of the per-frame budget
evidence.verbatim: Synthesis eats most of the per-frame budget[3].

evidence.gloss: RetinaFace and SCRFD chosen for speed; a false negative makes the swap flicker for that frame
evidence.verbatim: Face detectors such as RetinaFace and SCRFD are chosen for speed and for handling multiple scales and partial occlusions; a false negative at that stage makes the swap drop out and flicker for that frame[3].

evidence.gloss: Live format gives the defender real-time compute pressure as an artifact class
evidence.verbatim: So the live format hands the defender a class of artifact the recorded format does not: real-time compute pressure.

h3.h3: Where detection degrades: compression, unseen generation methods, and human review

evidence.gloss: The conditions that degrade detection are exactly the conditions of a live video call
evidence.verbatim: The conditions that degrade detection are exactly the conditions of a live video call.

evidence.gloss: Low resolution, noise, screen recordings, compression and reposting remove the signals a detector needs
evidence.verbatim: Low resolution, background noise, screen recordings, livestream compression, and repeated reposting all remove or distort the signals a detector needs[63].

evidence.gloss: 2025 Intelligent Systems with Applications study found detectors overfit to known datasets and fail on new generation methods
evidence.verbatim: A 2025 study of deepfake video detection and model generalization published in *Intelligent Systems with Applications* found that detectors overfit to known datasets and lose effectiveness against new generation methods[63].

evidence.gloss: 2025 academic review identifies cross-dataset generalization as a continuing challenge for multi-signal detection systems
evidence.verbatim: A 2025 academic review of deepfake detection and multimedia forensics describes systems combining spatial, temporal, audio, biometric, and metadata methods and identifies cross-dataset generalization as a continuing challenge[63].

evidence.gloss: Manual review is a listed common mistake because human accuracy on strong deepfakes is near a quarter
evidence.verbatim: Leaving manual review as the safety net is listed among the common mistakes IDV teams make, because human accuracy on strong deepfakes sits near a quarter, so a reviewer is not a reliable last line of defence[21].

h3.h3: Risk scoring and rules decide which interviews reach a human

evidence.gloss: Risk scoring prioritises cases for manual review
evidence.verbatim: **Risk scoring** prioritises which cases go to manual review[12].

evidence.gloss: Rule-based systems: base rules plus custom rules applied uniformly
evidence.verbatim: Rule-based systems start teams on base rules such as New Email, Poor Phone Name Match, or Risky IP Country, then allow custom rules: flagging when a candidate's device or location changes between application and interview, detecting reuse of identities across roles, or escalating interviews when high-risk behavior appears, so every candidate is evaluated against the same criteria[69].

sections_menu.h2: Why in-call deepfake detection tricks fail

h3.h3: Humans cannot reliably spot a deepfake on a live call

evidence.gloss: iProov survey: 57% believed they could spot a deepfake
evidence.verbatim: an iProov survey found 57% of respondents believed they could tell the difference between a real video and a deepfake

evidence.gloss: Only 24% of subjects could actually detect well-made deepfakes
evidence.verbatim: one study found only 24% of subjects could detect well-made deepfakes

evidence.gloss: Alan Turing Institute on the impossibility of telling authentic from synthetic media
evidence.verbatim: the Alan Turing Institute states it is now "increasingly challenging, potentially even impossible, to reliably discern between authentic and synthetic media"[13]

evidence.gloss: Human inspection and video calls are not a solution; biometric liveness detection closes the gap
evidence.verbatim: Human inspection and video call interviews are not a viable solution on their own; science-based biometric liveness detection is what closes the gap[13].

evidence.gloss: Humans cannot reliably spot altered video, voice manipulation or synthetic identity, so manual judgment is not enough alone
evidence.verbatim: The reason all of this matters at the human layer is that humans cannot reliably spot AI-altered video, voice manipulation, or synthetic identity signals, so manual judgment is no longer enough on its own[46].

h3.h3: The three-finger hand-wave test and its short shelf life

evidence.gloss: The three-finger hand-wave test went viral in early 2026 and should not be relied on
evidence.verbatim: The hand-wave or occlusion test — asking the person to hold three fingers across their face — went viral in early 2026 and should not be relied on as of the 2026 correction[12].

evidence.gloss: Viral detection tricks become specifications for fake builders
evidence.verbatim: The mechanism of failure is a feedback loop: every time a detection trick goes viral, it becomes a specification for the people building the fakes[12].

evidence.gloss: Colman says models fixed the gesture limitation; Ahmed warns it gives false confidence
evidence.verbatim: Reality Defender CEO Ben Colman has said the gesture was once a reliable tell but that current real-time models have already fixed that limitation, and OpenOrigins CEO Manny Ahmed warned that the trick now gives "false confidence, which is arguably worse than no check at all"[12].

evidence.gloss: Occlusion handling is one of the first problems face-swap developers solve
evidence.verbatim: Occlusion handling is no longer an exotic edge case; it is one of the first problems developers of real-time face-swap tools solve[12].

evidence.gloss: Keep the hand-wave request but treat a pass as zero evidence
evidence.verbatim: A candidate who waves a hand across their face and stays crisp has proved almost nothing — keep the request in the toolkit, because a fraudster running older software may still glitch and a guilty one may still hang up, but treat a pass as zero evidence[12].

evidence.gloss: The three-finger occlusion test went viral in early 2026 and has been largely neutralised
evidence.verbatim: The occlusion or "three finger test" (asking the person to hold three fingers across their face), which went viral in early 2026, has been largely neutralised

evidence.gloss: Reality Defender CEO says real-time models already fixed the occlusion limitation
evidence.verbatim: Reality Defender CEO Ben Colman has said the gesture was once a reliable tell but that current real-time models have already fixed that limitation

evidence.gloss: OpenOrigins CEO says the trick now gives false confidence, worse than no check
evidence.verbatim: OpenOrigins CEO Manny Ahmed warned that the trick now gives "false confidence, which is arguably worse than no check at all"[12]

evidence.gloss: Why detection tricks decay: a viral trick becomes a build specification for fake-makers
evidence.verbatim: The mechanism behind that decay is a feedback loop: every time a detection trick goes viral, it becomes a specification for the people building the fakes, and occlusion handling is now one of the first problems the developers of real-time face-swap tools solve[12].

evidence.gloss: Passing the hand-wave test should be treated as zero evidence; only a fail carries signal
evidence.verbatim: A candidate who waves a hand across their face and stays crisp has proved almost nothing; the request is worth keeping only because a fraudster running older software may still glitch and a guilty one may still hang up, but a pass should be treated as zero evidence[12].

evidence.gloss: A comparison table still rates hand-over-face high, and lip-sync and lighting analysis medium with decreasing efficacy
evidence.verbatim: One detection-method comparison still rates the hand-over-face test as high-effectiveness and easy, while flagging lip-sync monitoring and lighting/shadow analysis as medium effectiveness with decreasing efficacy against advanced deepfakes

evidence.gloss: Real-time deepfakes struggle with sudden movement, occlusion and spontaneity, so in-call requests are grouped as verification
evidence.verbatim: On the identity side, real-time deepfakes still struggle with sudden movement, occlusion, and spontaneity, which is why asking candidates to change their camera angle, hold up an ID, or respond to an unscripted prompt is grouped with in-call verification steps[43].

h3.h3: What replaces the visual trick: layered controls and interviewer-led probing

evidence.gloss: Recruiters shouldn't fight a visual arms race; make attackers defeat several independent controls
evidence.verbatim: Recruiters should not be expected to win a visual arms race against increasingly convincing media manipulation; the system should instead make an attacker defeat several independent controls[9].

evidence.gloss: The case for interviewer-led questioning rests on technical tells expiring, not sophistication
evidence.verbatim: The case for interviewer-led questioning does not rest on it being sophisticated. It rests on the fact that the technical tells keep expiring.

evidence.gloss: Visual instinct alone is not enough; a structured multi-signal process is required
evidence.verbatim: The same source concludes that visual instinct alone will not cut it and that a structured process stacking multiple signals is required[42].

sections_menu.h2: Proctoring and monitoring: what these tools actually watch during an interview

h3.h3: Proctoring is a stack of layers, not a single detector

evidence.gloss: Proctoring is eight components combined, not one detection model
evidence.verbatim: Online proctoring technology brings together several components rather than relying on a single detection model: computer vision, voice detection, face matching, browser controls, device checks, screen recording, event logs, and risk scoring[33].

evidence.gloss: Online proctoring is a stack of many components, not a single model
evidence.verbatim: Online proctoring technology is a stack, not one model: computer vision, voice detection, face matching, browser controls, device checks, screen recording, event logs, and risk scoring[33].

evidence.gloss: Once an assessment starts the platform combines video, audio, desktop, browser and device data to spot events
evidence.verbatim: Once an assessment starts, the platform may combine webcam video, microphone audio, desktop activity, browser events, and device information to identify another person appearing, the candidate leaving frame, unexpected speech, a tab change, a blocked application, or an additional device[33].

evidence.gloss: Monitoring can be automated flag-and-review or live AI alerts directing a human proctor
evidence.verbatim: Monitoring does not always mean continuous human watching: in an automated model, software records and flags events for scoring or later review; in a live model, AI alerts direct a human proctor's attention toward sessions needing intervention[33].

evidence.gloss: Defines AI proctoring as software that watches webcam, screen, keystrokes and audio in real time via computer vision, and notes it scales beyond a human invigilator and logs events for audit.
evidence.verbatim:
AI proctoring is software that monitors a candidate’s webcam, screen, keystrokes, and background audio in real-time, using computer vision and machine learning models to flag behavior that appears to be cheating.
Unlike a human invigilator, the system scales to thousands of test-takers at once and logs every event for later audit.

evidence.gloss: Defines AI proctoring, introduces the six-layer Testlify Assessment Integrity Framework, and cites a 2023 review finding 44.7% of students self-reported online-exam cheating
evidence.verbatim:
An AI proctoring solution is software that monitors a remote assessment as it happens. It confirms the candidate is who they claim to be, watches the test environment for unauthorized help, flags unusual behavior in real time, and stores evidence a reviewer can check later. The aim is simple: make a remotely taken result trustworthy enough to act on.
This sits inside the broader Testlify Assessment Integrity Framework, which protects the trustworthiness of results through six layers: identity assurance, environment control, behavior monitoring, AI-assistance detection, reviewable evidence, and configurable strictness, with the final judgment always kept human-led. Use it as the lens for everything below. A tool that covers only one or two layers will leak.
The need is not theoretical. One 2023 systematic review found 44.7% of students self-reported cheating on online exams. Hiring assessments face the same pressure, often with more on the line.

evidence.gloss: The four baseline jobs of a proctoring tool (verify identity, secure the environment, detect activity live, support fair review) in a table with why each matters for hiring
evidence.verbatim:
Good proctoring does more than point a webcam at someone. It should protect integrity across the whole session: confirm identity, lock down the environment, catch suspicious activity while the test is live, and give your team enough context to judge a flagged session fairly. If a tool cannot do these four basics well, it will struggle the moment real candidates start gaming it.
What it should doWhy it matters for hiring
Verify identityConfirms the person who registered is the person taking the test, not a stand-in.
Secure the environmentLimits tab switching, copy-paste, and outside tools that quietly inflate scores.
Detect activity in real timeFlags a second voice, a new face, or AI-assisted answering as it happens.
Support fair reviewGives recordings, logs, and timestamps so a human makes the final call.

evidence.gloss: TL;DR summary: what proctoring verifies, why it matters in 2026, Testlify's five integrity layers, three modes, and flags as human-reviewed evidence
evidence.verbatim:
- A proctored exam verifies identity and monitors the webcam, screen, and browser so a test score reflects the real candidate’s own work.
- Proctoring matters more in 2026 because more candidates use AI and stand-ins, so unmonitored scores are easier to fake.
- Testlify groups its controls into five integrity layers: identity, environment, behavior, AI-assistance detection, and reviewable evidence.
- Three modes (Standard, Strict, Custom) let you match proctoring strictness to the role instead of over-policing every test.
- Flags are evidence for a human reviewer, not an automatic reject. People make the hiring call.

evidence.gloss: The three-step mechanic of a proctored exam: verify identity, monitor camera/screen/tabs, then human review of flags
evidence.verbatim:
Proctored exams work in three steps: verify, monitor, review. First the candidate confirms their identity, often with a photo or ID check. During the test, the tool records the webcam, screen, and browser activity and watches for rule-breaking. After the test, recruiters review any flags in context and decide what they mean.
- Verify. Confirm the right person is taking the test before the first question loads.
- Monitor. Track the camera, screen, tabs, and copy or paste actions while the test runs.
- Review. Surface flagged moments to a human, who reads them in context, not as a verdict.
Some setups lean on automated software, some on a live person, and many blend the two. For a side-by-side of the trade-offs, see human and AI proctoring and the full breakdown of types of online exam proctoring.

evidence.gloss: Frames the three-stage mechanism: a pre-test check, live monitoring during the test, and a scored review afterward, with the AI running in the background and escalating anomalies to a person.
evidence.verbatim: Most systems run in three stages: a check before the test, live monitoring during it, and a scored review after. The candidate sees a short setup step and then takes the assessment as normal. The AI works in the background and hands anything unusual to a human.

evidence.gloss: Pre-test stage: webcam photo matched to a photo ID plus a room and desk scan, aimed narrowly at ruling out an impersonator or a hidden phone before questions load; dual-camera setups cover screen and room.
evidence.verbatim: The candidate confirms who they are, usually with a webcam photo matched to a photo ID, and does a quick scan of their room and desk. The goal is narrow: rule out an impersonator and a phone taped to the monitor before a single question loads. This is where dual-camera setups help, one angle on the screen and one on the wider room.

evidence.gloss: Defines online proctoring services and their components (ID verification, webcam/mic, screen recording, browser lockdown, behavior signals) and the automated vs live vs hybrid split.
evidence.verbatim:
Online proctoring services are tools that supervise a candidate during a remote test to keep the result trustworthy. They combine identity verification, webcam and microphone monitoring, screen recording, a locked-down browser, and behavior signals such as tab switching or a second face in frame. Some use software alone (automated), some add trained human reviewers (live), and many blend both (hybrid).
The point is not to accuse people. It is to give the person making a decision enough evidence to trust the score, or to know when they cannot. That distinction matters more in hiring than in a classroom, because a bad decision here follows the company for years.

evidence.gloss: Introduces the four categories of 2026 detection technology: identity verification, behavioural analysis, environmental controls, and assessment design
evidence.verbatim: Detection technology in 2026 covers four main categories: identity verification at session start, behavioural analysis during the session, environmental controls on the testing device, and assessment design that limits the value of external assistance. Each category addresses a different threat vector, and effective setups use all four in combination.

evidence.gloss: Interview proctoring / AI monitoring: what it flags and its positioning as a supplementary layer
evidence.verbatim: **Interview proctoring / AI-powered monitoring during assessments** — flags when a candidate looks away from the screen for extended periods, when multiple faces appear in the video frame, when audio suggests multiple people in the room, or when typing patterns are inconsistent with claimed experience levels. Not infallible; positioned as an additional layer of oversight that supplements human interviewer observation[6].

evidence.gloss: Key takeaways: proctoring protects decision quality, the fraud threat is growing, integrity is layered, match strictness to stakes, humans decide, transparency matters
evidence.verbatim:
- Proctoring protects decision quality. A score is only useful if it reflects the real candidate’s own work, so monitoring is what makes an assessment worth acting on. Skip it on a high-stakes role and you are hiring on data you cannot trust.
- The threat is growing, not shrinking. With about 4 in 10 candidates using AI in applications, 6% admitting interview fraud, and 63% of resume liars still landing offers, unmonitored tests get easier to game every year. That is why integrity controls belong on senior and remote assessments by default.
- Integrity is layered, not a single feature. Identity, environment, behavior, AI detection, and reviewable evidence each cover a different gap. Relying on one control (webcam alone, say) leaves the others wide open.
- Match strictness to stakes. Over-proctoring a first screen frustrates honest people and raises drop-off; under-proctoring a final round invites fraud. The right level is role-specific, which is why modes exist.
- Humans decide, tools inform. Every flag is evidence for a reviewer to read in context, not a verdict. Auto-rejecting on a flag is both unfair and legally risky, so keep a person in the loop.
- Transparency is part of integrity. Telling candidates what is monitored and why reduces anxiety, lowers abandonment, and makes your process defensible if a decision is ever questioned.

evidence.gloss: Proctoring platforms add environment signals like multiple faces or voices, and supplement human observation
evidence.verbatim: Proctoring platforms add environment-level signals: flagging when a candidate looks away from the screen for extended periods, when multiple faces appear in the video frame, when audio suggests multiple people in the room, or when typing patterns are inconsistent with claimed experience levels. These systems are not infallible but supplement human interviewer observation[6].

evidence.gloss: Proctoring described as lightweight alerts that help spot possible misconduct
evidence.verbatim: Proctoring is likewise described as surfacing clear, lightweight alerts that help a team spot signals of possible misconduct[48]

h3.h3: The behavioural signals: gaze, typing rhythm, answer velocity, code playback

evidence.gloss: Signal: typing rhythm distinguishes composed work from fed or pasted answers
evidence.verbatim: **Typing rhythm and cadence.** A candidate solving a problem types differently from one reading and copy-pasting. Models trained on genuine test-taking behaviour can detect when keystrokes feel "fed" rather than composed[32].

evidence.gloss: Signal: micro-eye movement analysis identifies where the candidate looks, not just that they look away
evidence.verbatim: **Micro-eye movement analysis.** Not just whether the candidate looks away but where. Consistently downward glances toward a hidden phone, lateral movement with a fixed head indicating off-camera notes, or the teleprompter effect of reading from an overlay above the screen are all detectable with the right eye-tracking model[32].

evidence.gloss: Signal: answer velocity far below the median is a high-confidence flag, especially early
evidence.verbatim: **Answer velocity.** A candidate who answers a complex SQL problem in 40 seconds when the median is 4 minutes either knows the material exceptionally well or has had help. Speed anomalies, especially early in a test when candidates are usually slower, are high-confidence flags[32].

evidence.gloss: Gaze detection boundary: brief glances pass, sustained off-camera reading is detectable, camera contact scores higher
evidence.verbatim: Gaze detection has a hard boundary worth naming. Brief glances at notes are generally not flagged, sustained off-camera eye contact (reading from a script) is detectable, and looking directly at the camera correlates with higher engagement scores.

evidence.gloss: The system cannot know about a second screen; it only sees gaze direction within the frame
evidence.verbatim: The system does not know whether the candidate has a second screen; it only sees where the gaze appears to be directed within the webcam frame[5].

evidence.gloss: arXiv pipeline (Özgen et al.): face detection, tracking and gaze estimation, real but imperfect
evidence.verbatim: The arXiv paper on interview cheating detection pipelines (Özgen et al.) describes the technical approach as face detection, face tracking, and gaze estimation within the video frame; the detection is real but imperfect, because it can tell you are not looking at the screen, not what you are looking at[5].

evidence.gloss: TestInvite 2025: suspicious eye movement is a top-three indicator but needs real eye-tracking software
evidence.verbatim: Research from TestInvite (2025) found that suspicious downward or lateral eye movements are among the top three behavioural indicators AI proctoring flags, but that this analysis requires actual eye-tracking software, not just a video feed[32].

evidence.gloss: Automated proctoring signals: looking away, multiple faces, multiple voices, inconsistent typing patterns
evidence.verbatim: Automated proctoring signals that do carry into live and assessed sessions include flags for a candidate looking away from the screen for extended periods, multiple faces appearing in the video frame, audio suggesting multiple people in the room, and typing patterns inconsistent with claimed experience[6].

evidence.gloss: Proctoring systems are not infallible and supplement rather than replace human observation
evidence.verbatim: These systems are "not infallible" and are framed as an additional layer supplementing human interviewer observation rather than replacing it[6].

evidence.gloss: Automated monitoring flags gaze, multiple faces, multiple voices and typing-pattern mismatch, but is not infallible
evidence.verbatim: Automated monitoring can flag when a candidate looks away from the screen for extended periods, when multiple faces appear in the video frame, when audio suggests multiple people in the room, or when typing patterns are inconsistent with claimed experience levels; these systems are not infallible but add a layer of oversight supplementing human interviewer observation[6].

evidence.gloss: Behavioural biometrics and AI anomaly detection: typing cadence, submission timing versus session baselines, flagging for review rather than auto-disqualification
evidence.verbatim:
Behavioural biometrics analyse typing cadence, mouse movement patterns, and answer submission timing across the full session. A candidate who types steadily for 45 minutes and then submits a complex technical answer in under 90 seconds presents a detectable anomaly.
AI-powered systems compare a candidate’s response pattern against baseline data from previous sessions for the same assessment. Responses that arrive faster than the assessed competency level would support, or that cluster around known AI output patterns, generate a review flag rather than an automatic disqualification.
Psychometric and skill assessments used in combination provide richer baseline data for anomaly detection than either type alone. A candidate who performs consistently across both types is statistically less likely to have used external assistance on either.

evidence.gloss: Coding platforms record every keystroke and pause so reviewers can replay the process
evidence.verbatim: Coding platforms extend this by recording the entire coding process — every keystroke, deletion, pause and revision — so a reviewer can replay how the candidate worked, whether they pasted a solution, and whether the rhythm matches the claimed experience level; long pauses followed by sudden bursts of perfect code warrant investigation[6].

evidence.gloss: Code playback records the whole coding process, exposing pasting and mismatched rhythm
evidence.verbatim: On coding platforms, code playback records not just the final submission but the entire coding process, every keystroke, deletion, pause, and revision, letting reviewers see whether the candidate copied and pasted and whether their coding rhythm matches their claimed experience. Long pauses followed by sudden bursts of perfect code warrant investigation[6].

evidence.gloss: Code playback and keystroke analysis records the whole coding process, not just the submission
evidence.verbatim: **Code playback and keystroke analysis** — advanced coding interview platforms record the entire coding process, every keystroke, deletion, pause, and revision, not just the final submission, so reviewers can see how the candidate approached the problem, whether they copied and pasted solutions, and whether their coding rhythm matches the claimed experience level.

evidence.gloss: Long pauses followed by bursts of perfect code warrant investigation
evidence.verbatim: Significant deviations, such as long pauses followed by sudden bursts of perfect code, warrant investigation[6].

evidence.gloss: Code playback and keystroke analysis reveal process, copy-paste, and suspicious bursts of perfect code
evidence.verbatim: Code playback and keystroke analysis record not just the final code submission but the entire coding process, every keystroke, deletion, pause, and revision, letting reviewers see how the candidate approached the problem, whether they copied and pasted solutions, and whether their coding rhythm matches their claimed experience level; significant deviations such as long pauses followed by sudden bursts of perfect code warrant investigation[6].

h3.h3: Continuous identity checks that run through the whole session

evidence.gloss: Continuous biometric authentication re-checks identity through the session, with keystroke dynamics catching handovers
evidence.verbatim: Some enterprise platforms add continuous biometric authentication that re-checks identity throughout the session rather than only at the start, comparing the live video feed against the initial identity verification and alerting interviewers if a different person appears on camera, with keystroke dynamics used to catch a sudden handover of the keyboard[6].

evidence.gloss: Some enterprise platforms run biometric continuous authentication through the session
evidence.verbatim: Some enterprise hiring platforms run biometric continuous authentication that re-checks the candidate throughout the session rather than only at the start[6].

evidence.gloss: Some enterprise platforms authenticate continuously through the session with facial recognition
evidence.verbatim: Some enterprise platforms incorporate biometric verification that continuously authenticates the candidate throughout the session rather than only at the start, using facial recognition comparison[6].

evidence.gloss: Biometric and continuous authentication: face match against the live feed plus keystroke dynamics
evidence.verbatim: **Biometric and continuous authentication** — some enterprise hiring platforms continuously authenticate the candidate throughout the session rather than only at the start; facial recognition compares the live video feed against the initial identity verification and alerts interviewers if a different person appears on camera, and keystroke dynamics analysis can identify when typing patterns suddenly change, suggesting a different person has taken control of the keyboard[6].

evidence.gloss: Cross-input validation compares document, voice and video identity signals for consistency
evidence.verbatim: **Cross-input validation** extends this idea across the stack: identity signals from documents, voice interactions, and video streams are compared for consistency to identify mismatches that may indicate synthetic manipulation[12].

evidence.gloss: Live interaction checks assess audio-video-behaviour consistency in real-time interviews
evidence.verbatim: Live interaction checks assess consistency across audio, video, and behavioral responses during real-time interviews to identify subtle irregularities[12].

evidence.gloss: HireVue Identity Checks captures session images for recruiter comparison without biometric recognition
evidence.verbatim: HireVue Identity Checks takes a similarly lightweight approach, capturing candidate images during the video session and making them available to recruiters for comparison against submitted documents or photos — linking identity evidence to interview sessions without introducing biometric recognition[11].

evidence.gloss: Reuse patterns across applications are hard to detect without cross-system checking
evidence.verbatim: Without cross-checking signals across systems, reuse patterns — the same identity artefacts appearing across multiple applications or onboarding attempts — can be difficult to detect[12].

evidence.gloss: Live meeting authenticity review works on Zoom, Teams, Meet and Webex without replacing hiring review
evidence.verbatim: **Live meeting authenticity review** — tools that help recruiting teams verify the authenticity of live audio and video during interviews on Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet, and Webex, without replacing the broader hiring review process[7].

h3.h3: Environment and device controls: lockdown, tab tracking, copy-paste, second devices

evidence.gloss: Documented async controls cluster around assessment lockdown, targeting copying and outside help
evidence.verbatim: Where async integrity controls are documented, they cluster around assessment lockdown rather than identity, and they target copying and outside assistance:

evidence.gloss: Control: copy-paste restrictions block copied questions and pasted pre-written answers
evidence.verbatim: **Copy-paste restrictions**, blocking candidates from copying test questions to share with others or pasting pre-written answers from external sources, which keeps responses original and prevents candidates building shareable question banks for future applicants [3].

evidence.gloss: Control: word count limits force brief original responses
evidence.verbatim: **Word count limits**, forcing brief, original responses instead of copied lengthy text from websites or documents, making it harder to paste irrelevant content [3].

evidence.gloss: Control: spellcheck disabling removes writing assistance so real communication skill shows
evidence.verbatim: **Spellcheck disabling**, removing automated spelling and grammar assistance so employers can assess actual communication skills without browser tools or writing software [3].

evidence.gloss: Control: screen or browser locking ends the session if the candidate navigates away
evidence.verbatim: **Screen or browser locking**, automatically ending the assessment session if candidates try to navigate away from the test page, preventing them from searching Google or using a chatbot [3].

evidence.gloss: These controls are layered on top of identity confirmation, filling gaps manual review misses
evidence.verbatim: These are browser control and monitoring measures layered on top of confirming candidates are who they claim to be, filling gaps manual review might miss [3].

evidence.gloss: Lockdown controls limit reach mid-assessment but do not answer the identity question
evidence.verbatim: They constrain what a candidate can reach mid-assessment. They do not answer the identity question.

evidence.gloss: Forward-only reveal hides all question types behind a gate with no scrolling back
evidence.verbatim: OneWayInterview's forward-only reveal hides every question type except section headers, so text, video, multiple-choice, and CV/LinkedIn questions all sit behind the gate, and the candidate has to commit to seeing a question before they can do anything else, with no ability to scroll back to compare or re-read [18].

evidence.gloss: Reveal state survives reload; wiping browser storage resets the gate but drops submitted answers
evidence.verbatim: The reveal state persists across a page reload, so the obvious bypass is closed; a determined candidate could wipe their browser storage to reset the gate, but that drops every answer they have already submitted in that interview [18].

evidence.gloss: Vendor calls the protection a deterrent by cost, not an absolute lockout
evidence.verbatim: The protection is described by its own vendor as a deterrent by cost, losing all progress, rather than an absolute lockout [18].

evidence.gloss: Control load should be role-dependent: full combination for technical roles, not entry-level
evidence.verbatim: The vendor is equally explicit about the load this places on candidates being role-dependent: technical roles where on-the-fly thinking matters earn the full combination, while entry-level positions where you want candidates to feel comfortable usually do not [18].

evidence.gloss: What the anti-cheat mode explicitly does not detect or record
evidence.verbatim: The anti-cheat mode does not detect AI use; it does not detect that the candidate is reading off a second screen, does not detect a teleprompter or notes off-camera, does not lock browser tabs or prevent application switching, does not record the candidate's screen or keystrokes, and does not generate an audit log of blocked retry attempts [18].

evidence.gloss: A second phone with live AI captions still beats the controls; the bar moves from passive to effortful
evidence.verbatim: A candidate with a second phone and AI generating live captions can still cheat; what the controls do is raise the bar from passively easy to actively requires effort and a second device [18].

evidence.gloss: Test environment controls: lockdown browser, full-screen enforcement, tab-switch and copy-paste tracking, mouse-out tracking, and pre-test system compatibility checks
evidence.verbatim:
Identity checks alone are not enough. A candidate can still switch tabs, copy a question into another tool, or slip outside the assessment window. Environment controls close those gaps. Look for lockdown browser settings, full-screen enforcement, tab-switch monitoring, copy-paste tracking, and a quick system check that confirms the camera, microphone, and browser work before the test starts.
Teams can set full-screen and tab proctoring rules based on the stakes of the assessment.
In Testlify, these live in the proctoring settings: full-screen mode, tab proctoring, copy-paste tracking, mouse-out tracking, and system compatibility checks.

evidence.gloss: Environment control features: full-screen mode, tab proctoring, copy/paste tracking, multi-monitor restriction, and timed tests
evidence.verbatim:
Full-screen mode. Forces the test into full screen so the candidate cannot quietly work in another window.
Tab proctoring. Logs every time the candidate leaves the test tab, a common tell for outside lookups.
Copy and paste tracking. Records copy and paste actions so pasted answers from a chatbot or doc stand out.
Restrict multiple monitors. Detects and blocks extra displays that could hide notes or a second person feeding answers.
Timed tests. Caps the time per test, which limits how much a candidate can look things up mid-question.

evidence.gloss: Explains disabling copy-paste and screen switching to stop candidates importing answers or toggling to prohibited resources mid-test.
evidence.verbatim:
In the digital landscape of online assessments, maintaining the integrity of the testing environment is of paramount importance. Our talent assessment platform takes this commitment seriously by disabling the copy-paste function and screen switching during the assessment. These features are essential safeguards against various forms of cheating, creating a level playing field for all candidates.
Disabling the copy-paste function is a critical step in preventing candidates from copying answers or content from external sources. Without this capability, candidates are unable to simply copy and paste information into their test, making it significantly more challenging to cheat by importing answers from unauthorized materials or websites.
Moreover, the prohibition of screen switching is a valuable security measure that ensures candidates remain within the assessment environment throughout the test. It prevents them from toggling between screens to access prohibited resources or seek assistance from external parties, thereby upholding the test’s integrity.
By implementing these measures, recruiters can have confidence that their assessments are fair, secure, and free from dishonest practices. This not only preserves the authenticity of the results but also reinforces the credibility of the entire recruitment process.

evidence.gloss: Environmental controls on the device and network: browser lockdown, screen recording, IP geolocation and VPN detection, ATS-logged evidence trails
evidence.verbatim:
Browser lockdown prevents candidates from switching tabs, opening new windows, or accessing clipboard content during the assessment. Screen recording supplements this by creating an auditable session record that reviewers can check against flagged behavioural events.
IP geolocation and VPN detection add a geographic layer. If a candidate’s registered location differs significantly from the session IP, that discrepancy is a signal worth reviewing.
ATS-integrated assessment platforms that log geographic signals alongside application data give hiring teams a complete evidence trail from application to hire. These controls raise the cost of fraud without claiming to eliminate it entirely.

evidence.gloss: Signal: tab switches, clipboard events, background processes and network requests leave fingerprints
evidence.verbatim: **Browser and process signals.** Tab switches, clipboard events, unusual background processes, and network requests all leave fingerprints that do not show up on a webcam at all[32].

evidence.gloss: Two options for catching phone use: hope someone notices, or cell phone detection plus smart speech detection
evidence.verbatim: Catching a candidate using a phone or another device comes down to two options: hoping the interviewer or a live proctor notices one of them, or using cell phone detection technology that identifies phones, smartwatches, and other secondary devices, plus, for technical interviews, smart speech detection that catches phrases such as "Hey Siri" and "Alexa" that may activate virtual assistants for outside help[34].

evidence.gloss: Desktop recording plus webcam workspace monitoring plus an optional second camera
evidence.verbatim: The candidate's desktop can be recorded, and their workspace recorded and monitored through their webcam, with an optional second camera for a complete view[34].

evidence.gloss: IP logging cross-referenced with claimed location can signal outsourcing
evidence.verbatim: Employers can log IP addresses and cross-reference them with the candidate's claimed location; while remote work allows flexibility, recurring mismatches might signal outsourcing or misrepresentation[14].

h3.h3: The proctoring report: what it scores and where you find it

evidence.gloss: Auto-proctoring integrity report generated at submission from a 7-dimension 0-100 model
evidence.verbatim: Auto-proctoring platforms generate an integrity report automatically at submission, with no video review and no manual queue, built from a 7-dimension model in which each dimension scores independently from 0 to 100: Identity Verification Score (confidence of biometric match and ID verification success), Session Continuity Score (internet disconnections, device changes, session pauses), Tab Activity Score (number, timing, and context of tab switches), Copy-Paste Events (frequency and timing of paste attempts relative to answers), Behavioural Consistency Score (answer timing anomalies, response to complex questions), Device Integrity Score (screen sharing, second monitors, unauthorized applications), and Submission Confidence (an overall assessment combining the above)[77].

evidence.gloss: Identity Verification Score dimension definition
evidence.verbatim: Identity Verification Score (confidence of biometric match and ID verification success)

evidence.gloss: Session Continuity Score dimension definition
evidence.verbatim: Session Continuity Score (internet disconnections, device changes, session pauses)

evidence.gloss: Tab Activity Score dimension definition
evidence.verbatim: Tab Activity Score (number, timing, and context of tab switches)

evidence.gloss: Copy-Paste Events dimension definition
evidence.verbatim: Copy-Paste Events (frequency and timing of paste attempts relative to answers)

evidence.gloss: Behavioural Consistency Score dimension definition
evidence.verbatim: Behavioural Consistency Score (answer timing anomalies, response to complex questions)

evidence.gloss: Device Integrity Score dimension definition
evidence.verbatim: Device Integrity Score (screen sharing, second monitors, unauthorized applications)

evidence.gloss: Submission Confidence as the combined overall dimension
evidence.verbatim: Submission Confidence (an overall assessment combining the above)[77]

evidence.gloss: Dimension weighting varies by exam type or jurisdiction
evidence.verbatim: The platform may weight the dimensions differently by exam type (practice versus high-stakes) or jurisdiction[77].

evidence.gloss: This report class replaces human review rather than triggering it
evidence.verbatim: A buyer evaluating this class of report should note that it replaces human review rather than triggering it, which is the opposite of the live-mode escalation path.

evidence.gloss: Jobma documents mobile-usage detection, screen-minimise timestamps, and a per-candidate proctoring report
evidence.verbatim: Jobma documents mobile-usage detection and timestamps for when a candidate minimises the interview screen, and produces a detailed per-candidate proctoring report that employers use as a record for comparing competency and integrity[17].

evidence.gloss: Where the Jobma proctoring report lives in-product
evidence.verbatim: The report is reached in-product at Applicants > Evaluate > open a candidate profile > Proctoring tab[17].

evidence.gloss: A second vendor documents proctoring mode choice, browser tracking, ID upload, timing, weighting and test libraries
evidence.verbatim: A second vendor in the set documents on-demand and real-time proctoring as a buyer choice, fraud protection measures, browser tracking, ID showcase and upload, per-question or whole-test time limits, per-question score weighting with automatic result calculation, automated scoring and ranking, and progression criteria that trigger automatic candidate notification, plus partner libraries of hundreds of pre-built tests covering typing speed, English proficiency, Excel knowledge and script reading[19].

evidence.gloss: Jobma's proctoring report is a per-candidate record reached through a specific navigation path
evidence.verbatim: Jobma's proctoring report is presented as a per-candidate record for comparing competency and integrity, reached via Applicants > Evaluate > candidate profile > Proctoring tab[17].

evidence.gloss: An End Interview action revokes editing access and finalizes the session timeline for reliable playback
evidence.verbatim: Session hygiene matters for the recorded artifact: an "End Interview" action immediately revokes editing access once the session is complete, preventing post-session edits or overwrites, finalizing the session timeline, and ensuring playback remains fully reliable for review[2 - source 6][47].

evidence.gloss: Overview table mapping Testlify's 19 proctoring controls to integrity layer and the specific risk each reduces
evidence.verbatim:
Testlify ships proctoring as 19 configurable controls, not a single on/off switch. The table below maps each feature to the integrity layer it serves and the risk it reduces. Detailed notes and screenshots follow.
FeatureIntegrity layerWhat it reduces
Face detection and snapshotsIdentityImpersonation, stand-ins
Full-screen and tab proctoringEnvironmentTab-switching to outside help
Copy and paste trackingEnvironmentPasting answers from elsewhere
Restrict multiple monitorsEnvironmentHidden second screens
IP and mouse-out trackingBehaviorLocation spoofing, leaving the window
Session and screen recordingReviewable evidenceDisputes with no audit trail
AI assistance detectionAI assistanceUnauthorized chatbot use

evidence.gloss: Behavior monitoring features: IP proctoring, mouse-out tracking, session and screen recording, and bundled video violation clips
evidence.verbatim:
IP proctoring. Tracks the candidate’s IP so a test taken from an unexpected location gets a second look.
Mouse-out tracking. Flags when the cursor leaves the test window, often paired with tab switches.
Session recording. Records the full session as a reviewable timeline for any later dispute.
Screen recording. Captures on-screen activity so reviewers see exactly what the candidate did, not just that something happened.
Video violation. Bundles webcam and on-screen flags into clear, reviewable clips instead of raw footage.

evidence.gloss: How proctoring and lockdown controls (full-screen enforcement, tab-switch and copy-paste monitoring, ID and webcam checks) produce reviewable evidence, and the six layers of the Testlify Assessment Integrity Framework.
evidence.verbatim:
Proctoring builds the clean room. Anti-cheating and proctoring controls such as full-screen enforcement, tab-switch detection, copy-paste monitoring, ID verification, and webcam checks make it hard to pull in outside help without leaving a trace. The point is not to accuse, it is to produce reviewable evidence.
That is the idea behind the Testlify Assessment Integrity Framework. It protects the trustworthiness of results across six layers: identity assurance, environment control, behavior monitoring, AI-assistance detection, reviewable evidence, and configurable strictness matched to the role. Every signal is context for a person to judge, never an automatic reject. A flag starts a conversation; a human decides.

evidence.gloss: Recordings should be HD with timestamped flags and side-by-side video and screen playback
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers should be able to access these recordings in HD with timestamped flags and side-by-side video and screen playback[34].

evidence.gloss: Post-test stage: flags are bundled into a session risk score and a scrubbable timeline, with severity-sorted alerts letting a reviewer spend two minutes on a clean session and ten on a messy one; that triage is the real productivity gain.
evidence.verbatim: When the test ends, the AI bundles the flags into a session score and a timeline a reviewer can scrub through. Good tools sort alerts by severity, so a reviewer spends two minutes on a clean session and ten on a messy one instead of watching every recording end to end. That triage is the real productivity win, not the flagging itself.

h3.h3: Reading the flags: evidence for a human, not a cheating verdict

evidence.gloss: Integrity criterion: which signals the platform captures, named specifically
evidence.verbatim: **Integrity.** Which signals the platform captures, named specifically

evidence.gloss: Integrity criterion: how flags are presented to a reviewer and with what context
evidence.verbatim: how flags are presented to a reviewer, and with what context

evidence.gloss: Integrity criterion: whether a human reviews every flag before any adverse decision
evidence.verbatim: whether a human reviews every flag before any adverse decision[35]

evidence.gloss: Integrity signals must be read correctly: a page reload or focus change is not proof of anything
evidence.verbatim: The integrity signals themselves need to be read correctly during evaluation. Detected anomalies such as a page reload or a window focus change are not proof of anything: a reload is usually a bad connection and a focus change is usually a notification[35].

evidence.gloss: Signals should direct reviewer attention, never trigger auto-rejection or be shown as a cheating verdict
evidence.verbatim: These signals exist to tell a reviewer where to look more closely; they should never trigger an automatic rejection, and they should never be presented to a hiring manager as a cheating verdict[35].

evidence.gloss: Lists the live signals read during the test (face presence and count, gaze, audio voices, tab switches, copy-paste, full-screen exits, second monitors) and argues each is ambiguous alone, so value comes from patterns rather than single moments.
evidence.verbatim: As the candidate works, the system reads a handful of signals: face presence and count, gaze direction, voices or coaching in the audio, tab switches, copy-paste, full-screen exits, and connections to a second monitor. None of these is a smoking gun on its own. Looking away could be thinking. Two voices could be a delivery at the door. The value is in patterns, not single moments.
