h3.h3: Capture scope and what the candidate notice has to say

evidence.gloss: Capture breadth varies by feature and is employer-configured, changing what the notice must say
evidence.verbatim: The breadth of capture varies by feature and is employer-configured, which affects what the notice must say.

evidence.gloss: HireVue recording spans camera, microphone, screen sharing and preserved code or session activity
evidence.verbatim: HireVue recording is feature-specific and employer-configured: video responses use camera and microphone capture, some tasks explicitly request screen sharing, and technical assessments can preserve code and session activity[29].

evidence.gloss: CodeSignal proctored assessments capture camera, mic, screen, a face photo and a government ID
evidence.verbatim: CodeSignal's proctored assessments prompt candidates to share camera, microphone, and screen for the duration of the assessment, plus a photo of the face and a government-issued photo ID[26].

evidence.gloss: Codility asks for front and back document photos plus a selfie, country and ID type
evidence.verbatim: Codility's identity verification asks for photos of the front and back of the document plus a selfie, along with country and ID type[26].

evidence.gloss: The phrase 'identity verification' tells a candidate nothing about scope
evidence.verbatim: As the source puts it, "identity verification" on an invitation email tells you almost nothing about scope, because a webcam snapshot and a document-plus-liveness check are both called the same thing[26].

evidence.gloss: Candidates are told to grant only required permissions; the employer's mirror duty is precise scope in the notice
evidence.verbatim: Guidance to candidates is to read the consent language and the employer's candidate privacy notice before granting permissions, and to grant only the permissions the stated assessment requires[29] — the mirror-image duty for the employer is to state the scope precisely in the notice, because reviewer behaviour and capture are not the same thing: a reviewer may start with a score or summary and open detailed evidence only when needed, but anything intentionally submitted can be reviewed by the employer[29].

evidence.gloss: Recording with disclosure and consent supports later review during onboarding or performance
evidence.verbatim: Recording interviews with proper disclosure and consent supports later review if inconsistencies emerge during onboarding or performance[6].

sections_menu.h2: What proctoring and a webcam feed cannot catch

h3.h3: The blind spots of a webcam stream

evidence.gloss: Webcam is the layer buyers trust most and the one with the narrowest view
evidence.verbatim: The webcam feed is the layer most buyers assume is doing the work, and it is the layer with the narrowest field of view.

evidence.gloss: Four things a webcam cannot see: system, processes, real desktop, who is typing
evidence.verbatim: A webcam has no visibility into what is running on the candidate's system, what processes are active in the background, whether the screen share is showing the real desktop or a sanitized version, or whether the typing on screen is actually coming from that candidate's fingers[32].

evidence.gloss: What webcam proctoring was actually designed to catch is blatant physical behaviour
evidence.verbatim: What webcam monitoring was originally designed to catch is comparatively narrow: blatant physical behaviour such as a second person walking into frame, the candidate leaving their chair, or obvious and repeated off-screen glancing[32].

evidence.gloss: On general conferencing software almost nothing is actually monitored
evidence.verbatim: For a live interview run on general-purpose conferencing software, the honest answer is that almost nothing is monitored.

evidence.gloss: Zoom, Meet and Teams do not see your screen, apps, tabs, gaze, clipboard or window focus
evidence.verbatim: Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams do not access your screen, other applications, or browser tabs; do not perform eye tracking or gaze analysis; do not log clipboard activity or window focus; and do not know whether you have notes in front of you[5].

evidence.gloss: The interviewer only sees webcam, audio, and what the candidate chooses to share
evidence.verbatim: The only things visible to the interviewer are the webcam feed, the audio, and anything the candidate chooses to share[5].

evidence.gloss: Human behavioural observation is the real monitoring on a plain video call
evidence.verbatim: Human behavioural observation is the actual monitoring at play: whether the candidate seems distracted, looks away repeatedly, or delivers rehearsed-sounding answers[5].

evidence.gloss: A webcam is a passive stream blind to system processes, screen-share authenticity, or who is typing
evidence.verbatim: A webcam feed is a passive video stream that records what is in front of the lens and nothing else. It has no visibility into what is running on the candidate's system, what processes are active in the background, whether a screen share is showing the real desktop or a sanitised version, or whether the typing on screen is actually coming from that candidate's fingers[32].

evidence.gloss: Webcam monitoring was designed for a narrow 2010 testing-centre threat model
evidence.verbatim: What webcam monitoring was originally designed to catch is narrow: a second person walking into frame, the candidate leaving their chair, or obvious and repeated off-screen glancing. That was sufficient in a proctored university testing centre in 2010; in a remote hiring assessment it barely scratches the surface[32].

evidence.gloss: The highest-risk candidates are the ones best equipped to bypass a webcam without a trace
evidence.verbatim: The candidates who pose the highest risk are technically sophisticated, motivated, and willing to invest time before the test starts, and they are exactly the ones most capable of bypassing a webcam feed without leaving a trace: they have read the documentation and know what the software watches and what it ignores[32].

evidence.gloss: Detection works only where the platform sees beyond the video frame
evidence.verbatim: Where detection has teeth, it is because the platform sees more than the video frame.

h3.h3: Desktop overlays that screen share never transmits

evidence.gloss: Desktop-overlay tools appear on the candidate's monitor but are excluded from screen capture
evidence.verbatim: The same blind spot shows up in the desktop-overlay category of assistance tools, which run as overlays that appear on the candidate's monitor but are excluded from screen-capture output[5].

evidence.gloss: Screen share in Zoom or Meet does not transmit the overlay
evidence.verbatim: When the candidate shares their screen in Zoom or Google Meet, the overlay is not transmitted, so the interviewer sees the shared content without it[5].

evidence.gloss: The overlay uses the same mechanism as notification centres and video-call UIs
evidence.verbatim: This is the same mechanism notification centres and video-conference UIs use to appear on a local display while staying invisible to screen recording[5].

evidence.gloss: A live Zoom interviewer cannot see an overlay through screen share
evidence.verbatim: a live Zoom interviewer cannot see the overlay through screen share

evidence.gloss: HireVue async records only the webcam, never the screen
evidence.verbatim: HireVue async does not capture the screen at all, only the webcam

evidence.gloss: HackerRank has no integration with external desktop overlays
evidence.verbatim: HackerRank does not integrate with external desktop overlays

evidence.gloss: Overlays differ from in-browser manipulation, which browser proctoring can detect
evidence.verbatim: the overlay approach is technically distinct from tools that manipulate what appears inside the browser window, which browser-based proctoring can detect[5].

h3.h3: Off-frame help: phones, notes, virtual machines, remote access

evidence.gloss: A phone below the frame: only indirect eye-movement tells, invisible to a basic webcam feed
evidence.verbatim: **A phone below the frame.** No technical setup, just a well-positioned phone. AI proctoring can flag it indirectly through eye movement that consistently dips downward, a subtle tilt of the chin, or the cadence of reading rather than thinking. A basic webcam feed sees nothing suspicious at all[32].

evidence.gloss: Notes on the wall, a second laptop outside frame, and sunglasses hiding eye direction
evidence.verbatim: **Notes and devices just outside the camera's view.** Notes taped to the wall beside or above the monitor, a second laptop positioned to the left or right behind the edge of the frame, and sunglasses worn to hide the direction of eye movement[32].

evidence.gloss: Virtual machines: proctoring watches the primary OS while the test is taken on a hidden VM
evidence.verbatim: **Virtual machines running a parallel OS.** The candidate runs two operating systems on one computer. The webcam and the proctoring session run on the primary OS while the actual test-taking, with full access to AI tools, browsers, and a remote helper, happens on the virtual machine running invisibly in the background. The proctoring software monitors the primary OS; the cheating happens where it cannot see.

evidence.gloss: Remote access via TeamViewer lets a ghost coder drive the test while the candidate sits in frame
evidence.verbatim: Some candidates go further and grant a technically skilled friend remote access via TeamViewer or similar tools, so a "ghost coder" navigates the test while the candidate sits in frame looking engaged[32].

evidence.gloss: Handwritten notes on a physical notepad are undetectable in either format
evidence.verbatim: Handwritten notes on a physical notepad beside the laptop register as nothing in either format and are completely undetectable[4].

h3.h3: Proctoring produces evidence, not a verdict

evidence.gloss: TL;DR bullets: proctoring flags but does not decide, it scales one reviewer across hundreds of sessions, its weak spots (demographic accuracy gaps, false positives, generative AI) are real, and strictness should match the stakes of the assessment.
evidence.verbatim:
- AI-powered proctoring verifies identity, monitors the test session, and flags suspicious behavior for a person to review. It does not decide who cheated and it does not make the hire.
- It scales screening: one reviewer can oversee hundreds of sessions instead of watching each live.
- Its weak spots are real. Facial-recognition accuracy varies by demographic group, false positives happen, and generative AI is a moving target.
- The honest use is as one integrity layer, paired with assessment design and human judgment, not a lie detector.
- Deploy it in proportion to the stakes: light-touch for early screens, stricter for final or credential-bearing assessments.

evidence.gloss: Defines AI proctoring as an automated invigilator that surfaces evidence rather than a judge that reaches a verdict, warns that auto-rejecting on a flag costs good hires and invites fairness complaints, and points to primers on online proctoring and AI vs human proctoring.
evidence.verbatim:
AI-powered proctoring is technology that supervises an online assessment on your behalf. It checks that the right person is present, watches the webcam, microphone, and screen during the test, and scores each session for signals that suggest a rule was broken. A recruiter or hiring manager then reviews anything it flags. Think of it as an automated invigilator that surfaces evidence, not a judge that reaches a verdict.
That distinction matters, so hold it throughout: proctoring produces evidence, people make the decision. The software can tell you a second face appeared on camera or a candidate switched tabs eleven times. It cannot tell you why, and it should never auto-reject anyone. Treating a flag as proof of cheating is the fastest way to lose a good hire and invite a fairness complaint.
If you are new to the category, start with the online proctoring basics and the difference between AI versus human proctoring before you pick a strictness level. The rest of this guide assumes you want proctoring for hiring assessments, not classroom exams.

evidence.gloss: Limitation three: proctoring deters more than it prevents, citing a 2025 Journal of Intelligence study finding no significant score difference between proctored and unproctored remote testing, so treat it as a strong lock plus evidence trail paired with privacy-by-design data handling.
evidence.verbatim: Proctoring changes behavior more than it stops it. A 2025 study in the Journal of Intelligence of remote testing found no significant overall difference in scores between proctored and unproctored conditions, which suggests the main effect is deterrence and a cleaner evidence trail, not a hard wall against cheating. Treat it as a strong lock, not an unbreakable one, and pair it with privacy-by-design: collect the minimum, disclose it, and store it no longer than you need.

evidence.gloss: Key takeaways restating the six core arguments: evidence not verdicts, strictness matched to stakes, bias planned for with demographic testing and human review, generative AI outpacing detection, deterrence and documentation over prevention, and humans staying in charge of the hire.
evidence.verbatim:
- Proctoring produces evidence, not verdicts. The AI flags and scores; a person decides. Keeping that line clear is what protects both your hires and your fairness posture, so never let a tool auto-reject.
- Match strictness to stakes. Light-touch monitoring for early screens, full controls for final or credential-bearing tests. Over-proctoring a practice test just adds friction and drop-off for no integrity gain.
- Bias is a real risk, so plan for it. Facial-recognition accuracy varies by demographic group, which means demographic testing and a human review step are not optional; they are how you avoid wrongly flagging real candidates.
- Generative AI outpaces detection. No monitor catches every chatbot. Assessment design, live explanation, follow-ups, and role-specific tasks carry the defense that detection alone cannot.
- It deters and documents more than it prevents. Research shows scores barely move with proctoring on, so value it as a strong lock plus an audit trail, and pair it with privacy-by-design data handling.
- Keep humans in charge. The best integrity setup makes reviewers faster and decisions more defensible without ever handing the hire to an algorithm.

evidence.gloss: FAQ covering four questions: whether proctoring detects phones or second devices, whether it tracks eye movement and looking away, how accurate and reliable it is (triage-grade, not judgment-grade, per NIST), and whether it detects ChatGPT or other AI assistance.
evidence.verbatim:
Can AI proctoring detect phones or a second device?
It can catch many of the signs. Environment scans, gaze tracking, and second-monitor detection flag a phone in view, eyes repeatedly dropping off-screen, or an external display, and dual-camera setups widen the field of view. It cannot see a device kept fully out of the camera’s frame, which is why identity checks and assessment design still matter.
Can AI proctoring detect eye movement or looking away?
Yes. Gaze and head-pose tracking flag when a candidate repeatedly looks away from the screen or off to a fixed point that could be notes. Treat these as signals, not proof: normal thinking, a wandering glance, or a screen reader can all trigger them, so a human should review the context before it counts.
Is AI-powered proctoring accurate and reliable?
It is reliable enough to triage sessions and surface risk, but not accurate enough to judge a candidate on its own. False positives happen, and facial-recognition accuracy varies across demographic groups per NIST testing. The reliable pattern is AI for flagging plus a person for the decision, never fully automated rejection.
Can AI proctoring detect ChatGPT or other AI assistance?
Partly. It can detect browser AI plugins, copy-paste, second screens, and off-screen reading. It cannot reliably detect a chatbot answer read from a hidden device or memorized in advance. Beating AI-assisted cheating depends as much on assessment design, live explanation and follow-up questions, as on monitoring.
Is AI-powered proctoring legal and GDPR compliant?
It can be, if you handle it right. Get clear consent, tell candidates exactly what is captured and why, collect the minimum data, and store it no longer than needed. Compliance depends on your practices and jurisdiction, so confirm your setup with your legal or data-protection team before you deploy at scale.

evidence.gloss: Honest assessment of what proctoring can and cannot catch on AI and deepfakes, with Gartner's one-in-four-fake-profiles-by-2028 projection and the 6% interview-fraud survey figure.
evidence.verbatim:
Partly, and the honest answer matters. Modern proctoring flags likely AI assistance, such as a paste from a chatbot or a sudden tab switch, and locks down the easy routes to one. Identity fraud is the harder problem: face-swap and deepfake candidates are rising fast, so identity and liveness checks now carry as much weight as screen monitoring.
The threat is no longer hypothetical. Gartner projects that by 2028, one in four candidate profiles will be fake, and in a survey of 3,000 job seekers, 6% admitted to some form of interview fraud, from impersonation to having someone else sit the session. For a remote hiring test that means two jobs at once: confirm the person is who they claim to be, and confirm the answers are theirs. AI-assistance detection handles the second by flagging chatbot-style behavior and, where the rules allow, ending a session when AI-generated responses are detected. The first needs photo ID and face verification at the door, which is exactly where software-only tools that never involve a human reviewer fall short. Pairing automated flags with human review turns a suspected deepfake or an AI-assisted answer into reviewable evidence, rather than a silent pass or an automatic reject.

evidence.gloss: FAQ answering what proctoring services are, how they detect cheating, whether they catch ChatGPT and deepfakes, and how the three pricing models work.
evidence.verbatim:
What are online proctoring services?
Online proctoring services are tools that supervise a candidate during a remote test using identity checks, webcam and screen monitoring, a locked-down browser, and behavior signals such as tab switching. They flag anything that looks like cheating so a human can review the session and trust the result.
How does online proctoring detect cheating?
Proctoring detects cheating by combining signals: photo ID and face verification confirm who is testing, webcam and microphone monitoring catch a second person or voice, screen recording and browser lockdown block copy-paste and outside tabs, and AI-assistance detection flags likely chatbot use. A reviewer then weighs the flags in context.
Can online proctoring detect ChatGPT and deepfakes?
Partly. AI-assistance detection flags patterns that suggest a candidate is pasting from a chatbot, and browser lockdown blocks the easy routes to one. Deepfake and face-swap fraud is harder, so identity verification and liveness checks matter more each year. Treat any flag as evidence for a human to review, not proof.
How much do online proctoring services cost?
Pricing follows three models: per exam or session, per seat as a subscription, or bundled into an assessment platform. Dedicated proctoring vendors usually bill per session, and live human proctoring costs more than automated software. A platform that bundles assessment and proctoring folds it into one subscription, so a hiring team pays once instead of running a separate tool.
How do I choose a proctoring service for hiring?
Weigh four things: what you are protecting, how strict the role needs to be, the candidate experience, and workflow fit. For hiring specifically, a platform that both builds the skills test and proctors it removes a second tool and a second login, so integrity signals sit next to the score your recruiter is reading.

evidence.gloss: Opens the case against single-layer proctoring: the most prevalent 2026 cheating methods operate outside what proctoring can observe
evidence.verbatim:
Most assessment platforms offer proctoring as a single-layer control. Proctoring catches what it can observe: screen activity, physical movement, and environmental anomalies.
The problem is that the most prevalent cheating methods in 2026 operate outside that field of view. A candidate using a secondary device in their lap, or an AI tool on a phone below the camera frame, generates no signal that standard proctoring can detect.

evidence.gloss: Why proctoring alone fails: it misses lap devices, earpieces, and off-frame phones, and a known attack surface invites the next iteration of evasion; CV fraud and assessment fraud travel together
evidence.verbatim:
AI proctoring flags physical and environmental cues: head movement away from the screen, multiple faces in frame, unusual noise, and device activity visible within the monitored environment. It does not observe a candidate using a secondary device in their lap, a noise-cancelling earpiece connected to a helper, or an AI tool running on a phone placed below the camera frame.
The core vulnerability of single-layer detection is that it creates a known attack surface. Once candidates understand what triggers a flag, the next iteration of cheating is designed to avoid those specific signals.
CV fraud and assessment fraud often appear together: a candidate who misrepresents their background on a CV is more likely to attempt to compensate with an assisted assessment. A layered system raises the cost of both forms of fraud by requiring independent verification at multiple stages.

sections_menu.h2: Live interviewing: the probes and tells that catch a proxy without a detection tool

h3.h3: Structured interviewing as the baseline defense

evidence.gloss: Definition of structured interviewing and its status as the top evidence-based method
evidence.verbatim: Structured interviewing is the practice of asking every candidate for the same role the same predefined questions and evaluating their responses against the same rating rubric, described as the single most important evidence-based method for improving hiring accuracy and reducing bias[34].

evidence.gloss: Structured interviewing increases predictive validity by up to 65%
evidence.verbatim: Research published in *Personnel Psychology* shows structured interviewing increases the predictive validity of hires by up to 65% compared with unstructured interviews[34], a figure VidCruiter also states as its product claim[35].

evidence.gloss: VidCruiter builds structure into every interview rather than as an add-on
evidence.verbatim: VidCruiter builds structured interviewing into every live and pre-recorded interview rather than offering it as an add-on, via standardized question sets tailored to each role and competency framework, in-window rating rubrics and scorecards, real-time question guides, multi-evaluator scoring, and auditable evaluation records[34].

evidence.gloss: Structure may suppress the payoff from cheating, but the evidence is from async
evidence.verbatim: There is a documented reason to believe structure suppresses the payoff from cheating, though the evidence comes from the async format.

evidence.gloss: HireVue 2024 whitepaper similarity-flag rates and flagged candidates' poor performance
evidence.verbatim: HireVue's 2024 whitepaper covers approximately 11,000 responses and reports that 0.65% of responses globally triggered a similarity flag above the detection threshold, under 2% in China (the highest rate among surveyed markets), and 0% in Japan showing shared-script patterns; flagged candidates showed "consistently poor performance" on underlying competency scores, meaning the cheating did not help them pass the bar[36].

evidence.gloss: Cheaters fail because the rewarded answer type is hard to fake, not because they get caught
evidence.verbatim: The stated takeaway is that candidates who cheat mostly do not advance, not primarily because they get caught, but because the kind of answers the system rewards — specific, behaviourally-evidenced, contextually relevant — are hard to fake[36].

evidence.gloss: Suspected cheaters were usually already weak; edge cases rarely escalate
evidence.verbatim: HireVue's own research also notes that in many cases where cheating was suspected, the candidate's underlying performance was already weak, so the flag was a secondary signal rather than the deciding factor; this also means edge cases such as a roommate talking in the background or a brief tab switch rarely escalate into real problems unless the employer is specifically looking for reasons to filter candidates[36].

evidence.gloss: Amazon's structural defense: Bar Raiser and multi-loop across five to six interviewers
evidence.verbatim: Amazon's secondary defense there is structural rather than technical — the Bar Raiser round and multi-loop format, which make it harder to sustain a manufactured performance across five to six interviewers[5].

evidence.gloss: Structured interviews expose inconsistencies, reduce bias, and make the process defensible
evidence.verbatim: Structured interviews, where every candidate is asked the same core questions, make inconsistencies much easier to detect, and they simultaneously reduce bias and make the process more defensible[10].

evidence.gloss: Design principle of structured interviews: same core questions, follow-ups, test for ownership
evidence.verbatim: The design principle is that structured interviews make it harder for a candidate to pass through a vague conversation alone: use the same core questions for the same role, ask follow-ups, and test for ownership, decision-making, and practical skill[7].

evidence.gloss: Role-specific application: ask technical candidates the why, ask finance/security/ops a scenario
evidence.verbatim: For technical roles this means asking the candidate to explain the "why" behind a decision; for finance, security, or operations roles, asking how they would handle a role-specific scenario[7].

evidence.gloss: Second benefit of structured interviewing: inconsistencies surface, bias drops, process is defensible
evidence.verbatim: Structured interviewing has a second benefit beyond fraud: when every candidate is asked the same core questions, inconsistencies are much easier to detect, and it reduces bias and makes the process more defensible[10].

evidence.gloss: Structured interviews expose inconsistencies and make the process defensible
evidence.verbatim: Structured interviews, where every candidate is asked the same core questions, make inconsistencies much easier to detect and make the process more defensible[10].

evidence.gloss: Structured interviews with the same core questions, follow-ups, and ownership tests are harder to fake through
evidence.verbatim: Structured interviews make it harder for a candidate to pass through a vague conversation alone: use the same core questions for the same role, ask follow-ups, and test for ownership, decision-making, and practical skill; for technical roles, ask the candidate to explain the "why" behind a decision, and for finance, security, or operations roles, ask how they would handle a role-specific scenario[7].

evidence.gloss: Panel interviews with multiple interviewers asking follow-ups reveal scripted answers
evidence.verbatim: Panel interviews, where multiple interviewers ask follow-ups, are especially effective at revealing whether answers are genuine or overly scripted[14].

evidence.gloss: Redesigning the process so a scored skills assessment carries the evaluation, with application-specific questions, structured panel scoring, and reference/background checks.
evidence.verbatim:
The strongest move is to stop relying on the live interview to do all the evaluating. Score a skills assessment or a role-specific test before the call, in a controlled environment, then use the interview to confirm the person and probe how they think. When you already have scored evidence, a polished-but-hollow interview answer stands out immediately.
Write questions only the real candidate can answer well. Ask about the specific projects on their application, the decisions they made, and what broke. Pair that with a structured panel interview so more than one person hears the answers and scores against the same rubric. Fabricated skills and references collapse faster when you also run reference and background verification.

evidence.gloss: Assessments should run on secure proctored platforms and questions should probe real-world experience
evidence.verbatim: On the assessment side, task-based exercises or live technical assessments should be completed on secure, proctored platforms where possible, and interview questions should probe real-world experience — how a candidate solved a specific challenge or approached a complex decision[14].

h3.h3: The unexpected follow-up question

evidence.gloss: Unpredictable follow-up questions expose a stand-in
evidence.verbatim: Candidates can prepare answers to common questions found online but cannot predict follow-up questions or in-depth clarifications, so a technical or behavioral problem-solving question requiring on-the-spot thinking exposes a stand-in[3].

evidence.gloss: In a live interview the challenge is an unscripted question, not a system prompt
evidence.verbatim: In a live hiring interview the challenge does not have to be a system prompt. The equivalent human move is an unscripted question.

evidence.gloss: Practitioner recommendation: off-script questions triggering facial reactions, with the sports-car-or-apple example
evidence.verbatim: Practitioners recommend live interactive assessments paired with off-script questions that can trigger facial reactions in real candidates you would not get from a deepfake, with the illustrative example "If you had the choice would you want to be a sports car or an apple?"[30].

evidence.gloss: Structured-interview version: one unexpected follow-up on the last answer exposes scripted answers
evidence.verbatim: The structured-interview version of the same principle: ask one unexpected follow-up question based on the candidate's last answer, because real experience can usually adapt to a follow-up while scripted answers often become weaker when the conversation moves away from the expected path[7].

evidence.gloss: The most frequently named mechanic is the unexpected follow-up
evidence.verbatim: The single mechanic named most often is the unexpected follow-up.

evidence.gloss: Rapid unscripted follow-ups work because a proxy cannot keep up with unexpected pivots
evidence.verbatim: Ask rapid, unscripted follow-up questions that require spontaneous, detailed responses about specific projects or technical decisions, because a proxy cannot keep up with unexpected pivots[42].

evidence.gloss: One unexpected follow-up off the last answer: real experience adapts, scripted answers weaken
evidence.verbatim: A useful test is to ask one unexpected follow-up question based on the candidate's last answer: real experience can usually adapt to a follow-up, while scripted answers often become weaker when the conversation moves away from the expected path[7].

evidence.gloss: Tactic: deep follow-ups on every answer, defending technical choices under scrutiny
evidence.verbatim: The tactical list is to ask deep follow-up questions on every answer, requiring candidates to explain their reasoning, discuss trade-offs, and defend their technical choices under scrutiny

evidence.gloss: Unexpected follow-up separates real experience from scripts
evidence.verbatim: Ask one unexpected follow-up based on the candidate's last answer: real experience usually adapts, while scripted answers become weaker when the conversation moves off the expected path[7].

evidence.gloss: Probing is the one control that works regardless of which fraud type you face
evidence.verbatim: There is a second reason probing carries disproportionate weight: it is the control that does not depend on which fraud you are facing.

evidence.gloss: Same table: rapid unscripted questions rate high effectiveness and work against advanced deepfakes; live screen-shared assessment rates very high
evidence.verbatim: in the same table, rapid unscripted questions rate high effectiveness at medium difficulty and are marked as working against advanced deepfakes specifically because they expose proxies, and live screen-shared assessment rates very high[42]

evidence.gloss: Tactic: plant nonsensical phrases in correspondence and quiz the candidate live
evidence.verbatim: Reported employer tactics include embedding small nonsensical phrases in email communication, assessments, and other correspondence and then quizzing the candidate on them when speaking directly

evidence.gloss: Hosea Chang's example phrase planted in an accounting exam
evidence.verbatim: Hosea Chang, COO of Hayden Girls, gives the example of a phrase such as "big blue elephants smoking cigars" dropped into an accounting exam, the point being to give little nuggets a candidate will notice that make no sense in any context until you bring them up [22].

evidence.gloss: Hosea's seeded-detail technique: plant details early, ask about them later
evidence.verbatim: Hosea's technique is to seed the earlier conversation with details the candidate will note but that "won't make sense in any context until you bring it up", then ask about them later[44].

evidence.gloss: Michael Hammelburger re-questions candidates about the test post-assessment to verify credibility
evidence.verbatim: Michael Hammelburger, CEO of The Bottom Line Group, asks candidates about the test in the post-assessment interview and has them further explain their answers, testing how well they understood the task and digging into their opinions to verify the credibility of their answers [22].

evidence.gloss: Hammelburger's post-assessment interview probes understanding of the test itself
evidence.verbatim: Michael Hammelburger, CEO of The Bottom Line Group, runs a post-assessment interview asking candidates about the test and to further explain their answers, testing how well they understood the task and digging deeper into their opinions to verify the credibility of their answers[44].

evidence.gloss: The probe has to be live because a proxy can complete asynchronous work
evidence.verbatim: Because a proxy can complete asynchronous work, the probe has to be live.

evidence.gloss: Post-assessment interviews asking candidates to explain their test answers verify credibility
evidence.verbatim: Practitioners describe post-assessment interviews that ask candidates to explain their test answers, testing how well they understood the task and digging into their opinions to verify credibility[22]

evidence.gloss: Test design as a detection control: question-bank randomisation defeats answer-sharing, adaptive follow-up logic exposes AI assistance that lacks contextual continuity
evidence.verbatim:
Assessment design is a detection control in its own right. Question banks that randomise item selection across candidates make coordinated answer-sharing less effective, since no two candidates taking the same assessment see the same question sequence.
Adaptive question logic adds a second layer. If a candidate answers the first five questions at the top of the competency range and then struggles with a follow-up testing the same competency at a deeper level, the system flags the divergence.
This pattern is difficult to fake with generalist AI assistance because the follow-up requires contextual continuity from the previous answer. Technical skills assessments built with adaptive logic are significantly harder to game than static question sets because the system responds dynamically to the candidate’s apparent knowledge level.

evidence.gloss: Interviewer-led probing does the same verification work inside the call
evidence.verbatim: Interviewer-led probing does the same work inside the call.

h3.h3: Cross-checking the resume inside the interview

evidence.gloss: Cross-check resume claims live: tools, contribution, teammates; fakes drift vague or repeat phrases
evidence.verbatim: Cross-checking resume claims during the interview itself is the specific probe: if a candidate lists a deployment, ask what tools they used, what their specific contribution was, and who else was on the team — real candidates answer with context, while fake candidates drift into vague language or repeat the same phrases[10].

evidence.gloss: The separating probe is resume cross-checking inside the interview itself
evidence.verbatim: The specific probe that separates a real practitioner from a stand-in is resume cross-checking during the interview itself.

evidence.gloss: How to cross-check a claimed deployment, and how real vs fake candidates answer differently
evidence.verbatim: If a candidate lists a deployment, ask what tools they used, what their specific contribution was, and who else was on the team; real candidates answer with context, while fake candidates often drift into vague language or repeat the same phrases[10].

evidence.gloss: The five-question set for the resume-versus-conversation gap
evidence.verbatim: A published question set for the resume-versus-conversation gap runs: What problem did the project solve? What part did you personally own? What trade-off did you make? What failed during the project? What would you change now?[7]

evidence.gloss: Red flag: complex projects listed but basic decisions from that work cannot be explained
evidence.verbatim: The underlying red flag is a candidate who lists complex projects but struggles to explain basic decisions from that work, because the gap can show the resume does not reflect the candidate's own experience[7].

evidence.gloss: Tactic: walk through resume details only the actual person would know
evidence.verbatim: to reference specific projects, technologies, or experiences from the candidate's resume and ask them to walk through technical details only the actual person would know

evidence.gloss: Cross-check resume claims live by asking for tools, contribution, and teammates
evidence.verbatim: Cross-check resume claims during the interview itself: if a candidate lists a deployment, ask what tools they used, what their specific contribution was, and who else was on the team.

evidence.gloss: Real candidates give context; fake ones drift vague or repeat phrases
evidence.verbatim: Real candidates answer with context; fake candidates often drift into vague language or repeat the same phrases[10].

evidence.gloss: Red flag 1: resume and conversation do not match
evidence.verbatim: **Resume and conversation do not match.** A candidate lists complex projects but struggles to explain basic decisions from that work, which can show the resume does not reflect their own experience.

evidence.gloss: Probe questions for a suspect project claim
evidence.verbatim: Useful probes: what problem did the project solve; what part did you personally own; what trade-off did you make; what failed during the project; what would you change now[7].

evidence.gloss: Red flag 5: claimed expert skills that fail one basic direct question
evidence.verbatim: Ask one direct question about any claimed expert-level skill. A candidate who cannot explain a basic concept in their stated speciality has inflated their proficiency.

evidence.gloss: Five probe questions for resume-versus-conversation gaps
evidence.verbatim: For resume-versus-conversation gaps, useful probes are: what problem did the project solve, what part did you personally own, what trade-off did you make, what failed during the project, and what would you change now[7].

h3.h3: Live exercises instead of take-home work

evidence.gloss: Embedded skills assessments force imposters to match resume claims
evidence.verbatim: Skills assessments, embedded into the interview where the platform supports it, force imposters to match the skills claimed on the resume[3].

evidence.gloss: Role-based reasoning evaluation beats keyword matching for technical roles
evidence.verbatim: Reasoning-based checks that require a candidate to explain their logic rather than produce a plausible-sounding response are harder for AI-generated answers to pass, which is why role-based reasoning evaluation, rather than keyword matching, is the recommendation for IT and technical roles[8].

evidence.gloss: Live technical assessments beat take-homes for raising the difficulty of cheating in IT roles
evidence.verbatim: For IT roles, live technical assessments that require real-time problem-solving, rather than take-home assignments, significantly raise the difficulty of cheating[10].

evidence.gloss: Technical interview formats to use instead of pure algorithmic challenges
evidence.verbatim: For technical interviews specifically, the guidance is to move beyond pure algorithmic coding challenges to include architectural discussions, debugging exercises with unfamiliar codebases, and pair programming sessions where the candidate must respond in real time to interviewer suggestions and direction

evidence.gloss: Why interactive formats break proxies: the deception cannot hold without the real candidate performing
evidence.verbatim: these interactive formats make it nearly impossible for a proxy to maintain the deception without the actual candidate being able to perform at the same level[6]

evidence.gloss: Tactic: virtual whiteboarding for system design discussion
evidence.verbatim: and to use virtual whiteboarding for system design discussion[6]

evidence.gloss: For high-risk roles, add a short live exercise where the candidate explains their approach while working
evidence.verbatim: For high-risk roles, add a short live exercise where the candidate explains their approach while working; the task does not need to be long or difficult, only specific enough to test whether the candidate can think through the work in real time[7].

evidence.gloss: Concrete live-exercise forms, and what comparing them lets you do before offer or onboarding
evidence.verbatim: Concrete forms include asking the candidate to walk through a past decision, revise a small part of their submission, explain a trade-off, or respond to a role-specific scenario, which lets you compare skills, explanations, and resume claims before the process moves to offer or onboarding[7].

evidence.gloss: Take-home work should not be the only proof of skill for roles with sensitive access
evidence.verbatim: Take-home work can still be useful but should not be the only proof of skill for roles with sensitive access[7].

evidence.gloss: Real-time problem-solving tools and observable shared coding environments raise the difficulty of cheating
evidence.verbatim: tools that require real-time problem-solving, not take-home assignments, significantly raise the difficulty of cheating, and shared coding environments where you can observe keystrokes and process are particularly effective[10]

evidence.gloss: Google reintroduced in-person technical rounds specifically to counter AI interview fraud
evidence.verbatim: Google reintroduced in-person technical interview rounds specifically to counter AI interview fraud, a move confirmed in multiple industry reports through 2025[10].

evidence.gloss: Hiring example: recorded presentation of a data analysis, with unnatural or scripted delivery disqualifying
evidence.verbatim: In the assessment layer, one hiring example asked candidates to do a data analysis and record a presentation of their findings, with candidates whose presentation did not look natural, or looked like they were reading from a script, not considered for the position; those who passed were then invited to a one-on-one interview with the hiring team[44].

evidence.gloss: Davis Nguyen used a recorded analysis presentation, screening out script-reading delivery
evidence.verbatim: Davis Nguyen, founder of My Consulting Offer, asked candidates for a remote marketing manager role to do a data analysis and record a presentation of their findings; if the presentation does not look natural, or looks like the candidate is reading from a script, they are not considered, and those who pass are invited to a one-on-one interview with the hiring manager [22].

evidence.gloss: A remote marketing manager process used a data analysis plus recorded presentation, rejecting scripted-looking ones
evidence.verbatim: one hiring process for a remote marketing manager required a data analysis plus a recorded presentation of findings, with candidates rejected if the presentation looked scripted rather than natural[22]

evidence.gloss: For high-risk roles, add a short live exercise rather than relying on take-home work alone
evidence.verbatim: For high-risk roles, take-home work should not be the only proof of skill; add a short live exercise where the candidate explains their approach while working, specific enough to test whether they can think through the work in real time, such as walking through a past decision, revising a small part of their submission, explaining a trade-off, or responding to a role-specific scenario[7].

evidence.gloss: Technology can monitor candidates during assessments to stop them looking up answers
evidence.verbatim: Technology can also monitor candidates during assessments to ensure they are not looking up answers online[22].

evidence.gloss: Step 5, live skills assessment run before the phone screen, with a tip to reorder it ahead of employer calls
evidence.verbatim:
This is the highest-signal step in the framework. A candidate who genuinely has the skills they claim will demonstrate them in real time. Run a skills assessment matched to the actual role: give a data analyst a messy dataset, a developer a real debugging task, a sales candidate a live objection scenario.
Testlify provides 3,500+ test libraries for efficient role-based skill assessment.
Pro Tip: Run Step 5 before Step 3, not after. You identify fabrication in 20 minutes instead of discovering it two interviews in. A candidate who fails a live skills test does not need an employer call.

evidence.gloss: Answers whether proctoring catches ChatGPT: it detects visible tells (phone below the desk, second monitor, copy-paste, off-screen gaze, browser AI plugins) but not a chatbot read off an unseen device or a memorized answer, so assessment design must carry part of the load through live reasoning, follow-ups, role-specific tasks, and an AI-assistance signal.
evidence.verbatim:
Partly, and honesty here matters. Proctoring can catch the visible tells of AI use: a phone held below the desk, a second monitor, copy-paste from another window, eyes tracking off-screen text, or an AI plugin running in the browser. What it cannot reliably catch is a candidate reading a chatbot answer off a device it never sees, or memorizing an AI-generated response beforehand.
This is why detection alone loses. The same research that warns detectors and proctoring will not be foolproof against generative AI concludes that assessment design has to carry part of the load. The durable defenses are structural: ask candidates to explain their reasoning live, use follow-up questions that a pre-written answer cannot survive, favor role-specific tasks over recall, and combine proctoring with an AI-assistance signal that flags when an on-device model is likely in play.

h3.h3: Behavioral tells of a scripted, coached, or AI-assisted answer

evidence.gloss: Behavioral signals of a scripted or assisted response
evidence.verbatim: Signals that a scripted or assisted response is in play include long pauses before simple answers, unusually polished responses, or answers that do not change much when the question becomes more specific[7].

evidence.gloss: Detection tools watch machine correlates: gaze drift and unnatural pause structure
evidence.verbatim: Detection-tool analogues watch for the machine correlates of the same behavior, including gaze drift and unnatural pause structure before answers[8].

evidence.gloss: Caution: one odd moment is not proof; concern rises when several inconsistencies cluster
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers should not treat one odd moment, such as a short audio delay or a camera issue, as proof of fraud; a stronger concern appears when several inconsistencies show up together, such as a thin profile, repeated camera refusal, scripted answers, a weak live exercise, and identity details that do not match the rest of the hiring record[7].

evidence.gloss: Video and audio artifacts: blur on movement, lighting mismatch, skin tone shifts at face edges, unnatural blinking
evidence.verbatim: Video and audio artifacts that support this pattern include a face that blurs and twitches unnaturally on movement, lighting mismatches where the face is lit differently from the background or neck, unnatural skin tone shifts along the edges of the face, and unnatural eye movement such as rare blinking or blinking at the exact same interval, which can occur because the AI is struggling to render a new face over the real one in real time[12].

evidence.gloss: Indicators of outside help: long pauses, over-polished answers, answers that do not sharpen with specificity
evidence.verbatim: In detection terms, indicators of outside help include long pauses before simple answers, unusually polished responses, or answers that do not change much when the question becomes more specific[7].

evidence.gloss: A formulaic or off-topic reply to a conversational question may be AI-generated
evidence.verbatim: Be wary if a normally conversational question, such as "What did you enjoy about working at Company X?", yields an overly formulaic or off-topic response, possibly generated by AI[12].

evidence.gloss: Longer pauses can mean the candidate is waiting for an accomplice to feed answers
evidence.verbatim: Longer pauses can indicate the candidate is waiting for an accomplice to feed answers[12].

evidence.gloss: Interviewers report reliable tells even with no tooling
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers report reliable tells even without tooling.

evidence.gloss: Sharon Robinson: you can tell when people are reading and pausing
evidence.verbatim: "We've experienced it a few times… You can absolutely tell when people are reading and pausing," says Sharon Robinson, HR director at Nova Scotia Pension[40].

evidence.gloss: The pattern: an overlong pause, eyes drifting off-screen, an answer that is too polished
evidence.verbatim: The pattern to watch for is a pause that runs a bit too long, eyes that drift off-screen, and an answer that is a bit too polished[40].

evidence.gloss: Long pauses may signal an accomplice; formulaic answers to conversational questions suggest AI
evidence.verbatim: Long pauses before answers may mean the candidate is waiting for an accomplice to feed answers; a normally conversational question such as "What did you enjoy about working at Company X?" that yields an overly formulaic or off-topic response may be AI-generated[12].

evidence.gloss: Disconnect between an avatar's steady gaze and obvious offscreen reading is itself a signal
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers have also noticed candidates reading offscreen, with eyes darting to something just beyond the camera, while their on-screen avatar maintained an oddly steady gaze, and that disconnect between apparent eye contact and obvious reading is itself a signal[12].

evidence.gloss: Employers and HR lean on human observation rather than automated flagging
evidence.verbatim: This is why employers and HR lean on human observation rather than automated flagging[40].

evidence.gloss: Mo Zhang: latency, AV mismatch, and eye-tracking anomalies spike with a proxy
evidence.verbatim: Dr. Mo Zhang, a behavioral analytics researcher, notes that latency in responses, audio-visual mismatches, and eye-tracking anomalies all spike when someone else is answering the questions.

evidence.gloss: Off-camera coaching creates a measurable half-beat delay before answers
evidence.verbatim: A second person off-camera feeding answers via chat or earpiece creates a measurable delay between the question being asked and the response beginning: the lips move, but there is a half-beat of silence as the proxy reads the prompt.

evidence.gloss: Red flag 2: scripted or delayed answers and their indicators
evidence.verbatim: **Answers sound scripted or delayed.** Indicators include long pauses before simple answers, unusually polished responses, or answers that do not change much when the question becomes more specific.

evidence.gloss: Detection protocol splits signals into three categories, each layer adding cost to the fraudster
evidence.verbatim: Framed as a detection protocol, the signals fall into three categories: behavioural, environmental, and identity-based, with each layer adding cost to the fraudster and increasing detection probability[45].

evidence.gloss: Response latency is the most reliable proxy signal, and the relay mechanism that creates it
evidence.verbatim: The most reliable proxy detection signal is response latency: when a proxy candidate receives a question, they must relay it to the surrogate, often via text or a secondary audio channel, wait for the surrogate to formulate an answer, and then repeat or synthesize the response, which creates a measurable delay[45].

evidence.gloss: Audio-visual mismatch as a secondary indicator, caused by a surrogate's voice dubbed over the video
evidence.verbatim: Dr. Zhang's research points to audio-visual mismatches, moments where the candidate's lip movements do not fully sync with the audio, as a secondary indicator, often caused by a surrogate's voice being dubbed over the candidate's video feed[45].

evidence.gloss: A sudden shift in technical depth is a third behavioural tell
evidence.verbatim: Another behavioural tell is a sudden shift in technical depth[45].

evidence.gloss: The named in-interview behavioral cues
evidence.verbatim: The behavioral cues named include looking off-screen repeatedly, screen reading, unusual background changes, drastic mid-interview voice-tone shifts, switching devices, and inconsistent facial positioning[4].

evidence.gloss: Cues are a reason to rewatch, not a verdict or automatic disqualification
evidence.verbatim: The recommended handling is explicit: these cues do not automatically disqualify a candidate, but they give recruiters a reason to take a closer look, and system alerts should be a reason to rewatch the video, not a verdict[4].

evidence.gloss: Interview-native signals are unavailable to any external checker
evidence.verbatim: The second is that interview-native signals are unavailable to any external checker.

evidence.gloss: Natural speech is more reliable than rehearsed; Willo's Real Talk monitors speech patterns
evidence.verbatim: Candidates who share genuine stories and speak naturally tend to give more reliable information than those who sound overly rehearsed, and Willo's Real Talk monitors for natural speech patterns to help spot rehearsed responses [15].

evidence.gloss: Polish-based suspicion penalises the nervous and over-prepared as well as the fraudulent
evidence.verbatim: The same caution about polish applies in reverse: it penalises the nervous and the over-prepared alongside the fraudulent.

evidence.gloss: Manual tells for deepfaked video interviews
evidence.verbatim: for video interviews, unnatural facial movements, lighting and shadow anomalies, behavioral inconsistencies, audio-visual asynchrony not explained by connection issues, and notable lag[3]

evidence.gloss: Detection fails when teams lack familiarity or flagging technology
evidence.verbatim: Failures happen where hiring teams have not encountered these signs before, are not familiar with them, or lack the technology to automatically flag AI-generated content[3].

evidence.gloss: Reported tell: eyes darting offscreen while the on-screen avatar holds a steady gaze
evidence.verbatim: In some reported cases, interviewers noticed candidates reading offscreen, with eyes darting to something just beyond the camera, while their on-screen avatar maintained an oddly steady gaze; that disconnect is a potential sign of trickery[12].

evidence.gloss: January 2026 case: Jason Rebholz of Evoke caught a fake candidate on an accumulation of small tells
evidence.verbatim: One high-value tell is specific to LLM assistance. In a January 2026 case, Jason Rebholz, founder of AI security firm Evoke, interviewed a referred candidate for a security researcher role and caught the fake on an accumulation of small things, including the candidate parroting questions back before answering them.

evidence.gloss: The clincher: answers quoted the interviewer's own published writing verbatim, an LLM tell
evidence.verbatim: The clincher was not visual: some answers quoted Rebholz's own published statements verbatim, which is what an LLM does when it has been fed the interviewer's public writing[12].

evidence.gloss: Rebholz on 'What if I'm wrong?' — why single-signal tricks are dangerous and process must carry the weight
evidence.verbatim: Rebholz also named the part nobody talks about: "What if I'm wrong?" Even at 95% confidence he worried about damaging a real person's shot at a job, which is why single-signal tricks are dangerous and why process rather than gut feel has to carry the weight[12].

evidence.gloss: Kuczynski's advice without software: ask the candidate, and trust your gut
evidence.verbatim: Kuczynski's advice for employers without detection software is to trust what they observe: "If you notice that your candidate keeps looking to the right every time you ask a question and pausing for a bit, ask them. And if you're still not convinced, it's better to trust your gut than otherwise. That's my policy on it"[40].

evidence.gloss: Never act on one odd event; look for several inconsistencies together
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers should not treat one odd event, such as a short audio delay or camera issue, as proof of fraud; the stronger concern is several inconsistencies together, such as a thin profile, repeated camera refusal, scripted answers, a weak live exercise, and identity details that do not match the rest of the hiring record[7].

evidence.gloss: Live observation produces tells the recorded format cannot
evidence.verbatim: Live observation also supplies tells the recorded format cannot produce.

evidence.gloss: Check voice-to-mouth match and lip-synching; a third person may answer off-screen
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers are advised to check whether the voice matches the mouth of the person on video, and whether the candidate appears to be lip-synching or covering their mouth, because the person on camera may not be the person speaking — the face may even be the real applicant who can produce ID, with a third person off-screen answering the questions[11].

evidence.gloss: Behavioral observation alone is insufficient when synthetic video or voice is a concern
evidence.verbatim: Live interviews need more than behavioral observation when synthetic video or voice manipulation is a concern[7].

h3.h3: Live challenges that break a deepfake in real time

evidence.gloss: The live format's structural advantage is real-time challenge against deepfake weaknesses
evidence.verbatim: The live format's structural advantage is that the interviewer can issue challenges in real time, and real-time deepfake systems have documented technical shortcomings that create detection opportunities[37]:

evidence.gloss: Deepfake weakness: temporal consistency under rapid head movement
evidence.verbatim: **Temporal consistency issues** — rapid head movements cause noticeable artifacts as the tracking system struggles to maintain accurate landmark positioning[37].

evidence.gloss: Deepfake weakness: occlusion handling when a hand passes over the face
evidence.verbatim: **Occlusion handling** — when the operator's hand passes over their face, the deepfake system fails to properly reconstruct the partially obscured face[37].

evidence.gloss: Deepfake weakness: lighting adaptation reveals rendering inconsistencies at face edges
evidence.verbatim: **Lighting adaptation** — sudden changes in lighting conditions reveal inconsistencies in the rendering, particularly around the edges of the face[37].

evidence.gloss: Deepfake weakness: audio-visual synchronization lag between lips and speech
evidence.verbatim: **Audio-visual synchronization** — slight delays between lip movements and speech are detectable under careful observation[37].

evidence.gloss: Passing a hand over the face is the most effective challenge method
evidence.verbatim: The most effective method appears to be passing a hand over a face, which disrupts facial landmark tracking[37].

evidence.gloss: NYU researchers' additional challenge strategies
evidence.verbatim: Govind Mittal et al. of New York University suggest additional strategies: rapid head movements, exaggerated facial expressions, and sudden lighting changes[37].

evidence.gloss: These challenge techniques exploit deepfake weaknesses to produce human-detectable artifacts
evidence.verbatim: These techniques exploit weaknesses in real-time deepfake systems, causing visible artifacts that help humans detect fakes[37].

evidence.gloss: Live format compensates for thin instrumentation with on-the-spot human interrogation
evidence.verbatim: The live format's compensation for its thin technical instrumentation is that a human can interrogate on the spot.

evidence.gloss: None of these live probes exist in the one-way format
evidence.verbatim: None of this exists in the one-way format, where there is no interlocutor to ask the follow-up.

evidence.gloss: Inability to use a camera on any device is a signal of unpreparedness or a different person
evidence.verbatim: A candidate who cannot use a camera on a laptop, desktop or smartphone may be unprepared, or may not be the individual who applied[11].

evidence.gloss: Camera reluctance as a signal: deepfake scammers prefer voice-only, and refusing camera adjustments counts too
evidence.verbatim: Reluctance is its own signal: beware of candidates who refuse to turn on their camera claiming it is broken or that their connection cannot handle video, since many deepfake scammers will initially try to stick to voice only because a visual deepfake adds complexity and risk of detection, and equally of a candidate on video who refuses any request to adjust their camera or environment[12].

evidence.gloss: High-risk live interviews can add audio and video authenticity review before advancing
evidence.verbatim: Live interviews need more than behavioral observation when synthetic video or voice manipulation is a concern, and for high-risk interviews live meeting protection can add audio and video authenticity review before a candidate advances[7].

evidence.gloss: Live meeting protection adds audio/video authenticity review for high-risk interviews
evidence.verbatim: For high-risk interviews where synthetic video or voice manipulation is the concern, live meeting protection can add audio and video authenticity review before a candidate advances, because live interviews need more than behavioural observation when that is the threat[7].

h3.h3: Identity and logistics checks around the call

evidence.gloss: Photo ID refusal, LinkedIn photo comparison, and pre-interview scrubbed ID copies as signals
evidence.verbatim: Inability to produce photo ID during the call is another signal, alongside comparing the candidate's appearance against LinkedIn and social profile photos and requesting a copy of the ID with private details scrubbed before the interview[11].

evidence.gloss: Pre-interview cross-referencing across LinkedIn, GitHub and other platforms, and what fraudulent profiles look like
evidence.verbatim: Before the interview starts, cross-reference the applicant's photo, work history, and credentials across LinkedIn, GitHub, and other professional platforms, since fraudulent applicants often have recently created profiles, very few connections, sparse activity history, or employment records that do not match publicly available data[42]

evidence.gloss: Cross-platform profile audit is rated high effectiveness and works against advanced deepfakes
evidence.verbatim: cross-platform profile audit is rated high effectiveness at medium difficulty and works against advanced deepfakes[42]

evidence.gloss: Logistics signals: location/network mismatch, equipment shipped elsewhere, pressure to skip verification
evidence.verbatim: logistics signals include a mismatch between stated location and network or payment details, requests to ship equipment to a different address, and pressure to skip verification steps[43]

evidence.gloss: LinkedIn message confirming interview time flushes out fraud either way
evidence.verbatim: Messaging the candidate on LinkedIn to confirm the interview time produces clarity either way: if the application is fraudulent, either the real person responds ("um…who??") or the scammer disappears[49].

evidence.gloss: A confirmation email framed around fraud volume is acceptable to legitimate candidates
evidence.verbatim: An email that says "we've been seeing a lot of fraudulent applications, would you mind confirming X?" is something most legitimate candidates won't mind at all[49].

evidence.gloss: GitHub link plus private-repo add is a 30-second engineer check
evidence.verbatim: For engineers, asking for a GitHub link in the application questions and asking them to add you to a private repo takes 30 seconds[49].

evidence.gloss: Combined signals across the funnel make a stronger escalation case than any one
evidence.verbatim: A thin profile, vague project ownership, video anomalies, inconsistent assessment performance, and unusual onboarding details together create a stronger case for escalation than any one of them alone[7].

evidence.gloss: Financial-services-style identity verification asks a logged-in applicant three to five history questions
evidence.verbatim: as are secure identity verification services of the type used in financial services, where a logged-in applicant answers three to five questions about their history[22]

evidence.gloss: Stage 2: one real identity check at the first live stage, because identity is verifiable and intent is not
evidence.verbatim: **Stage 2 should happen exactly once**, at the first live stage, and should be a real identity check rather than a behavioural guess. Identity is verifiable; intent is not[8].

evidence.gloss: Jessica Robinson: request e-signatures with resumes and verify them live on video
evidence.verbatim: Jessica Robinson of The Speaking Polymath recommends asking candidates to send e-signatures with their resumes so interviewers can verify the e-signature on the spot during the video interview, pointing to platforms such as signNow [22].

evidence.gloss: Other listed tactics: ID checks on video, identification scoring, verification questions, monitoring, third-party resources
evidence.verbatim: Other listed strategies are checking IDs during video interviews, introducing identification scoring (a fraud-detection method borrowed from business settings such as the mortgage industry, per Charles McMillan of Stand With Main Street), asking verification questions, monitoring candidates, and using third-party resources [22].

h3.h3: A second interviewer and who reviews a flag

evidence.gloss: A second interviewer catches different signals and is harder for a coached candidate to manage
evidence.verbatim: Adding a second interviewer for high-stakes roles means two observers catch different signals, no single person is making the call alone, and it is harder for a coached or AI-assisted candidate to manage two interviewers at once[10].

evidence.gloss: A second interviewer on high-stakes roles catches different signals and is harder to game
evidence.verbatim: Bringing in a second interviewer for high-stakes roles means two observers catch different signals, no single person is making the call alone, and it is harder for a coached or AI-assisted candidate to manage two interviewers simultaneously[10].

evidence.gloss: A second interviewer for high-stakes roles: two observers, shared call, harder to manage two people at once
evidence.verbatim: Bring in a second interviewer for high-stakes roles: two observers catch different signals, a single person is not making the call alone, and it is harder for a coached or AI-assisted candidate to manage two interviewers simultaneously[10].

evidence.gloss: Operational advice: proctoring by default, trained reviewers, role-based thresholds
evidence.verbatim: The operational advice is to use platforms offering AI-enhanced interview proctoring by default with unusual-activity detection, voice consistency and multi-face alerts enabled; to train recruiters to review flagged interviews carefully instead of jumping to conclusions; and to customize thresholds or alerts based on role sensitivity, with remote customer support or compliance roles warranting tighter monitoring than internal junior roles[4].

evidence.gloss: Monitoring framed as protecting the process, not surveillance
evidence.verbatim: Monitoring is framed as protecting the process from manipulation rather than turning hiring into surveillance[4].

evidence.gloss: Stage 5: a named human must review context, or you have built an automated decision system
evidence.verbatim: **Stage 5 is the guardrail that makes the rest safe.** If a flag can trigger a rejection without a named human reviewing the full context, you have built an automated decision system and inherited every obligation that comes with it[8].

evidence.gloss: Interview design itself carries part of the detection load
evidence.verbatim: Interview design itself carries part of the detection load.

h3.h3: Tools that watch the live call

evidence.gloss: Sherlock AI analyzes live-interview behavioral, visual and interaction patterns
evidence.verbatim: Specialized interview-integrity platforms are emerging beyond basic proctoring: Sherlock AI's interview fraud detection analyzes behavioral, visual and interaction patterns during live interviews to identify deepfake usage, hidden assistance, and AI-assisted responses that traditional monitoring tools often miss[4].

evidence.gloss: BrightHire adds Zoom-powered deepfake detection with flag-to-moment traceability
evidence.verbatim: On the video-conferencing side, BrightHire adds deepfake interview detection for Zoom users powered by Zoom's own proprietary models, passively surfacing and combining fraud signals with no extra verification steps for legitimate candidates, and links every flag back to the moment that triggered it so decisions stay explainable and human[9].

evidence.gloss: Sova's anti-cheating stack and Integrity Guard without lockdown software
evidence.verbatim: Sova combines adaptive testing that changes difficulty in real time so order and complexity differ per candidate, a large randomised question bank with shuffled options, strictly timed exams, browser and tab navigation tracking that records and flags a candidate leaving the assessment window, and cursor and interaction tracking for non-human movement patterns, with its Integrity Guard technology monitoring in the background without requiring computer lockdown or intrusive software installation[10].

evidence.gloss: Willo's RealTalk flags AI scripts without invasive surveillance and limits algorithmic scoring to multiple choice
evidence.verbatim: Some vendors deliberately restrict what they automate. Willo's RealTalk detection analyses response patterns in video interviews to flag candidates using AI-generated scripts or coaching tools, framed as authentic communication assessment without an invasive surveillance experience, and the platform limits algorithmic scoring to multiple-choice questions with factual right/wrong answers rather than scoring video responses for communication style or cultural fit[41].

evidence.gloss: A structured-interview platform embeds rating guides in the live interface and adds proctoring, reference checks, audio-only
evidence.verbatim: One platform offers live and pre-recorded structured interviews with rating guides embedded directly into the live interview interface, plus skills testing, automated reference checks, audio-only interviews, and video proctoring for assessments; standardized questions and evaluation criteria across every candidate help reduce interviewer bias at scale[1].

evidence.gloss: That platform's pricing starts at $5,000/yr and fits regulated industries needing auditable processes
evidence.verbatim: Pricing starts at $5,000/yr with custom per-module pricing, one-time setup and training costs, and scales with team size and volume; it suits organizations in regulated industries needing auditable, structured interview processes with compliance documentation, and expects an implementation timeline rather than same-day activation[1].

h3.h3: Designing the process so cheating is pointless

evidence.gloss: For assistance the control is process design: make cheating pointless instead of detecting it
evidence.verbatim: For assistance, process design is the control, and the teams handling this well have stopped trying to detect and started trying to make cheating pointless[8].

evidence.gloss: Fixing assistance is a process change, not a purchase
evidence.verbatim: That is a process change, not a purchase[8].

evidence.gloss: Stating acceptable AI use in the invitation is the highest-leverage and most-skipped step
evidence.verbatim: Telling candidates what AI use is acceptable, in the interview invitation itself, removes the ambiguity that produces most of the 35%, and this disclosure stage is described as the highest-leverage and the one most teams skip[8].

evidence.gloss: Disclosure is the cheapest deterrent and a growing compliance matter
evidence.verbatim: Disclosure is both the cheapest deterrent available and increasingly a compliance matter[8].

evidence.gloss: Buying detection before rewriting questions pays to measure a removable problem
evidence.verbatim: The buying-order error follows directly from the conflation: buying detection software before rewriting questions means paying a subscription to measure a problem you could have removed[8].

evidence.gloss: Each stage is cheap; the order matters more than the steps
evidence.verbatim: Each stage of the sequence is cheap on its own, and the order matters more than the individual steps[8].

evidence.gloss: The teams doing this well aim to make cheating pointless rather than detectable
evidence.verbatim: The teams handling this well have stopped trying to detect and started trying to make cheating pointless.

evidence.gloss: Stage 1: state acceptable AI use in the invitation, removing the ambiguity behind most of the 35%
evidence.verbatim: **Stage 1 is the highest-leverage and the one most teams skip.** Telling candidates what AI use is acceptable, in the interview invitation itself, removes the ambiguity that produces most of the 35%[8].

evidence.gloss: Buying detection before rewriting questions pays to measure a problem the process should have removed
evidence.verbatim: Reordering these is where teams go wrong: buying detection software before rewriting questions means paying a subscription to measure a problem the process should have removed[8].

evidence.gloss: Best-performing teams make cheating pointless rather than detecting it; a process change, not a purchase
evidence.verbatim: The teams handling this well have stopped trying to detect and started trying to make cheating pointless, which is a process change rather than a purchase, run in a defined sequence where the order matters more than the individual steps[8].

evidence.gloss: Verification is the right tool for identity fraud, detection's one legitimate job
evidence.verbatim: The corollary for scope: detection has one legitimate narrow job. For identity fraud, where the question is whether this human is that human, verification is the right tool[8].

evidence.gloss: For everything else redesign beats detection, which inherits the process's weaknesses
evidence.verbatim: For everything else, redesign beats detection, because detection is a filter bolted onto an unchanged process that inherits that process's weaknesses while adding a false positive rate on top[8].

evidence.gloss: Buying detection before rewriting questions pays to measure a problem the design creates
evidence.verbatim: Buying detection software before rewriting questions means paying a subscription to measure a problem the interview design is still creating[8].

evidence.gloss: Transparency is the paired requirement: disclose checks upfront and define acceptable versus unacceptable AI use
evidence.verbatim: Transparency is the paired requirement: tell candidates from the outset that the process includes identity checks, skill validation, and possibly consent for video recording or screen sharing, and outline what AI use is acceptable (help polishing a resume) versus what is not (AI writing interview answers)[14].

evidence.gloss: An authenticity declaration in the application deters dishonesty and sets the tone
evidence.verbatim: An authenticity declaration in the application, a brief statement confirming the resume, cover letter, and interview responses are the applicant's own, deters dishonesty and sets the tone[14].

evidence.gloss: Disclosure is the cheapest deterrent and increasingly a compliance requirement
evidence.verbatim: Disclosure is described as both the cheapest deterrent available and increasingly a compliance requirement[8].

h3.h3: Training interviewers to catch the casual attempts

evidence.gloss: A trained recruiter noticing 1.5-second latency beats a $100,000 platform for obvious cases
evidence.verbatim: A recruiter trained to notice a 1.5-second response latency across a 45-minute interview can flag the session for deeper review; you do not need a $100,000 enterprise platform to catch the obvious cases, you need a systematized set of observations and a protocol for escalation[45].

evidence.gloss: Recommended training package: a 30-minute module on the three behavioural signals
evidence.verbatim: The recommended training package is a 30-minute training module on the three behavioural signals, response latency, audio-visual sync, and technical depth inconsistency, which gives a frontline screening team a detection vocabulary[45].

evidence.gloss: The stated limit: recruiter observation catches casual attempts, not sophisticated operations
evidence.verbatim: The stated limit is explicit: recruiter observations alone will not catch sophisticated operations, but they will catch the long tail of casual proxy attempts[45].

evidence.gloss: A 30-minute training module on three behavioural signals catches the casual long tail
evidence.verbatim: A 30-minute training module on the three behavioural signals, response latency, audio-visual sync, and technical depth inconsistency, gives the frontline screening team a detection vocabulary; recruiter observations alone won't catch sophisticated operations, but they will catch the long tail of casual proxy attempts[45].

sections_menu.h2: Liveness and anti-spoof certifications: what each standard actually proves

h3.h3: ISO/IEC 30107 and why Part 3 is the part that counts

evidence.gloss: ISO 30107 certification is tiered and the tier signals the attack class proven against
