evidence.verbatim: Certification against ISO 30107 is tiered, and the tier tells you what class of attack the system was proven against:

evidence.gloss: Liveness is rated on certification because an external checkable standard exists
evidence.verbatim: This is the dimension with an external, checkable standard behind it, so the rating uses certification rather than vendor phrasing.

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-1 defines presentation attack terminology and Presentation Attack Instruments
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107-1 defines the terminology of presentation attacks and names fake materials Presentation Attack Instruments (PAIs)

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines test methods and per-attack-type reporting
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines the methods for measuring system performance and reporting results by attack type[15]

evidence.gloss: Claiming ISO/IEC 30107 compliance without Part 3 testing does not demonstrate effectiveness
evidence.verbatim: The distinction is load-bearing for scoring: when a vendor says its system complies with ISO/IEC 30107 but does not state Part 3 testing, it has not demonstrated that the system is effective in practice[15].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107 was published in 2017 for remote identity proofing systems
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107 was published in 2017 and defines safety measures and presentation attack tests on remote identity proofing systems[16].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107 Part 1 vs Part 3, and the Part 3 omission as a vendor gap
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107-1 describes the fundamentals of presentation attacks and the methods of detecting them, while ISO/IEC 30107-3 covers the evaluation and reporting of PAD effectiveness in actual security threat tests; when a vendor says its system complies with ISO/IEC 30107 but does not state Part 3 testing, that is flagged as a gap[15].

evidence.gloss: Certification claims without Part 3 testing leave effectiveness unevaluated
evidence.verbatim: Vendor certification claims can be hollow: compliance with ISO/IEC 30107 that does not state Part 3 testing leaves effectiveness unevaluated[15].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-3 is the primary PAD evaluation standard
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107-3 is the primary standard for evaluating PAD systems, providing standardized performance metrics and consistent testing protocols[29].

h3.h3: How presentation attack detection works: active versus passive liveness

evidence.gloss: Both active and passive PAD can be certified under ISO/IEC 30107-3
evidence.verbatim: Both active and passive PAD methods can achieve certification under ISO/IEC 30107-3[15]

evidence.gloss: Passive PAD runs silently with no extra user steps
evidence.verbatim: passive PAD runs liveness detection silently in the background without extra user steps[15]

evidence.gloss: Active PAD: challenge-response actions, blocks pre-recorded video, slower verification
evidence.verbatim: Active PAD asks users to perform actions such as blinking, turning their head, or smiling, checks these as real-time responses, and does not allow pre-recorded videos because they cannot react to new challenges; it is very good at preventing spoofing but makes verification slower, a trade-off described as important for high-value transactions and situations needing extra authentication[15].

evidence.gloss: Passive PAD: no user input, model-dependent, lower onboarding drop-off
evidence.verbatim: Passive PAD works without any user input, with an AI model analysing a natural facial capture and deciding whether the person is real based on surface detail, depth, and tiny movements, reducing drop-off during busy onboarding but requiring a detection model strong enough to spot attacks without challenge-response checks[15].

evidence.gloss: PAD method choice affects both friction and which attack surfaces are addressed
evidence.verbatim: The choice of method affects both verification friction and the specific attack surfaces addressed[15].

evidence.gloss: Liveness relies on micro-movements printed images cannot display
evidence.verbatim: Liveness relies on parts of a face that printed images cannot display: micro-movements such as changes in skin tone due to pulse, eye blinking, and breathing, which may be more perceptible when observing the recording process than the video[15].

evidence.gloss: PAD operates at the capture stage before facial recognition
evidence.verbatim: PAD operates at the capture stage to stop fake faces before they reach facial recognition, checking the input first so spoofing attempts do not compromise the rest of the verification process[15].

evidence.gloss: ENISA's four types of facial presentation attack
evidence.verbatim: ENISA's remote verification research identifies four types of facial presentation attack — photo, video replay, 3D mask, and deepfake — all of which a remote verification system should prevent[15].

evidence.gloss: Supporting detection techniques: texture analysis and 3D scanning
evidence.verbatim: Supporting detection techniques include texture analysis, examining small-scale skin surface variation such as sebaceous glands, pores and hair follicles that cannot be represented by printed photos and masks, and 3D scanning of the face using structured light, time-of-flight and stereo cameras to capture what printed images cannot[15].

evidence.gloss: Three named research issues in deepfake artifact detection
evidence.verbatim: For deepfakes specifically, researchers studying AI artifacts have to compare real and fake videos, and three issues are named: detection of rare compression artifacts, detection of time-inconsistent synthetic video, and generation of fake face features by face recognition algorithms[15].

evidence.gloss: Active PAD slows verification; passive PAD depends on model strength
evidence.verbatim: Active PAD's challenge-response step slows verification down[15], and passive PAD's speed advantage depends entirely on the detection model being strong enough to catch attacks with no challenge at all[15].

h3.h3: The iBeta PAD levels and the attacks each one survives

evidence.gloss: iBeta PAD Level 1 covers common spoofing methods as a baseline
evidence.verbatim: **iBeta PAD Level 1** covers the most common spoofing methods, establishing a baseline of protection across channels[7].

evidence.gloss: iBeta PAD Level 2 raises difficulty substantially
evidence.verbatim: **iBeta PAD Level 2** raises the difficulty substantially.

evidence.gloss: Level 2 requires resisting depth/texture-mimicking materials and digitally synthesized faces
evidence.verbatim: At Level 2 the system must resist sophisticated attacks made with materials that mimic human depth and texture, as well as faces synthesized by digital imaging.

evidence.gloss: Level 2 artefacts include silicone, resin, and latex masks replicating specific faces
evidence.verbatim: The artefacts used include silicone, resin, and latex masks designed to replicate specific faces[7].

evidence.gloss: Passing systems detect subtle light-reflection anomalies on mask materials
evidence.verbatim: Passing systems work by identifying subtle anomalies in light reflection on these materials[7].

evidence.gloss: Level 2 is extremely demanding with few providers passing, making it a harder claim than ISO compliance
evidence.verbatim: Level 2 is described as extremely demanding, with few providers passing successfully[7], which makes "certified to Level 2" a meaningfully harder claim to make than "ISO 30107 compliant.

evidence.gloss: iBeta: NVLAP-accredited lab certified to ISO 30107-3, offering PAD certification at two levels
evidence.verbatim: iBeta Quality Assurance is an independent testing lab accredited under NIST NVLAP and certified to ISO 30107-3, and offers presentation attack detection (PAD) certification at two levels[15].

evidence.gloss: PAD Level 1 covers printed photos and normal video playback
evidence.verbatim: PAD Level 1 examines readily available physical artifacts such as printed photos and normal video playback[15].

evidence.gloss: PAD Level 2 covers silicone masks and 2D dynamic attacks, zero violations across 750 tests
evidence.verbatim: PAD Level 2 covers more complex artifacts, including 3D custom silicone masks and 2D dynamic attacks built from biometric samples of specific persons, and requires zero violations across 750 individual test situations, with no rounding or partial credit[15].

evidence.gloss: iBeta Level 2 under ISO/IEC 30107-3 is the bar for a PAD tool to count as valid
evidence.verbatim: The framework treats iBeta Level 2 under ISO/IEC 30107-3 as the bar for a PAD tool to count as a valid fraud-catching control[15].

evidence.gloss: Facia's iBeta Level 2 certification and its 1,500-attack March 2024 test scenario
evidence.verbatim: As a concrete example of what a real certification claim looks like, Facia's liveness detection has been certified at iBeta Level 2 under ISO/IEC 30107-3, and per the March 2024 certification announcement the test scenario consisted of 1,500 presentation attacks across both Android and iOS devices[15].

evidence.gloss: Level 3 test plans follow ISO/IEC 30107-3 and score with APCER, BPCER and IAPMR
evidence.verbatim: Level 3 test plans are customized but still follow ISO/IEC 30107-3, scoring subsystems via APCER (attack success rate) and BPCER (user rejection rate), and assessing end-to-end systems with IAPMR, which reflects whether the full identity pipeline is compromised by a spoof[13].

evidence.gloss: An accuracy figure only means something against the attack class it was tested on
evidence.verbatim: An accuracy figure is only meaningful against the attack class it was tested on, and the two relevant classes are tested by entirely different frameworks.

evidence.gloss: iBeta Level 1: attacks, budget, pass thresholds and test volume
evidence.verbatim: | Level 1 | Printed photos, smartphone screen selfies, simple paper masks | ~8 hours prep, max $30 per attack attempt | APCER = 0%, BPCER ≤ 15% | ~900 attempts (~6 attack types × ~150 trials) |

evidence.gloss: iBeta Level 2: attacks, budget, pass thresholds and test volume
evidence.verbatim: | Level 2 | 3D masks, high-resolution video replays, deepfake clips | 2-4 days prep (~24 hours hands-on), up to $300 per attack type | APCER ≤ 1%, BPCER ≤ 15% | ~1,100 attempts (multiple PAIs × ~150 each, plus ~200-250 bona fide samples) |

evidence.gloss: iBeta Level 3: professional-grade attacks, no cost limits, custom test plan
evidence.verbatim: | Level 3 | Professional-grade, resource-intensive attacks | No fixed cost limits, prep up to seven days | Custom test plan, still under ISO/IEC 30107-3 | Fully customized |

evidence.gloss: Level 3 is where testing starts to resemble a real hiring-fraud attacker
evidence.verbatim: Level 3 is where the test starts resembling a real hiring-fraud attacker.

evidence.gloss: Level 3 testers match spoofs to the target system's angle, illumination and framing
evidence.verbatim: Testers craft spoofs matched to the target system's expected angle, illumination, and framing so it perceives them as native, real-time input[13].

evidence.gloss: Level 3 spoof prompts defeat active liveness with blinking masks and smiling deepfakes
evidence.verbatim: Against active liveness prompts, Level 3 testers build **spoof prompts** that mimic the required response: a mask with mechanically controlled eyelids that blink on command, or a deepfake animation that smiles and replicates head movements[13].

evidence.gloss: Dynamic liveness checks lose protective value against responsive spoofs
evidence.verbatim: The result is that dynamic liveness checks lose their protective value, because the spoof appears animated and responds convincingly to system instructions[13].

evidence.gloss: The governing question at Level 3 shifts to surviving a precision-engineered expert spoof
evidence.verbatim: The governing question at Level 3 shifts from "can you stop a spoof?" to "can you survive a precision-engineered, expert-grade spoof attempt designed specifically to defeat your system?

h3.h3: Where PAD certification stops: injection attacks and CEN/TS 18099

evidence.gloss: CLR Labs also evaluates biometric data injection and deepfake-based facial recognition attacks
evidence.verbatim: CLR Labs' evaluation work covers both presentation attacks and biometric data injection tests, including facial recognition attacks based on deepfake technology[16].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 is the European standard built for this threat and splits attack method from attack instrument
evidence.verbatim: CEN/TS 18099, the European standard built specifically for this threat, separates the injection attack *method*, meaning how the fake is delivered, from the injection attack *instrument*, meaning what gets delivered[21].

evidence.gloss: Examples of method versus instrument under CEN/TS 18099
evidence.verbatim: The method might be a virtual camera, an emulator, a hooked software function, or manipulated network traffic; the instrument is the payload itself, the deepfake video, synthetic face, or manipulated image sequence the attacker wants the system to accept[21].

evidence.gloss: PAD certification under ISO/IEC 30107-3 tests only spoofs shown to a camera
evidence.verbatim: Presentation attack detection certification under ISO/IEC 30107-3 tests only spoofs shown to a camera[21].

evidence.gloss: Injection resistance is tested separately under CEN/TS 18099
evidence.verbatim: Injection resistance is tested separately, under the CEN/TS 18099 specification[21].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 is the first technical specification dedicated to injection attack detection, lab-tested against named methods
evidence.verbatim: CEN/TS 18099 is the first technical specification dedicated to injection attack detection, tested by independent labs against methods including virtual cameras, USB cameras, function hooking, and rooted devices[21].

evidence.gloss: Forthcoming ISO/IEC 25456 aims to globalize the CEN/TS 18099 requirements
evidence.verbatim: The forthcoming ISO/IEC 25456 aims to globalize those requirements[21].

evidence.gloss: NIST digital identity guidelines require higher assurance levels to confirm the signal came from a real, live person
evidence.verbatim: NIST's updated digital identity guidelines now require, at higher assurance levels, that a biometric system confirm the signal came from a real, live person rather than a replayed or manipulated input[21].

evidence.gloss: NIST 2025 guidelines separate identity verification from media protection and treat injection, virtual cameras, modified media, and presentation attacks as distinct risks
evidence.verbatim: NIST's 2025 Digital Identity Guidelines distinguish identity verification from media protection, and address video and image injection, virtual cameras, modified media, and presentation attacks as separate risks requiring additional controls[27].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines presentation attack detection testing and was never designed for injection
evidence.verbatim: ISO/IEC 30107-3 defines how to evaluate presentation attack detection, the ability to catch photos, masks, and replays shown to a camera; it was never designed to address injection, which enters below the sensor[21].

evidence.gloss: iProov: a vendor can hold PAD certification and still have zero injection resilience
evidence.verbatim: The consequence is blunt: as iProov puts it, a vendor can hold PAD certification and still have zero resilience to injection attacks[21].

evidence.gloss: A PAD-only stack approves virtual-camera deepfakes because PAD checks the face, not the frame's origin
evidence.verbatim: A verification stack that only runs PAD will confidently approve a deepfake delivered through a virtual camera, because PAD examines the face in the frame while injection attacks compromise how the frame got there[61].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 is the first technical specification dedicated to injection attack detection
evidence.verbatim: Injection resistance has to be tested on its own terms, against CEN/TS 18099, the first technical specification dedicated to injection attack detection[21][61].

evidence.gloss: What CEN/TS 18099 covers: definitions, attack use cases, instruments, detection guidance, and test-plan creation
evidence.verbatim: That specification covers definitions of biometric data injection attack, the attack use case on enrolment and verification hardware, injection attack instruments across one or several biometric modalities, guidance on detection systems and mitigation, and creation of a test plan for evaluating an injection attack detection system[62].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 scope excludes presentation attack testing, though bona fide presentation testing is in scope
evidence.verbatim: Its scope explicitly excludes presentation attack testing: a PAD system may be assessed as a defence mechanism against injection attack instruments or methods, and bona fide presentation testing is in scope to check the target of evaluation correctly classifies legitimate users, but no presentation attack testing is performed by the laboratory to be compliant with the TS[62].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 25456 is forthcoming and NIST's digital identity guidelines require injection safeguards at higher assurance levels
evidence.verbatim: The forthcoming ISO/IEC 25456 aims to globalize injection-detection requirements, and NIST's digital identity guidelines require injection safeguards at higher assurance levels[21].

evidence.gloss: Equating liveness certification with injection resistance is a named common mistake
evidence.verbatim: Equating liveness certification with injection resistance is named as a common mistake teams make[21].

evidence.gloss: Analyzing only the image and not the camera path is a second named mistake, since the path carries the strongest signals
evidence.verbatim: So is analyzing only the image and not the path: a system that scores the pixels but never asks where the frames came from cannot see a virtual camera or a hooked SDK, and the camera path carries the strongest injection signals[21].

evidence.gloss: Active liveness prompts fail against injected feeds because a deepfake can perform blink or turn on cue
evidence.verbatim: Relying on active liveness prompts fails for a related reason: asking a user to blink or turn does not help when the entire feed is injected, since a pre-rendered or real-time deepfake can perform the requested action on cue[21].

evidence.gloss: Trusting the SDK as a boundary fails because attackers reverse-engineer it and hook frame-capture calls
evidence.verbatim: Trusting the SDK as a fixed boundary fails because attackers reverse-engineer client SDKs and hook the frame-capture calls, so integration integrity has to be verified rather than assumed[21].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 30107-3 PAD certification does not cover injection detection
evidence.verbatim: Presentation attack detection (PAD) certification under ISO/IEC 30107-3 says nothing about whether a system can detect an injected stream, because injection resistance requires its own testing against a different standard[21].

evidence.gloss: Definition of the difference between a presentation attack and an injection attack
evidence.verbatim: The two attacks are defeated by completely different controls: a presentation attack shows something fake to a real camera, while an injection attack removes the camera from the equation entirely, inserting a synthetic or pre-recorded video stream directly into the software capture layer before any liveness or face-match check runs[21].

evidence.gloss: Passing every presentation-attack test leaves injection exposure open
evidence.verbatim: A system can pass every presentation-attack test and still be wide open to injection.

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 is the standard to name, first spec dedicated to injection attack detection
evidence.verbatim: The standard to name in a vendor conversation is **CEN/TS 18099**, the European technical specification created specifically to test resilience against these internal, data-level assaults and the first technical specification dedicated to injection attack detection[21][78].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 complements rather than replaces ISO/IEC 30107-3
evidence.verbatim: It complements rather than replaces ISO/IEC 30107-3[21].

evidence.gloss: CEN/TS 18099 separates injection attack method from injection attack instrument
evidence.verbatim: CEN/TS 18099 separates the **injection attack method** (how the fake is delivered: a virtual camera, an emulator, a hooked software function, or manipulated network traffic) from the **injection attack instrument** (what gets delivered: the deepfake video, synthetic face, or manipulated image sequence)[21].

evidence.gloss: Effective defense must address both halves because no single signal suffices
evidence.verbatim: Both halves matter, and effective defense has to address both, because no single signal is sufficient[21].

evidence.gloss: ISO/IEC 25456 and NIST digital identity guidelines are the other two standards to raise
evidence.verbatim: The forthcoming **ISO/IEC 25456** aims to globalize injection-detection requirements, and **NIST's digital identity guidelines** require injection safeguards at higher assurance levels[21].

h3.h3: Reading a vendor's certification claim: labs, scope and the questions to ask

evidence.gloss: Native and web environments need separately optimised liveness algorithms
evidence.verbatim: One environment-specific caveat is worth carrying into a vendor conversation: native and web environments present different challenges for liveness detection because of hardware variation, and algorithms have to be optimised separately so that security is not compromised in a browser[7].

evidence.gloss: App-only certified performance is a weaker proposition when buyers won't force app downloads
evidence.verbatim: A tool that only achieves its certified performance inside a native mobile app is a different proposition from one that holds up on the web, which matters when a buyer does not want to force candidates to download an app[7].

evidence.gloss: CLR Labs and LSTI launched an ISO/IEC 30107 conformity assessment scheme on 24 May 2023
evidence.verbatim: On 24 May 2023, CLR Labs (a European biometric and security technology evaluation laboratory) and LSTI (a conformity assessment body created in 2004, a member of Apave Digital since September 2021, with a European franchise LSTI Worldwide based in Ireland) launched an ISO/IEC 30107 conformity assessment scheme[16].

evidence.gloss: Before that, certification was US-only and Europe ran compliance projects only
evidence.verbatim: Until then the only certification scheme available was from the United States, and in Europe only compliance projects had been carried out[16].

evidence.gloss: IDnow was first to obtain an LSTI ISO/IEC 30107 certificate, for VideoIdent
evidence.verbatim: IDnow became the first company to obtain an LSTI ISO/IEC 30107 certificate, for its VideoIdent product, an expert-assisted video identity verification product run by trained agents alongside backend AI controls that validates face biometrics and performs liveness checks to detect presentation attacks[16].

evidence.gloss: LSTI rated VideoIdent's level as substantial
evidence.verbatim: LSTI assessed VideoIdent's level as "substantial"[16].

evidence.gloss: NIST FATE 2023 report evaluated 82 PAD algorithms from 45 developers
evidence.verbatim: The field is large enough to be measured: in 2023 NIST published a Face Analysis Technology Evaluation (FATE) research report evaluating 82 software-based PAD algorithms submitted by 45 developers[15].

evidence.gloss: NIST FATE 2023 report evaluated 82 PAD algorithms from 45 developers
evidence.verbatim: In 2023 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published a research report from its Face Analysis Technology Evaluation (FATE) program that evaluated 82 software-based PAD algorithms submitted by 45 developers[15].

evidence.gloss: Ask which specific injection techniques were tested
evidence.verbatim: Ask specifically which injection techniques were tested.

evidence.gloss: Accredited lab evaluations covered virtual cameras, emulators, and direct API manipulation
evidence.verbatim: Real evaluations by accredited labs have covered virtual camera outputs, emulator-driven attacks, and direct API manipulation[78].

evidence.gloss: Ingenium offers five-level independent IAD testing as third-party procurement evidence
evidence.verbatim: Independent IAD testing is available in graded tiers: one lab, Ingenium, provides independent injection attack detection testing across five levels, from CEN/TS 18099 compliance baselines to advanced assessments, and positions the results as third-party evidence for procurement[24].

evidence.gloss: "iBeta certified" alone is not a sufficient vendor answer
evidence.verbatim: "iBeta certified" is not an answer on its own.

sections_menu.h2: What the certifications, accuracy numbers and risk scores actually prove

h3.h3: Grading a vendor's own integrity claims

evidence.gloss: HireID announced an Interview Integrity Platform on August 17, 2026
evidence.verbatim: HireID announced an "Interview Integrity Platform" on **August 17, 2026**[26].

evidence.gloss: HireID's claims: pre-interview identity, document fraud screening, 20+ live fraud signals, 98% accuracy
evidence.verbatim: The company says it verifies identity **before** interviews, screens documents "for document fraud, tampering, forgery, and synthetic or altered records," and monitors "more than 20+ fraud signals during live interviews," claiming "over 98% accuracy on synthetic identity detection in internal benchmark testing" (HireID press release)[26].

evidence.gloss: The 98% figure is an internal vendor claim, not independently evaluated
evidence.verbatim: The caveat is in the source and must travel with the number: "That accuracy figure is a vendor claim from internal testing, not an independent evaluation, and should be read as such"[26].

evidence.gloss: How to grade any vendor integrity claim: who benchmarked, on what, and can outsiders check
evidence.verbatim: This is the template for how every vendor integrity claim in the article should be graded — who ran the benchmark, on what population, and whether anyone outside the vendor can check it.

evidence.gloss: HireID's August 2026 platform claims 20+ live fraud signals and 98% synthetic identity accuracy
evidence.verbatim: HireID announced an "Interview Integrity Platform" on August 17, 2026, claiming it verifies identity before interviews, screens documents "for document fraud, tampering, forgery, and synthetic or altered records," monitors "more than 20+ fraud signals during live interviews," and reaches "over 98% accuracy on synthetic identity detection in internal benchmark testing"[26].

evidence.gloss: The 98% figure is an internal vendor claim, not an independent evaluation
evidence.verbatim: That accuracy figure is a vendor claim from internal testing, not an independent evaluation, and should be read as such[26].

h3.h3: Independent lab testing and the metrics it reports

evidence.gloss: The testing regime is part of the evaluation because vendor claims outrun capability
evidence.verbatim: Because vendor claims outrun vendor capability, the testing regime is itself part of the evaluation.

evidence.gloss: Lab testing uses photos, videos and 3D masks under a strict protocol
evidence.verbatim: In a lab, experts use various spoofing tools to try to bypass the biometric sensor — photos, videos, and 3D masks — to find where the system fails, following a strict protocol so every evaluation is fair[7].

evidence.gloss: Without lab tests you cannot know if a system blocks professional attackers
evidence.verbatim: Without these tests it is hard to know whether a system can really block professional attackers[7].

evidence.gloss: Four examination types: facial recognition, voice, liveness, and document verification tests
evidence.verbatim: The examination types map onto the stack: facial recognition tests focus on identifying features and detecting physical or digital masks; voice tests analyze audio patterns against deepfakes and recordings; liveness detection tests check whether a user is a real person or just an image; and document verification tests check whether ID cards or passports are authentic and untampered[7].

evidence.gloss: APCER and BPCER score subsystems; IAPMR scores end-to-end systems
evidence.verbatim: Subsystems are scored via **APCER** (attack success rate) and **BPCER** (user rejection rate); end-to-end systems are assessed with **IAPMR**, which reflects whether the full identity pipeline is compromised by a spoof[13].

evidence.gloss: Ask for the end-to-end IAPMR number, not the subsystem APCER
evidence.verbatim: Ask for the end-to-end number. A subsystem APCER tells you the matcher held; IAPMR tells you the pipeline did.

evidence.gloss: BPCER is the candidate-experience metric buyers skip
evidence.verbatim: BPCER is the candidate-experience number, and it is the one buyers skip.

evidence.gloss: A passing system may reject up to 15% of genuine users at Level 1 and 2
evidence.verbatim: Even a passing system may reject up to 15% of genuine users under both Level 1 and Level 2 thresholds[13].

evidence.gloss: The 15% rejection is a cost paid by honest candidates and a negotiating point
evidence.verbatim: That is the cost the honest candidate pays for the vendor's fraud control, and it is a legitimate negotiating point.

evidence.gloss: A 15% rejection rate plus heavy setup compounds two taxes on the honest applicant
evidence.verbatim: Pair this with the BPCER number above: a system that rejects up to 15% of legitimate users[13] and adds a heavy setup burden compounds two separate taxes on the honest applicant.

h3.h3: What iBeta liveness certification covers, and the injection gap it leaves

evidence.gloss: A PAD-certified system can have zero injection defense
evidence.verbatim: A system can be PAD certified and still have no defense against injection, and a product can pass PAD certification with zero resistance to injection attacks[21].

evidence.gloss: Liveness certification as table stakes creates false buyer confidence about scope
evidence.verbatim: Liveness certification has become table stakes, which can create false confidence: a buyer sees a liveness certification and assumes the system is secure, when the certification speaks only to spoofs shown to the lens[21].

evidence.gloss: Didit Passive Liveness iBeta Level 1 PAD result: 0% attack success, 0% IAPAR across 360 attempts
evidence.verbatim: A concrete illustration of the scope limit: Didit's Passive Liveness is certified to iBeta Level 1 PAD (ISO/IEC 30107-3) with 0% attack success and 0% IAPAR (Impostor Attack Presentation Accept Rate) across 360 tested attempts covering printed photos, screen displays, and video replay[22].

evidence.gloss: Level 1 covers presentation attacks only; no equivalent third-party certification standard exists for injection
evidence.verbatim: Level 1 covers presentation attacks; the vendor does not claim Level 2, and there is no equivalent third-party certification standard for injection attacks the way there is for PAD[22].

evidence.gloss: Didit's injection defense comes from a 200+ fraud signal layer and device/session integrity analysis beyond iBeta Level 1
evidence.verbatim: Injection attack defense there is provided instead through a 200+ fraud signal layer and device/session integrity analysis, which sits beyond what iBeta Level 1 tests[22].

evidence.gloss: Procurement scorecards ask about liveness but never about virtual camera detection (Victor Mendez, Verifyo, in Finextra)
evidence.verbatim: An analysis in Finextra by Victor Mendez, CMO of Verifyo, argues that the current landscape demands a reorientation of the procurement process, noting that "most procurement scorecards ask 'do you have liveness?' and never ask 'do you detect a virtual camera?'"[26].

evidence.gloss: A PAD-certified but injection-blind system is weaker than its certification implies
evidence.verbatim: A verification system certified against presentation attacks but blind to injection is meaningfully weaker than the certification implies[22].

evidence.gloss: Buyer consequence: VCD claims are largely unverifiable, making CEN/TS 18099 independent-lab testing the available substitute
evidence.verbatim: For a buyer, this means claims about virtual camera detection are largely unverifiable against published, independently reproduced methods, which is what makes the CEN/TS 18099 independent-lab testing route the available substitute.

evidence.gloss: Certification scope matters when a vendor cites challenge-response capability
evidence.verbatim: Certification scope matters when a vendor cites a challenge-response capability.

evidence.gloss: iBeta Level 1 vs Level 2 scope, and a vendor claiming only Level 1
evidence.verbatim: But iBeta Level 1 covers printed, digital, and replay presentation attacks, while Level 2 extends to 3D masks and prosthetics; one vendor states plainly that its certification is Level 1 and that it does not claim Level 2[22].

evidence.gloss: No third-party certification standard exists for injection attacks; handled via fraud signals and device/session integrity
evidence.verbatim: The same vendor notes there is no equivalent third-party certification standard for injection attacks the way there is for PAD, so injection defense is handled through a 200+ fraud signal layer and device/session integrity analysis instead[22].

h3.h3: Accuracy numbers move with the threshold, and so does who absorbs the errors

evidence.gloss: Vendor accuracy numbers are quoted at an operating threshold that changes who absorbs the errors
evidence.verbatim: Vendor accuracy numbers are quoted at an operating threshold, and the threshold changes who the errors fall on.

evidence.gloss: At least six top identification algorithms flipped the direction of the black/white male false-positive gap between two thresholds
evidence.verbatim: NIST demonstrated this directly: at least six of the most accurate identification algorithms had higher false-positive rates for black men than white men at one threshold, but lower false-positive rates for black men than white men at another[37].

evidence.gloss: Threshold set to 0.01 percent false positives for white males: over half of the top 17 hit 0.03 percent or better for three other groups
evidence.verbatim: When NIST set thresholds so algorithms had a false-positive rate of 0.01 percent for white males, more than half of the 17 most accurate verification algorithms achieved 0.03 percent or better for black males, Asian men, and white women, meaning three or fewer false matches per 10,000 impostor comparisons versus one per 10,000 for white males[37].

evidence.gloss: At another threshold seven top algorithms showed no false-positive bias, and several favoured black and Asian women over white males
evidence.verbatim: At another threshold, seven of the top algorithms displayed no false-positive bias at all between white men, black men, Asian men, and white females, and several had false-positive rates of 0.003 percent or less for black women or Asian women against 0.001 percent for white males[37].

evidence.gloss: Five of the 17 most accurate algorithms kept false negatives under one percent across all demographics at a 0.01 percent false-positive threshold
evidence.verbatim: Five of the 17 most accurate algorithms had false-negative rates below one percent across all demographic groups when the threshold was set to a 0.01 percent false-positive rate[37].

evidence.gloss: The same data supports two opposite headlines, the reporting trap for buyers
evidence.verbatim: The same data supports two headlines, which is exactly the reporting trap for a buyer reading vendor material.

evidence.gloss: Low absolute error rates make small absolute differences look large in relative terms

evidence.gloss: VisionLabs' Visionlabs-007: 4x relative false-negative gap sitting on a 0.63 percent absolute rate

evidence.gloss: Camvi verification algorithm: 13x relative false-positive gap that is barely one false match per 10,000
evidence.verbatim: A verification algorithm from Camvi, a Silicon Valley firm, had a false-positive rate 13 times higher for American Indian females than for white men at one threshold — a 13x relative gap that amounted to barely more than one false match per 10,000 impostor comparisons among American Indian females[37].

evidence.verbatim: Lab matching accuracy and end-to-end system accuracy are different things.

sections_menu.h2: Layered, continuous identity verification across the hiring funnel

h3.h3: The signal stack: why no single detection feature is a gate

evidence.gloss: Interview integrity is a stack of independent signals, not one feature
evidence.verbatim: The checks that separate a real candidate from a stand-in or a synthetic face are not one feature but a stack of independent signals, each catching a different attack and each failing in a different way.

evidence.gloss: A tool is rated by how many layers it runs and what its docs claim each is tested against
evidence.verbatim: A tool's interview-integrity rating comes down to how many of these layers it actually runs, and what its own documentation says each one is tested against.

evidence.gloss: Multi-layer detection frameworks beat single-method detection for reliability
evidence.verbatim: Modern systems combine audio, video, and behavioral analysis in **multi-layer detection frameworks** rather than relying on a single method, which improves reliability in complex environments[12].

evidence.gloss: Deepfake detection is decision support, not a standalone gate, and depends on conditions
evidence.verbatim: Deepfake detection does not provide absolute certainty. It is a decision support system, not a standalone gate, and its effectiveness depends on input quality, model design, and environmental conditions[12].

evidence.gloss: Named failure modes: quality variance, false positives/negatives, weakened signals, human review needed
evidence.verbatim: Specifically: results vary with audio or video quality; false positives and negatives can occur; advanced synthesis can reduce detectable signals; and human review is often needed for high-risk cases[12].

evidence.gloss: Detection works best inside a layered verification system
evidence.verbatim: Because of this, detection works best inside a layered verification system[12].

evidence.gloss: Detection as a signal with escalation of ambiguous cases to human review
evidence.verbatim: **Detection as support, with a human review layer.** Treat detection as an additional signal rather than a standalone decision-making system, so results are interpreted in context alongside other checks, and escalate ambiguous or flagged cases to manual review where contextual judgment is needed[12].

evidence.gloss: The fragmentation argument: current tools only offer fragments
evidence.verbatim: The fragmentation argument is explicit: current tools only offer fragments, with background checks verifying history, scanners hunting AI text, and risk signals sitting elsewhere[1]

evidence.gloss: The layered approach pairs identity verification, proctoring and real skill assessment
evidence.verbatim: The first is integration: pairing identity verification with AI proctoring during the assessment itself, and with a genuine skill assessment rather than a self-reported claim, is the layered approach[6]

evidence.gloss: Glider's Candidate 360 view integrates identity, behavior and skill signals
evidence.verbatim: integrating identity, behavior, and skill signals so they can be reviewed together rather than in separate systems is the reasoning behind Glider's Candidate 360 view[6].

evidence.gloss: Live interviews recommended as a verification step alongside references and IDV tools
evidence.verbatim: Live interviews are also recommended as a verification step in their own right: a fake candidate can be identified by checking references, using identity verification tools, and conducting live interviews on video interview platforms that can detect anomalies[3].

evidence.gloss: Deepfake detection technology catches fake personas and AI-generated responses
evidence.verbatim: Alongside that, deepfake detection technology uses advanced algorithms to identify artificially generated or manipulated video and audio content, catching candidates who might use fake personas or AI-generated responses to misrepresent themselves[3].

evidence.gloss: Anti-cheating confidentiality agreements as a control
evidence.verbatim: Anti-cheating confidentiality agreements require candidates to sign a document promising not to cheat[3].

evidence.gloss: HYPR Affirm's five documented identity verification controls
evidence.verbatim: For interview-time identity assurance, the vendor-documented control set from an identity verification provider (HYPR Affirm) shows what a hardened live check contains: biometrics using unique physical or behavioural characteristics such as facial recognition; document verification authenticating government-issued IDs, passports and other official documents for signs of tampering or forgery; liveness detection ensuring the person presenting the identity is a real, live individual and not a spoof, a photograph, or a sophisticated deepfake; location verification checking the candidate's physical location against expected or declared information; and manager attestation, a step-up escalation allowing a manager or help desk agent to conduct a live chat and video call for final verification in complex cases[31].

evidence.gloss: Verification applied at hiring-journey touchpoints against three threat types
evidence.verbatim: Verification is applied at critical touchpoints throughout the hiring journey, from initial application through onboarding, against synthetic identities (by cross-referencing multiple data points and using algorithms to detect fabricated personal details), deepfake impersonations (by employing liveness detection and forensic analysis during video interactions to ensure the person on screen is genuinely real), and stolen credentials (by verifying the applicant is the legitimate holder of the presented identity documents)[31].

evidence.gloss: Effective prevention requires IDV, better interviewing, background checks and zero trust
evidence.verbatim: Effective prevention is stated to require a comprehensive identity verification solution, improved interviewing techniques, enhanced background checks, and zero trust principles[31].

evidence.gloss: Recommended layered hiring workflow: AI triage, recruiter time on high-signal candidates, pre-interview verification, emphasis on spontaneity
evidence.verbatim: On the hiring workflow specifically, the recommended shape is layered: use AI to triage and flag risks early, reserve recruiter time for high-signal candidates, add lightweight verification steps before live interviews, and place added emphasis on human interaction and spontaneity in interviews.

evidence.gloss: Claimed outcome of the layered hiring shape: fewer false positives, fake candidates caught, better real-candidate experience
evidence.verbatim: This is described as reducing false positives while ensuring fake candidates do not progress unnoticed, and as improving the experience for real candidates, who move faster through a cleaner funnel[31].

evidence.gloss: Forensics inspects frames, metadata, spectrograms and chain of custody but cannot help during a live call
evidence.verbatim: Investigators can inspect original frames, metadata, audio spectrograms, encoding history, source files, and chain of custody in far greater detail after the event, which supports incident response and legal review, but it does not help someone who must decide during a live call[27].

evidence.gloss: Tactic switching: a defence is not layered if a fraudster can switch from deepfakes to injection attacks
evidence.verbatim: can the system detect tactic switching, given that sophisticated attackers test defences and adapt, and that a defence is not truly layered if a fraudster can find an undefended pathway by switching from deepfakes to injection attacks[28]

evidence.gloss: HireID's 98% synthetic-identity accuracy claim is internal, not independent
evidence.verbatim: HireID's August 17, 2026 "Interview Integrity Platform" announcement claims "over 98% accuracy on synthetic identity detection in internal benchmark testing", which is a vendor claim from internal testing, not an independent evaluation, and should be read as such[58].

h3.h3: Where the checks fire: one top-of-funnel gate is not enough

evidence.gloss: Identity checks need to be continuous, not a single gate at the top of the funnel
evidence.verbatim: This is also the reason identity checks need to be continuous rather than a single gate at the top of the funnel[6].

evidence.gloss: Persona places the same ID+selfie check at up to three funnel points
evidence.verbatim: Persona's candidate verification runs the same primitive — government ID photo plus selfie — but places it at up to three points in the funnel rather than one: at application or screening to establish a verified identity record, before key interviews such as final rounds or technical interviews to confirm the person interviewing is the same person, and at the offer stage to ensure the person hired is the person who interviewed[10].

evidence.gloss: 2FA keeps the same individual participating throughout the hiring process
evidence.verbatim: Adding two-factor authentication (2FA) ensures the same individual is consistently participating throughout the hiring process[14].

evidence.gloss: Risk-based controls: stronger verification for high-access roles, lighter for low-risk
evidence.verbatim: **Risk-based controls.** Apply stronger verification for high-access or high-impact roles while keeping lighter workflows for lower-risk positions, balancing security against resource use[12].

evidence.gloss: Persona makes verification timing buyer-configurable by need, role and risk tolerance
evidence.verbatim: Persona frames the same idea as buyer-configurable: you decide when and how verification happens based on hiring needs, role requirements, and risk tolerance[10].

evidence.gloss: Ongoing verification beyond onboarding guards against delayed or staged impersonation
evidence.verbatim: **Ongoing verification and workflow integration.** Extend identity validation beyond initial onboarding, using early-stage checkpoints to reduce the risk of delayed or staged impersonation attempts[12].

evidence.gloss: The failure mode to buy against is disconnected checks run at multiple stages
evidence.verbatim: The failure mode to buy against is the opposite: organizations that run disconnected checks at multiple stages[36].

evidence.gloss: Checkpoints at application, interview, and offer or onboarding
evidence.verbatim: checkpoints at application, interview, and offer or onboarding stages

evidence.gloss: The most repeated design point: one top-of-funnel check is not enough
evidence.verbatim: The single most repeated design point is that one check at the top of the funnel is not enough.

evidence.verbatim: Cross-session re-verification, checking identity again at assessment, interview, and sometimes onboarding rather than only once at the start, closes the gap that lets a proxy step in later in the process[6].

evidence.gloss: Multi-stage verification catches a later switch
evidence.verbatim: Verification at more than one stage means a switch later still gets caught[6].

evidence.gloss: Vendor framing: a continuous identity record, unbroken from application to Day One
evidence.verbatim: One vendor frames this as a continuous identity record across every stage of the funnel rather than isolated checkpoints, an unbroken chain from application to Day One, so that if the thread breaks anywhere you know before they start[1]

evidence.gloss: Most hiring tools verify once and move on
evidence.verbatim: Most hiring tools verify once and move on[1].

evidence.verbatim: The "front-door only" design premise treats identity verification as a one-time event, judging the session by the token or login state rather than by who is physically present[35].

evidence.gloss: Definition of continuous identity verification: repeated reassessment after login
evidence.verbatim: Continuous identity verification repeatedly reassesses whether the person, device, behaviour, and session remain consistent after login or initial verification[27].

evidence.gloss: Continuous verification beats one-time checks but still needs deepfake detection and approval controls
evidence.verbatim: It is stronger than a one-time check, but high-value decisions still require deepfake detection and independent approval controls[27].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification comes early, framed as standard process rather than suspicion
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification comes early, with a government-issued ID requested as part of pre-screen onboarding and framed as standard process rather than suspicion[10].

evidence.gloss: SHRM June 2025 floor: two-factor identity checks before any live interview round
evidence.verbatim: SHRM's June 2025 guidance sets a floor of at minimum two-factor identity checks before any live interview round, described as enough to deter casual fraud without creating disparate impact while creating a documented audit trail if a placement goes bad and the agency needs to prove due diligence[45].

evidence.gloss: Veriff/iCIMS August 2025 partnership cut proxy fraud 52% by embedding ID verification in scheduling
evidence.verbatim: Layering identity verification into the interview scheduling flow is called the highest-ROI move, with the August 2025 Veriff/iCIMS partnership embedding identity verification directly into interview scheduling and reducing proxy fraud by an average of 52% in pilot programs[45].

evidence.gloss: A standardized second-round identity checkpoint before the final stage is recommended
evidence.verbatim: A standardized second-round identity checkpoint before the final stage is also recommended[45].

evidence.gloss: Automated conversational screens standardize early questions and surface fraud clustering by channel
evidence.verbatim: an automated conversational screen can standardize early questions, capture structured responses, and flag inconsistencies before a recruiter spends time on a live interview, and looking for duplicate applicants, mismatched locations, and patterns across applications, with source-level transparency, shows whether fraud is clustering around specific channels[43]

evidence.verbatim: But the boundary of one-time checks is explicit: one-time background checks, document uploads, and manual review processes cannot validate who is actually behind the screen or guarantee continuity of identity from screening to interview to Day 1 and beyond, and those gaps make it easier for impostors to move through recruiting workflows undetected[46].

evidence.verbatim: The challenge is bigger in remote, frontline, and third-party hiring environments, where shared devices, high churn, fragmented ownership across HR and IT, and staffing or recruiting intermediaries all create blind spots[46].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification happens once at the first live stage, as a real check not a behavioural guess
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification should then happen exactly once, at the first live stage, and should be a real identity check rather than a behavioural guess, because identity is verifiable and intent is not[8].

evidence.gloss: One identity check is not enough because a verified person can front for another actor
evidence.verbatim: A single identity check is not enough, because the individual who passes one stage can be a real person helping another actor get through the next one[9].

evidence.gloss: A robust control asks the longitudinal question: is this still the same verified person
evidence.verbatim: A robust control therefore asks a longitudinal question: is this still the same verified person?[9]

evidence.verbatim: Recommended controls include government ID verification before the offer stage, reference and background checks, signed employment agreements before day one, and cameras on for all remote work rather than just interviews[49].

evidence.gloss: Request identity verification early in pre-screen onboarding, framed as standard process
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification should be requested early, as part of pre-screen onboarding, framed as standard process rather than suspicion, with legitimate verification platforms handling it professionally and unobtrusively[10].

evidence.gloss: SHRM June 2025: two-factor identity checks before any live round as a floor, not a ceiling
evidence.verbatim: SHRM's June 2025 guidance recommends implementing at minimum two-factor identity checks before any live interview round, described as a floor rather than a ceiling: enough to deter casual fraud without creating disparate impact, and enough to create a documented audit trail if a placement goes bad and the agency needs to prove due diligence[45].

evidence.gloss: It is a process change in a defined sequence; buying detection first wastes the subscription
evidence.verbatim: That is a process change, not a purchase, and it runs in a defined sequence where the order matters more than the individual steps; buying detection software before rewriting questions means paying a subscription to measure a problem the process change would have removed[8].

evidence.gloss: Highest-ROI move: ID check plus liveness selfie before the calendar invite; Veriff/iCIMS 52% proxy fraud reduction
evidence.verbatim: Layering identity verification into the interview scheduling flow is described as the highest-ROI move: if the candidate must complete a government-ID check and a liveness selfie before the interview calendar invite fires, the lowest-effort proxy attacks are eliminated, and the August 2025 Veriff/iCIMS pilot data showing a 52% average reduction in proxy fraud indicates the impact ceiling[45].

evidence.gloss: A standardised second-round identity checkpoint before the final stage
evidence.verbatim: A standardised second-round identity checkpoint sits before the final stage[45].

evidence.verbatim: The question is not whether proxy detection will become standard, but whether a team implements it before a $50,000 bad hire forces the conversation[45].

evidence.gloss: SHRM June 2025: two-factor identity checks before live rounds create a due-diligence audit trail
evidence.verbatim: SHRM's June 2025 guidance recommends at minimum two-factor identity checks before any live interview round, described as enough to deter casual fraud without creating disparate impact, and as creating a documented audit trail if a placement goes bad and the agency needs to prove due diligence [45].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification is not a one-time gate
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification is not a one-time gate either.

evidence.gloss: Continuous identity assurance reuses the trust anchor across every later hiring stage
evidence.verbatim: Continuous identity assurance begins once the trust anchor is established, and in organizations with multiple interview rounds that anchor is used to confirm that the same verified person appears for the second interview, the third interview, the background check, the offer review, and Day 1[46].

evidence.gloss: Codility supports re-sending a verification after a failed check

evidence.verbatim: Vendors like HireID market this repetition explicitly as "identity continuity"[58].

h3.h3: Wiring verification into the ATS and HR stack

evidence.gloss: Detection outputs should embed into HR and identity systems without major redesign
evidence.verbatim: Detection outputs should embed into existing HR platforms and identity management systems so they directly support operational decisions[12], without requiring major process redesign[12].

evidence.gloss: Persona carries one identity across the employee life cycle, closing the HR-IT gap
evidence.verbatim: Persona's version of this runs one identity across the employee life cycle: the identity confirmed during hiring carries into onboarding, IT provisioning, credential issuance, system provisioning, account recovery, and ongoing authentication, closing a gap between HR and IT that point solutions verifying identity once leave open[10].

evidence.gloss: Persona integrates with Greenhouse, Ashby and Workday
evidence.verbatim: It integrates directly with Greenhouse, Ashby, and Workday so buyers do not have to overhaul the hiring process[10].

evidence.gloss: iCIMS ID Verification embeds checks inside the iCIMS talent platform and candidate profiles
evidence.verbatim: iCIMS ID Verification embeds identity checks early inside the iCIMS talent platform, with verification data flowing into candidate profiles and hiring stages so teams keep a connected workflow without leaving the system of record[11].

evidence.gloss: ATS and interview-tool integration so identity and exam integrity check together
evidence.verbatim: integration with existing ATS and interview tools including the vendor's own AI proctoring environment so identity and exam integrity are checked together

evidence.gloss: Single-pipeline platform for hourly and frontline hiring at volume
evidence.verbatim: One platform argues that combining identity verification, proctoring and conversational AI interviews in a single pipeline reduces the risk of verification gaps between screening stages, and is purpose-built for hourly and frontline hiring at volume where speed and consistency matter as much as detection depth[8].

h3.h3: What each added check costs the real candidate

evidence.gloss: Every verification step adds a new drop-out point for real candidates
evidence.verbatim: Every added verification step (document upload, face capture, browser lockdown) lands on top of this existing failure surface, and each one is a new place for a genuine candidate to drop out.

evidence.gloss: Candidate-side cost is a real evaluation input; some candidates will not complete a recorded interview
evidence.verbatim: Candidate-side cost is a real evaluation input. Some proportion of candidates in competitive markets simply will not complete a recorded interview; the mitigation is not to abandon the format but to use it where the trade is favourable — high applicant volume, early stage, clearly explained, with a short question set[35].

evidence.gloss: An easy-to-request alternative route for disadvantaged candidates is a design requirement, not an edge case
evidence.verbatim: Candidates who face barriers, including those with disabilities or connectivity constraints, may be disadvantaged by a timed recorded or conversational format, so an alternative route must be available and easy to request; this is a design requirement, not an edge case[35].

evidence.gloss: The standard objection to buying identity verification is added funnel friction
evidence.verbatim: The standard objection to buying identity verification is that it adds funnel friction.

evidence.gloss: Counter-argument: verification is designed for the 99.9%; a two-minute ID check finishes before the recruiter moves on
evidence.verbatim: The counter-argument in the collected material is that the verification process is designed for the 99.9% who move through it, while a fraudulent candidate relying on a stolen identity or a deepfake is the one for whom each layer creates an obstacle; a real candidate completing a two-minute ID check on their phone is done before the recruiter has moved to the next application[36].

evidence.gloss: Proof runs 100+ passive risk indicators on application with no candidate step, returning a risk signal in the ATS
evidence.verbatim: Mechanically, the first check a candidate encounters can be invisible: on application, Proof runs passive signals in the background, over a hundred risk indicators tied to the email address, phone number, and other submitted contact details, with no extra step, no link to click, and no form to fill out, returning a risk signal to the recruiter in the ATS[36].

evidence.gloss: Real candidates with real contact details pass the passive check without knowing it happened
evidence.verbatim: Real candidates with real contact information pass without any awareness it happened[36].

evidence.gloss: Government ID and liveness checks can be triggered at whatever stage the team configures
evidence.verbatim: For candidates who move into active consideration, a government ID and liveness check can be triggered at whatever stage the team configures[36].

evidence.gloss: A uniform check applied to every candidate is better for fairness and compliance, and documents fairness
evidence.verbatim: A uniform process also means every candidate gets the same check applied the same way, regardless of who a recruiter thinks might be suspicious, which is better for candidates and for compliance; a documented, consistent process is a record of fairness, not just a record of risk[36].

evidence.gloss: Sets the under-five-minutes benchmark as a time budget and explains which inputs belong before a first call versus later in the process.
evidence.verbatim:
A job application should take under five minutes to complete on a phone. That is the working benchmark most talent teams land on, because it lines up with how long a motivated candidate will spend before their attention drifts. Past five minutes, drop-off climbs sharply, and the people you lose skew toward the experienced candidates who have other offers.
Five minutes is a time budget, not a feature list. It forces the useful question: what do you truly need before a first conversation? Usually that is a resume, contact details, a couple of role-specific questions, and consent to be contacted. Everything else (availability windows, salary history, long-form essays, work samples) belongs later in the process, once both sides have shown real interest. If a step does not help you decide who moves forward this week, it does not belong in the first five minutes. When you are unsure, pull the step out and watch whether decision quality actually drops. It rarely does.

evidence.gloss: Worked example of a 500-person software company cutting 38 fields across four pages down to 14 fields plus a 6-minute mobile assessment, and what the sequence achieved.
evidence.verbatim:
Picture a 500-person software company hiring 20 support agents a quarter. Their old flow ran 38 fields across four pages, desktop-tuned, with a mandatory account. Most phone applicants gave up on page two. The rework was not fancy: 14 fields, resume parsing to pre-fill the top of the form, no account, a progress bar, and a 6-minute mobile skills assessment sent by automatic invitation right after submission.
The point of the example is the sequence, not a promised number. By moving one short assessment early and stripping the form down, the team got scored evidence on every finisher before the first call, and candidates spent their five minutes proving they could do the work instead of retyping a resume. That is a user-friendly application process doing two jobs at once: better experience for the candidate, better shortlist for the recruiter.

evidence.gloss: Key takeaways: treat the form as product, design for phone (58% mobile stat), cost every field, move evidence earlier, measure and fix one step, keep humans deciding.
evidence.verbatim:
- Treat the form as the product. The application is a first impression, so a short, clear flow signals respect and keeps strong candidates in your pool. Audit it as often as you audit your careers page.
- Design for the phone, not the laptop. With 58% of job seekers searching on mobile, a desktop-only form leaks most of your traffic, which is why every step needs to work on a real phone before launch, on a normal connection.
- Every field has a cost. Extra fields screen for patience, not skill, and the best candidates quit first. Cut to what you will read this week and pre-fill the rest from the resume.
- Move evidence earlier, not later. A short, role-relevant assessment right after a lean application scores fit before the first call, which shortens the loop and raises shortlist quality at the same time.
- Measure, then fix a specific step. Completion rate, time to apply, satisfaction, and acceptance point to exactly where people drop, so review them monthly and tie each dip to one fixable step.
- Keep humans in the decision. AI can parse resumes and summarize results, but your team owns the call. Automation should remove typing and waiting, never judgment.

evidence.gloss: Argues the 2026 talent market favors candidates, citing SHRM cost per hire above $4,700, IBM's 70% hire-quality lift, and Gartner's 60% application abandonment, plus three benchmark outcomes (85%+ acceptance, sub-20-day time to hire, higher quality of hire).
evidence.verbatim:
The talent market shifted permanently in favor of candidates. Workers now expect speed, respect, and clarity at every stage of the hiring process.
SHRM data places the average cost per hire above $4,700, which makes every drop-off expensive. IBM research connects strong candidate experience to a 70% lift in hire quality across roles.
Gartner finds that 60% of candidates abandon applications because of friction or poor communication. Recruiters who close these gaps win measurable business outcomes within one hiring cycle.
Three outcomes separate top recruiters from the rest:
- Offer acceptance rates climb above 85%.
- Time to hire drops below 20 days.
- Quality of hire scores rise across every team.
Related resources: For deeper analysis, see our breakdown of recruitment metrics that matter.

evidence.gloss: Tactic 1: write outcome-driven job descriptions under 400 words that state purpose, impact, responsibilities, must-have skills, and salary range in the first 100 words.
evidence.verbatim:
Long, vague job posts drive top candidates away within seconds. Top recruiters now write outcome-driven job descriptions that clearly define responsibilities, expectations, and growth opportunities
Keep job descriptions under 400 words whenever possible. In the first 100 words, explain the role’s purpose, business impact, core responsibilities, must-have skills, and salary range.
This helps candidates quickly decide whether the opportunity aligns with their career goals.
Related resources: Use our guide on creating effective job descriptions, and try our free job description generator to create inclusive job descriptions

evidence.gloss: Tactic 2: cut applications to under five minutes, citing Korn Ferry's finding that longer forms lose 40% of qualified candidates, and defer deep questions to the assessment stage.
evidence.verbatim:
Korn Ferry research shows that applications longer than five minutes lose 40% of qualified candidates. Top recruiters strip their applications down to name, contact, resume, and one signal question.
Ask candidates only what you need to make an initial decision. Save deep questions for the assessment stage.

sections_menu.h2: Deploying these checks: matching verification strictness to role risk

h3.h3: Which roles justify stronger identity checks

evidence.gloss: Roles with access to code, customer data, finance, infrastructure or admin tools need stronger checks
evidence.verbatim: Roles with access to code, customer data, finance systems, infrastructure or admin tools need stronger checks than the rest[7].

evidence.gloss: Which roles need stronger checks
evidence.verbatim: Roles with access to code, customer data, finance systems, infrastructure, or admin tools need stronger checks[7].

evidence.gloss: Match the verification process to the risk the role creates
evidence.verbatim: The practical goal is to match the verification process to the risk created by the role[7].

evidence.gloss: Set response thresholds by business impact, not by treating a score as a final identity judgment
evidence.verbatim: Response thresholds should be set around business impact rather than treating a score as a final identity judgment.

evidence.gloss: Low-access roles: consequence is hiring waste, delays, replacement search
evidence.verbatim: In a low-access role, candidate fraud may lead to hiring waste, delayed projects, or a replacement search[7].

evidence.gloss: High-access roles turn fraud into an identity and access-control problem
evidence.verbatim: In roles tied to engineering, finance, cybersecurity, IT administration, or customer-data operations, the same issue can become an identity and access-control problem because the wrong person may receive credentials, devices, or sensitive system access[7].

evidence.gloss: Fake hires create compliance risk and costly replacement cycles post-onboarding
evidence.verbatim: Fake candidates that slip through also create compliance and security risks and expensive replacement hiring cycles if discovered after onboarding[19].

h3.h3: The proctoring and monitoring tiers to choose between

evidence.gloss: The four proctoring models compared: AI/automated, live, record-and-review, and hybrid, with which exam stakes and volumes each suits
evidence.verbatim:
Not every assessment needs the same level of control. Most setups fall into four models, and the right one depends on exam stakes, review capacity, budget, and how much friction your candidates will tolerate. For a deeper breakdown, see the types of online exam proctoring.
- AI (automated) proctoring: the system monitors the session and flags suspicious activity in real time, with no human watching live. Best for volume.
- Live proctoring: a human proctor watches the session as it happens and can step in. Best for small, high-stakes batches.
- Record-and-review: the session is recorded and reviewed afterward. A middle ground when live coverage is not practical.
- Hybrid proctoring: AI monitors every session and a person reviews the flags or joins live when needed. The model most hiring teams land on.

evidence.gloss: Introduces the three-tier integrity model that scales controls by role risk instead of applying uniform policy
evidence.verbatim: The most defensible integrity setups in 2026 use three tiers of control that activate based on role risk level rather than uniform policy. This structure reduces candidate friction on lower-risk roles while maintaining rigorous detection coverage where it matters most.

evidence.gloss: Tier 1 passive always-on controls: browser lockdown, basic webcam capture, question randomisation, IP monitoring, catching opportunistic cheating with no friction or manual review
evidence.verbatim:
Tier 1 controls run on every assessment regardless of role level. These include browser lockdown, basic webcam capture, question randomization from a validated item bank, and IP-level monitoring for geographic anomalies.
These controls create no friction for compliant candidates and detect opportunistic cheating, which accounts for the majority of violations in volume hiring pipelines. No manual review is required when sessions pass without flags.
Digital hiring optimisation frameworks treat Tier 1 controls as the default layer for all assessment types. Escalation to Tier 2 happens only when the role’s criticality or access level warrants it.

evidence.gloss: Tier 2 active role-sensitive monitoring: facial comparison, gaze tracking, behavioural biometrics, triggered by role criticality and access level rather than seniority
evidence.verbatim:
Tier 2 controls activate for roles where the assessment result directly determines the hiring decision. This includes real-time facial comparison, gaze tracking, behavioural biometrics, and AI anomaly detection on response timing and pattern.
The trigger for Tier 2 should be role criticality and access level, not seniority alone. A junior developer with direct access to production code warrants the same monitoring tier as a senior engineer, and hiring teams that conflate seniority with risk level consistently under-protect high-access junior roles.
Interview scorecards used alongside Tier 2 assessment results create a dual data point for hiring decisions. A candidate whose monitored assessment score diverges significantly from their interview performance warrants a closer review before an offer goes out.

evidence.gloss: Tier 3 human post-assessment review of flagged sessions, preventing false positives and negatives and providing compliance documentation in regulated sectors
evidence.verbatim:
Tier 3 is a human review step for sessions that generated composite anomaly flags in Tiers 1 or 2. A reviewer examines the flagged session recording, compares the anomaly against the candidate’s full response pattern, and makes a pass, re-test, or disqualification decision.
Post-assessment review prevents both false positives and false negatives. A candidate whose internet connection caused timing anomalies should not be disqualified without review, and a candidate with a perfect score whose timing pattern matches AI output should not advance without one.
This review step also serves a compliance function in regulated sectors. Organisations where job specifications include minimum assessment score requirements need documented review trails to demonstrate that thresholds were applied consistently.

evidence.gloss: Testlify's three proctoring modes (Standard, Strict, Custom) in a table matching strictness to role type
evidence.verbatim:
Testlify offers three proctoring modes so strictness fits the role, not a one-size policy. Standard balances monitoring with candidate comfort, Strict enforces the full set of controls, and Custom lets you pick exactly which signals run.
ModeBest forHow it behaves
StandardEarly screens, high volumeCore monitoring with flexibility for honest candidates
StrictFinal rounds, senior or sensitive rolesFull control set enforced, minimal leeway
CustomRoles with specific riskYou choose which controls run, per assessment

evidence.gloss: How to pick a proctoring level by weighing role stakes against candidate friction, with four practical selection rules
evidence.verbatim:
Choose your proctoring level by weighing the stakes of the role against the friction for the candidate. The higher the cost of a bad or faked result, the more controls are worth it. For a quick first-round screen, lighter monitoring keeps good candidates moving; for a final technical test, strict lockdown earns its keep.
- Map the risk: how damaging is a fake or assisted score for this specific role?
- Start light on early, high-volume steps and tighten as candidates advance.
- Tell candidates what is monitored and why. Transparency cuts anxiety and drop-off.
- Treat every flag as a prompt to review, never as an automatic rejection.

evidence.gloss: Configurable strictness by assessment stakes (violation limits, snapshot intervals, per-control toggles) plus a pro tip to trial on candidates' real devices because setup friction, not detection, is the usual failure
evidence.verbatim:
A short screening test and a final-round assessment do not deserve the same rules. Light monitoring suits one; stricter limits and stronger evidence suit the other. Look for a platform that lets you decide when to warn, when to flag, and when to end a session based on the test you are running, instead of forcing one setup on everyone.
Testlify lets hiring teams configure proctoring rules directly inside the assessment workflow.
In Testlify, you can configure violation limits, snapshot intervals, and individual monitoring controls to fit the assessment rather than the other way round.
Pro tip: before you roll a proctor out widely, run one real assessment through it on the exact devices your candidates use, including older laptops and mobiles. Most failures are not detection misses, they are setup friction: a camera that will not start or a lockdown setting that blocks an honest candidate. Catch that in a trial, not on a finalist.

h3.h3: Human review on every flag, no automatic rejections

evidence.gloss: AI should assist verification, not replace judgment; sensitive roles need human review
evidence.verbatim: AI should assist verification and screening, not replace judgment, and final decisions, especially for sensitive or access-heavy roles, should include human review[43].

evidence.gloss: The defensible question in a live interview is about documented controls and identity, not suspicion
evidence.verbatim: The defensible question during a live interview is not "does this person look suspicious to me?" It is "can we establish, using the same documented controls we apply to comparable candidates, that this is the same person and that this person produced the evidence we are evaluating?

h3.h3: What candidates are told, and how they tell it from a scam

evidence.gloss: The signals monitored should be stated clearly in candidate instructions
evidence.verbatim: The exact signals monitored should be stated clearly in the candidate instructions[33].

evidence.gloss: Candidate-facing IDV preparation: mobile-first instructions, acceptable IDs, a provider FAQ
evidence.verbatim: Candidate-facing preparation includes mobile-first instructions and guidance on acceptable IDs and selfies, requesting a candidate FAQ from the provider, and agreeing best practices for handling candidate issues or drop-offs[47].

evidence.gloss: Running IDV creates a communications duty: timing and channel let candidates tell it from a scam
evidence.verbatim: An employer running IDV inherits a communications duty: the timing and channel of your request are what let a candidate distinguish it from a scam.

evidence.gloss: Scammers imitate verification requests; FTC says real employers do not ask before hiring
evidence.verbatim: Separately, the request itself can be counterfeited: scammers now imitate verification requests, and the FTC's guidance is that "Real employers won't ask for that kind of information before they've actually interviewed and hired you," referring to driver's licenses, Social Security numbers, and bank account details requested as "employment paperwork" (FTC Consumer Alert, July 7, 2025)[26].

evidence.gloss: Rollout advice to protect candidate experience: disclose proctoring in the invite, tier strictness by funnel stage, plan who reviews flags and how candidates respond, and pilot on one role first.
evidence.verbatim:
The fastest way to waste a proctoring tool is to switch every control to maximum and surprise applicants with it. Strong candidates have options, and a clunky, invasive test is an easy reason to walk. A few practical moves keep integrity high and drop-off low.
Tell candidates up front. A short line in the invite that explains the test is proctored, what gets recorded, and why, removes the surprise and filters out people who were planning to cheat anyway. Transparency is a deterrent on its own. Next, tier the strictness. Early-funnel screens for a large applicant pool can run light monitoring, while final-round assessments for a senior or high-trust role earn full lockdown and identity verification. One setting for every role is the mistake that generates a flood of low-value flags.
Then plan for the review, not just the capture. Proctoring produces evidence, and someone has to read it. Decide in advance who reviews flagged sessions, what counts as a real violation versus noise (a glance away is not a second person in the room), and how a candidate can respond before any decision is made. That last point protects both fairness and your brand.
