Run a small pilot on one role before you turn proctoring on across the pipeline, so you learn your own false-positive rate on friendly candidates first. Get these basics right and proctoring stops feeling like surveillance and starts working as quiet insurance on every score.

h3.h3: Piloting before rollout: the metrics that decide whether it scales

evidence.gloss: IDV deployment is framed as cross-functional, not a feature toggle
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification guidance frames deployment as a cross-functional exercise, not a feature toggle.

evidence.gloss: The IDV quick action checklist, from mapping high-risk roles to piloting before rollout
evidence.verbatim: The quick action checklist: map hiring stages and high-risk roles where IDV will be implemented; define internal policies for handling failed or canceled results with HR, Risk, and Legal; train teams on the candidate experience and workflow; confirm legal/privacy compliance for data collection and handling; test the IDV flow internally or with a small pilot group; and refine the workflow before full rollout[47].

evidence.gloss: The IDV pilot tracks completion, time-to-verify, drop-off and fraud detected before scaling
evidence.verbatim: The pilot stage tracks completion rates, time-to-verify, drop-off, and fraud detected, refining communications, policies, and workflow before scaling[47].

evidence.gloss: Deployment guidance built on the Testlify Assessment Integrity Framework's six human-led layers, with five rules: set strictness by stakes, verify identity then step back, route every flag to a human with no auto-rejections, keep evidence but drop surveillance, and design assessments to resist shortcuts; ends with a support-team hiring example (truncated).
evidence.verbatim:
The way to get value without the fairness problems is to treat proctoring as a system, not a switch. The Testlify Assessment Integrity Framework protects the trustworthiness of results through six layers that stay human-led: identity assurance, environment control, behavior monitoring, AI-assistance detection, reviewable evidence, and configurable strictness matched to the role. The point of the framework is restraint as much as coverage, dial up only the controls a given role justifies.
- Set strictness by stakes. A first-round skills screen needs identity plus light monitoring. A final assessment for a finance or security role earns full controls and a live reviewer.
- Verify identity, then step back. Confirm the person once, then let monitoring run quietly so an honest candidate mostly forgets it is there.
- Route every flag to a human. No auto-rejections. A reviewer reads the flag in context and decides whether it changes anything.
- Keep the evidence, drop the surveillance. Store the session score and timeline you would defend to a candidate, and nothing you would be uncomfortable explaining.
- Design the assessment to resist shortcuts. Follow-ups, live explanation, and role-specific tasks do more against AI cheating than any single monitor ever will.
Here is how that looks in practice. A support team hiring 40 remote agents a quarter runs a 25-minute situational judgment and typing assessment as the first screen, with record-and-review proctoring and identity verification on. AI scores every session overnight; a coordinator reviews only the 6 or 7 flagged as high risk the next morning. Candidates who reach the final round retake a shorter task under AI-assisted live proctoring, where a recruiter can watch in real time. The team keeps its shortlist honest without asking a human to watch 300 hours of webcam footage.
Proctoring earns its place only when people stay in charge of the call. As Testlify’s founder Abhishek Shah put it when describing the company’s approach to AI in hiring:
It’s not about replacing recruiters. It’s about empowering them to focus on high-value decisions rather than repetitive tasks.
Abhishek Shah, Founder, Testlify
If you are choosing a tool, weigh it against these layers rather than a feature checklist; the AI proctoring buyer’s guide walks through the questions to ask, and the high-stakes proctored exam guide covers setup for the highest-stakes cases.
Run fairer, more secure assessments. Turn on identity checks and AI proctoring, keep every decision human-led, and give your team an evidence trail it can stand behind. Start free with Testlify, or book a demo to see proctoring configured for your specific roles.

sections_menu.h2: Fraud flags: what a detection score proves, and the human process that has to sit behind it

h3.h3: A detection score is a signal, not proof

evidence.gloss: Algorithms identify anomalies but do not evaluate them; the flag is not the decision
evidence.verbatim: An algorithm identifies anomalies; it does not evaluate them, so the flag is not the decision [20].

evidence.gloss: AI Check is a context signal, not a verdict, and can false-positive on certain natural styles
evidence.verbatim: AI Check flags responses with patterns consistent with AI-assisted phrasing, off-screen reading, or copy-pasted output, and is a context signal rather than a verdict; the model can produce false positives, especially for candidates whose natural style happens to match generated text patterns [21].

evidence.gloss: A detector gives a risk signal, not a guarantee; attacks can combine real person, fake face, cloned speech, manipulated feed
evidence.verbatim: A detector produces a risk signal rather than an absolute guarantee, and a convincing attack can combine a real person, a fake face, cloned speech, and a manipulated camera feed[27].

evidence.gloss: Definitions of false positive and false negative in media detection
evidence.verbatim: A false positive occurs when authentic media is incorrectly flagged as synthetic; a false negative occurs when manipulated media is incorrectly accepted as genuine[27].

evidence.gloss: Detection failure modes: missed unfamiliar manipulations, false flags under poor lighting, blindness on compromised device with real feed
evidence.verbatim: Detection can miss an unfamiliar manipulation, flag a legitimate person under poor lighting, or lose visibility entirely when an attacker uses a compromised device and a real camera feed[27].

evidence.gloss: Guidance: set response thresholds around business impact rather than treating a score as a final identity judgment
evidence.verbatim: Security teams should set response thresholds around business impact rather than treat a score as a final identity judgment[27].

evidence.gloss: The buyer distinction: AI that spots signals vs process that interprets them
evidence.verbatim: The important distinction for a buyer is between the AI that identifies signals and the institutional process that decides what those signals mean[33].

evidence.gloss: Detection can see what happened but not why or whether it was illegitimate
evidence.verbatim: A system may detect that a face disappeared, that another voice was present, or that the exam window lost focus, but it cannot always determine why that happened or whether it was illegitimate[33].

evidence.gloss: Detection tools work on signal, not proof
evidence.verbatim: Detection tools work on signal, not proof.

evidence.gloss: Text detectors score perplexity and burstiness, asking if writing is too smooth to be human
evidence.verbatim: Text detectors score perplexity and burstiness, essentially asking whether writing is statistically too smooth to be human.

evidence.gloss: Video and audio tools watch gaze drift, pause structure, keystrokes and lip-sync artefacts
evidence.verbatim: Video and audio tools watch for gaze drift, unnatural pause structure before answers, keystroke patterns, and lip-sync artefacts.

evidence.gloss: These tools observe correlates of cheating, and a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation
evidence.verbatim: None of these observe cheating; they observe correlates of cheating, and then a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation[8].

evidence.gloss: Separate the AI that identifies signals from the process that decides meaning; systems can't say why
evidence.verbatim: The distinction to hold onto is between the AI that identifies signals and the institutional process that decides what those signals mean: the system may detect that a face disappeared, another voice was present, or the exam window lost focus, but it cannot always determine why that happened[33].

evidence.gloss: Definitions: false positive flags authentic media, false negative accepts manipulated media
evidence.verbatim: A false positive occurs when authentic media is incorrectly flagged as synthetic; a false negative occurs when manipulated media is incorrectly accepted as genuine.

evidence.gloss: Detection tools produce signal rather than proof
evidence.verbatim: Detection tools work on signal, not proof.

evidence.gloss: What text detectors and video/audio tools actually measure
evidence.verbatim: Text detectors score perplexity and burstiness, essentially asking whether writing is statistically too smooth to be human; video and audio tools watch for gaze drift, unnatural pause structure before answers, keystroke patterns, and lip-sync artefacts.

evidence.gloss: Tools observe correlates of cheating, and a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation
evidence.verbatim: None of these observe cheating. They observe correlates of cheating, and then a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation[8].

evidence.gloss: Storing "AI detected" without which kind supports neither a fair nor a defensible decision
evidence.verbatim: A record that stores "AI detected" without preserving which of these two things was detected cannot support either a fair decision or a defensible one, since candidate fraud is a spectrum and different behavior requires different controls [9].

evidence.gloss: Detection tools work on signal rather than proof
evidence.verbatim: Detection tools work on signal, not proof.

evidence.gloss: Detectors observe correlates, and a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation
evidence.verbatim: None of these observe cheating; they observe correlates of cheating, and then a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation[8].

evidence.gloss: Probabilistic outputs mean the same tool flags fraudsters and honest applicants
evidence.verbatim: Outputs are probabilities rather than proof, which is why the same tool that flags a fraudster also flags a share of honest applicants[8].

evidence.gloss: Identity verification answers only whether the person in the chair is the applicant; tool use is a separate policy
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification answers exactly one question: whether the person in the chair is the applicant. It says nothing about which tools that person used; the tool question is governed by a separate employer policy that varies and is worth reading before the interview rather than during it[58].

evidence.gloss: Proxy interviewing is misrepresentation of identity; permitted assistance is a different act
evidence.verbatim: Having someone else sit the interview is misrepresentation of identity, and identity verification exists precisely to catch it; preparing thoroughly and using assistance within whatever the employer's stated policy permits is a different act with different consequences[58].

evidence.gloss: How an online detection service reports: authentic/manipulated/inconclusive, suspected region, probability score
evidence.verbatim: An online service typically labels media as likely authentic, likely manipulated, or inconclusive, and may identify a suspected region such as a face, voice track, background, or edited segment, attaching a probability or confidence score[63].

evidence.gloss: A detection score describes only the model's reading of the pixels and waveforms, nothing beyond them
evidence.verbatim: That number describes the model's reading of the pixels and waveforms in front of it, and nothing beyond them[63].

evidence.gloss: A confidence score is a triage signal: high scores trigger preservation and verification, low scores must not end a high-stakes investigation
evidence.verbatim: A confidence score is a triage signal that should route a file toward a decision rather than replace one: a high score should trigger preservation of the original file, review of its source and transmission history, and independent verification through a trusted channel, while a low score should not end an investigation involving money, credentials, confidential data, or executive authority, because compression, cropping, re-recording, and other alterations can remove the artifacts a detector expects[63].

evidence.gloss: Detection scores are not verdicts
evidence.verbatim: Detection scores are not verdicts.

evidence.gloss: False positive and false negative defined for media detection
evidence.verbatim: A false positive occurs when authentic media is incorrectly flagged as synthetic; a false negative occurs when manipulated media is incorrectly accepted as genuine[27].

evidence.gloss: Set thresholds by business impact and verify independently on low-confidence calls
evidence.verbatim: The recommended posture is to set response thresholds around business impact rather than treat a score as a final identity judgment, and to trigger independent verification on low-confidence calls in high-consequence situations even when the participant looks familiar[27].

evidence.gloss: Detection degrades in poor lighting and goes blind against a compromised device feed
evidence.verbatim: Detection also degrades under ordinary conditions, including poor lighting, and can lose visibility entirely when an attacker uses a compromised device feeding a real camera feed[27].

h3.h3: False positives and who pays for them

evidence.gloss: The false-positive cost falls almost entirely on the candidate
evidence.verbatim: A false positive is a cost borne almost entirely by the candidate.

evidence.gloss: Definition of a proctoring false positive
evidence.verbatim: A false positive is when a proctoring system flags a test taker for suspected misconduct that did not occur

evidence.gloss: Without human review, false positives are designed into the process
evidence.verbatim: When a flag becomes an outcome without human review, false positives are built into the process by design [20].

evidence.gloss: Stanford/Cell Press: over half of non-native English writing samples misclassified as AI-generated
evidence.verbatim: Stanford research published in Cell Press found that over half of writing samples from non-native English speakers were misclassified as AI-generated by automated detectors, while native samples were identified accurately, and the same bias risk exists in proctoring systems that act on flags [20].

evidence.gloss: The buying question: is every flagged session human-reviewed before any outcome, at every price point
evidence.verbatim: The buying question that follows is not whether a platform offers human review but whether every flagged session is reviewed by a person before any outcome is issued, at every price point, without paying extra, because where human review is optional the vast majority of flagged sessions never receive it [20].

evidence.gloss: Rapport advice conflicts with monitoring posture because anxiety mimics fraud cues
evidence.verbatim: That rapport-building advice sits in tension with the monitoring posture: the same behavioural cues that indicate coaching or fraud — looking away, tone shifts, hesitation — are also what an anxious, under-prepared, or badly-connected genuine candidate produces, which is precisely why the guidance treats a flag as a prompt to rewatch rather than a verdict[4].

evidence.gloss: No standardized testing of automation bias in face recognition operators; informing reviewers mitigates it
evidence.verbatim: there is no standardized third-party testing measuring the impact of automation bias — the propensity to overly rely on or trust technological system outputs — on face recognition technology operators, and some research suggests face recognition results can bias human reviewers' analysis of face similarity, at least when reviewers are not fully informed about the potential for algorithm errors; informing them about that potential helps mitigate the risk[18].

evidence.gloss: Do not accuse on one odd pause or bad connection, and do not confuse nerves with fraud
evidence.verbatim: Do not accuse someone based on one odd pause or a bad internet connection, and do not confuse nerves with fraud: some strong candidates are simply awkward on video or unaccustomed to high-pressure interviews[10].

evidence.gloss: A probability does not survive a hiring committee that wants a yes or no
evidence.verbatim: A detector score is a probability, and probabilities do not survive contact with a hiring committee that wants a yes or a no.

evidence.gloss: A score on a scorecard becomes a finding, turning a 61% false positive rate into a rejection
evidence.verbatim: Once a number is on a scorecard, it gets treated as a finding, which is exactly how a 61% false positive rate turns into a rejection letter[8].

evidence.gloss: Stanford/Patterns study details: 7 detectors, 91 TOEFL essays, 61.22% false positive rate, 97.8% flagged
evidence.verbatim: The Stanford research behind that figure, published in the Cell Press journal Patterns by Weixin Liang and colleagues, ran seven widely used GPT detectors against 91 human-written TOEFL essays and 88 essays by US eighth graders: near-perfect on the American students, an average 61.22% false positive rate on the non-native English writers, with 97.8% of the TOEFL essays flagged as AI-generated by at least one detector[8].

evidence.gloss: Rejecting on a detector score alone discards qualified candidates at a high rate
evidence.verbatim: Any rejection based solely on a detector score will discard qualified candidates at a high rate[8].

evidence.gloss: The accused bears the cost and a probability score has no appeal
evidence.verbatim: The cost is borne by the accused, not the accuser, and there is no appeal built into a probability score.

evidence.gloss: Jason Rebholz of Evoke caught a synthetic candidate in January 2026
evidence.verbatim: Jason Rebholz, the founder of AI security firm Evoke who caught a synthetic candidate in January 2026, named the part nobody talks about: "What if I'm wrong?"

evidence.gloss: Even at 95% confidence Rebholz worried about damaging a real person's job chances
evidence.verbatim: Even at 95% confidence he worried about damaging a real person's shot at a job[12].

evidence.gloss: That hesitation is why process, not gut feel, must carry a flag
evidence.verbatim: That hesitation is precisely why single-signal tricks are dangerous and why process, not gut feel, has to carry the weight of a flag[12].

h3.h3: The tells a trained interviewer can spot without software

evidence.gloss: A well-trained hiring team can spot AI fraud without fraud-detection software
evidence.verbatim: A well-trained hiring team can identify many types of AI fraud and deepfakes even without fraud-detecting software, because AI-generated content has known limitations that can be exploited[3].

evidence.gloss: The documented deepfake tells in video interviews
evidence.verbatim: For video interviews specifically, the documented tells are unnatural facial movements, inconsistencies and anomalies in lighting and shadows, behavioural inconsistencies, audio and visual that are asynchronous for reasons other than connection issues, and notable lags between questions and responses[3].

evidence.gloss: The documented tells in phone interviews
evidence.verbatim: For phone interviews the tells are inconsistent voice patterns, lack of voice and tone variation, strange background noises, and notable lags between questions and responses[3].

evidence.gloss: Live-specific behavioural cues: screen reading and unusual background changes
evidence.verbatim: Live-specific behavioural cues include screen reading and unusual background changes[4].

evidence.gloss: Worked example of a suspicious behavioural shift mid-interview
evidence.verbatim: The worked example given is a candidate who appears confident on one question then suddenly looks off-screen repeatedly during the next, or whose voice tone shifts drastically mid-interview[4].

evidence.gloss: Behavioural cues are a reason to look closer, not an automatic disqualification
evidence.verbatim: The stated caveat matters for false positives: these cues do not automatically disqualify a candidate, they give recruiters a reason to take a closer look, and while they may have innocent explanations, when paired with anomalies like switching devices or inconsistent facial positioning they could indicate coaching or fraud[4].

h3.h3: Human review is the guardrail, and a recruiter rewatching the tape is not one

evidence.gloss: Willo's product language keeps humans in control of every hiring decision
evidence.verbatim: Vendor product language echoes the human-in-the-loop framing: Willo describes transcripts, summaries, benchmarks, and role-specific insights as giving teams clearer evidence "while keeping people in control of every hiring decision," supporting faster shortlisting "without handing decisions over to AI"[44].

evidence.gloss: Automated fraud agent assigns high/medium/low risk with 90% accuracy and explanations; recruiters decide
evidence.verbatim: One model for a live-review flag is a risk level rather than a raw signal — an automated fraud agent that evaluates fraud signals together and assigns high, medium or low risk to each application with 90% accuracy, returning a complete risk assessment with transparent explanations rather than individual flags for a recruiter to interpret, while recruiters make the final decision on every candidate[14].

evidence.gloss: Human review of the flag is the guardrail that makes the rest safe
evidence.verbatim: The guardrail that makes the rest safe is human review of the flag itself.

evidence.gloss: A flag that rejects without a named human reviewer makes it an automated decision system
evidence.verbatim: If a flag can trigger a rejection without a named human reviewing the full context, you have built an automated decision system and inherited every obligation that comes with it[8].

evidence.gloss: Manual review is not a backstop
evidence.verbatim: Manual review is not a backstop either.

evidence.gloss: Humans identify high-quality deepfakes about 24.5% of the time, worse than chance, and are worse on live video than stills
evidence.verbatim: Human reviewers identify high-quality deepfakes only about 24.5% of the time, worse than a coin flip, and people are even less able to catch a live video deepfake than a still image[21].

evidence.gloss: Reviewers navigate by timestamp, flag type and risk indicator instead of replaying whole sessions
evidence.verbatim: Reviewers are given navigation by timestamp, flag type, and risk indicator so they can examine the relevant moments rather than replaying every session end to end[33].

evidence.gloss: The final review workflow can be automated, human, or both
evidence.verbatim: The final workflow may be automated, human-reviewed, or both[33].

evidence.gloss: What Tofu checks: account age, email/LinkedIn match, scam-linked phone, repeat resumes across the network
evidence.verbatim: Tofu can tell you if an email address or LinkedIn was created yesterday, whether the email matches the LinkedIn signup, whether the phone number is tied to prior scams, and whether the same resume shows up under multiple names at your company or across the countless others in the network[49].

evidence.gloss: BrightHire centralises signals in one view with evidence linked to each
evidence.verbatim: Centralising flags matters for the same reason: BrightHire brings signals together in a single view so teams see the full picture across touchpoints and across candidates instead of chasing one flag, with each signal linked back to the evidence behind it so hiring teams can review, investigate, and decide[50].

evidence.gloss: BrightHire coverage spans applications, AI screens, and Zoom interviews, not one checkpoint
evidence.verbatim: Its coverage runs from applications to AI screening interviews on BrightHire Screen through every live video interview on Zoom, so signals get raised wherever fraud appears, not just at a single checkpoint a bad actor can plan around[50].

evidence.gloss: A flag that can reject without named human review makes it an automated decision system
evidence.verbatim: If a flag can trigger a rejection without a named human reviewing the full context, you have built an automated decision system and inherited every obligation that comes with it[8].

evidence.gloss: Human review is the guardrail that makes the process safe to run
evidence.verbatim: This human-review stage is the guardrail that makes the rest of the process safe to run[8].

evidence.gloss: Strongest control combines technical detection with human verification
evidence.verbatim: The strongest control design combines technical detection with human verification[27].

evidence.gloss: Manual review as last line of defense is a listed IDV mistake; human deepfake accuracy near a quarter
evidence.verbatim: Leaving manual review as the last line of defense is listed among the common IDV mistakes, for a measurable reason: human accuracy on strong deepfakes sits near a quarter, so a reviewer is not a reliable final check[21].

evidence.gloss: An escalation path ending in a recruiter watching the recording is no real backstop
evidence.verbatim: If a vendor's escalation path terminates in "a recruiter looks at the recording," the pipeline has no real backstop.

evidence.gloss: Ask what automated evidence the human reviewer is handed
evidence.verbatim: Ask what automated evidence the reviewer is handed, not just whether a review step exists.

evidence.gloss: A flag must not trigger rejection without a named human reviewing full context
evidence.verbatim: A flag must not be able to trigger a rejection without a named human reviewing the full context.

evidence.gloss: Without a human in the loop you have built an automated decision system with its obligations
evidence.verbatim: If it can, you have built an automated decision system and inherited every obligation that comes with it[8].

evidence.gloss: Ask contractually whether auto-rejection on a fraud or AI-use score can be disabled
evidence.verbatim: This is a contractual requirement of the vendor as much as a process requirement of your team: ask whether the product permits auto-rejection on a fraud or AI-use score, and whether that behaviour can be disabled.

evidence.gloss: Review evidence that makes flags actionable: session recordings, snapshots, question-level activity logs, timestamps, and violation summaries for human judgment
evidence.verbatim:
Flags on their own are noise. Your team needs evidence it can actually look at, because not every alert means cheating. A modern solution should capture session recordings, snapshots, question-level activity logs, timestamps, and plain violation summaries. Sometimes a reviewer needs the full picture before deciding either way.
Trust insights bring key proctoring signals into one review view for faster decision-making.
Testlify supports this with session recording, question-level logs, snapshot proctoring, and proctoring flags, so teams move faster without trading away fairness.
Screen recordings give hiring teams more context when they review flagged sessions.

h3.h3: What happens after a flag: escalation, verification, appeal

evidence.gloss: Prescribed response to an AI flag: follow-up question, cautious weighting, or live verification, never auto-disqualification
evidence.verbatim: The prescribed response is to ask a sharper follow-up question, weight the response with caution, or schedule a quick live verification, and explicitly not to use it as a basis for automatic disqualification [21].

evidence.gloss: Recommended handling: proctoring defaults, recruiter training, role-sensitive thresholds
evidence.verbatim: The recommended handling is to use platforms offering AI-enhanced interview proctoring by default with unusual activity detection, voice consistency and multi-face alerts enabled; to train recruiters to review flagged interviews carefully rather than jumping to conclusions, treating a system alert as a reason to rewatch the video rather than a verdict; and to customise thresholds or alerts by role sensitivity, so that remote customer support or compliance roles warrant tighter monitoring than internal junior roles[4].

evidence.gloss: A failed check is an ambiguous event needing a documented human path, not automatic rejection
evidence.verbatim: Note what "define internal policies for handling failed or canceled results" concedes: a failed check is an ambiguous event needing a documented human path, not an automatic rejection.

evidence.gloss: Flagged cues are a reason to rewatch, not a verdict, and thresholds should vary by role sensitivity
evidence.verbatim: Guidance for monitored interviews is that flagged cues do not automatically disqualify a candidate but give recruiters a reason to look closer, that recruiters should be trained to review flagged interviews carefully rather than jumping to conclusions and treat an alert as a reason to rewatch the video rather than a verdict, and that thresholds or alerts should be customised by role sensitivity — remote customer support or compliance roles may warrant tighter monitoring than internal junior roles[4].

evidence.gloss: Monitoring is framed as protecting the process, not surveillance
evidence.verbatim: Monitoring is framed as protecting the process from manipulation rather than turning hiring into surveillance[4].

evidence.gloss: A fraud flag should escalate the process rather than end it
evidence.verbatim: A fraud flag should escalate the process, not end it.

evidence.gloss: Handle flag conversations neutrally and avoid accusations without clear evidence
evidence.verbatim: Interviewers should remain professional and respectful at all times, handle conversations neutrally, and avoid making accusations until there is clear evidence[14].

evidence.gloss: Explain verification as protecting legitimate applicants and candidates are generally receptive
evidence.verbatim: Verification should be explained rather than imposed: when candidates understand that verification protects everyone, including legitimate applicants competing against fraudulent ones, they are generally receptive to reasonable requirements[14].

evidence.gloss: Fraud detection can be enabled per job based on risk level and application volume
evidence.verbatim: That deployment can be enabled per job, so which roles get fraud detection depends on risk level and application volume[14].

evidence.gloss: Look for graduated responses instead of binary pass/fail
evidence.verbatim: To preserve the experience for legitimate users, look for a system that supports graduated responses rather than a binary pass/fail[28].

evidence.gloss: Define the post-flag response in advance because flag causes differ
evidence.verbatim: Institutions should define what happens after a flag appears, because technical issues, background interruptions, approved accommodations, and potential rule violations should not automatically receive the same response[33].

evidence.gloss: Review criteria, escalation, evidence rules and appeals make decisions consistent
evidence.verbatim: Clear review criteria, escalation routes, evidence requirements, and appeals make decisions more consistent[33].

evidence.gloss: Define post-flag response: different causes need different handling, plus review criteria and appeals
evidence.verbatim: Institutions and employers should define what happens after a flag appears. Technical issues, background interruptions, approved accommodations, and potential rule violations should not automatically receive the same response, and clear review criteria, escalation routes, evidence requirements, and appeals help make decisions more consistent[33].

evidence.gloss: Goal is reducing risk with multiple signals; one strange answer should prompt a follow-up, not a conclusion
evidence.verbatim: The goal is not to "catch" everyone but to reduce risk using multiple signals evaluated together, and one strange answer should prompt a better follow-up, not an immediate conclusion[10].

evidence.gloss: One flag is not fraud; multiple flags mean pause and verify
evidence.verbatim: One flag alone does not mean fraud; multiple flags together should make the interviewer pause and verify[49].

evidence.gloss: Fonzi AI combines multiple anomalies into a determination a human verifies
evidence.verbatim: Fonzi AI, which screens for fake candidates on remote engineering roles, builds its determination the same way: it looks for a number of different anomalies and combines the signals into an overall fraud determination that a human then verifies[49].

evidence.gloss: A missing LinkedIn photo is a prompt to check, not a conclusion
evidence.verbatim: Signals such as a missing LinkedIn photo appear on fake identities, but the signal is a prompt to check, not a conclusion[49].

evidence.gloss: The next action after a flag is another verification step, not an accusation
evidence.verbatim: The next action after a flag is an additional verification step, not an accusation.

evidence.gloss: Candidates must be allowed to explain apparent discrepancies
evidence.verbatim: Candidates should be allowed to explain apparent discrepancies, because there may be legitimate reasons for what looks suspicious[14].

evidence.gloss: Follow-up call with the same interviewer plus a new reviewer
evidence.verbatim: A follow-up call with the same interviewer plus one new reviewer[7]

evidence.gloss: Live walkthrough of a submitted work sample
evidence.verbatim: A live walkthrough of a submitted work sample[7]

evidence.gloss: A shorter role-specific exercise as a follow-up check
evidence.verbatim: A shorter role-specific exercise[7]

evidence.gloss: A second reference check through a verified path
evidence.verbatim: A second reference check through a verified path[7]

evidence.gloss: Identity verification at the next risk-based stage
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification at the next risk-based stage[7]

evidence.gloss: Named escalation owners: HR, Legal, IT, Security
evidence.verbatim: A confirmed or strengthening flag hands off to named owners: HR owns candidate communication and process; Legal advises on policy and employment risk; IT reviews device, account, and access details; Security assesses identity and access risk[7].

evidence.gloss: Frame discrepancy conversations neutrally; involve counsel where fraud is suspected
evidence.verbatim: Discrepancy conversations should be framed neutrally, and where organized fraud or identity theft is suspected, legal counsel should be involved before any action with legal implications is taken [14].

evidence.gloss: The three advancement decisions and the basis they must rest on
evidence.verbatim: Decisions on advancement (move forward, request more information, or remove from consideration) are to be made on the evidence plus additional verification, in a way that complies with applicable regulations [14].

evidence.gloss: NIST 2025 Digital Identity Guidelines separate identity verification from media protection
evidence.verbatim: NIST's 2025 Digital Identity Guidelines distinguish identity verification from media protection, addressing video and image injection, virtual cameras, modified media, and presentation attacks as separate risks requiring additional controls[27].

evidence.gloss: Three steps: verify the requester, detect manipulation, confirm through a trusted channel
evidence.verbatim: Three steps follow: verify who is requesting the action, detect whether the call has been manipulated, and confirm the action through a trusted channel[27].

evidence.gloss: Develop an internal fraud investigation protocol involving HR, legal and hiring managers
evidence.verbatim: develop a clear internal protocol for investigating suspected fraud that involves HR, legal, and hiring managers[6]

evidence.gloss: The escalation path a flag feeds is process, not product
evidence.verbatim: The published mid-interview and post-interview escalation path is process, not product.

evidence.gloss: Keep factual escalation notes: stage, concern, role, access level, next check, outcome, no assumed intent
evidence.verbatim: Keep notes factual, recording the stage of the process, the concern observed, the role being hired for, the access level tied to the role, the next check requested, and the final review outcome, and avoid language that assumes intent by writing what was observed rather than what it is thought to prove[7].

evidence.gloss: Ask for a second data point with one matched follow-up check, without accusing
evidence.verbatim: Then ask for a second data point, adding one follow-up check matched to the concern without accusing the candidate: a follow-up call with the same interviewer plus one new reviewer, a live walkthrough of a submitted work sample, a shorter role-specific exercise, a second reference check through a verified path, or identity verification at the next risk-based stage[7].

evidence.gloss: Compare inconsistencies across the funnel to build an escalation case
evidence.verbatim: Then compare inconsistencies across the funnel, since a thin profile, vague project ownership, video anomalies, inconsistent assessment performance, and unusual onboarding details together build a stronger case for escalation[7].

evidence.gloss: Escalation team split: HR, Legal, IT and Security each own a piece
evidence.verbatim: Then bring in the right team: HR owns candidate communication and process, Legal advises on policy and employment risk, IT reviews device, account, and access details, and Security assesses identity and access risk[7].

sections_menu.h2: After a fraud flag: the review record, escalation, and legal exposure

h3.h3: The session record a reviewer actually works from

evidence.gloss: Truffle transcribes and scores against a rubric written before any candidate records
evidence.verbatim: Truffle transcribes every response then scores against a rubric whose decision logic is written down before any candidate records, so the scoring measures what the employer actually cares about rather than a generic hiring formula [21].

evidence.gloss: Score output breaks into per-criterion alignment, written reasoning, and timestamp citations into the transcript
evidence.verbatim: The output is not a single number: the overall match percentage breaks down into per-criterion alignment scores, each criterion carries a written reasoning paragraph explaining what the AI weighted and why, and every reasoning paragraph cites a timestamp in the transcript, so clicking a criterion skips the player to the second the AI cited [21].

evidence.gloss: Reviewers can override a score with a note, stored alongside the AI output for the audit record
evidence.verbatim: A reviewer who disagrees can leave a note and override the score, and the override stores alongside the AI output for the audit record, letting the team see how human reviewers diverge from AI on each role [21].

evidence.gloss: The score is the start of the conversation, not the verdict
evidence.verbatim: The framing throughout is that the number is the start of the conversation, not the verdict [21].

evidence.gloss: Reviewers work from a consolidated session record with timestamps and risk indicators
evidence.verbatim: Reviewers work from a consolidated session record after the fact. The system brings together camera, audio, desktop, identity, and event data, and reviewers see timestamps, recordings, event types, and risk indicators, letting them examine the relevant moments rather than replaying every session from beginning to end. The final workflow may be automated, reviewed by a person, or both[33].

evidence.gloss: Structural weakness: hiring, IT and security each see only their part of the record
evidence.verbatim: The structural weakness this addresses is that risk builds when no one sees the full picture: a background check may happen later through a third-party process, IT may ship a laptop after the offer is accepted, and security may not see warning signs until the person starts accessing company systems, with each team seeing only its own part of the hiring record[7].

h3.h3: Documenting a flag: fields, evidence, and neutral language

evidence.gloss: A flagged mismatch should carry the specific evidence attached
evidence.verbatim: Clear audit trails matter in both directions: a flagged mismatch should come with the specific evidence attached, which serves internal review and compliance documentation[6].

evidence.gloss: Document concerns with evidence instead of gut feeling
evidence.verbatim: Document specific concerns with evidence rather than relying on gut feeling.

evidence.gloss: What to write down after a flag: inconsistencies, timestamps, screenshots, correspondence
evidence.verbatim: Write down exactly what raised suspicion, the specific inconsistencies, unusual behaviours, or verification failures, and include timestamps, screenshots, and any relevant correspondence[14].

evidence.gloss: Documentation over time reveals org-specific fraud patterns
evidence.verbatim: Over time this documentation lets a team identify patterns in what fraudulent candidates look like for their own organisation[14].

evidence.gloss: The factual fields a flag record should capture
evidence.verbatim: Keep the notes factual. The useful fields are: the stage of the process, the concern observed, the role being hired for, the access level tied to the role, the next check requested, and the final review outcome[7].

evidence.gloss: Avoid language assuming intent in the notes
evidence.verbatim: Avoid language that assumes intent: write what was observed, not what you think it proves[7].

evidence.gloss: The standard the file must meet is objective, not subjective
evidence.verbatim: The bar the file should clear is not a subjective one.

evidence.gloss: The defensible question is documented-controls sameness, not looking suspicious
evidence.verbatim: The defensible question is not "Does this person look suspicious to me?" but "Can we establish, using the same documented controls we apply to comparable candidates, that this is the same person and that this person produced the evidence we are evaluating?" [9].

evidence.gloss: Two further records recommended: a fraud-pattern log and updated team training
evidence.verbatim: Two further records are recommended: a running log of fraud patterns seen in your specific context, which becomes the organization's institutional knowledge, and updated training shared across the recruiting team as tactics evolve [14].

h3.h3: The four escalation steps

evidence.gloss: Red flags decide between clarification, a second check, or escalation
evidence.verbatim: Interview red flags are used to decide whether to ask for clarification, run a second check, or escalate through the agreed process[7].

evidence.gloss: Escalation Step 1: keep factual notes recording stage, concern, role, access level, next check, outcome
evidence.verbatim: Step 1 is to keep notes factual, recording the stage of the process, the concern observed, the role being hired for, the access level tied to the role, the next check requested, and the final review outcome, avoiding language that assumes intent and writing what was observed rather than what you think it proves[7].

evidence.gloss: Escalation Step 2: ask for a second data point with one follow-up check matched to the concern
evidence.verbatim: Step 2 is to ask for a second data point, adding one follow-up check matched to the concern and without accusing the candidate: a follow-up call with the same interviewer and one new reviewer, a live walkthrough of a submitted work sample, a shorter role-specific exercise, a second reference check through a verified path, or identity verification at the next risk-based stage[7].

evidence.gloss: Escalation Step 3: compare inconsistencies across the funnel for a stronger case
evidence.verbatim: Step 3 is to compare inconsistencies across the funnel, checking whether the same concern shows up elsewhere in the hiring record, since a thin profile, vague project ownership, video anomalies, inconsistent assessment performance, and unusual onboarding details together create a stronger case for escalation[7].

evidence.gloss: Escalation Step 4: bring in HR, Legal, IT and Security, each with a defined remit
evidence.verbatim: Step 4 is to bring in the right team: HR owns candidate communication and process, Legal advises on policy and employment risk, IT reviews device, account, and access details, and Security assesses identity and access risk[7].

h3.h3: Lawful verification and the cost of a botched protocol

evidence.gloss: Audit-ready identity records are a product requirement, not optional
evidence.verbatim: Audit-ready records documenting when and how each candidate's identity was confirmed are listed as a product requirement, not an optional extra[2].

evidence.gloss: Lawfulness: verification is permitted with notice, consent, secure purpose-limited handling
evidence.verbatim: On lawfulness, in most jurisdictions employers can verify candidate identity as part of a lawful hiring process, provided candidates are informed and consent is obtained where required, and the data collected is handled securely and only for that purpose; requirements vary by country and by role, so hiring teams should confirm their specific obligations with legal counsel[2].

evidence.gloss: Regulated industries mandate checks; others adopt voluntarily
evidence.verbatim: Requirements also vary by industry, role, and jurisdiction: some regulated industries and government contracts mandate specific identity checks, but even where it is not legally required more employers are adopting it voluntarily given the rise in remote hiring fraud[6].

evidence.gloss: A botched detection protocol carries legal exposure
evidence.verbatim: There is also legal exposure in a botched detection protocol[45].

evidence.gloss: Legal exposure of a botched detection protocol is as real as the fraud
evidence.verbatim: The legal exposure of a botched detection protocol is as real as the fraud itself[45].

h3.h3: Flag rate is not the metric

evidence.gloss: A stored flag rate does not prove the system worked
evidence.verbatim: A stored flag rate is not proof the system worked.

evidence.gloss: Flag rate measures sensitivity; the real metric is six-month hire performance
evidence.verbatim: Flag rate is not a success metric; it measures the tool's sensitivity, not hiring quality, and the discipline is to track whether the people hired after the change perform better six months in [8].

sections_menu.h2: What these checks cost the honest candidate

h3.h3: The friction genuine applicants absorb

evidence.gloss: Every integrity control has a candidate-side cost: device, document, time, tolerance for refusal
evidence.verbatim: Every integrity control on an interview costs the candidate something: a device that supports it, a document they hold, minutes spent verifying, and a tolerance for being told no.

evidence.gloss: Tools speed screening but cannot fix a disorganized hiring process
evidence.verbatim: The sources are explicit that expectations should stay realistic: these tools can dramatically speed up early screening, **yet they cannot fix a disorganized hiring process on their own**, and even the most polished platforms can frustrate candidates if the interface is clunky, the instructions are unclear, or the automation feels a little too robotic[23].

evidence.gloss: Every anti-fraud safeguard lands on the honest candidate
evidence.verbatim: Every safeguard you add to stop a fraudster lands on the honest candidate, often as a cost to experience; candidates already loathe the recruiting process, so balance is critical, and getting it wrong in either direction means everyone loses[11].

evidence.gloss: Invasive verification hurts completion rates, so low friction is a requirement
evidence.verbatim: A verification step that feels invasive or slow can hurt completion rates for legitimate candidates just as much as it blocks fraudulent ones, which is why a fast, low-friction candidate experience is listed as a requirement alongside the detection features[6].

evidence.gloss: The goal: more signal, minimum friction, via staged checks, transparency, trained recruiters
evidence.verbatim: The stated goal is more signal while minimizing friction, achieved through verification at every stage, transparency about why you are asking, and recruiters trained to read behavior[11].

evidence.gloss: Legitimate applicants absorb the friction, and identity-proving stages are increasing
evidence.verbatim: Legitimate applicants absorb the friction created by fraudulent ones, and the number of hiring stages that ask a candidate to prove who they are is going up[58].

evidence.gloss: Most verification failures are mundane, so the cost is preparation and rework not rejection
evidence.verbatim: Most verification failures for honest candidates are mundane, which means most of the cost is preparation and rework rather than rejection[58].

evidence.gloss: The friction settles less than candidates assume
evidence.verbatim: Finally, the friction settles less than candidates assume.

evidence.gloss: Part of the integrity cost falls on genuine candidates and the sources treat it as a real constraint
evidence.verbatim: The cost side of any integrity purchase falls partly on genuine candidates, and the collected sources treat that as a real constraint rather than a footnote.

evidence.gloss: Goal is to reduce risk without treating every remote applicant as suspicious
evidence.verbatim: Candidate experience still matters, and the stated goal is to reduce risk without treating every remote applicant as suspicious[7].

evidence.gloss: A hostile process damages candidate experience and costs qualified people
evidence.verbatim: A hostile process damages the candidate experience and can cost qualified people.

h3.h3: Device, browser and accessibility requirements

evidence.gloss: Platform choice drives completion rates
evidence.verbatim: Platform choice affects completion rates directly.

evidence.gloss: Buying criterion: works on 99.9% of devices and browsers, no app or download
evidence.verbatim: Buyers are told to look for platforms that work across 99.9% of devices and browsers with no apps or downloads required, on the reasoning that the easier a check is to complete, the better the completion rate [15].

evidence.gloss: Over 60% of candidates use smartphones, so desktop-only flows filter on hardware
evidence.verbatim: Mobile is the majority case, not the exception: over 60% of candidates use smartphones, so a verification or interview flow that only behaves on desktop is filtering on hardware rather than on ability [15].

evidence.gloss: ID verification has a harder device dependency than interviews
evidence.verbatim: ID verification carries a harder device dependency.

evidence.gloss: TestGorilla troubleshooting starts with supported browser/device, so a bad combo mimics a fraud signal
evidence.verbatim: TestGorilla's troubleshooting guidance for failed verification starts with ensuring the candidate uses a supported browser and device, which is an admission that an unsupported combination produces a failure indistinguishable from a fraud signal [16].

evidence.gloss: Candidates struggle with video interview tech requirements
evidence.verbatim: A documented reason candidates struggle with or are cautious about video interviews is unfamiliarity with the tech requirements: internet connection hiccups, unfamiliar video interview software, or camera and microphone setup[31].

evidence.gloss: Connection problems only surface during the interview itself
evidence.verbatim: A candidate's connection may be fine for regular web surfing while video calls require more capacity, so instability only shows up during the interview itself[31].

evidence.gloss: Recommended mitigation: simple guidelines sent ahead of the call
evidence.verbatim: The recommended mitigation is sending simple guidelines ahead of the call covering how to join, how to check camera, microphone and speaker quality, how to practise recording themselves before submitting final answers in a one-way interview, and how to troubleshoot common issues — while accepting that no amount of preparation eliminates the problem[31].

evidence.gloss: Verification device and environment requirements are an accessibility question
evidence.verbatim: Verification steps impose device and environment requirements that become an accessibility question.

evidence.gloss: Talview ID verification requires a camera device, good lighting, clear lens and an accepted document
evidence.verbatim: Talview's ID verification requires a device equipped with a camera — laptop, desktop with webcam, or smartphone — meeting the platform's technical requirements for supported operating systems and browser compatibility, and candidates need good lighting, a clear camera lens, and an accepted identification document ready before starting[45].

evidence.gloss: Accepted ID document types vary by provider policy and jurisdiction
evidence.verbatim: Accepted documents typically include government-issued IDs such as passports, national ID cards, and driver's licenses, with the specific types varying by the provider's policies and the legal requirements of the jurisdiction[45].

evidence.gloss: A mandatory camera step with a documented human fallback is where ADA accommodation duties land
evidence.verbatim: A mandatory, camera-dependent step with a documented human fallback is the shape a defensible policy needs; the fallback is where ADA and equivalent accommodation duties land.

evidence.gloss: Document checks require a live photograph of the physical ID card
evidence.verbatim: - **Physical ID in the room before the session starts.** Document checks generally require a live photograph of the card, not a scan or a photo of a photo[58].

evidence.gloss: Verification flows often reject virtual camera devices, so candidates should check the webcam
evidence.verbatim: - **Webcam choice.** Candidates should check which webcam the platform will actually use, and disable virtual-camera software routed through for other reasons, because many verification flows reject virtual camera devices outright[58].

h3.h3: Liveness prompts and the completion-rate trade-off

evidence.gloss: Active liveness catches simple replay but adds abandonment and misses sophisticated deepfakes
evidence.verbatim: Active liveness may help identify simple replay attacks but can create more abandonment and may not detect sophisticated deepfakes on its own[28].

evidence.gloss: Case data: multi-step active liveness produced about 60% completion
evidence.verbatim: At one organization that implemented active liveness requiring users to follow on-screen prompts through a multi-step process, customer dropoff was significant, producing a completion rate of only about 60%.

evidence.gloss: Switching to passive liveness raised completion above 95%
evidence.verbatim: After a strategic decision to switch to passive liveness, requiring only a selfie with no prompts or gestures, completion rates rose to over 95%[28].

evidence.gloss: The completion swing is roughly 35 percentage points from prompt friction
evidence.verbatim: That is roughly a 35-percentage-point swing in completion attributable to prompt friction alone.

evidence.gloss: Trade-off statement: passive reduces friction, active catches replay but raises abandonment
evidence.verbatim: Passive liveness can reduce friction for legitimate users, while active liveness may help identify simple replay attacks but can create more abandonment[28].

evidence.gloss: Active liveness as a risk-triggered escalation, not a universal toll
evidence.verbatim: Active liveness is applied as an escalation triggered by risk, not as a toll on every candidate.

evidence.gloss: Anti-deepfake probes the genuine candidate must also perform on camera
evidence.verbatim: Interviewer-led probes that expose real-time fakes are things the genuine candidate must also perform: changing camera angle on request, holding up an ID on camera, responding to an unscripted prompt, and making sudden movements, since real-time deepfakes still struggle with sudden movement, occlusion, and spontaneity[43].

h3.h3: What happens when verification fails

evidence.gloss: Once enabled on a TestGorilla assessment, IDV is mandatory for every invitee and cannot be disabled after publishing
evidence.verbatim: On TestGorilla, once ID verification is enabled for an assessment, every invited candidate must complete it, and it cannot be disabled after publishing [16].

evidence.gloss: Failing or not completing IDV blocks the rest of the assessment
evidence.verbatim: Candidates who do not complete or fail IDV cannot proceed with the rest of the assessment [16].

evidence.gloss: Verification sessions resumable for up to 7 days
evidence.verbatim: Verification sessions can be resumed for up to 7 days [16].

evidence.gloss: A failed IDV locks the assessment; a retry needs a new invitation and a new credit
evidence.verbatim: But a failure is terminal within that invitation: once a candidate fails IDV, the assessment is locked, and the employer must send a new invitation, using a new credit, for another attempt [16].

evidence.gloss: The retry decision sits with the recruiter and costs a credit, so the candidate depends on that choice
evidence.verbatim: That means the retry decision sits with the recruiter and carries a cost, so a candidate whose licence photo is worn or whose lighting is poor depends on someone choosing to spend a credit on them.

evidence.gloss: Three reasons a candidate shows no test results
evidence.verbatim: A candidate has no test results when they did not pass IDV, never completed the verification step, or abandoned the assessment before completing IDV [16].

evidence.gloss: Status badge meanings: blue verified, grey not completed, orange failed and disqualified
evidence.verbatim: Status badges read: blue for verified; grey, or no badge yet, meaning the candidate has not completed the ID verification step; orange for failed ID verification, where the ID or selfie did not match or verification failed for another reason, and those candidates are disqualified and will not have test results [16].

evidence.gloss: On a mismatch the candidate may retry, with manual human-proctor verification as the fallback
evidence.verbatim: Where a potential error or mismatch is detected, the test-taker may be asked to retry or provide additional information, and in some cases manual verification by a human proctor is initiated to resolve ambiguities, with clear instructions given on how to proceed[45].

evidence.gloss: Codility shows the employer a pass or fail with reasoning, and the check can be re-triggered
evidence.verbatim: Codility's employer-side view is a pass or fail with reasoning attached, and the check can be re-triggered[26]

evidence.gloss: Candidates cannot skip Codility ID verification when it is enabled for the test
evidence.verbatim: candidates cannot skip ID verification when it is enabled for the test[26].

evidence.gloss: Failed checks need clear resolution instructions, and a practice check cuts avoidable disruption
evidence.verbatim: Candidates who fail a check should receive clear instructions for resolving the problem rather than a generic error screen, and a practice check before the assessment window reduces avoidable disruption by giving candidates time to update permissions, change devices, test their connection, or contact support[33].

evidence.gloss: A fallback process is required for unclear images, expired documents, name differences, accessibility needs
evidence.verbatim: Institutions should provide a fallback process for unclear images, expired documents, name differences, accessibility needs, or candidates who cannot complete automated matching[33].

h3.h3: Framing, transparency and handling a flag

evidence.gloss: Candidate-side risks and the recommended mitigations: make it human, tech checks, clip highlights, limit use to hiring
evidence.verbatim: The candidate-side risks named elsewhere are the same shape: candidates can freeze on camera, formats can feel robotic, and sloppy follow-ups hurt accuracy, so the recommended mitigations are to make it human, run tech checks, clip highlights, and limit use strictly to hiring unless explicitly agreed[38].

evidence.gloss: Vendor answer one: refusal to verify is itself a data point
evidence.verbatim: One reframes it as signal: a candidate refusing to verify identity is telling you something important, and that is a data point rather than a drop-off problem[1].

evidence.gloss: Vendor answer two: real-time AI ID checks are faster and scale without delay
evidence.verbatim: Others point to speed: AI-driven tools perform real-time ID checks with higher accuracy than slow, error-prone manual checks, providing real-time results so candidates do not face unnecessary friction, and scaling to high-volume recruitment without delay[7].

evidence.gloss: BrightHire: signals trigger human review, never automated rejection
evidence.verbatim: BrightHire's position is that catching fraud produces a faster, fairer process for honest applicants, that signals trigger human review and never automated rejection, and that they are captured in the flow of work with no friction for legitimate candidates[9].

evidence.gloss: Biometric accuracy is qualified: depends on technology and image quality
evidence.verbatim: Modern biometric verification combining facial matching with liveness detection is described as highly accurate for legitimate use cases, though accuracy depends on the specific technology and image quality, which is exactly why leading solutions layer in document verification and re-verification at later stages rather than relying on one single scan[6].

evidence.gloss: Camera reluctance is scored as a fraud signal, converting preference or bad connection into suspicion
evidence.verbatim: Reluctance to turn on camera or to change camera angle on request is itself scored as a fraud signal[43], which converts an ordinary preference or a bad connection into suspicion.

evidence.gloss: What happens to the uploaded ID differs sharply between vendors
evidence.verbatim: What happens to a candidate's identity document after they upload it is the question candidates should ask more often, and the answers differ sharply between vendors[58].

evidence.gloss: Candidates are receptive when verification is framed as protecting everyone
evidence.verbatim: Framed to candidates, verification protects everyone including the legitimate applicants competing against fraudulent ones, and when that is explained candidates are generally receptive to reasonable requirements[14].

evidence.gloss: Gartner: 62% of candidates more likely to apply to a position requiring in-person interviews
evidence.verbatim: There is also evidence candidates will accept the heavier version: Gartner found 62% of candidates said they were more likely to apply to a position that required in-person interviews[8].

evidence.gloss: Frame verification as standard procedure and keep suspicion conversations neutral until there is evidence
evidence.verbatim: Verification should be framed as standard procedure rather than a reflection on any individual candidate; candidates should be treated with dignity throughout, and even when fraud is suspected the conversation should stay professional, neutral, and free of accusations until there is clear evidence[14].

evidence.gloss: Interviewers overcorrect: do not read one odd pause or nerves as fraud
evidence.verbatim: On the interviewer side, it is easy to overcorrect and that usually makes the process worse: do not accuse someone based on one odd pause or a bad internet connection, and do not confuse nerves with fraud, because some strong candidates are simply awkward on video or unaccustomed to high-pressure interviews.

evidence.gloss: Aim is risk reduction with multiple signals, one strange answer prompts a follow-up not a conclusion
evidence.verbatim: The goal is not to catch everyone but to reduce risk using multiple signals evaluated together, and one strange answer should prompt a better follow-up rather than an immediate conclusion[10].

evidence.gloss: Monitoring software signals distrust, mitigated by explaining why the check happens
evidence.verbatim: On the tooling side, monitoring software carries a trust cost of its own: it could indicate a lack of trust on the employer's part, and the recommended mitigation is messaging so the candidate fully understands why the check is happening and that it is not representative of how they would be treated as an employee[44].

evidence.gloss: Monitored signals must be stated clearly in the candidate instructions
evidence.verbatim: The exact signals monitored should be stated clearly in the candidate instructions[33].

sections_menu.h2: What these checks cost honest candidates: the false-positive surface

h3.h3: Detectors measure signal, not proof

evidence.gloss: Detection tools work on signal, not proof
evidence.verbatim: Detection tools work on signal, not proof.

evidence.gloss: What text, video and audio detectors actually measure
evidence.verbatim: Text detectors score perplexity and burstiness, essentially asking whether writing is statistically too smooth to be human, while video and audio tools watch for gaze drift, unnatural pause structure before answers, keystroke patterns, and lip-sync artefacts[8].

evidence.gloss: Detectors observe correlates of cheating, and a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation
evidence.verbatim: None of these observe cheating. They observe correlates of cheating, and then a threshold turns a correlate into an accusation[8].

evidence.gloss: Procedural failure: a probability on a scorecard gets treated as a finding
evidence.verbatim: The third failure mode is procedural: a detector score is a probability, and probabilities do not survive contact with a hiring committee that wants a yes or a no — once a number is on a scorecard it is treated as a finding, which is how a 61% false positive rate turns into a rejection letter[8].

evidence.gloss: Summary line: a detector catches an unusual sentence, not a liar
evidence.verbatim: As the summary puts it, "a detector does not catch a liar, it catches an unusual sentence"[8].

evidence.gloss: Source quote: a detector catches an unusual sentence, not a liar
evidence.verbatim: As the source puts it, "A detector does not catch a liar, it catches an unusual sentence"[8].

h3.h3: The AI-detector false-positive rate on non-native English writers

evidence.gloss: AI-text detectors flagged non-native writers at 61.3% false positive, dropping to 11.6% after vocabulary enrichment
evidence.verbatim: The clearest documented case is AI-text detection, where a study found detectors flagged non-native writers at a 61.3% false positive rate, driven by significantly lower perplexity — a narrower range of linguistic expression that reads statistically like a machine; enriching the same essays' vocabulary with an LLM dropped the false positive rate to 11.6%, showing the tool was measuring vocabulary range and calling it authorship[8].

evidence.gloss: Stilted over-structured sentences are what a second language sounds like
evidence.verbatim: That caveat has a concrete failure mode behind it, captured in the observation that a stilted, over-structured sentence "is what a second language sounds like"[8].

evidence.gloss: Stanford study in Patterns tested seven GPT detectors on 91 TOEFL and 88 US eighth-grader essays
evidence.verbatim: The hardest evidence on the cost of that threshold comes from research published in the Cell Press journal *Patterns*, where Weixin Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran seven widely used GPT detectors against 91 human-written TOEFL essays and 88 essays by US eighth graders.

evidence.gloss: Detectors were near-perfect on US students but hit 61.22% false positives on non-native writers; 97.8% flagged at least once
evidence.verbatim: The detectors were near-perfect on the American students. On the non-native English writers they produced an average false positive rate of 61.22%, and 97.8% of those TOEFL essays were flagged as AI-generated by at least one detector[8].

evidence.gloss: The bias is structural, not a bug: low linguistic variety is what a second language sounds like
evidence.verbatim: The mechanism matters because it means this is not a bug awaiting a patch: the essays that were unanimously misclassified were the ones with lower linguistic variety, and, as the source puts it, a plainer sentence is what a second language sounds like[8].

evidence.gloss: Lower perplexity in misclassified essays means second-language fluency reads as machine
evidence.verbatim: The Stanford study found misclassified essays had significantly lower perplexity, meaning detectors penalise writers with a narrower range of linguistic expression, so fluency in a second language reads, statistically, like a machine[8].

evidence.gloss: Enriching vocabulary dropped the false positive rate from 61.3% to 11.6%
evidence.verbatim: When the researchers used an LLM to enrich the vocabulary of the same essays, the false positive rate fell from 61.3% to 11.6%, confirming the tools were measuring vocabulary range and calling it authorship[8].

evidence.gloss: The Stanford false-positive study setup: seven detectors, TOEFL essays vs US eighth graders
evidence.verbatim: In research published in the Cell Press journal Patterns, Weixin Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran seven widely used GPT detectors against 91 human-written TOEFL essays and 88 essays by US eighth graders.

evidence.gloss: 61.22% average false positive rate on non-native writers; 97.8% of TOEFL essays flagged
evidence.verbatim: On the non-native English writers they produced an average false positive rate of 61.22%, and 97.8% of those TOEFL essays were flagged as AI-generated by at least one detector[8].

evidence.gloss: Low linguistic variability drove misclassification, so it is a mechanism not a bug
evidence.verbatim: Essays that were unanimously misclassified had lower linguistic variability, which is why this is not a bug awaiting a patch: the mechanism that makes a detector work is the same mechanism that penalises a non-native speaker[8].

evidence.gloss: The false positive burden falls on the candidates a hiring team most needs to evaluate fairly
evidence.verbatim: For a hiring team, that lands hardest on exactly the candidates it most needs to evaluate fairly[8].

evidence.gloss: AI-writing detection gives the clearest published false-positive numbers and a warning for candidate-facing detectors
evidence.verbatim: The clearest published false-positive numbers in this space come from AI-writing detection, and they are a warning about deploying any probabilistic detector against candidates.

evidence.gloss: Stanford study in Patterns: seven GPT detectors averaged 61.22% false positives on non-native English writing
evidence.verbatim: Stanford research published in *Patterns* found seven leading GPT detectors produced an average 61.22% false positive rate on non-native English writing, against near-perfect accuracy on US student essays[8].

evidence.gloss: Mechanism of the false positives: detectors score linguistic predictability, penalising lower-perplexity writing
evidence.verbatim: The mechanism is diagnostic: the detectors score linguistic predictability, and misclassified essays had significantly lower perplexity, meaning the tools penalise writers with a narrower range of linguistic expression[8].

evidence.gloss: Second-language fluency reads statistically like a machine
evidence.verbatim: Fluency in a second language reads, statistically, like a machine[8].

evidence.gloss: Enriching essay vocabulary with an LLM dropped the false positive rate from 61.3% to 11.6%
evidence.verbatim: When researchers used an LLM to enrich the vocabulary of the same essays, the false positive rate fell from 61.3% to 11.6%, confirming the tools were measuring vocabulary range and calling it authorship[8].

evidence.gloss: Operational conclusion: rejecting on a detector score alone discards qualified candidates at a high rate
evidence.verbatim: The direct operational conclusion: any rejection based solely on a detector score will discard qualified candidates at a high rate[8].

evidence.gloss: Stanford study in Patterns tested seven GPT detectors on TOEFL and eighth-grader essays
evidence.verbatim: In research published in the Cell Press journal *Patterns*, Weixin Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran seven widely used GPT detectors against 91 human-written TOEFL essays and 88 essays by US eighth graders[8].

evidence.gloss: Detectors were near-perfect on American students
evidence.verbatim: The detectors were near-perfect on the American students.

evidence.gloss: 61.22% average false positive rate on non-native writers; 97.8% flagged by at least one detector
evidence.verbatim: On the non-native English writers they produced an average false positive rate of **61.22%**, and **97.8%** of those TOEFL essays were flagged as AI-generated by at least one detector[8].

evidence.gloss: The false positive mechanism is not a bug awaiting a patch
evidence.verbatim: The mechanism means this is not a bug awaiting a patch[8].

evidence.gloss: Ask AI-detection vendors for false positive rates broken out by candidate population
evidence.verbatim: Any vendor selling AI-answer or AI-content detection into a hiring process should be asked for its false positive rate broken out by candidate population, and what happens to a flagged candidate who is simply a non-native speaker.

h3.h3: Webcam proctoring and face match: benign behaviour that reads as cheating

evidence.gloss: Webcam-only proctoring both misses cheating and flags innocent behaviour
evidence.verbatim: Webcam-only proctoring does not just miss genuine cheating; it also flags innocent behaviour as suspicious[32].

evidence.gloss: Concrete false positives: pushing up glasses, looking away while thinking
evidence.verbatim: A candidate who pushes their glasses up gets flagged for "touching face"; someone who looks away while thinking gets flagged too[32].

evidence.gloss: Fabric 2026: 61% of candidates flagged for cheating would have performed adequately anyway
evidence.verbatim: The Fabric 2026 report found that 61% of candidates who were flagged for cheating would have performed adequately anyway, which reframes the question from whether assistance tools are detectable to whether they improve performance at all[5].

evidence.gloss: Webcam-only proctoring flags benign acts like adjusting glasses or looking away while thinking
evidence.verbatim: Webcam-only proctoring produces the same errors in the other direction: a candidate who pushes their glasses up gets flagged for "touching face", and someone who looks away while thinking is flagged too[32].

evidence.gloss: Weak signals have benign explanations: camera issues, nerves, low online presence, privacy, bandwidth, devices
evidence.verbatim: A whole range of weak signals have benign explanations, including camera issues, nervous answers, limited online presence, privacy concerns, bandwidth problems, and device limitations[7].

evidence.gloss: Kuczynski's brilliant-engineer example shows behaviour-based flagging misfiring in a live call
evidence.verbatim: Behaviour-based flagging carries the same risk in a live call. Kuczynski gives a concrete example: "We have one engineer on our team who is probably the most brilliant engineer I've ever worked with in my entire life. But you ask her a question, she's going to stare off into space for 30 seconds and then come back at you with what sounds like a PhD thesis. And to anything like that, or even just off a quick eye check, you'd be like, 'OK, this person just typed everything into ChatGPT and is now reading it off verbatim'"[40].

evidence.gloss: Limitation one, bias: cites NIST report NISTIR 8280 (2019, ~200 algorithms, 18 million images) finding demographic false-match differentials often 10x to 100x, higher for Asian, African American, women, elderly, and child faces, and advises choosing vendors that publish demographic testing plus keeping a human between flag and rejection.
evidence.verbatim: Facial recognition, the backbone of identity and face-presence checks, does not perform the same for everyone. In a landmark test of nearly 200 algorithms drawn from 18 million images (report NISTIR 8280, published 2019), the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology found demographic differentials in false-match rates, often by a factor of 10 to 100 depending on the algorithm, with higher error rates for Asian, African American, women, elderly, and child faces. In hiring, a false flag is not a rounding error; it is a real person wrongly suspected. Pick tools that publish demographic testing and always keep a human between a flag and a rejection.

evidence.gloss: Limitation two: flags are not proof, since tab switches, second voices, and frozen cameras have innocent explanations, and false positives fall hardest on candidates with disabilities, caregiving interruptions, or poor bandwidth.
evidence.verbatim: A tab switch might be an accidental keystroke. A second voice might be a roommate. A frozen camera might be a weak connection. Automated systems generate false positives, and the candidates most likely to be flagged for “unusual” behavior are often those with disabilities, caregiving interruptions, or poor bandwidth. Every flag needs context before it counts against anyone.

h3.h3: Where ID and document checks fail an honest candidate

evidence.gloss: Practitioner account: more signal, minimal friction, but every safeguard lands on the honest candidate
evidence.verbatim: One practitioner account states the aim is "more signal while minimizing friction," via verification at every stage, transparency about why we're asking, and recruiters trained to read behavior — but then concedes: "every safeguard you add to stop a fraudster lands on the honest candidate, often as a cost to experience. Candidates already loathe the recruiting process. So balance is critical. Get it wrong in either direction and everyone loses"[11].

evidence.gloss: Failure modes for honest candidates are mundane and configuration-driven
evidence.verbatim: The documented failure modes for honest candidates are mundane and configuration-driven[26]:

evidence.gloss: Document checks need a live photo of the physical card, not a scan
evidence.verbatim: Document checks generally require a **live photograph of the card**, not a scan or a photo of a photo, so the physical ID must be in the room before the session starts.

evidence.gloss: Backlighting is the most common cause of a failed selfie match
evidence.verbatim: **Backlighting from a window behind you is the most common cause of a failed selfie match**; front lighting is the fix.

evidence.gloss: Preferred-name vs legal-name mismatch triggers manual review
evidence.verbatim: A **mismatch between a preferred name and a legal name is a frequent manual-review trigger**.

evidence.gloss: These failure modes are the false-positive surface a buyer inherits
