evidence.verbatim: These are the false-positive surface a buyer inherits the moment they switch a check on.

h3.h3: Friction, drop-off and completion rate

evidence.gloss: Cost one: friction and drop-off, with top candidates holding multiple offers
evidence.verbatim: First, friction and drop-off: every additional step in the hiring process creates an opportunity for candidates to leave, so verification must be thorough enough to catch fraud without being so slow that top candidates, who often hold multiple offers, are lost[14].

evidence.gloss: Invasive or slow verification hurts legitimate completion rates as much as it blocks fraud
evidence.verbatim: A verification step that feels invasive or slow hurts completion rates for legitimate candidates just as much as it blocks fraudulent ones[16].

evidence.gloss: The candidate-side cost of keeping the record is real
evidence.verbatim: The candidate-side cost of the record is real.

evidence.gloss: Invasive verification hurts legitimate completion rates, so low friction is a design requirement
evidence.verbatim: A verification step that feels invasive or slow can hurt completion rates for legitimate candidates just as much as it blocks fraudulent ones, which is why a fast, low-friction candidate experience is listed as a design requirement alongside multi-stage verification, liveness and deepfake detection, integration with proctoring and assessment data, and clear audit trails [16].

evidence.gloss: Vendors market low-friction workflows, flexible scheduling, transparent guidance for time-to-hire
evidence.verbatim: Vendors position low-friction workflows, flexible scheduling, and transparent guidance as what keeps friction low and speeds time-to-hire [53].

evidence.gloss: The candidate-experience cost of over-monitoring: asymmetric dropout among high-performing candidates, sub-70% completion as a warning signal, calibrating intensity to role risk
evidence.verbatim:
Intrusive monitoring produces a dropout effect that is measurable and asymmetric. Candidates who feel monitoring is disproportionate to the role they are applying for are more likely to abandon the session mid-assessment.
Higher-performing candidates, who hold more competing offers, are disproportionately represented in this dropout group. Assessment completion rates below 70% in a high-volume pipeline indicate either an excessive difficulty threshold or an invasive monitoring setup, and calibrating monitoring to role risk level reduces dropout without reducing detection coverage on critical roles.
A well-calibrated candidate experience and assessment integrity are not in opposition. Screening approaches that match detection intensity to role risk protect both hiring quality and the candidate pipeline from dropout at the assessment stage.

h3.h3: Who the false flags land on, and why they stay invisible

evidence.gloss: Cost two: misdirected suspicion falls on international, neurodivergent, disabled, low-bandwidth or anxious candidates
evidence.verbatim: Second, misdirected suspicion: a badly designed anti-fraud process turns recruiters into amateur investigators and makes international, neurodivergent, disabled, low-bandwidth or simply anxious candidates bear the cost of false suspicion[9].

evidence.gloss: Detection's economics: raises casual cheating cost slightly, determined cheating not at all
evidence.verbatim: Detection also loses on economics: it raises the cost of casual cheating slightly and of determined cheating not at all, because countermeasures are free and widely shared, while every false flag costs a real candidate you never learn about, since rejected people do not appear in any report you read[8].

evidence.gloss: Detection loses on economics; false flags cost candidates you never learn about
evidence.verbatim: Detection also loses on economics: adding a detector raises the cost of casual cheating slightly and the cost of determined cheating not at all, because the countermeasures are free and widely shared, while every false flag costs a real candidate and you never learn which ones you lost, since the people your detector rejects do not appear in any report you read[8].

evidence.gloss: Rejected candidates never appear in reports, so false flags stay invisible
evidence.verbatim: The people a detector rejects never appear in any report the employer reads, so every false flag costs a real candidate and the employer never learns which ones were lost [8].

evidence.gloss: Behaviour-based judgment carries a fairness cost
evidence.verbatim: Behaviour-based judgment carries the same fairness cost.

evidence.gloss: Bad anti-fraud design shifts the cost of false suspicion onto vulnerable candidates
evidence.verbatim: That shift matters for fairness as much as security, because a badly designed anti-fraud process turns recruiters into amateur investigators and makes international, neurodivergent, disabled, low-bandwidth or simply anxious candidates bear the cost of false suspicion [9].

evidence.gloss: Employers cannot ask about protected characteristics even to verify identity
evidence.verbatim: Employers generally cannot ask candidates about specific protected characteristics even if those details would help verify identity, and should consult legal counsel about which verification questions are permissible [14].

h3.h3: Designing the process so it does not punish the honest candidate

evidence.gloss: Bad anti-fraud process turns recruiters into investigators and penalises vulnerable candidates
evidence.verbatim: A badly designed anti-fraud process can turn recruiters into amateur investigators and make international, neurodivergent, disabled, low-bandwidth or simply anxious candidates bear the cost of false suspicion[9].

evidence.gloss: Reduce risk without treating every remote applicant as suspicious
evidence.verbatim: Candidate experience still matters: the goal is to reduce risk without treating every remote applicant as suspicious[7].

evidence.gloss: A badly designed process turns recruiters into amateur investigators and taxes vulnerable candidates
evidence.verbatim: A badly designed anti-fraud process does the opposite: it turns recruiters into amateur investigators and makes international, neurodivergent, disabled, low-bandwidth or simply anxious candidates bear the cost of false suspicion[9].

evidence.gloss: The process must not punish nervous, camera-shy, or unpolished candidates
evidence.verbatim: Recruiters therefore need a process that identifies problems without punishing legitimate candidates who are simply nervous, camera-shy, or not polished on video[10].

evidence.gloss: Benefit two: faster shortlists because sessions score as they finish, plus a defensible evidence trail (timeline, snapshots, session score) that protects candidate and employer; includes a pro tip on disclosing monitoring upfront in plain language to cut anxiety, drop-off, and disputes.
evidence.verbatim:
Because sessions are scored as they finish, you are not waiting on manual review to move a shortlist forward. You also get a reviewable evidence trail: a timeline, snapshots, and a session score you can point to if a rejected candidate asks why. That record protects the candidate as much as the employer.
Pro tip: Tell candidates what the proctoring will and will not capture before they start, in plain language. A one-line note (“we use webcam and screen monitoring during this 30-minute test; a person reviews any flags”) cuts anxiety, cuts drop-off, and heads off the “nobody told me” complaint that turns a flag into a dispute.

sections_menu.h2: The consent and biometric-privacy rules behind face match, liveness and voice checks

h3.h3: What BIPA actually covers: the faceprint, not the photo

evidence.gloss: Illinois BIPA adds notice, consent and a private right of action
evidence.verbatim: **Illinois biometric privacy law (BIPA)** adds a separate notice and consent requirement, **with a private right of action**, for any product that scans face geometry[24].

evidence.gloss: BIPA scope decides whether a vendor identity feature is in or out
evidence.verbatim: BIPA's scope is documented at the definitional edge that decides whether a vendor's identity feature is in or out.

evidence.gloss: BIPA excludes photographs but covers face-geometry scans from them
evidence.verbatim: The statute **excludes photographs themselves from "biometric identifiers"** — but Illinois courts have repeatedly held that **a scan of face geometry derived from a photograph is covered**[26].

evidence.gloss: Storing photos is outside BIPA; face-matching them is inside
evidence.verbatim: So a company storing employee photos is generally outside BIPA; software that runs those photos through face-matching is generally inside it.

evidence.gloss: The BIPA line is the geometry scan, not the image
evidence.verbatim: **The line is the geometry scan, not the image**[26].

evidence.gloss: ID-document-to-live-face matching crosses the BIPA line
evidence.verbatim: That is the precise line an ID-document-to-live-face match crosses.

evidence.gloss: BIPA is Illinois-only but the case signals verification does not exempt disclosure of what is collected and kept
evidence.verbatim: BIPA's protections are specific to Illinois, but the case signals that "we need to verify you" does not exempt an employer from disclosing what it collects and how long it keeps it[26].

evidence.gloss: Face match, liveness checks and voice-consistency monitoring process exactly the identifiers BIPA names
evidence.verbatim: That matters directly for the integrity features rated in this article: face match against a live candidate, liveness checks, and voice-consistency monitoring all process exactly the identifiers BIPA names.

evidence.gloss: Illinois BIPA definition of a biometric identifier and the common workplace examples
evidence.verbatim: Under Illinois BIPA, a biometric identifier is a retina or iris scan, a fingerprint, a voiceprint, or a scan of hand or face geometry, with fingerprint timeclocks and facial recognition for employee access or timekeeping the common workplace examples[65].

evidence.gloss: A photo is not a biometric identifier, but a faceprint derived from it is biometric information under BIPA
evidence.verbatim: A simple photograph is not a biometric identifier, but if a system takes a photo and then uses software to create a mathematical map of the face, a "faceprint," to verify identity, that map is biometric information and BIPA rules apply[65].

evidence.gloss: What BIPA excludes: PINs, ID cards, keys, writing samples, physical descriptions, demographic data
evidence.verbatim: PIN numbers, ID cards, keys, writing samples, physical descriptions such as height and hair colour, and demographic data are all excluded from coverage[65].

evidence.gloss: What BIPA covers and what a biometric identifier is
evidence.verbatim: BIPA applies to businesses that collect, store, or use "biometric identifiers" or "biometric information," and a biometric identifier is a scan of a unique physical human characteristic[65].

evidence.gloss: BIPA reaches out-of-state vendors collecting from Illinois residents
evidence.verbatim: It applies to any private entity that collects biometric data from Illinois residents, including where the timeclock or verification vendor is based out of state[65].

evidence.gloss: Buying face match or continuous biometric auth puts the buyer inside the BIPA regime
evidence.verbatim: Any purchase of face match or continuous biometric authentication puts the buyer inside that regime.

h3.h3: Sosa v. Onfido: the ID-document-plus-selfie check itself is in scope

evidence.gloss: BIPA reaches the mechanics of an ID-document-plus-selfie check
evidence.verbatim: BIPA's reach extends past fingerprint and face scans into the exact mechanics of an ID-document-plus-selfie check.

evidence.gloss: Sosa v. Onfido: how the ID-plus-selfie verification product works
evidence.verbatim: In *Sosa v. Onfido, Inc.*, No. 20-CV-4247, 2022 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 74672 (N.D. Ill. Apr. 25, 2022), the plaintiff alleged the defendant sells proprietary facial recognition software used by online businesses to verify consumers' identities: the consumer uploads a copy of an identification document and a facial photograph, and the software scans both, locates the facial images, and extracts a unique numerical representation of the facial geometry[68].

evidence.gloss: Sosa plaintiff alleged no notice and no written release
evidence.verbatim: The plaintiff alleged he was not informed his biometric identifiers would be collected, stored, or used and never signed a written release[68].

evidence.gloss: Sosa holding: photographs and derived information are protected by BIPA
evidence.verbatim: The court denied the motion to dismiss, holding that photographs and information derived from photographs are protected by BIPA, that the plaintiff sufficiently pleaded liquidated damages, and that BIPA does not violate the First Amendment[68].

evidence.gloss: Seyfarth's takeaway: BIPA can apply to photographs, not just scans
evidence.verbatim: Seyfarth described it as putting businesses and employers on notice that BIPA can apply to photographs in addition to the typically-alleged facial and hand scans[68].

evidence.gloss: Sosa v. Onfido citation and its extension of BIPA into ID-verification tooling
evidence.verbatim: *Sosa v. Onfido, Inc.*, No. 20-CV-4247, 2022 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 74672 (N.D. Ill. Apr. 25, 2022), extended the statute's reach directly into ID-verification tooling [68].

evidence.gloss: What the Sosa plaintiff sued over: ID plus facial photograph scanned for facial geometry
evidence.verbatim: The plaintiff sued over facial recognition software marketed and sold to online businesses to verify consumers' identities, where the consumer uploads identification plus a facial photograph and the software scans both, locates the facial images, and extracts a unique numerical representation of facial geometry [68].

evidence.gloss: The Sosa holding: photographs and derived information are protected by BIPA, liquidated damages pleaded, no First Amendment violation
evidence.verbatim: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that photographs and information derived from photographs are protected by BIPA, that the plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a claim for liquidated damages, and that BIPA does not violate the First Amendment [68].

evidence.gloss: Seyfarth's read: a plaintiff-friendly decision putting employers on notice that BIPA covers photographs
evidence.verbatim: Seyfarth characterised this as the latest plaintiff-friendly BIPA decision, putting businesses and employers on notice that the statute applies to photographs in addition to the typically alleged facial and hand scans [68].

h3.h3: The HireVue settlement: facial geometry and voiceprints, $3.75m

evidence.gloss: HireVue publishes ADA and EEOC guidance; fits large structured-video enterprises
evidence.verbatim: HireVue has published ADA and EEOC guidance, which gives compliance teams a documented starting point, and is described as best suited to large enterprises already running structured video interviewing who want to add proctoring without switching core infrastructure[8].

evidence.gloss: HireVue's stated compliance stack
evidence.verbatim: HireVue's stated compliance stack in these sources is FedRAMP authorization, SOC 2, ISO certifications, and third-party algorithmic audits built in[24].

evidence.gloss: The $3.75m HireVue BIPA settlement over facial geometry and voiceprints
evidence.verbatim: HireVue agreed to a **$3.75 million settlement**, granted **preliminary approval on June 25, 2026**, resolving claims that its video interview software extracted **facial geometry and voiceprints** from Illinois applicants without the notice and consent required by Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), which requires written notice and consent before a private entity collects biometric identifiers such as face geometry (Deyerler v. HireVue settlement coverage)[26].

evidence.gloss: Why the settlement is the key consent-and-notice fact: face analysis is the processing that got sued
evidence.verbatim: This is the single most load-bearing vendor fact in the collected set for the consent-and-notice part of the article: the facial analysis that would underpin any face-match or liveness capability is exactly the processing that produced a seven-figure BIPA settlement.

evidence.gloss: The HireVue settlement is the applied BIPA case
evidence.verbatim: The HireVue settlement above is the applied case[26].

evidence.gloss: HireVue's $3.75M BIPA settlement, preliminary approval June 25, 2026, over facial geometry and voiceprints
evidence.verbatim: HireVue agreed to a $3.75 million settlement, granted preliminary approval on June 25, 2026, resolving claims that its video interview software extracted facial geometry and voiceprints from Illinois applicants without the required notice and consent (Deyerler v. HireVue)[26].

h3.h3: What a BIPA claim costs after the 2024 amendment

evidence.gloss: Illinois BIPA as the sharpest quantified cost of an identity check
evidence.verbatim: Illinois BIPA is the sharpest quantified example of what an identity check can cost an employer.

evidence.gloss: BIPA statutory damages: $1,000 negligent, $5,000 intentional or reckless
evidence.verbatim: $1,000 per violation for a negligent violation, and $5,000 per violation for an intentional or reckless violation[65].

evidence.gloss: Cothron v. White Castle made every scan a separate violation
evidence.verbatim: Under the Illinois Supreme Court's ruling in *Cothron v. White Castle*, a violation occurred with every single scan made without prior consent.

evidence.gloss: 100 employees clocking twice daily meant 400 potential violations a day
evidence.verbatim: For a company with 100 employees clocking in and out twice a day, that meant 400 potential violations daily, pushing potential liability into the millions or billions and driving a wave of class actions[65].

evidence.gloss: August 2024 amendment caps liability at one violation per employee
evidence.verbatim: In August 2024 the Illinois legislature amended BIPA to cap damages: an employer is liable for only one violation per employee for repeated collection of the same biometric data, not for every scan[65].

evidence.gloss: Post-cap risk math: 50 employees without consent equals 50 counts
evidence.verbatim: If you failed to get proper consent from 50 employees, statutory risk is now calculated on those 50 people[65].

evidence.gloss: Unresolved: whether the cap applies retroactively to pre-August-2024 conduct
evidence.verbatim: The amendment's biggest unresolved issue is whether the cap applies to conduct before August 2024. Courts are still resolving this gray area, so a business can still face a suit computed on the old per-scan model for past non-compliance[65].

evidence.gloss: Five-year limitations period; a new policy does not erase past liability
evidence.verbatim: A five-year statute of limitations still reaches past conduct. Adopting a compliant policy today limits future liability and demonstrates good faith, but does not erase liability for past actions[65].

evidence.gloss: Courts split on how much identifiability a plaintiff must plead
evidence.verbatim: Courts have not converged on how much identifiability a plaintiff must plead.

evidence.gloss: BIPA's private right of action drives numerous Illinois lawsuits and makes compliance a priority
evidence.verbatim: The enforcement teeth are the private right of action: BIPA gives individuals the right to sue if their biometric information is collected or used in violation of the law, which has produced numerous Illinois lawsuits and made compliance a top priority for any business collecting biometric data [73].

evidence.gloss: Recent amendments make lawsuits more manageable but a BIPA claim in court is still significant
evidence.verbatim: That right is what inspired the recent amendments; under the new rule lawsuits are more manageable for businesses, but handling a BIPA claim in court remains significant, and organisations should not take the additional grace for granted [73].

evidence.gloss: Unresolved BIPA questions: per-scan vs one-time accrual under 15(b) and 15(d), and the limitations period
evidence.verbatim: Open questions in the surrounding case law include whether claims under sections 15(b) and 15(d) accrue only once on initial collection or disclosure, or each time a private entity collects or discloses biometric information, and the applicable limitations period [68].

evidence.gloss: Illinois BIPA as previously interpreted counted each biometric use as a separate violation
evidence.verbatim: Under Illinois BIPA as previously interpreted, each use of an individual's biometric data without complete consent could be considered a separate violation; the illustrative example given is an employee using retina biometrics to unlock a company computer ten times a day for two years, where each instance would have counted separately, with penalties described as astronomical and potentially bankrupting a business[73].

evidence.gloss: BIPA amendments push claims into simplified class actions and out of federal court
evidence.verbatim: Amendments to the law dissuade single-plaintiff lawsuits and eliminate lawsuits in federal court in favor of simplified class action lawsuits, making it easier for employers to navigate compliance violations through a single court process[73].

evidence.gloss: BIPA amendments allow digital consent through standardized state-approved language
evidence.verbatim: The amendments also introduce streamlined consent and notice procedures, so businesses still required to obtain informed consent can now do so through digital platforms and standardized language approved by the state[73]

evidence.gloss: BIPA amendments add clearer biometric data retention schedules
evidence.verbatim: provide clearer data retention guidelines, including retention schedules for how long businesses can store biometric data[73]

h3.h3: What the employer owes: notice, written consent, retention, security

evidence.gloss: Recording versus evaluating are legally different acts; duty sits with employer
evidence.verbatim: The collected information states the allocation of duty plainly: **recording an interview and having software evaluate that recording are legally different acts, and several states regulate the second. The duty sits with the employer, not with the vendor selling the feature**[24].

evidence.gloss: BIPA requires written notice and consent before collecting face geometry
evidence.verbatim: Illinois' BIPA requires written notice and consent before a private entity collects biometric identifiers such as face geometry[26].

evidence.gloss: Illinois BIPA requires written notice and consent before collecting biometric identifiers like face geometry
evidence.verbatim: Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act requires written notice and consent before a private entity collects biometric identifiers such as face geometry[26].

evidence.gloss: A public written biometric policy with a destruction schedule is mandatory
evidence.verbatim: A public written policy is mandatory: a published document stating what biometric data you collect, the specific purpose, and the schedule for permanent destruction[65].

evidence.gloss: BIPA requires written employee consent; the 2024 amendment accepts an electronic signature
evidence.verbatim: Written consent must be obtained from the employee, and the 2024 amendment explicitly confirms that an electronic signature is a valid form of written consent, which simplifies onboarding [65].

evidence.gloss: BIPA security standard: same protection as financial records or Social Security numbers
evidence.verbatim: Collected biometric data must be protected with the same level of security applied to other confidential and sensitive information such as financial records or Social Security numbers, meaning reasonable steps to prevent data breaches [65].

evidence.gloss: State law requires encryption, access controls and regular audits
evidence.verbatim: By state law, businesses must use industry-standard security practices including encryption, access controls, and regular audits [73].

evidence.gloss: Profiting from employee biometric information is forbidden with very few exceptions
evidence.verbatim: Selling, leasing, trading, or otherwise profiting from an employee's biometric information is strictly forbidden, with very few exceptions [65]

evidence.gloss: No disclosure of biometric data to third parties without explicit consent
evidence.verbatim: businesses may not disclose biometric data to third parties without the individual's explicit consent [73].

evidence.gloss: Vendor liability does not transfer away
evidence.verbatim: Vendor liability does not transfer away.

evidence.gloss: You stay liable for a third-party provider's BIPA failures; contracts requiring compliance are the proof
evidence.verbatim: If you use a third-party provider, you remain liable for their BIPA compliance failures; it is your responsibility to ensure they handle the data correctly, and proving your case often depends on showing that your contracts required full compliance with all BIPA rules [65].

h3.h3: Outside Illinois: Maryland waivers, GDPR, FCRA and no-go jurisdictions

evidence.gloss: Maryland requires a signed waiver for facial recognition in interviews
evidence.verbatim: **Maryland** runs a narrower rule aimed at facial recognition specifically: an employer must obtain a **signed waiver** before using facial recognition to create a facial template during an interview[24].

evidence.gloss: GDPR obligations frame any EU identity-data processing by a vendor
evidence.verbatim: For any vendor feature that processes candidate identity data in the EU, the collected information sets out the surrounding obligations.

evidence.gloss: What GDPR is and its aim
evidence.verbatim: GDPR is a comprehensive legal framework in the EU providing universal rules for collecting, storing and using personal data, applying to automatic and systematic data processing, with one of its biggest goals being to give EU citizens more control over their personal data[27].

evidence.gloss: GDPR breach fines reach seven figures
evidence.verbatim: **Personal data regulation breaches can result in fines in seven-digit figures**[27].

evidence.gloss: You are accountable for your vendors under GDPR
evidence.verbatim: **You are accountable for your vendors.** Under GDPR, your company is responsible for who it does business with, for example an ATS provider or sourcing service; **if your contractors fail to comply with the law, your company is accountable as well**[28].

evidence.gloss: Facial recognition confirms hire matches interviewee but state and local laws may prohibit it
evidence.verbatim: Facial recognition may be effective at confirming the worker hired is the same person as the worker interviewed, but many states and localities have laws governing and potentially prohibiting its use, and a remote applicant's location can change which laws apply[38].

evidence.gloss: FCRA may impose disclosure requirements if the process counts as a background check
evidence.verbatim: The law here is not fully developed with respect to these new technologies, and if a process is considered a background check, the **Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA)** may impose special requirements before it can be used, including specific disclosures[38].

evidence.gloss: Ask the vendor which jurisdictions it will not run face-match in and if output is a consumer report
evidence.verbatim: Ask the vendor directly which jurisdictions it will not operate its face-match feature in, and whether it treats its own output as a consumer report.

sections_menu.h2: Consent, disclosure and data rules for recorded and monitored interviews

h3.h3: US recording consent law: one-party, two-party, and the stricter rule across state lines

evidence.gloss: Two-party consent states named; guidance to always inform in advance and consult counsel
evidence.verbatim: Two-party consent jurisdictions, including California, Florida, Illinois, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Washington among others, make explicit consent a requirement; one-party-consent states allow recording without it, but candidate trust is cited as its own reason to ask, so the guidance is to always inform candidates in advance and consult counsel for jurisdiction-specific guidance [19].

evidence.gloss: Recording interviews is legal but consent is required nearly everywhere; secret recording is a bad idea
evidence.verbatim: Recording a job interview is legal, but consent is the requirement in nearly every jurisdiction, and secret recording is almost never a good idea even where it is technically permitted[38].

evidence.gloss: US recording law splits in two, and the stricter law governs across state lines
evidence.verbatim: In the U.S., recording law splits into two categories, and the general principle when interviewing across state lines is that the stricter law governs: if you are in a one-party state but the candidate is in a two-party state, follow the two-party rules[38].

evidence.gloss: One-party consent defined, with example states
evidence.verbatim: | One-party consent | Only one person on the call (you) needs to consent to the recording | New York, Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Colorado, Virginia, North Carolina, and the majority of U.S.

evidence.gloss: Two-party/all-party consent defined, with example states
evidence.verbatim: | Two-party / all-party consent | Every person on the call must agree to the recording | California, Florida, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Washington, Maryland, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Montana, New Hampshire[38] |

evidence.gloss: In two-party states, recording without all-party consent can be a criminal misdemeanour
evidence.verbatim: In two-party states such as California, Florida and Illinois, recording without all parties' consent can be a criminal misdemeanour, with fines and civil liability as real rather than hypothetical risks[38].

evidence.gloss: What 'explicit' consent means; a buried terms-of-service notice does not count
evidence.verbatim: "Explicit" consent means the candidate clearly agrees, either verbally on the call or in writing beforehand; a notification buried in a terms-of-service page does not count[38].

evidence.gloss: A second source confirms the two-party set and says tell the candidate anyway, because trust is its own reason
evidence.verbatim: A second source lists the same two-party set (California, Florida, Illinois, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Washington and others) and reaches the same conclusion: even where the law allows one-party consent, the right answer is still to tell the candidate, because candidate trust is its own reason to ask[19].

evidence.gloss: Exposure for recording without consent: criminal charges, civil suits, penalties, plus complication risk in one-party states
evidence.verbatim: Recording without proper consent in a two-party state exposes the employer to criminal charges, civil suits and regulatory penalties, and even in one-party states, failing to disclose a recording can create complications if a candidate files a complaint[38].

evidence.gloss: Checklist step 1: confirm one-party or two-party consent in both states, default to stricter, keep a reference document
evidence.verbatim: **Confirm legal requirements in your jurisdiction.** Before setting up any recording tool, check whether your state and the candidate's state requires one-party or two-party consent; when hiring across state lines, default to the stricter standard, and create a simple reference document the team can check before each interview[38].

evidence.gloss: International candidates warrant local counsel for cross-border recording rules
evidence.verbatim: Anything involving international candidates warrants local counsel: the rules get strict, and the advice on the record is to consult local counsel for cross-border recording and jurisdiction-specific guidance[38][19].

h3.h3: What the candidate is told, and when the consent is captured

evidence.gloss: Consent ask lands before the call: one sentence in the invite plus a reply-to opt-out
evidence.verbatim: The consent ask should land before anyone presses join: a single sentence in the invite description plus a reply-to opt-out path [19].

evidence.gloss: Consent wording: specific purpose, scoped use, costless opt-out
evidence.verbatim: What you say matters as much as when: make the purpose specific (accuracy, fairness, training), scope the use to this interview and this hiring decision, and make opting out genuinely costless [19].

evidence.gloss: Common mistake: making the recording visible during the conversation
evidence.verbatim: The most common mistake is making the recording visible to the conversation: a red dot blinking on screen, a typing recruiter who cannot make eye contact, a pause to check the recording is running mid-question, all of which pull the candidate out of the interview [19].

evidence.gloss: Integrity criterion: what the candidate is told and when consent is captured
evidence.verbatim: what the candidate is told, and when consent is captured

evidence.gloss: The safe default: tell every candidate, explain why, get agreement before recording starts
evidence.verbatim: The safe default is to tell every candidate the interview will be recorded, explain why, and get their agreement before the recording starts[38].

evidence.gloss: Put consent language in the scheduling email so the candidate can process, ask, or opt out
evidence.verbatim: The practical mechanism is to put consent language in the interview scheduling email so the candidate has time to process it, ask questions, and opt out, rather than feeling pressured to agree in the moment[38].

evidence.gloss: Verbal confirmation at the start is additional, not the candidate's first notice
evidence.verbatim: Verbal confirmation at the start of the call is a good additional step but should not be the first time the candidate hears about it[38].

evidence.gloss: Checklist step 3: notify the candidate in advance in the scheduling email with an invitation to raise concerns
evidence.verbatim: **Notify the candidate in advance,** in the scheduling email, giving them time to process, ask questions, and opt out, with an invitation to raise questions or concerns before the interview[38].

evidence.gloss: Checklist step 5: start recording, confirm the indicator is visible, state it verbally
evidence.verbatim: **Start the recording,** confirm the recording indicator is visible, and state it verbally[38].

evidence.gloss: Communicating verification steps upfront reduces anxiety and normalises them
evidence.verbatim: Communicate verification requirements clearly upfront so candidates know what verification steps are part of the process; this reduces anxiety and demonstrates that verification is standard procedure rather than suspicion[14].

evidence.gloss: The record only defends the employer if the candidate was told about it
evidence.verbatim: The record only defends the employer if the candidate was told it was being made.

evidence.gloss: Announcing what you check deters cheating at zero cost and protects against challenges
evidence.verbatim: announcing that you check, and what you check for, deters casual cheating at zero cost and protects you when a candidate challenges a decision [8].

evidence.gloss: Candidate instructions should state the exact signals monitored
evidence.verbatim: the exact signals monitored should be stated clearly in the candidate instructions [33]

evidence.gloss: Disclosure is the cheapest deterrent and increasingly a compliance requirement
evidence.verbatim: Disclosure is both the cheapest deterrent available and increasingly a compliance requirement[8].

evidence.gloss: Obtain explicit recording consent and explain use and storage
evidence.verbatim: obtain explicit consent before recording interviews and clearly communicate how recordings will be used and stored

evidence.gloss: Setting and communicating an acceptable-AI-use policy up front, with stated observation methods and consequences, which deters casual cheating and protects honest candidates.
evidence.verbatim: State the rules before the interview, not after. Tell candidates which tools are allowed, how the session is observed, and what happens if the rules are broken. Gartner recommends exactly this kind of layered, communicated policy, and it works partly because most casual cheating stops once people know detection is active and consequences are real. Clear expectations also protect honest candidates from a false accusation.

evidence.gloss: Trust benefit: research finds well-designed proctoring with clear privacy cues lowers test-taker stress, and Testlify's onboarding discloses what is captured and when it is deleted.
evidence.verbatim:
Academic studies have found that well-designed AI proctoring with clear privacy cues reduces test-taker stress compared to unfamiliar test-center environments.
Testlify’s onboarding flow clearly indicates what data is captured and when it is automatically deleted, turning a potential surveillance concern into a transparency win.

h3.h3: The disclosure gap: most candidates are never told AI is evaluating them

evidence.gloss: 70% of candidates were never told upfront that AI would evaluate them
evidence.verbatim: Greenhouse found 70% of candidates were never told upfront that AI would evaluate them

evidence.gloss: Greenhouse: 63% interviewed by AI, up 13 points in six months; 70% not told upfront; one in five found out mid-interview
evidence.verbatim: Greenhouse found 63% of job seekers have now been interviewed by an AI, up 13 percentage points in six months, and that 70% were never clearly told upfront that AI would be evaluating them; one in five only found out once the interview had started[8].

evidence.gloss: The disclosure asymmetry damages what detection is meant to protect
evidence.verbatim: That asymmetry damages the thing detection is meant to protect.

evidence.gloss: Gartner: only 26% of applicants trust AI to evaluate them fairly; only half believed the jobs were legitimate
evidence.verbatim: Gartner found only 26% of applicants trust AI to fairly evaluate them, and only half of candidates believed the jobs they were applying for were even legitimate[8].

evidence.gloss: Distrust of the screener and the posting shifts the candidate's calculus on using AI
evidence.verbatim: When a candidate assumes an unaccountable model is screening them, and assumes the posting might be fake, the calculus around using AI to answer shifts[8].

h3.h3: The fallback when a candidate refuses recording or the check fails

evidence.gloss: Refusal fallback: manual notes and a structured post-call summary against the same rubric
evidence.verbatim: If a candidate refuses to be recorded, the interview goes ahead manually: the interviewer takes notes during the call and writes a structured post-call summary against the same rubric they would use for a recorded interview, and the team uses those notes the same way they would use a transcript, so no recording does not mean no structure [19].

evidence.gloss: Around 5% or fewer of candidates refuse recording, per Metaview
evidence.verbatim: Metaview reports that around 5% or fewer of candidates take this path, in their experience [19].

evidence.gloss: The manual fallback when a candidate refuses: notes plus a structured post-call summary against the same rubric
evidence.verbatim: The interview goes ahead manually: the interviewer takes notes during the call and writes a structured post-call summary against the same rubric they would use for a recorded interview, and the team uses those notes the same way they would use a transcript[19].

evidence.gloss: Around 5% or fewer of candidates refuse recording, per one vendor's experience
evidence.verbatim: One vendor reports that around 5% or fewer of candidates take this path, based on its own experience[19].

evidence.gloss: A fallback process is required for unclear images, expired docs, name differences, accessibility needs
evidence.verbatim: institutions should provide a fallback process for unclear images, expired documents, name differences, accessibility needs, or candidates who cannot complete automated matching [33]

h3.h3: Storage, access, retention and deletion of recordings and scores

evidence.gloss: Compliance question: retention periods for recordings, transcripts, scores, and who decides
evidence.verbatim: - How long are recordings, transcripts, and scores retained, and who decides?

evidence.gloss: Compliance question: can a candidate request deletion and what is the process
evidence.verbatim: - Can a candidate request deletion, and what is the process?

evidence.gloss: 'Your data is stored securely' is a claim, not a guarantee
evidence.verbatim: The practical caution for anyone evaluating a vendor's identity or integrity claims: "your data is stored securely" is a claim, not a guarantee[39].

evidence.gloss: Secure storage: role-based access, no personal drives or shared folders
evidence.verbatim: **Secure storage.** Role-based access, no personal drives, no shared folders, so only the people who need the recording can reach it[19].

evidence.gloss: Move the recording to encrypted storage with role-based access after the interview
evidence.verbatim: Operationally, that means moving the recording to encrypted storage with role-based access after the interview rather than leaving it in a personal Downloads folder or an unlocked cloud drive[38].

evidence.gloss: Purposeful use only: the original stated purpose and nothing else
evidence.verbatim: **Purposeful use only.** Use recordings for the original stated purpose (decision-making, calibration, training) and nothing else[19].

evidence.gloss: Under GDPR the same discipline maps onto controller/processor, access disclosure, processors and cross-border transfer
evidence.verbatim: Under GDPR terms, the same discipline maps onto the controller/processor split, disclosure of who has access, whether processors are used, and whether data is transferred abroad, all of which the privacy notice must state upfront[27].

evidence.gloss: Checklist step 6: save to encrypted storage with role-based access and set a retention window
evidence.verbatim: **Save and store securely** in encrypted storage with role-based access, and set a retention window[38].

h3.h3: Face match and liveness as biometric special-category data

evidence.gloss: Biometric identity checks in the live format carry a heavier compliance burden than a stored recording
evidence.verbatim: Where the live format leans on biometric identity checks, the compliance burden is heavier than for a stored recording alone.

evidence.gloss: Identity verification uses special-category data such as facial images for liveness and 1:1 face match
evidence.verbatim: Identity verification relies on technologies that often involve special categories of data: biometric data such as facial images used for liveness detection and 1:1 face match is the prime example[17].

evidence.gloss: GDPR Article 9: biometric identification needs a robust legal basis and often explicit consent
evidence.verbatim: Under GDPR, biometric data processed for unique identification is a special category and triggers the full force of Article 9 protections, so companies using passive and active liveness and 1:1 face match must have a robust legal basis; simply having a user agree to terms and conditions may not suffice, and explicit consent that clearly distinguishes the sensitive nature of the data and its specific processing purposes is often required[17].

evidence.gloss: GDPR Article 9 makes facial biometrics special category data needing a defensible legal basis
evidence.verbatim: Under GDPR, facial biometrics are special category data under Article 9, so the vendor must support a defensible legal basis[17].

evidence.gloss: Explicit consent requires disclosing data type, purpose, retention, via a clear affirmative act
evidence.verbatim: Explicit consent is often the most straightforward path, and it requires clearly informing candidates of the specific types of special category data collected (for example, facial biometrics), the purpose (identity verification and fraud prevention), and the retention period, with consent given by a clear affirmative act such as an unchecked box or a distinct agreement separate from general terms[17].

evidence.gloss: The governing GDPR principles are transparency and proportionality
evidence.verbatim: The governing principles are transparency and proportionality: collect only what is strictly necessary, and be clear about how it will be used and protected[17].

evidence.gloss: Substantial public interest basis fits AML financial services, not hiring
evidence.verbatim: Note the limit on the alternative basis: substantial public interest requires a clear legal framework and operations mandated or explicitly permitted by national law, which is available to fraud prevention in financial services under AML rules but is not a ready-made fit for hiring[17].

h3.h3: The compliance questions to put to a vendor, and the documented controls behind them

evidence.gloss: A separate, harder question set applies to anything that monitors a candidate
evidence.verbatim: A separate, harder question set applies to anything that monitors a candidate[35]:

evidence.gloss: Compliance question: what consent is captured, at what point, in what wording
evidence.verbatim: - What consent is captured from the candidate, at what point, and in what wording?

evidence.gloss: Compliance question: what exactly is monitored and whether the candidate is told beforehand
evidence.verbatim: - What exactly is monitored during the interview, and is the candidate told before they start?

evidence.gloss: Compliance question: is human review before adverse decisions enforced by the product or only by policy
evidence.verbatim: - Is a human required to review before any adverse decision, and is that enforced by the product or only by our policy?

evidence.gloss: AEDT, notice, consent and biometric obligations vary by jurisdiction and must be verified, not assumed
evidence.verbatim: Obligations around automated employment decision tools, candidate notice, consent, and biometric data vary significantly by jurisdiction and change often, so current requirements have to be verified per jurisdiction rather than assumed[35].

evidence.gloss: The structured compliance framework and its working checklist of ten line items
evidence.verbatim: The structured compliance framework recruitment teams and talent platforms are expected to hold covers transparency, lawful bases, retention, security, vendor management and candidate rights, and a working checklist includes: data processing agreements with all vendors; secure ATS and CRM with MFA enabled; role-based access controls; secure data transfers to clients; a clear log of candidate rights requests; documented screening and profiling logic; international transfer safeguards; employee confidentiality and GDPR training; a data breach response plan; and periodic reviews of sourcing and retention practices[27].

evidence.gloss: Two checklist items where integrity features land hardest: documented screening logic, and Articles 22 and 35
evidence.verbatim: Two of those line items are where integrity features land hardest. "Documented screening and profiling logic"[27] is the item an ID-match or deepfake-detection model has to satisfy, and Article 22 (automated decision-making) plus Article 35 (data protection impact assessments) are the specific exposures that biometric matching and algorithmic screening raise[25].

evidence.gloss: The full recruitment GDPR compliance checklist
evidence.verbatim: The recruitment GDPR compliance checklist covers: a current privacy notice tailored to recruitment operations; a lawful basis register for sourcing, screening, and contacting; a strict CV and data retention schedule; consent mechanisms for talent pools and sensitive data; Data Processing Agreements with all vendors; a secure ATS and CRM with MFA enabled; role-based access controls; secure data transfers to clients; a clear log of candidate rights requests; documented screening and profiling logic; international transfer safeguards; employee confidentiality and GDPR training; a data breach response plan; and periodic reviews of sourcing and retention practices[27].

evidence.gloss: Documented screening and profiling logic is the checklist item integrity tooling most often misses
evidence.verbatim: Documented screening and profiling logic is the item most likely to be missing when integrity tooling is bolted on: the deepfake score and the proctoring threshold are screening logic.

evidence.gloss: Recommended posture: AI-use rules, safeguards, background checks, identity verification, system-level validation
evidence.verbatim: The recommended posture is rules around acceptable AI use, safeguards in assessments, stronger background checking, identity verification, anomaly alerts, and "system-level validation" rather than reliance on individualized surveillance[9].

evidence.gloss: Reframe the defensible question from personal suspicion to documented controls and evidence provenance
evidence.verbatim: The defensible question is not "does this person look suspicious to me?" but "can we establish, using the same documented controls we apply to comparable candidates, that this is the same person and that this person produced the evidence we are evaluating?

evidence.gloss: The defensible question replaces 'does this look suspicious' with documented same-person controls
evidence.verbatim: The defensible question is not "Does this person look suspicious to me?" It is "Can we establish, using the same documented controls we apply to comparable candidates, that this is the same person and that this person produced the evidence we are evaluating?"[9]

evidence.gloss: The audit trail doubles as the deterrence artifact
evidence.verbatim: The audit trail is also the deterrence artifact.

evidence.gloss: Buying detection brings process obligations the tooling does not discharge
evidence.verbatim: A purchase decision here comes with process obligations the tooling does not discharge.

evidence.gloss: Fraud prevention measures must comply with privacy, anti-discrimination and data protection law
evidence.verbatim: Interview processes and fraud prevention measures must comply with privacy laws, anti-discrimination regulations, and data protection requirements in the relevant jurisdiction.

evidence.gloss: Apply verification measures consistently to all candidates to avoid discrimination claims
evidence.verbatim: apply identity verification and fraud prevention measures consistently to all candidates to avoid discrimination claims

evidence.gloss: Put misrepresentation consequences into offer letters and employment contracts
evidence.verbatim: include language in offer letters and employment contracts about the consequences of misrepresentation during the hiring process

evidence.gloss: Two-sided legal exposure, negligent hiring claims from insecure assessments versus privacy claims from invasive monitoring, heightened in regulated industries
evidence.verbatim:
Assessment security creates legal exposure in two directions. If a hiring team uses assessments that are not secure, they face negligent hiring claims when a fraudulently placed employee causes harm.
If monitoring practices are excessively invasive, they risk privacy claims from candidates in jurisdictions with strong data protection requirements. In regulated industries, the exposure is compounded: financial services, healthcare, and government contractors operate under frameworks that require documented evidence of assessment integrity for specific roles.

evidence.gloss: FAQs on AI-generated answers during live tests, common cheating methods, detection versus privacy under the EU AI Act and ICO guidance, handling anomaly flags, and proctoring's effect on candidate experience
evidence.verbatim:
Can AI tools really generate answers during a live online assessment?
Yes. AI tools available in 2026 can monitor on-screen content through a secondary device and generate formatted answers without any copy-paste activity from the candidate. Standard browser lockdown does not detect this because the AI tool runs on a separate physical device outside the controlled browser environment.
How do candidates cheat in online assessments?
Candidates may attempt to cheat by using AI tools, searching for answers online, collaborating with others, using multiple devices, or having another person take the test on their behalf.
How do hiring teams balance detection with candidate privacy?
The standard approach in regulated markets is to collect only the data required for integrity verification, retain it for a defined period, and notify candidates explicitly at session start. The EU AI Act and ICO guidance on automated hiring tools both address assessment data collection practices that enterprise platforms now need to comply with.
What should HR teams do when a session flags an anomaly?
Treat every flag as a review trigger, not an automatic disqualification. A human reviewer should examine the session recording, compare the flagged event against the candidate’s full response pattern, and decide whether to pass, disqualify, or invite a re-test.
Does proctoring create a poor candidate experience?
Not necessarily. Transparent communication about assessment rules and the use of non-intrusive monitoring can help maintain a positive candidate experience while protecting assessment integrity. The goal is to create a fair process for all applicants.
